That is both the design's § 9.2 rule — a silent fallback would change who the caller is, and with `(tid, oid)` that changes which business they resolve — and what stops `/auth` becoming a redirect loop. `AppComponent`'s redirect handler reports a refused or broken callback and navigates to `/sign-in` instead of leaving the callback page saying "Signing you in..." for ever, and a cancelled journey is told apart from a broken one by the provider's own error code so the two get different sentences.

**How the choice reaches every route.** `SignInAuthorityGuard` is registered under the `MsalGuard` token, with the real guard beside it under `MSAL_REDIRECT_GUARD`. It intervenes only when all three of "a second authority is configured", "nobody is signed in" and "no choice is on record" hold; otherwise every decision is `MsalGuard`'s, unchanged. **With no customer identity tenant configured it never intervenes at all**, which is why the shipped behaviour — one authority, redirect straight to it — is byte for byte what it was. Overriding that one token is how forty route definitions stay untouched, and is the same mechanism the end-to-end build already uses (see [End-to-end testing authentication](#end-to-end-testing-authentication-issue-46) below).

**The destination survives the round trip without becoming a caller-supplied return URL.** The guard records the page it refused — from the router state, never from a query parameter or anything the authorize response carries — in the tab's `sessionStorage` (`intended-destination.ts`, the pending invite token's store and 15-minute window), and it is handed to MSAL as the redirect start page. `isInternalDestination` refuses an absolute URL, a protocol-relative `//host` or `/\host`, anything carrying a backslash, whitespace or a control character, and the two authentication addresses `/auth` and `/sign-in`. An invite is unaffected: `inviteTokenAddressBarGuard` still strips the token into its own store and redirects to the tokenless `/invite` during route recognition, before any `canActivate` guard runs, so `/invite` is the only thing the sign-in ever carries or returns to — see [Invite acceptance page](#invite-acceptance-page-issue-535).

**It survives a cancelled or broken one too, and that is what "preserve the destination through cancellation" means.** The destination is held until a sign-in **completes**, not until it is first read: a redirect that could not start leaves the person on `/sign-in` pressing an action again, and a cancelled hosted journey comes back to `/auth` carrying nothing and is sent to `/sign-in` for the same reason, so consuming it at the start of the attempt would quietly land the retry on the application's home page instead — and for `/invite`, on a home page that says nothing about the invitation still waiting. `peekIntendedDestination` therefore reads without consuming and re-validates every time (dropping an expired, tampered or unreadable one as it reads), and `AppComponent` calls `clearIntendedDestination` on the one callback that completes, which is also MSAL's own cue to navigate there. **A retry never extends the window**: reusing a destination only reads it, so `storedAt` stays the instant the guard recorded it and an abandoned sign-in expires exactly when it would have. Only a fresh refusal by the guard records a new destination with a new instant.

**With no destination held, a sign-in returns to the home page, and a signed-in person never stays on `/sign-in`.** MSAL returns a redirect to the page it started from when it is given no start page, so a sign-in pressed on `/sign-in` with nothing held — every one, on a deployment with no customer identity tenant, where the guard never records a destination — came back to `/sign-in` signed in, showing the chooser again. `SignInService.signIn` therefore hands MSAL `/` whenever `peekIntendedDestination` has nothing, and the `/sign-in` route carries `signInPageGuard` (`auth/sign-in-page.guard.ts`): once any redirect in progress has been handled, a visitor with a signed-in account is sent to `/`, and a signed-out one, or one whose redirect just failed and is being told so, stays. It is not an authentication guard, so the page stays public. `auth/sign-in.service.spec.ts`, `auth/sign-in-page.guard.spec.ts` and `app.routes.spec.ts` pin both halves.

**Nothing is linked, and the welcome page says so.** Identity linking is deferred (#713), so a Google identity is a new actor: no membership, no role, no inherited access, and nothing written by presenting a token. A matching email address links nothing — an address is display-only data here and no authorization, membership, invite or onboarding decision reads one — and Google sign-in on its own never redeems an invite. The person therefore lands on the existing `NoMembership` welcome page, which is now the one place that explains why: each way of signing in is a separate account, and the supported advice is to keep using the same one.

**What proves it.** `auth-config.spec.ts` pins the two authorities' separate client ids, authorities and audiences, the explicit `profile` scope, and that every half-filled or non-`https` configuration means "not configured". `auth/selected-authority.spec.ts` pins the three-part question, the per-tab snapshot — another tab's write reaching neither a bootstrapped tab nor one whose redirect is in flight — and that clearing the configuration takes a browser that chose the second authority back to workforce sign-in, the design's § 15.1 rollback lever. `auth/intended-destination.spec.ts` pins the refusals above, that a destination survives repeated reads until it is cleared, and that reading it never extends its window. `auth/sign-in.service.spec.ts` pins which instance a redirect is made on, the start page, the absence of any provider hint, that no failure falls back to the other authority, and that a redirect which could not start — including one whose client could not be built, with `/invite` held — leaves the destination for the retry. `auth/sign-in.component.spec.ts` and `auth/browser-auth-providers.spec.ts` pin the rendered actions, their loading and error states, the guard's three-part condition, and that the guard and interceptor configurations stay on one authority while the shared choice changes under them; `app.component.spec.ts` pins the header action, the sign-out forgetting the choice, the refused callback keeping the destination, and the completed callback releasing it. On the API side, `TrustedIssuerTokenValidationTests` adds the two regressions this journey turns on: a Google identity sharing an existing member's mailbox inherits nothing and gains no membership row, and a customer identity resolves through its directory `oid` while the upstream Google `sub` resolves nobody.

#### The local email and password journey (issue #712)

Issue #711 made the customer identity tenant's hosted journey reachable; this is the other journey that same flow offers — a person registering or signing in with any deliverable email address and a password, including a custom company domain, with no Microsoft or Google account involved (design § 4 journey D, and § 16's #712 row). It is the same authority, the same MSAL configuration, the same `(tid, oid)` actor and the same user flow as the Google journey: **the only new thing in this repository is what the sign-in page says.**

**The managed credential boundary: this application has no credentials to handle.** There is no password field, no registration form, no verification page and no recovery link anywhere in it; no password, password hash, verification code, reset code or recovery token is ever received, stored, logged, put in a URL or sent to the API; and there is no endpoint, DTO, column or configuration key for one. Registering, verifying the mailbox with the provider's one-time code, signing in, and resetting a forgotten password all happen on the External ID tenant's own hosted pages, which is the whole point of choosing a managed provider (design § 3: credential storage, credential-stuffing defence, verification and recovery are a permanent liability this repository has no reason to own). `SignInService` starts one redirect carrying scopes and, at most, the in-application page to return to — `sign-in.service.spec.ts` asserts the request has exactly those two keys, so a `loginHint`, a `prompt` or an invented query parameter cannot be added without a failing test.

**One action, because one hosted flow offers both journeys.** An External ID application has exactly one user flow, and which providers that flow offers is tenant configuration (design § 13 items 5 and 6). Nothing in the verified record confirms a supported way for a relying application to preselect one of them, and this application invents none, so a second button would send the person to the identical page and promise a choice the application does not make. The single action therefore names both journeys, and the line beside it says the hosted page is where you choose a Google account or use an email address and password. A second line says where creating an account, verifying an address and resetting a password happen, states that Inventory Manager never sees or stores a password and cannot reset one, and answers the expired-code case — start again from `/sign-in` and the hosted page issues a new code — because an expired verification or reset code is entirely inside the provider's journey and never reaches a URL here.

**Email verification is the provider's gate, and the application reads no address for any decision.** External ID verifies the mailbox with a one-time code *during sign-up, before the account exists* (design § 13 item 7), so there is no "unverified account" state for this API to recognise: an incomplete registration has no directory object, hence no `oid`, hence no token. Beyond that, verification could not widen anything here even if it were asserted, which is the property that makes the boundary robust rather than configuration-dependent: no authorization, membership, invite, onboarding or Super Admin decision reads an email address, `email_verified` or any other profile claim (see [Member display name and email](#member-display-name-and-email-issue-524)). A customer identity that holds no membership gets `403` from every business endpoint and reaches only `GET /api/me/account-state`, exactly as a workforce stranger does.

**Nothing is linked, duplicated or inherited by mailbox.** Identity linking stays deferred (#713), so a local account that registers an address an existing member already uses — through a work account or through Google — is a new actor with no membership, no role and no inherited access, and presenting its token writes no membership row. A duplicate registration of one address is a second directory object and therefore a second actor. An email change or a password reset at the provider changes no `(tid, oid)`, so it can neither move nor widen a membership: the same pair resolves the same business and role whether the token carries a different address, an unverified one, or none at all. The `NoMembership` welcome page is where this is explained, and it now names an email address beside the work account and Google.

**A failure says one of two fixed sentences.** A refused credential journey is where "no such account" leaks, because the provider's own error text names the mailbox, the directory and often the reason. `classifySignInFailure` reduces a failure to *cancelled* or *failed* from the provider's error **code** alone, and only those two application-authored sentences are rendered, so the page never discloses whether an address has an account here and never shows provider text.

**No new configuration, and the same rollback lever.** Journey D needs no identifier, flag or setting beyond issue #710's `ExternalId` section and issue #711's `externalIdSettings` — it is the same tenant, registration and flow — so clearing those settings removes both journeys at once (design § 15.1), and a deployment no human has configured shows no customer identity action, says nothing about passwords, and signs in exactly as it did before. Everything that makes the journey *work* is human portal configuration: enabling email with password inside the user flow, its verification and self-service password reset, and the available anti-abuse and MFA controls — see [README.md § Signing in with an email address and password](../README.md#signing-in-with-an-email-address-and-password-issue-712) for the recorded control set, its verified gaps (no built-in bot or sign-up fraud protection, no built-in per-IP throttling) and the staging checks a human performs.

**What proves it.** `auth/sign-in.component.spec.ts` pins the single action's label, the hosted-flow line, the registration/verification/reset help line, the absence of any `input` or `form` element on the page, that a deployment with no customer identity tenant says nothing about passwords at all, and that a refused sign-in renders one generic sentence and never the provider's description, account name or error code. `auth/sign-in.service.spec.ts` pins the exact keys of the redirect request. `access/welcome.component.spec.ts` pins that the separate-accounts explanation names an email address. On the API side, `TrustedIssuerTokenValidationTests` adds four regressions: a local account sharing a member's mailbox inherits nothing and gains no membership row, a second registration of one mailbox is a second actor with nothing of the first, neither an unverified nor a verified mailbox claim reaches a business endpoint on a direct API request, and a member's changed, unverified or absent address decides nothing about their membership.

#### Verifying the customer identity rollout (issue #714)

Issues #710, #711 and #712 each proved their own piece. This is the consolidated validation of the whole rollout, and the thing it is most careful about is **what a passing build does not mean**. [docs/identity-rollout-verification.md](identity-rollout-verification.md) is the document of record: the verification matrix, the staging smoke tests, the phased enablement, the observability signals, the incident and rollback procedure, and the production go/no-go checklist.

**Three kinds of evidence, declared per row and never pooled.** A *synthetic API/JWT* test says what the API accepts, refuses and resolves for a given token. A *synthetic browser journey* says what the SPA decides, stores, refuses and asks MSAL for. Only a *human hosted-provider staging run* can say that a tenant exists, that a provider is enabled inside its user flow, that the application is associated with that flow, and that a real token carries the claims the design assumes. Each row is `passed`, `failed` or `not verified`, and the automated suites cannot produce the third kind of evidence — which is why `docs/identity-rollout-verification.md` § 2.6 lists every hosted-provider row as **not verified** and § 7 treats that as blocking.

**What the automated half covers, and where it lives.** `backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/CustomerIdentityRolloutMatrixTests` runs the provider × account-state × role matrix through the real pipeline with real tokens from **both** trusted issuers, reusing issue #710's signing keys and stubbed metadata documents so the validation under test is the one that ships: invitation redemption in both directions, the already-a-member `409` that stands in for a linking conflict, every non-member account state reported identically per issuer with `403` from every business endpoint, revocation taking effect on the next request, deactivation ending access and cancelling live invites with reactivation restoring the member's own role, a role granting the same capabilities whichever issuer signed the member in, the whole platform-admin surface refusing a customer identity (T9), and two-business isolation across the issuers (T8). `CustomerIdentityRollbackRehearsalTests` rehearses design § 15's lever 1 over **one database read by three hosts in turn** — configured, rolled back, configured again — so "memberships and outstanding invites are retained and work again when the settings are restored" is asserted as a property of data surviving a configuration change; it also keeps the legacy Super Admin recovery route tested while customer identity sign-in is off, and asserts that a refused issuer, an expired token and a successful redemption leave no bearer token, invitation token or mailbox in the logs. On the browser side, `frontend/inventory-app/src/app/auth/customer-identity-journey.spec.ts` composes the real units into whole journeys: an interrupted invite acceptance through a cancellation and a retry with the token reaching no MSAL request, cache or stored destination; the two authorities sharing no client id, authority or audience while both keep one cache location, so the partition is the client id; a provider switch asking only the newly chosen authority for a token; the § 15.1 rollback lever landing on a tab part-way through; and a destination outside this application never becoming a redirect start page.

**Nothing in the application changed.** This is a verification task: no production code, no configuration default, no contract and no schema is touched by it, and the suites above are evidence rather than behaviour. A test here that fails is a finding about #710, #711 or #712, not about #714.

#### End-to-end testing authentication (issue #46)

There is exactly one exception to the two bullets above, and it exists so the browser-level end-to-end suite can reach protected pages and endpoints without an interactive Entra sign-in — which issue #46 explicitly does not test. Everything about it is in `backend/InventoryApi/Auth/E2ETesting/`.

**The gate.** `E2ETestEnvironment.IsEnabled` is the only way into any of it, and it answers `true` for exactly one hosting environment name, `E2ETest`, compared ordinally. The decision is made from the host the process was started as, before any request exists: no header, query string, route value, cookie or request body takes part in it, there is no endpoint that turns it on, and there is no configuration key that can. A near-miss name (`e2etest`, `E2ETest2`) is not that environment. The `E2ETest` host is a local test host only; it is never deployed, and `deploy-production.yml` deploys the API with its own environment.

**What the host swaps, and nothing else.** `AddInventoryApiAuthentication` (`InventoryApiAuthenticationExtensions`) makes one either/or decision: the E2E host registers `E2ETestAuthenticationHandler` and no other scheme, and **every** other environment — Production, Development, the backend suite's `Testing`, and any future one — registers the real `AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi` bearer scheme this composition always registered — and, in those other environments alone and only when one is configured, the pinned customer identity scheme of issue #710, which this host never gets whatever is configured. There is no public method that registers the test scheme, so no other part of the application can add it to a host. The same gate also registers `E2ETestNayaxLynxClient` (`Adapters/Nayax/`) in place of the real Nayax HTTP client, so the E2E host has nothing configured that could call the live operator account, and `E2ETestFixture` seeds the suite's two synthetic businesses into the disposable database that host was pointed at.

**It authenticates; it does not authorise.** The synthetic principal carries the same `(tid, oid)` claim pair and the same `scp: access_as_user` scope a real access token carries, from a closed, compile-time set of three synthetic actors (`E2ETestActors`). Everything after authentication is the production pipeline: `[Authorize]`, `[RequiredScope]`, `BusinessScopeMiddleware`, the `BusinessMembership` lookup, the tenant query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`. One of the three actors is deliberately given no membership, so the suite proves that an authenticated caller outside every business is refused `403`. The `X-E2E-Test-Actor` header only chooses between those three already-permitted identities, exactly as a bearer token identifies a user; a missing, unknown, blank or repeated value authenticates nobody and the request is answered `401`. The fixture itself never runs unscoped: businesses and memberships are not tenant-owned rows, and every tenant-owned row it writes goes through a `BusinessScope` resolved to one business, so `UnscopedBusinessScope` stays reserved for the three human-invoked commands.

**The frontend half is a build replacement, not a runtime flag.** `src/app/auth/browser-auth-providers.ts` holds the real MSAL wiring (`MSAL_INSTANCE`, `MsalGuard`, `MsalInterceptor`, …) that `app.config.ts` spreads into the application config. The `e2e` build configuration in `angular.json` — and only that configuration — replaces that one module with `browser-auth-providers.e2e.ts`, which lets the router through, stubs `MsalService`/`MsalBroadcastService` so no MSAL call reaches `login.microsoftonline.com`, and registers no HTTP interceptor and therefore attaches no token. A production or development bundle does not contain that module at all, so there is nothing in it to enable.

**What proves it.** `backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/E2ETestAuthenticationCompositionTests` pins the gate and what each environment registers; `E2ETestAuthenticationFailsClosedTests` hosts the real pipeline as Production, Development, `Testing`, `Staging` and `e2etest` and asserts the synthetic header authenticates nobody (`401`), the scheme is not registered, and no fixture data is seeded; `E2ETestAuthenticationTests` hosts the E2E environment and asserts the `401`/`403`/`200` boundary and two-business isolation by listing and by id. `browser-auth-providers.spec.ts` asserts the production module keeps the real guard and interceptor and that the replacement is declared in one build configuration only. All of these run in `scripts/validate.sh`; the Playwright suite itself does not (see [Frontend tests](#frontend-tests)).

### Tenant ownership (issue #64)

Authentication answers "who is this?". Tenant ownership answers "whose data is this?", and the two are deliberately not the same question. An Entra directory tenant is not a vending business: the mapping between them is application-owned data, so the business a caller belongs to is a decision this application makes and can audit, not one inherited from the token.

**Identity and membership.** The actor is identified by the validated `(tid, oid)` claim pair — never by email, display name, or the Entra directory tenant alone, all of which are mutable or shared. Since issue #524 the membership row does *store* a display name and an email address, refreshed from that same validated token, and they are display-only personal data that decides nothing: see [Member display name and email](#member-display-name-and-email-issue-524). `BusinessMembership` rows map an actor to one application-owned `Business`. `BusinessMembershipResolutionPolicy` (Domain) decides the outcome: exactly one active membership on a business whose lifecycle status is `Active` resolves; none, or several, or any other business status, denies — see [Business lifecycle status and profile](#business-lifecycle-status-and-profile-issue-540). Ambiguity is denied rather than resolved by picking one, because silently choosing a business is how data ends up in the wrong ledger. Since issue #522 the database also refuses to *create* that ambiguity, so the resolution denial is the second line of defence rather than the first — see [One active membership per identity](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522).

**Layering.** Claims parsing stays at the API boundary (`EntraActorIdentityAccessor`, the only implementation of the Application's `IAuthenticatedActorAccessor` port). `ICurrentBusinessProvider` is the Application-facing abstraction; `Inventory.Domain` and `Inventory.Application` never reference ASP.NET claims or principals. EF query filters and `SaveChanges` enforcement are persistence concerns and live with the `AppDbContext` adapter.

**Per-request resolution.** `BusinessScopeMiddleware` runs after authentication and authorization and before the endpoint, resolves membership once, and publishes the answer into the request-scoped `BusinessScope`. The resolution is memoised in the request's own scope, so the capability policies that run earlier in the pipeline (see [Capability authorization](#capability-authorization-issue-525)) and this middleware read one membership lookup between them and cannot disagree about the caller's role. An authenticated caller with no usable membership gets `403` and never reaches an action; the response carries no detail about why, because telling an unrecognised caller whether a business exists is information they have not earned. `IBusinessScope` exists as a separate synchronous port because query filters and `SaveChanges` cannot await a membership lookup. Two endpoint markers, and only two, are eligible to proceed without a membership — the platform diagnostics surface of issue #336 and the account-state family of issue #523 — and a request that does carries the same *denied* scope, so neither reads business data; see [Platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336) and [Account state and the membership-not-required marker](#account-state-and-the-membership-not-required-marker-issue-523). One other middleware takes part in a request that presents a support session, and it is deliberately the **outermost** one rather than another step beside this one: `SupportSessionAuditMiddleware` (issue #672) runs ahead of `UseExceptionHandler`, because the trail of what somebody from outside the business asked for has to include the attempts authorization refused above this middleware and has to record the status the exception handler finally mapped — see [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**One other way a business is resolved, and it is not a membership.** Since issue #551 a platform administrator who presents an active support session's id in the `X-Support-Session` header has that session's business published as `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` — the same business key the filters compare against, and nothing writable. It is the third documented exception to "the business comes only from the caller's membership", and it is not an exception to "never from request input": the header carries a session id, which is a credential, and the business is the one the server stored when the session started. Everything about it — how a request joins one, the read-only enforcement in three layers, the fixed capability set and the Nayax block — is in [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**Fail closed.** `BusinessScope` starts denied and can only move forward to a resolved business, once — either an ordinary `Resolved` one or a support session's `SupportReadOnly` one, and never across from one to the other. A denied scope yields a `null` business ID, and the filters compare with `==`, so an unresolved caller matches no row. "No current business" must never be read as "no filter" — that would convert a resolution bug into a cross-business leak. A scope cannot be repointed mid-request.

**Tenant-owned versus global.** Everything persisted is tenant-owned — products, categories, suppliers, purchases and items, stock adjustments, supplier orders and allocations, sales, imports and their children, expenses, commissions, fee rates, costing transition records, each business's own Nayax credentials (issue #518) and report facts — except **five** structural exceptions: `Business` (the boundary itself), `BusinessMembership` (what resolves the boundary, so filtering it would be circular), `BusinessBackfillAudit` (operational evidence about the rollout, which must stay readable precisely when a run assigned rows to the wrong business), `MemberInvite` (the reviewed decision on issue #532: the redemption has to find an invite by the token a caller with no membership presents, and under the denied scope such a request carries a filtered read matches no row at all — see [Invite redemption](#invite-redemption-issue-532)), and `SupportSession` (the reviewed decision on issue #550: every request that reaches it is a platform-admin request, and a platform administrator is a member of no business, so such a request resolves nothing — a filter would match none of its rows and the ownership stamp would have no business to stamp — see [Support sessions](#support-sessions-the-store-and-the-control-endpoints-issue-550)). There is no "global reference data" among *business* tables: the enum-like constants live in code as C# enums, not tables. `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` enforces this — a new entity with no ownership fails the build rather than quietly arriving unfiltered — and it asserts the exemption list itself, so a sixth table is a visible edit rather than an addition nobody reviewed.

**And eleven *platform* tables, which are a different classification (issues #848, #873, #923, #925, #924, #937 and #966).** `SupplierPreset` is the platform's own list of suggested suppliers, kept by the Super Admin (see [Super Admin supplier presets](#super-admin-supplier-presets-issue-848)). Issue #931 widened that table — served states, whether its published prices include GST, and a price connector with its key ([The supplier-master fields](#the-supplier-master-fields-issue-931)) — and issue #925 added one more column to it, the per-supplier price-check freshness limit ([Supplier price observations and comparison](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925)); **it is still a platform table on exactly the terms below**: every one of the new columns says something about a *supplier*, none of them says whose supplier it is, so the table still carries no `BusinessId`, has no query filter and takes no ownership stamp. Adding a column to a platform table is not a tenancy decision; giving one a business key would be. `PlatformOptionVisibility` is the single shared row that says whether the one switchable Admin option is offered to anybody but a Super Admin (see [Switchable Admin option visibility](#switchable-admin-option-visibility-issue-873)). `MasterProduct`, `SupplierListing` and `ProductMatchSuggestion` are the shared supplier price catalogue's three tables (issue #923, see [Supplier price catalogue](#supplier-price-catalogue-issue-923)), and they are platform tables for the reason the parent issue exists: a product is looked up at a supplier **once** for every business, so a brand, a name, a size, a supplier's shelf and a matcher's opinion about them are facts about *products*. A `ProductMatchSuggestion` in particular names a folded product description and never the business whose product produced it, which is what keeps one business from being able to learn that another is tracking anything. `PriceCollectorRun` and `SupplierPriceObservation` are issue #925's two, and the same reason one step further on: what a supplier charged for a pack, and the run that read it, are facts about that supplier's shelf and about no business either (see [Supplier price observations and comparison](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925)). An observation names the listing it is a price *of* and never anybody who wanted that price. `PriceCollectorWorkItem` is issue #924's one, and the same reason again: one issued piece of work is a product description — a master product, or the folded search text of one nothing has matched yet — and a supplier's shelf, so it is about no business either, and it carries no `BusinessId`, no query filter and no ownership stamp (see [Collector work list](#collector-work-list-issue-924)). `PriceCollectorResultRow` and `SupplierListingPendingObservation` are issue #937's two, and the same reason once more: a reading a collector submitted, the decision this application made about it, and a reading that was held back rather than priced are facts about a supplier's shelf and about no business (see [Collector results](#collector-results-issue-937)). A result row names the run, the issued work item and the supplier's own product id — a product description and a shelf, never anybody who wanted the search. The business's own half of that catalogue is a separate, ordinary **tenant-owned** table, `ProductPriceTracking` — a business saying it wants one of its own products priced is that business's data, so it implements `IBusinessOwned` and is stamped, filtered and enforced centrally with nothing added for a business's own request, and it is asserted as owned in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` rather than classified here. The two writes to it that do not come from a business are issue #941's automatic match and issue #928's Super Admin review — the same four match columns, through the narrow matching and review windows described in § The second reviewed write and § The fourth reviewed write below. Issue #982 adds the Super Admin's own write of that grant and the append-only `BusinessPlanGrantAudit` beside it — both tenant-owned on the same terms, both asserted as owned, and neither a platform table — through the third reviewed denied-scope write lease below (see [Super Admin sets a business's plan](#super-admin-sets-a-businesss-plan-issue-982)). `SubscriptionGrandfathering` is issue #966's one, and the same reason from a different direction: the grandfathering step of the plan rollout runs **once, over every business**, so the fixed cutoff instant it grants by and the completion marker enforcement waits for are one answer for the whole application and there is no business whose key the row could carry (see [Business subscriptions and plan entitlements](#business-subscriptions-and-plan-entitlements-issue-966)). What that step writes *per business* is an ordinary **tenant-owned** `BusinessPlanGrant`, and the paid record beside it, `BusinessBillingSubscription`, is tenant-owned too: a plan a business was granted and a plan it paid for are facts about that one business, so both implement `IBusinessOwned`, get the ordinary central treatment with nothing added, and are asserted as owned in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` rather than classified here. Each of the eleven is about **no business at all**, which is what distinguishes them from the five above: each of those *is* about one business and carries its key in every statement, while these have no `BusinessId` to carry, no query filter to apply and no ownership stamp to make. The two lists are therefore kept apart in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` — `PlatformEntities` beside `DeliberatelyGlobalEntities`, each closed and asserted, with a test that they do not overlap and that a platform table carries neither a business column nor a filter — so neither table is ever read as an unassigned tenant table somebody forgot to stamp, and the "still carries a business key" rule stays exactly as strong for the five it is about. What keeps them bounded is not ownership but authorization: the two that are written today are written only by the platform-admin surface, every such request carries a **denied** `BusinessScope` (so everything tenant-owned stays unreachable to it), and the copying issue #835 child C does (issue #849) goes one way only — into a business, as an ordinary tenant-owned `Supplier` row that business then owns outright. Nothing reads back out of a business. The copy *write* is the one reviewed provisioning exception below; it writes a `Supplier`, never a platform table. Of the price catalogue's eight tables, every one now has a writer, and the last to get one was `MasterProducts`: the Super Admin review of [#928](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928) is its **only** writer and the only way a master product is ever created, which no automatic match ever does. The rest are written by exactly three collector paths, all under the **denied** scope a collector request carries: the work list of issue #924 through `IPriceCollectorRunStore` (one run, its work items, and the expiry of whatever run was still open, in one transaction — see [Collector work list](#collector-work-list-issue-924)); the results of issue #937 through `IPriceCollectorResultStore`, which writes the listings, the observations, the held readings, the recorded outcome of every submitted row and matching evidence on `ProductMatchSuggestions`, each call in one transaction (see [Collector results](#collector-results-issue-937)); and the matches of issue #941 through `IPriceCollectorMatchStore`, which records one suggestion per decided waiting key — this run's own row always, the proposal itself when nothing of that pair is waiting for a reviewer and otherwise the `Repeated` record of having decided the key, never a relabelling of a row another run wrote — and moves the listings that key had already collected onto the master product a match applied (see [Collector product matching](#collector-product-matching-issue-941)). Those are the second, third and fourth write-capable paths to a platform table and all are bounded the same way the first is — by authorization, not by ownership. The **sixth** is the Super Admin review of [#928](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928), through `IPriceCatalogueReviewStore`: it creates master products, confirms or refuses listings at the identity a person reviewed, accepts a held reading as an observation and clears it from the pending store, and records every match decision on the suggestions — all of them platform tables, each decision one transaction, and bounded by authorization in exactly the same way. The **fifth** is issue #966's, and it is the one that is not a request path at all: the human-run `grandfather-business-plans` command writes the grandfathering record under a denied scope, and each eligible business's grant through a context scoped to that one business. No endpoint reads or writes that record's cutoff or marker — starting the web host and running a command are separate branches of `Program.cs` — and the per-request read beside it publishes one boolean (see [Business subscriptions and plan entitlements](#business-subscriptions-and-plan-entitlements-issue-966)). Since issue #938, `MasterProducts` is also *read* from a member-facing endpoint under the third reading exception below. And since issue #1023 the platform-admin surface **reads the master catalogue in its own right**, beside the review that decides it: `GET api/super-admin/master-products` and `GET .../master-products/{id}` read `MasterProducts`, `SupplierListings`, the `SupplierPresets` that publish those listings and the `SupplierPriceObservation` a listing points at for its current price — four platform tables, **no tenant-owned one at all**, so that surface adds no writer, no reviewed denied-scope write and no `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement anywhere: a platform table carries no business key, so the denied scope those requests run under reads the whole catalogue and none of anybody's own rows (see [Super Admin master products](#super-admin-master-products-issue-1023)). The review of [#928](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928) is still the only writer of a master product.

**Reading has exactly four documented exceptions, and each was reviewed on its own issue.** The first is issue #873's one boolean: `GET /api/me/access` publishes `historicalGstClassificationVisible` to every signed-in member, because an option the application has switched off has to stop being offered to the people it was switched off for. That read reaches one column of `PlatformOptionVisibility` through a one-method port, takes no caller-supplied input, and publishes nothing about any business or member. The second is the "Available to add" suppliers of issue [#935](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/935), which is reviewed on that issue and bounded by it: `GET /api/suppliers/available-presets` publishes the **id, name and website** of the *enabled* `SupplierPreset` rows that serve the caller's own business's recorded state and that it holds no copy of. It exists because the alternative was pushing a record the platform added later into every business that serves — a write into somebody else's data on the platform's schedule — so the business is *offered* it instead and takes it up itself. It reaches that one table through `IAvailableSupplierPresetStore` with no caller-supplied filter, predicate, page or sort, publishes none of the supplier-master fields (served states, price basis, connector), and says nothing about any other business, because a platform record is about none. The **add** beside it is not a platform-table write at all: it inserts an ordinary tenant-owned `Supplier` in the caller's own resolved scope, stamped by the central enforcer. See [Supplier records by business state, and "Available to add"](#supplier-records-by-business-state-and-available-to-add-issue-935). The **third** is a matched master product's name and size, reviewed on issue [#938](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/938) — that issue's own "known constraints" section *is* the review, and it fixed the limit before the code existed: `GET /api/products/{id}/price-tracking` publishes `MasterProduct.Name` and its `SizeValue`/`SizeUnit`, and nothing else about the shared catalogue. It exists because a mapping's *matched* status is unreadable without saying what the product was matched to — "Matched" alone tells a business nothing it can check. It is bounded in every direction at once: only a `ProductPriceTracking` row of the caller's **own** business (the central tenant filters, with no `IgnoreQueryFilters` and no unscoped context on the path), only while that mapping is in one of the two **matched** states, and only those two values — not the brand, the row key, the normalised key, the instants, a supplier listing, a price, or anything at all about another business. The master product is reached through the mapping's own navigation in `EfProductPriceTrackingStore`, so a master product no mapping of this business names is unreachable; there is no method on `IProductPriceTrackingStore` that takes a master product id, and no caller-supplied filter, predicate, page or sort anywhere on the path. See [Tracking supplier prices on a product](#tracking-supplier-prices-on-a-product-issue-938). The **fourth** is the cheapest-supplier summary, reviewed on issue [#930](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/930), whose third acceptance criterion *is* that review: `POST /api/cheapest-suppliers/summary` publishes, for each of the caller's own products, what the business's own linked, not-hidden suppliers charge per vending unit. It exists because a price comparison that cannot name the suppliers and their prices is not a comparison; and it is bounded the same way the third is. The way into the shared catalogue is always one of this business's **own matched mappings**: `ICheapestSupplierSummaryStore` has no method that takes a master product id, a supplier listing id or a supplier record id, and no caller-supplied filter, predicate, page or sort anywhere on the path, so a listing no mapping of this business names is unreachable. What it publishes is a supplier the business already holds its own copy of (its own `Supplier.Name`, tenant-owned), that supplier's pack size, pack price, unit price on both GST bases, special, stock answer, last check and source link, and the reason an offer could not be compared — and **nothing that identifies the shared catalogue or anybody else**: no master product name, brand or key, no listing key, no supplier preset id, and no count of who else tracks the product. There is nowhere for such a value to travel, because a master product, a listing and an observation are facts about products and shelves rather than about businesses. See [The cheapest-supplier summary and the Cheapest supplier column](#the-cheapest-supplier-summary-and-the-cheapest-supplier-column-issue-930). A **fifth** member-facing platform-table read, or a wider projection of any of these four, is a boundary change needing its own reviewed issue.

**Two tenant-owned tables reference a platform table, and each is a reviewed decision of its own (issues #934 and #923).** `Suppliers.SupplierPresetId` is nullable and points at `SupplierPresets.Id`: a supplier a business received from the master records which suggestion it came from, so its name and website stop drifting and a later price comparison can follow it back ([Supplier presets copied into an approved business](#supplier-presets-copied-into-an-approved-business-issue-849)). It changes nothing about either classification. The `Supplier` is still tenant-owned, still filtered, still stamped; the `SupplierPreset` is still about no business and still carries no business key; the copying still goes one way, and nothing reads a business's rows from the platform side. The key is **`Restrict`** and has no navigation property in either direction: the platform cannot delete a row a business depends on (a preset is disabled, never deleted), nothing is cascaded or nulled into a business's data, and no `Include` can pull a platform entity into a tenant-owned object graph. At most one supplier per business may carry a given preset, which is a filtered unique index on `(BusinessId, SupplierPresetId)` — led by `BusinessId`, because two businesses legitimately hold a copy of the same preset, and filtered to the linked rows, because "no preset" is the normal case. The second is issue #923's `ProductPriceTracking.MasterProductId`, nullable and pointing at `MasterProducts.Id` with **`Restrict`**: a business's mapping records which shared master product its own product is, so the platform cannot delete a master product a business is tracking, and a mapping still waiting for a match carries no link at all ([Supplier price catalogue](#supplier-price-catalogue-issue-923)). It changes neither classification either: the mapping is still tenant-owned, filtered and stamped, and the master product still names no business. `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` accepts these two keys **by name**, asserts they are the only ones of their kind, asserts that no platform table points the other way (a shared row depending on one business's data would be the real boundary break), and pins the index — so a third tenant-to-platform key is a decision somebody has to make there rather than an implementation detail.

**The one-time seed, and why it is a migration (issue #848).** The four shipped presets — Coles, Woolworths, Big W, Costco — are inserted by `AddSupplierPresets` with a single `InsertData`, and by nothing else. EF Core's `HasData` and a startup seeding step both re-apply themselves, and **Production applies migrations at startup** (see [Database and migrations](#database-and-migrations)), so either one would quietly undo a Super Admin's edit, or switch a deliberately disabled preset back on, at the next deployment. A one-off `InsertData` runs exactly once, when that migration is applied; `AddSupplierPresetsMigrationTests` proves it by editing and disabling a seeded row, migrating and starting again, and finding the edit intact and no row re-inserted or re-enabled. Name uniqueness ignoring case is the database's rule too, not a query's: a stored normalised name (`Name.Trim().ToUpperInvariant()`) under a unique index, with a pre-check that turns the ordinary case into a clear `409` and the index's own violation translated into the same `409`, so two creates of one name leave one row and one conflict rather than a `500`. The normalisation is invariant rather than culture-dependent, and stored rather than computed by a collation, because SQLite's `NOCASE` folds ASCII only.

**"Not tenant-owned" never means "not owned".** Each of the four exempt tables that is not the `Business` itself carries a `BusinessId`, and the boundary for it is that column named in **every** statement over it, by the adapter rather than by the central filter: `EfBusinessMemberStore` and `EfMemberProfileWriteStore` for memberships, `EfMemberInviteStore` and `EfMemberInviteRedemptionStore` for invites, `EfSupportSessionStore` for support sessions. The id is only ever one tenancy resolution produced from the authenticated actor's membership, or — for the redemption alone — the one the invite row itself reports, or — for a support session — the business row the session's own write transaction read; it never comes from a route, query, body or header. (A support session additionally carries the Entra `(tid, oid)` pair it was granted to, and every "my session" statement names that pair, which is the authenticated actor and never a request value.) That is deliberately *not* the per-controller `Where` clause this section warns against: those adapters have no central mechanism to defer to, and each keeps its statements behind one private helper so the owner cannot be omitted on one method.

**Central read enforcement.** `AppDbContext.ConfigureBusinessOwnership` walks the model rather than naming entities: every `IBusinessOwned` type gets a required business key, an index leading with it, and a global query filter. A new tenant-owned entity is protected the day it implements the interface. There is no per-entity list to forget and no controller `Where` clause that could be omitted on one endpoint — which is why adding redundant filters in controllers or services is discouraged rather than merely unnecessary.

**Central write enforcement.** Query filters protect reads only. `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` runs on both `SaveChanges` overloads. Since issue #849 the denied-scope refusal has reviewed exceptions, each narrower than the rule rather than a way around it — the supplier provisioning write below, and since issue #941 the collector's automatic match beside it. Since issue #551 it enforces one rule before the other four: a request in `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` may write **nothing at all** — every table, not only the tenant-owned ones — because in that state there is no write this application wants. The other four rules are about ownership: new rows are **stamped** with the caller's business (callers never supply it); inserts, updates, and deletes of another business's row are **rejected**, which is what stops a detached entity attached by ID from slipping through to an `UPDATE`; the business key is **immutable**, so a record cannot be moved between businesses; and every foreign key between tenant-owned entities must **stay inside one business**. The relationship rule is driven by EF model metadata, not a hand-written list, so a new foreign key is covered as soon as it is mapped. Resolving a principal's owner deliberately uses `IgnoreQueryFilters`, because a principal in another business must be reported as a boundary violation rather than mistaken for "does not exist".

**Tenant-scoped uniqueness.** Constraints over externally supplied values are scoped by business, because two businesses may legitimately hold the same external value: Nayax transaction IDs, import file hashes, site commission agreements, fee effective dates, and costing baselines. `NayaxSales` consequently has its own local key with `TransactionID` unique *per business* — a remote identifier is an external identity, not a primary key. This also keeps import de-duplication correct: one business must never be told its own import is a duplicate because another imported the same bytes first, and a shared remote ID must never cause one business's import to update another's row. The one-active-membership index of issue #522 is deliberately *not* scoped this way, and is not an exception to this rule: `BusinessMembership` is one of the five structural non-tenant-owned tables above, and the value it constrains is an Entra identity that must mean the same person everywhere rather than an externally supplied value two businesses may legitimately share. The invite token hash *is* scoped this way — `(BusinessId, TokenHash)` — even though the invite table is now non-tenant-owned too, because that value is not an identity: a global constraint over it would let one business's row deny another's, and 256 bits of cryptographic randomness is what makes a token unambiguous. The support-session id hash of issue #550 is deliberately the other way round — unique across the whole table — and that is not an exception either: the rule is about values a *business* supplies, and a session id is generated by this server, supplied by nobody, and matched by a request that carries no business to narrow the lookup with, so global uniqueness is what makes "which session is this?" have one answer.

**Protected documents.** A document's bytes live outside the database, so hiding the row is not enough. Retrieval always resolves the tenant-owned parent record first — `GET /api/purchases/{id}/file` and `GET /api/operating-expenses/{id}/attachment` both go through the filtered `DbSet` — and the stored file name is read from that record, never from the request. Adding a purchase document (`POST /api/purchases/{id}/file`, issue #976) resolves it the same way and writes the stored name the server generated, so another business's purchase id is simply not found and the bytes that request had written are removed again. No endpoint accepts a file name or path as input, and `FileSystemDocumentStorage` reduces any stored name with `Path.GetFileName` and then proves the result is inside the category folder, so a crafted value cannot escape it. Knowing another business's purchase ID, attachment ID, stored file name, and on-disk path therefore yields nothing.

**The unrestricted-context rule.** `new AppDbContext(options)` is fail-closed. Unrestricted, all-business access requires passing `UnscopedBusinessScope.Instance` explicitly, so every such place is greppable. Outside tests it exists only in the four human-invoked commands — `migrate-database`, `bootstrap-business`, `migrate-documents`, which reads every business's document metadata to migrate it (see [Document storage](#document-storage)), and `reconcile-attachment-storage` (issue #968), which reads every business's attachment records because a stored file is an orphan only if **no** business refers to it (see [Attachment storage quotas](#attachment-storage-quotas-issue-968)). Being a human-invoked command is not what grants it: `migrate-nayax-connection` (issue #519) is a fourth such command and constructs no unrestricted context at all, because it needs none — the tenancy tables it reads to resolve the target business carry no tenant filter, and the credential itself is read and written through a context scoped to that one business (see [Migrating the Nayax connection](#migrating-the-nayax-connection-issue-519)). `resolve-nayax-sale-products` (issue #758) is a fifth, on the same pattern: it enumerates businesses through a denied-scope context and reads and writes every sale, product and audit row through a context scoped to the one business that sale belongs to (see [The sale's own product](#the-sales-own-product-issue-758)). `grandfather-business-plans` (issue #966) is a sixth and does the same again: the businesses and the one platform grandfathering row are read under a denied scope, and each business's plan grant is written through a context scoped to that business (see [Business subscriptions and plan entitlements](#business-subscriptions-and-plan-entitlements-issue-966)). No controller, service, or request path may run unrestricted; a composition-root test pins down that the DI container never produces an unscoped context, and issue #544 extended that test to the platform-admin store below — it is registered scoped and its only constructor dependency is the request's own `AppDbContext`, so nothing can hand it anything else. Issue #550's support-session store is held to the same three things, for the same reason: it is the second adapter a platform administrator's denied-scope request reaches. **A support session is not unrestricted either, and is narrower than a membership rather than wider** (issue #551): `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` names exactly one business and is compared by the same filter expression as `Resolved`, so such a request reads that one business and — because `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` refuses every `SaveChanges` in that state — writes nothing at all. See [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551). The platform diagnostics API (issue #336) does **not** change this and is deliberately not implemented with it: a diagnostics request carries a *denied* `BusinessScope`, so the query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` stay in force and it reads nothing at all through `AppDbContext`. Its cross-business read is a separate read-only SQLite connection restricted by SQLite's own authorizer — see [Platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336) for the exception's exact boundaries.

**The two reviewed denied-scope writes (issues #849 and #982), the first of which is the provisioning one.** A denied scope writes nothing tenant-owned — that is the rule immediately above, and it is what makes the whole platform-admin surface unable to touch a business's own data. Approving a business application needs exactly one thing more: the business being approved has to receive its own copies of the enabled platform supplier presets, which are tenant-owned `Supplier` rows, in the same transaction as the status change. The exception is therefore cut as narrowly as the fact requires and no wider. `AppDbContext.BeginSupplierProvisioning(businessId)` opens a lease; while it is open `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` accepts **new `Supplier` rows of that one business and nothing else**, stamping them through the same `StampOrVerifyNewRow` every ordinary insert goes through; disposing it closes the window. It is narrower than the denied-scope rule in four directions at once: **one entity type** (a product, a purchase, a sale are all still refused), **one state** (an insert — never an update, never a delete, so no existing row of any business can be changed or removed), **one business**, whose id is the key of the row the approval's own write transaction read rather than anything a request supplied, and **one save** rather than one request. The method is `internal`, its only caller is `EfBusinessSupplierProvisioningStore`, and a lease may be taken only while the context's own scope is `Denied` — so neither an ordinary member's request nor a support session can open one, and an endpoint cannot borrow the adapter to write a supplier outside the ordinary tenant path. Nothing becomes *readable*: `CurrentBusinessId` and `TenantFilteringEnabled` deliberately do not consult the lease, so while it is open every tenant-owned query still matches nothing — the copy path cannot see another business's suppliers, or even the ones it has just created, and there is no `IgnoreQueryFilters` over `Suppliers` anywhere. See [Supplier presets copied into an approved business](#supplier-presets-copied-into-an-approved-business-issue-849).

**The second reviewed write, and the one that names no business (issue #941).** A match decided for a waiting *key* — the folded search name and unit label several businesses' products share, which is what makes one product one search — has to reach the mappings that carry it, and the collector that reported it is a member of nothing. `AppDbContext.BeginPriceCatalogueMatching()` opens a lease; while it is open `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` accepts **updates to `Status`, `MasterProductId`, `MatchSource` and `UpdatedAtUtc` of `ProductPriceTracking` rows and nothing else**. It is narrower than the denied-scope rule in the directions the fact allows: **one entity type**, **one state** (an update — never an insert and never a delete, so the collector can neither start nor withdraw a business's request to be priced), **four columns**, which do not include the business key, the product, the waiting key or the captured search text, and **one save**. It names no business, because the mappings that carry one key may belong to any number of them; what bounds it is *what may be written* rather than whose row it is, and the enforcer asserts the modified columns as a **set** rather than a lower bound, so a mapping can neither be moved between businesses nor re-pointed at another product through it. Relationship enforcement still runs. The method is `internal`, its only caller is `EfPriceCollectorMatchStore`, it may be taken only while the scope is `Denied`, and never beside a provisioning lease. Nothing becomes readable by it either: the mappings are read by that adapter's one reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement below. See [Collector product matching](#collector-product-matching-issue-941).

**The third reviewed write is the Super Admin's manual plan grant (issue #982, the owner-approved amendment of 29 October 2026), on exactly the same terms.** `AppDbContext.BeginPlanGrantWrite(businessId)` opens a lease under which `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` accepts **one business's `BusinessPlanGrant` row and the `BusinessPlanGrantAudit` row beside it, and nothing else**: two entity types rather than one, because the grant and the record of who gave it must commit together; an insert or an update of the grant and an insert of the audit row, never a delete, because a grant that was given is ended rather than unsaid and an audit trail that could be rewritten is not one; one business, whose id is the key of the row the decision's own write transaction read; and one save. The method is `internal`, its only caller is `EfPlatformPlanGrantStore`, a lease may be taken only while the scope is `Denied`, and only one may be open at a time, never beside a provisioning or matching lease. Nothing becomes *readable* through it either — the filters do not consult the lease, which is why that adapter's read is the explicit, business-pinned `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement described below rather than something the lease quietly permits. See [Super Admin sets a business's plan](#super-admin-sets-a-businesss-plan-issue-982).

**The fourth reviewed write is the Super Admin's review of the shared price catalogue (issue #928), and it is the second one's rule for the other decider.** `AppDbContext.BeginPriceCatalogueReview()` opens a lease under which `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` accepts **updates to `Status`, `MasterProductId`, `MatchSource` and `UpdatedAtUtc` of `ProductPriceTracking` rows and nothing else** — the same written-out column set the matching window uses, asserted as a *set* rather than a lower bound, so the ownership key, the product, the waiting key and the captured search text are all outside it. One entity type, one state (an update: this surface can no more create or withdraw a business's request to be priced than a matcher can), four columns, one save. It names no business, because a match and an undo of one are decided for a waiting *key* and the mappings that carry it may belong to any number of businesses; what bounds it is *what may be written*. The method is `internal`, its only caller is `EfPriceCatalogueReviewStore`, a lease may be taken only while the scope is `Denied`, and never beside another lease. It is a **separate window** from the matching one rather than a second caller of it, deliberately: each lease in that context names the one adapter that may take it, so "who may write a mapping's match columns?" has two answers with two issues behind them instead of one answer that has quietly grown a caller. A **fifth** denied-scope write exception, a lease taken anywhere else, or a wider entity set in any of the four is a boundary change needing its own reviewed issue. See [Super Admin review of the supplier price catalogue](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928).

**The six reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` paths in a request, each with its own issue (issues #544, #983, #924, #941, #982, #977 and #928).** The first is the Super Admin's business directory: it reports whether each business has stored Nayax credentials and the connection status stored beside them, `BusinessNayaxConnection` is tenant-owned, and the request carries a denied scope — so the central filter matches none of its rows and those facts are otherwise unreadable. `EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` makes exactly one `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement, projecting `BusinessId` and `Status` alone (the second added by issue #983 under the repository owner's approval — see [The business's Nayax connection status](#the-businesss-nayax-connection-status-issue-983)), and the rest of the adapter is ordinary reads and writes of the structurally non-tenant-owned tables. It is a *narrowed* exception rather than a loosened rule: what it reads is the ownership key, which is not business data, and one stored status that says how usable a connection was at its last test — no credential column, and nothing a business trades, buys, sells, counts or costs — and the alternatives — an unscoped request context, a second read-only cross-business connection, or resolving each business into the request scope in turn — were each strictly worse. See [Super Admin businesses API](#super-admin-businesses-api-issue-544).

The second is the collector work list (issue #924): `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` reads `ProductPriceTracking` across businesses, projecting the waiting key, the search name, the unit label and the master product id — **a product description, and nothing that says whose product it is**. It is the exception issue #923 left for #924 to review, and it is narrowed in the same four directions the first one is: one table, one projection, read-only, and reachable from exactly one endpoint, which no person can call at all. See [Collector work list](#collector-work-list-issue-924).

The third is the collector's automatic match (issue #941): `EfPriceCollectorMatchStore` reads the `ProductPriceTracking` rows whose stored waiting key is one the run was issued work for, because a key the central filters hide is a key whose mappings a match could not reach. It is the same table, the same authorization and the same kind of content — a waiting key, the search name and unit label it folds from, and the mapping's own match state — and it is the one of the three that is not read-only, because those rows are loaded in order to have four of their columns written through `SaveChanges`, where the enforcer judges the write. What *leaves* the adapter is less than what it reads: no business id, no product id, no mapping id, and **no count of the mappings a match moved**, which would be a count of the businesses tracking the product. See [Collector product matching](#collector-product-matching-issue-941). The fourth is the Super Admin's manual plan grant (issue #982, the owner-approved amendment of 29 October 2026): `EfPlatformPlanGrantStore` reads `BusinessPlanGrants` for the **one** business a platform decision names — the statement is pinned to that business id *and* to the complimentary grant source, projecting the plan, the period, the reason, the revision and the instant — because a grant is tenant-owned and the request carries a denied scope, so the central filter matches none of its rows. It is narrowed the same way the first two reads are: one table, one business per statement, one projection, and reachable from exactly one controller that no business role, support session or member can call. The grandfathered grant of issue #966 is excluded by the source predicate, so it is not readable through this path either. See [Super Admin sets a business's plan](#super-admin-sets-a-businesss-plan-issue-982).

The fifth is the collector work list's **plan read** (issue #977), and it is in the same adapter as the second: before those two mapping statements run, `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` reads `BusinessPlanGrants` and `BusinessBillingSubscriptions` across businesses — projecting the ownership key, the plan and the half-open period, and **nothing else about either record**: no reason text, no revision, no decision instant, no billing identifier — asks the Domain's single entitlement rule which businesses include the observed supplier prices, and restricts the two mapping statements to those businesses. Its *only* effect is to narrow the second path. It is read-only, makes no raw SQL statement, takes no unscoped context, is made only while plan enforcement is on and the grandfathering step has completed, and is reachable from the same one class-5 endpoint no person can call; nothing it reads is published — a business id, and a count of businesses, still cannot leave that adapter — and nothing is written or removed by a business ceasing to be eligible. The reason the read lives behind the port rather than in front of it is that whatever decided eligibility *outside* the adapter would have to hand it a set of business ids, which is exactly what this boundary exists to keep out of the work list. See [Plan enforcement on supplier price data](#plan-enforcement-on-supplier-price-data-issue-977).

The sixth is the Super Admin's review of the shared price catalogue (issue #928): `EfPriceCatalogueReviewStore` reads the `ProductPriceTracking` rows that are awaiting a match or auto-matched, and those carrying the waiting key a decision names, for the reason the third does — a platform-admin request carries a denied scope, so the central filters match no mapping at all and a review of the shared catalogue would see nothing to decide. It is **one statement in one place** (`MappingsAcrossBusinesses`), which every read and every write on that adapter goes through, and what crosses it is the same kind of content as the third's — a waiting key, the search name and unit label it folds from, the mapping's own match state — plus one thing the third deliberately does not publish: the **count of distinct businesses waiting** under a key. That count is issue #928's own criterion and is bounded by the same sentence that asks for it, "a count of businesses waiting, never which business asked": the reviewer is deciding a shared catalogue and needs to know whether a decision matters to one business or to twelve, and the collector — which is an application searching a shelf — still gets no count at all. Nothing else about a business leaves the adapter: no business id, no business name, no product id and no mapping id. See [Super Admin review of the supplier price catalogue](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928). A **seventh** such path, a wider projection, or any further predicate over a tenant-owned table in any of the five adapters is a boundary change needing its own reviewed issue.

**Schema and data are separate steps, and only the data step is exclusively human-controlled.** `DatabaseSchemaStartup` decides per environment: Production, Development, and `Testing` all migrate automatically and fail closed if the attempt fails (issue #201); any other non-Production environment does so only under the `Database:AllowAutomaticMigrationUnsafeOutsideDevelopment` override. Migrations never assign ownership, automatically or otherwise. The backfill is exclusively `bootstrap-business`, run by a human: deterministic, idempotent (it touches only unassigned rows), restartable, transactional, dry-runnable, and verified by before/after counts and financial totals, with a `BusinessBackfillAudit` record of what it did. `TenantOwnershipReadiness` reports at startup whether ownership has actually been bootstrapped, so "all my data is gone" cannot be the first symptom of an unfinished rollout.

**Known limits of this rollout.** One business is live. The Nayax **catalogue** is no longer part of that limit either: its products and categories used to be keyed by the Nayax `NayaxProductID`/`ProductGroupID`, which is one global identifier space, so two businesses could not both import the same Nayax product — issue #735 made a created row's key the database's own and left the provider's id as a per-business column, and `EfCatalogueReviewStoreTenancyTests` proves two businesses importing the same ids (`EfNayaxProductCatalogImportStoreTenancyTests` pinned the same thing for the direct import, until issue #739 replaced it), see [Provider identity on the local row](#provider-identity-on-the-local-row-issues-732-759-and-735). The Nayax **credential** is no longer part of that limit: issue #518 added the per-business storage, issue #519 the human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command that moves the existing credential into it, and issue #520 made the client read the current business's own operator id and token on every call with no global fallback — see [Per-business Nayax credentials](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520). Since issues #536 and #537 an Owner's own credential can also reach the database through the API: a test holds the pasted pair as an encrypted draft and a save promotes it, with a re-test for the stored one — see [Saving a tested connection and re-testing it](#saving-a-tested-connection-and-re-testing-it-issue-537). Since issue #538 an Owner can drive those endpoints from Admin → Integrations, through the connection wizard — see [The Nayax connection wizard](#the-nayax-connection-wizard-issue-538). Since issue #539 every Nayax-dependent screen explains an unready connection instead of failing silently, and points an Owner at the wizard — see [Nayax connection status banners](#nayax-connection-status-banners-issue-539). What is still outstanding before a second business goes live is the rest of #328's self-service work; the business that is live today had its credential moved in by the human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command, which is a human step described in `docs/tenant-rollout.md` § Migrating the Nayax connection into the business. The database foreign keys from `BusinessId` to `Businesses` are a deliberate, still-outstanding deferral — see `docs/tenant-rollout.md`. Issue #39 (document storage) consumes this ownership key and must not introduce blob storage before it.

#### Membership roles and capabilities (issue #521)

Ownership answers "whose data is this?". A role answers "what may this member do with it?", and that is again a separate question: every member of a business sees the same data, and the role decides which of it they may read and change.

**Three roles, on the membership.** `BusinessMembership.Role` is a `required` `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessRole` — `Operator`, `Manager` or `Owner` — stored as that constrained vocabulary's integer value. The values are spaced (`20`, `30`, `40`) so the read-only Viewer role #328 anticipates can be added below `Operator` without renumbering a value that is already persisted, and `0` is deliberately not a declared role, because `0` is what an unfilled integer column and a default-constructed enum both hold. Nothing compares two roles numerically.

**A role is always explicit, and an omitted role grants nothing** (issue #679). The property has no default: `required` makes a creation path that states no role a compile error, so the invite redemption, the self-service application, `bootstrap-business` and the E2E fixture each say which role they mean. `IsActive` is `required` on the same terms — whether a membership grants anything at all is not a value a write should be able to leave unsaid. It used to default to `Owner`, the most privileged role in the business, which is the fail-open shape issue #584 removed from `Business.Status`: a creation path that said nothing got everything. The database half is `RemoveBusinessMembershipRoleOwnerDatabaseDefault`, which replaces the `DEFAULT 40` that `AddBusinessMembershipRole`'s backfill left behind with `DEFAULT 0` — a value no role is declared at — in four in-place statements (add, copy, drop, rename) that preserve every stored role and rebuild no table, the shape `RemoveBusinessStatusActiveDatabaseDefault` established. So an `INSERT` that never goes through EF and names no role now produces a membership that is denied rather than an Owner. `IsActive` needed no migration: that column has never carried a database default, so a row that states no activation fails its `NOT NULL` constraint outright. What the entity still cannot refuse is a *cast* undeclared role — `(BusinessRole)99` from inside the code — which is stored and then denied on every request by the policy below rather than refused on the way in; a `SaveChanges` enforcer for it, on `BusinessStatusEnforcer`'s pattern, is deliberately left to its own reviewed change.

**An unknown stored role denies access.** `BusinessMembershipResolutionPolicy` checks the role of the membership that would otherwise have resolved, and a value this code does not declare — a hand-written `UPDATE`, or a role a newer deployment wrote — is denied as `RoleUnrecognised`. It is never read as the lowest declared role, which would grant access nobody recorded, and the adapter does not normalise it on read for the same reason. A membership denial still outranks it, so an operator investigating a refusal is shown the cause they can act on. The role is checked in the Domain policy rather than by a database CHECK constraint: SQLite cannot add one to an existing table without rebuilding it, and a value written by a future deployment has to fail closed in the policy anyway.

**The role travels with the resolved business.** `BusinessMembershipResolution` carries the business id and the role together, so the two always come from one membership lookup and cannot disagree. `ICurrentBusinessProvider.RequireRoleAsync` is how the Application layer reads it, memoised per request exactly like the business id — so a role change applies on the member's next request, with no cache to wait for and no sign-out needed. The one-active-membership fail-closed rule is unchanged.

**One capability table.** `Inventory.Application.Access.RoleCapabilities` is the single role → capability definition, over the fifteen-capability `Capability` vocabulary (`Dashboard.View`, `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, `PickList.View`, `Inventory.Operate`, `Purchasing.Operate`, `Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults`, `Expenses.Manage`, `Reports.View`, `Imports.Run`, `SiteCommissions.Manage`, `Integration.Manage`, `Data.Repair`, `Members.Manage`, `Roles.View`, `Business.Manage`). An Operator holds the four operational ones; a Manager adds the financial, expense, import and commission work; an Owner adds the business's own configuration — integration, data repair, members, roles and the business record. Each role's set is written out in full, so the table reads the way the agreed table in #328 reads, and the hierarchy it happens to describe is asserted by a test rather than assumed by the code. There is no second table, no per-controller list and no capability derived from a role's stored value.

**Defining a capability is not enforcing one.** Issue #521 stores the role, publishes the vocabulary and reports it, and enforces nothing. Enforcement is [Capability authorization](#capability-authorization-issue-525) below, which reads `RoleCapabilities.Allows` so that what an endpoint enforces and what `GET /api/me/access` reports cannot drift apart.

**`GET /api/me/access`** returns the caller's role, that role's capability names, and their business's name and time zone (issue #499). It takes no parameter of any kind and describes the caller alone: no other member, no other business, and no identifier for either.
