The capability is declared on each action rather than on `BusinessController`, because the controller's other action is the shell read `GET /api/business/current`, which every role holds `Dashboard.View` for; the settings **read** is restricted with the write rather than following it, because it reports the business's own contact address, ABN, GST registration and state rather than anything a page needs to render. See [Capability authorization on the Manager and Owner endpoints](#capability-authorization-on-the-manager-and-owner-endpoints-issue-526) for the matrix row.

**A save is the whole set, validated before anything is stored.** `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessSettingsPolicy` is the one rule: a name is required and bounded at 200 characters, a contact address must be a single well-formed address (`Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessContactEmail`, a format check that never claims the mailbox exists — see [The contact-address format rule](#the-contact-address-format-rule-issue-593) below), the ABN is optional but checksum-validated whenever it is present, the GST registration must be *stated* — an absent `gstRegistered` is a `400` and never `false`, because "registered", "not registered" and "not recorded" are three different facts and a missing form field must not record a tax one — and the state must be one of the eight Australian states and territories. The four profile columns stay nullable in the schema for the business that predates the application form, so the read reports "not recorded" honestly, while a save is narrower: it may leave the ABN unrecorded (`null`, its single representation of absence — a blank string is refused) and may not leave the address, the registration or the state unstated. A refusal stores nothing at all, so the six settings move together.

##### The business's state or territory (issue #933)

Issue #933, one slice of #817, adds `Businesses.State`: the Australian state or territory a business trades in, so a supplier record that serves only some states can be offered to the right businesses. It exists because the time zone cannot answer that question — `Australia/Sydney` is New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory alike — and it is therefore **recorded, never derived**: not from `TimeZoneId`, not from an address, not from an ABN.

- **The vocabulary is closed and written out once.** `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.AustralianStates` holds the eight codes (`NSW`, `VIC`, `QLD`, `SA`, `WA`, `TAS`, `ACT`, `NT`), the one normalisation (trim and upper-case, so `" nsw "` is stored as `NSW`) and the one refusal sentence. `BusinessSettingsPolicy.Validate` — and so `BusinessApplicationPolicy.Validate`, which delegates to it — refuses anything else with that sentence and a `400`, storing nothing. A long name (`New South Wales`), another country's subdivision and a plausible-looking code that is not one of ours are all refusals rather than interpretations.
- **It is required on a submission and nullable in the schema.** The application form (issue #543) collects it, so a business created by an application always has one; every business that existed before the column has `NULL`, the migration backfills nothing, and nothing is blocked while it is unset. The Owner records it on the Business Settings page (issue #549), where the existing legacy-profile prompt — `LegacyBusinessSettingsPromptComponent`, judged by `isLegacyBusinessProfile`, which now also treats an unrecorded state as an incomplete profile — asks for it beside the contact email and the GST registration.
- **The value is validated centrally too.** `Inventory.Infrastructure.Data.BusinessStateEnforcer` refuses anything but one of the eight — in its canonical stored form — on `SaveChanges`, beside `BusinessTimeZoneEnforcer`, `BusinessAbnEnforcer`, `BusinessStatusEnforcer` and `BusinessSalesProviderEnforcer`, so no write path to a business can store a value this vocabulary does not declare. `NULL` is accepted and is the single representation of "not recorded".
- **Changing it adds the supplier records the new state serves, and changes nothing else** (issue #935, which is the "separate work under #817" this bullet originally deferred). In the settings save's own transaction, every enabled platform supplier record that now matches and that this business holds no copy of is added as a linked copy; **no supplier is removed, hidden, relinked or edited**, and no product, purchase, sale, cost or report value moves. The audit event still names `State` among the changed fields without carrying the value, and says nothing about the suppliers. See [Supplier records by business state, and "Available to add"](#supplier-records-by-business-state-and-available-to-add-issue-935).
- **The Super Admin's directory reports it** so an application can be reviewed with it: one more column of the fixed set of the business's own published details `IPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` reaches (`GET /api/super-admin/businesses` → `state`), `null` for a business that recorded none. Nothing tenant-owned becomes reachable, no predicate is added, and no other method of that port changes — see [Super Admin businesses API](#super-admin-businesses-api-issue-544).
- **The migration is additive**: `AddBusinessState` adds one nullable `TEXT` column bounded at the longest abbreviation, with no `CHECK` constraint for the reason `Status` and `BusinessMemberships.Role` carry none (SQLite would rebuild the table, and the vocabulary is enforced on `SaveChanges` anyway). `AddBusinessStateMigrationTests` proves the upgrade: the column arrives, both seeded businesses read `NULL` — including the ones in `Australia/Sydney` and `Australia/Brisbane`, the two zones a backfill would have guessed from — and every other column comes through unchanged.

##### The contact-address format rule (issue #593)

`BusinessContactEmail.TryNormalize` is the one contact-address rule, read by `BusinessSettingsPolicy` and by nothing else: the controller holds no email check of its own, and adding a second one anywhere would be two answers to one question. It is a **format** rule and claims nothing more — no SMTP, DNS, mailbox-ownership or deliverability check runs, and a well-formed address is never a reachable one.

Issue #548's first version checked that the domain's dot-separated labels were non-empty, which was not the same question: `owner@!.com` and `owner@example.com>` both passed it, so `PUT /api/business/settings` could store them as the business's published contact address. Issue #593 replaced that check with what the rule was always meant to be, in the same two-part shape:

- **The mailbox** is dot-separated parts, each non-empty, of ASCII letters, digits and RFC 5322's unquoted symbols (``!#$%&'*+-/=?^_`{|}~``). The characters that set leaves out are the point: `<`, `>`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `:`, `;`, `,`, `"` and `\` are how a mail client delimits an address, a display name, a comment or a second recipient, so one arriving in this field is a paste that brought its surroundings with it. A quoted local part (`"owner name"@example.com`) is legal in RFC 5322 and refused here deliberately, because accepting quotes is what lets a pasted `"Owner" <owner@example.com>` through.
- **The domain** must be able to be a host name: at least two labels, each non-empty, made of ASCII letters, digits and interior hyphens, ending in an alphabetic top-level label of at least two characters. So `example.com`, `ex-ample.co.uk` and `e.co`, and not `example`, `.com`, `example..com`, `!.com`, `exa_mple.com`, `-example.com` or `example.c0m`. An internationalised domain must be submitted in its ASCII-compatible (punycode) form, and a bracketed IP literal is refused: neither is how a business publishes its own contact address.

Everything issue #548 already refused is still refused — a missing or blank value, whitespace anywhere inside the address, two addresses in one field, a second `@`, an empty domain label, and anything longer than the 254 characters an SMTP envelope allows — and every supported valid example is still accepted unchanged: `owner@example.com`, `owner.name@example.com`, `owner+vending@example.com.au`, `o@e.co` and `Owner@Example.com`. Surrounding whitespace is still the only thing removed, and the submitted case is still stored exactly as typed, because case is meaningful to a local part. A refusal is the same `DomainValidationException` with the same message, which names the rule and never echoes the submitted address, so the endpoint's `400`, its response shape, the Owner-only capability, the trusted current-business resolution, the ABN/GST/time-zone handling and the audit redaction are all unchanged. Nothing reads or rewrites an address already stored: the rule applies to what a save submits, and issue #593 backfilled, cleared and corrected nothing.

**The time zone's resolvability is still decided centrally.** The policy checks only that an id was submitted; whether the host's time-zone database can keep a calendar in it is answered by `Inventory.Infrastructure.Data.BusinessTimeZoneEnforcer` on `SaveChanges`, exactly as it is for the bootstrap and any other write path (see [Per-business time zone](#per-business-time-zone-issue-499)). Both refusals are a `DomainValidationException` and so the same `400`. That is also why `EfBusinessSettingsStore` writes through a tracked entity and `SaveChanges` rather than an `ExecuteUpdate`: a set-based update would write straight past that enforcer and past `BusinessAbnEnforcer`. The row is read, compared and written inside one transaction, so the audit trail's change set describes the state the write actually replaced.

**Since issue #680 that transaction is [`MembershipWriteGuard`](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522)'s, and the business's lifecycle status is re-read inside it.** The store joins the ambient transaction rather than opening a second one, which SQLite would refuse anyway. The reason for the change is serialisation rather than isolation: the business was resolved from the caller's membership when the request arrived, and a save that commits after the Super Admin's deactivation would rename, re-address or re-register a business that has been switched off — a change nobody inside it can see, undo or administer, and one the `409` the caller's *next* request gets would not explain. The intent names the business and no membership rule, because a settings save activates nothing and removes no Owner, and a save arriving after the deactivation is refused with `409` and `ActiveBusinessWritePolicy.NotActiveMessage`, storing nothing and auditing nothing. A business row that has gone keeps its own separate refusal in the use case; the status re-check reaches it first and refuses the same way, which is the fail-closed direction.

**Changing the zone re-derives every business day, and rewrites nothing.** This is the decision recorded on issue #499 and now reachable: the zone is resolved per request from the business's own record, so from the next request onwards *all* business days and report boundaries — past data as much as future — are derived in the new zone, including that zone's own daylight-saving transitions. **On the next request, and not during the saving one:** `BusinessScopeMiddleware` publishes the zone into the request's `BusinessTimeZoneScope` before the action runs, and that scope can only move forward once, so a `PUT` that changes the zone still *runs* in the old one. That is deliberate rather than incidental — a request deriving two different business dates depending on how far through itself it was would be worse than a change that lands cleanly at a request boundary — and it is why the submitted zone is a value this endpoint *stores*, never the zone the request itself reports in. The repository rule that a business's reporting timezone is never taken from route, query, body or header input is therefore unchanged: resolution still reads the business record and nothing else. No stored instant, sale, purchase, expense, commission, costing row or document changes, because nothing stored is a business date: a business date is derived from a stored UTC instant through `IBusinessCalendar` every time it is needed. The visible consequence is that a figure already printed for a Sydney business day may fall on the adjacent day once the business is in another zone, which is why the page that will call this endpoint (#549) is the one that has to show the warning #499 asked for - the API refuses nothing on that account, because the re-derivation is the agreed behaviour rather than an accident to be guarded against. `BusinessSettingsPersistenceTests` proves both halves on a relational database: an already-stored sale's business date and its business day's UTC boundaries move with the saved zone, the stored instant is unchanged, and a past transition day becomes 23 hours long in the new zone while the other business in the same database is untouched.

**Every change is audited, and the audit carries no values.** `Inventory.Application.Businesses.IBusinessSettingsAudit` takes one entry per stored change — the actor's Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, the business id, the instant from `IClock`, and which settings changed as the closed `BusinessSettingsField` vocabulary — and `InventoryApi.Adapters.Businesses.LoggingBusinessSettingsAudit` emits it as one structured `ILogger` event with the request's correlation id. It is a log port rather than a table for the reason the diagnostics audit is (see [Platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336)); destination and retention are platform configuration a human verifies. The event deliberately names fields and never values: no contact address, no ABN, no business name and no before-or-after of anything, so the audit trail cannot become a second, unprotected copy of the business's contact and tax detail. A save that changed nothing is not audited, because the event is evidence about a change rather than about an attempt; a rejected save and a save against a business row that has gone are not audited either, for the same reason. The actor is read **before** the write, so a change that could not be attributed is refused rather than stored with an anonymous event.

**What this slice does not do.** It writes no lifecycle status (approve, reject and deactivate are #509's), touches no membership, no role and no Nayax setting, and deletes or transfers nothing. It does not change what a GST report does with `GstRegistered` — still nothing reads that flag, which stays the deliberate follow-up issue #540 described.

**What proves this slice.** `BusinessSettingsPolicyTests` and `BusinessContactEmailTests` (the validation and change-set rules, including that a present zone id is deliberately *not* resolved there, that a refusal never echoes the submitted address or ABN, and — for issue #593 — both reported malformed addresses with the malformed-domain and pasted-delimiter families they belong to, beside the supported valid examples and the trimming and case-preserving behaviour they must not disturb), `BusinessSettingsUseCaseTests` (the business coming from the membership and never the submission, validation before any write, the audit entry's contents, the permitted save running inside the committed write transaction with the status re-read first, the save refused once the business is no longer `Active` and when a deactivation commits while the write lock is awaited, and nothing audited for an unchanged save, a refused one, a missing business or an unattributable actor), `OwnerWriteDuringDeactivationTests` (the relational race against a real deactivation), `BusinessSettingsPersistenceTests` (the relational read and write with two businesses present: the other business untouched, both central enforcers still refusing and storing nothing, the change set, and the zone re-derivation above), `BusinessSettingsApiTests` (the whole pipeline: an Owner's read and save, a Manager and an Operator refused on both, `401` and the missing-scope `403`, every validation rule answering `400` and storing nothing — including each malformed address of issue #593, against a business whose five settings have all been recorded, leaving every one of them and the audit trail alone — the ABN cleared, the saved zone visible in `/api/me/access` and `/api/business/current` on the next request, and the audit event's contents including the two values it must never carry) and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests`/`CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` (the capability on each endpoint, and the role matrix).

#### Self-service business application (issue #541)

Until this slice a business existed in exactly one way: a human ran `bootstrap-business`, which adopts the one Australian vending operation this application was built for. Issue #541, one slice of #507 under #328, is the second and only other way — a person signing in for the first time applies to start a business, and the application waits as a `Pending` business until the Super Admin decides on it. It adds no table and no migration: issue #540's lifecycle status and profile columns are what it writes.

**An application *is* the business.** There is no separate application entity, and deliberately so: a `Pending` business row carries the submitted details, `AppliedAtUtc`, and the applicant's own active Owner membership from the moment it is created, so approving it later changes a status rather than copying anything anywhere. `Inventory.Application.Onboarding.BusinessApplication` is what the Application layer reports about one — the business id, the stored `BusinessSettings`, the status and the submission instant — and `Inventory.Application.Onboarding.IBusinessApplicationStore` is the narrow port it runs on, implemented by `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfBusinessApplicationStore`.

**`POST /api/onboarding/business-applications`, class 3, denied scope.** `InventoryApi.Controllers.OnboardingController`'s one action carries `MembershipNotRequiredEndpointAttribute` and is the reviewed third entry on that marker's allowlist (see [Account state and the membership-not-required marker](#account-state-and-the-membership-not-required-marker-issue-523)). It is its own controller for the reason the invite redemption is: `BusinessController` declares capabilities a person with no membership could not possibly hold, so an endpoint with the opposite authorization shape gets its own story rather than an exception inside somebody else's. The request still requires authentication and the delegated `access_as_user` scope — "membership not required" is not "anonymous" — and still runs with a **denied** `BusinessScope`, so the tenant query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` stay fully in force and it reads no business data at all. The two tables it writes, `Businesses` and `BusinessMemberships`, are two of the five structurally non-tenant-owned ones (see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)), and the business id in every statement comes from the server's own side of the operation: the key the database assigns the row being created, or — for a resubmission — the id the caller's *own* membership row reported. Never from the request, which carries no identifier of any kind.

**The request carries the business's details and nothing else.** `name`, `contactEmail`, `abn`, `gstRegistered`, `timeZoneId` and — since issue #933 — `state`: the same six an Owner can later edit through `PUT /api/business/settings`, validated by the same rule. `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessApplicationPolicy.Validate` delegates to `BusinessSettingsPolicy.Validate` rather than restating it, because a second validation would eventually disagree with the first about what a business may record about itself — so a missing or over-long name, an address that cannot be an address, an unstated `gstRegistered`, a malformed ABN, a missing time zone and a missing or unrecognised state are refused with that policy's own `400` sentences, and the zone's resolvability is still decided centrally on the way into the database by `BusinessTimeZoneEnforcer`. Everything else is the server's: the identifier, the `Pending` status (stated explicitly, as issue #584 requires), the Owner role, and who the applicant is — the validated `(tid, oid)` claim pair, with the display name and email address from the same token (issue #524).

**Eligibility is `MembershipEligibility` and nothing else.** An applicant becomes the new business's Owner, so applying is a membership gain, and the states the issue lists as eligible — `NoMembership`, `MembershipRevoked` (including somebody released from a deactivated business) and `ApplicationRejected` — are exactly the states with no active membership. A caller holding one anywhere, in an `Active`, `Pending` or `Deactivated` business alike, gets `409`; the state their own account is in chooses only the *wording*, through `BusinessApplicationPolicy.IneligibleMessage`, which returns the same two sentences the invite redemption uses from the same two constants, so a caller attached to a deactivated business is told to be released by the platform administrator rather than sent looking for an Owner who cannot be reached. No refusal names a business, a role or another member.

**The write is one operation.** `MembershipWriteGuard` opens the `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, re-checks `MembershipEligibility` inside it, and only then is the business and its Owner membership created and committed — one `SaveChanges` through the business's own navigation, so there is no moment at which a `Pending` business exists with no Owner, and a refusal at any step takes both rows back. The application instant is sampled *inside* the transaction, after the write lock was granted (issue #608's lesson), and is stamped as the business's `AppliedAtUtc` and `CreatedAtUtc` and the membership's creation and state-change instant alike. The write goes through tracked entities rather than an `ExecuteUpdate` for the reason `EfBusinessSettingsStore`'s does: `BusinessStatusEnforcer`, `BusinessTimeZoneEnforcer` and `BusinessAbnEnforcer` run on `SaveChanges`, and a set-based insert would write straight past all three.

**Resubmitting the identical application returns the one already waiting.** A lost response or a double submission must not create a second business or refuse the person looking at the same screen again, so an identical submission while an application is `Pending` is answered with that application — same name, same status, same `appliedAtUtc` — and writes nothing, not even an audit event. The comparison is `BusinessApplicationPolicy.IsResubmission`, which is `BusinessSettingsPolicy.ChangedFields` over the *validated* values, so retyped whitespace and ABN spacing are not part of an application while a corrected capitalisation is. A submission that **differs** is `409` with its own sentence: changing details an operator is reviewing is a different request, and this slice does not implement it. That comparison writes nothing, so there is nothing about it to serialise — what has to be one operation is the creation, and that is what runs inside the guard's transaction. **Which answer two *simultaneous* identical submissions get is therefore the interleaving's to decide — and the answer is the only thing it decides:** the second attempt's read either runs after the first committed, sees the application waiting and reports it back as a second `200` for that one application, or runs before it and reaches the guard, whose re-check refuses it as `409`. Both are correct answers to one form submitted twice, and what is fixed either way is the state they leave: exactly one `Pending` business with exactly one active Owner membership, because the creation is serialised by the guard's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction and the filtered unique index behind it. A refused attempt leaves nothing — not a business row — and succeeds on its next try as the ordinary idempotent resubmission.

**The new business is not usable, and nothing existing changes.** Only `Active` resolves, so the applicant's very next request is answered with the same `403` as before and `GET /api/me/account-state` reports `ApplicationPending`. The business starts completely empty — no machine, product, purchase, sale, site, invite or `BusinessNayaxConnection` row, so its Nayax status is `NotConfigured` by virtue of nothing being stored — and no `DecidedAtUtc` or `RejectionReason` is written, because nobody has decided anything. The business that was already trading is untouched in every respect, including its members' own access. Approving and rejecting arrived with issue #544 (see [Super Admin businesses API](#super-admin-businesses-api-issue-544)) and deactivating remains #545's work; after a rejection a new application creates a **new** business while the rejected one is kept as the record of what happened.

**Behind a flag that is off by default.** `Inventory.Application.Onboarding.ISelfServiceOnboardingFlag` is read **first**, before an actor is read, a submission is validated, an allowance is spent or a membership is looked up, and a deployment with it off answers the framework's generic `404` with no detail of any kind — so a prober cannot tell a disabled deployment from one where the feature does not exist, or a malformed submission from an ineligible caller. "First" includes model binding: `[ApiController]` answers a body it cannot bind (malformed JSON, an empty body, a field of the wrong type) with its automatic `400` before the action runs, so the endpoint also carries `InventoryApi.Http.SelfServiceOnboardingGateAttribute`, a resource filter that reads the **same port** after authentication and the delegated scope have decided and before the body is bound, and short-circuits to that `404`. The use case keeps its own check, so it is closed whoever calls it; there is still one flag and one source. `InventoryApi.Adapters.Onboarding.ConfiguredSelfServiceOnboardingFlag` reads `SelfServiceOnboarding:Enabled` once at startup, because only the composition root reads configuration, and an absent, blank or unparseable value is **off**: the one answer that must never come from a mistyped setting is "yes, strangers may create tenants here". The same port is what `GetAccountState` reports as `onboardingEnabled`, so the screen that offers "Start a new business" and the endpoint behind it cannot disagree — and that field describes the *deployment*, never the caller, because whether a particular account may apply is this use case's decision from their own membership records and must not be duplicated. Switching the flag on in production is a human decision with a verified release gate in front of it; see [docs/tenant-rollout.md § Enabling self-service onboarding](tenant-rollout.md#enabling-self-service-onboarding-issue-541).

**Rate-limited per applicant, and audited.** `Inventory.Application.Onboarding.BusinessApplicationRateLimiter` is a sliding window — five submissions per identity per ten minutes — claimed *before* the membership read and the write, so simultaneous submissions cost one allowance each rather than all passing a count nothing has incremented yet. The identity is the bucket because there is no business to rate-limit by and the validated `(tid, oid)` pair is the only thing a request cannot choose; validation failures are deliberately *not* counted, so correcting a typo in a form is not what runs somebody out of attempts. It is in-process state, like `NayaxConnectionTestRateLimiter` and `MemberProfileRefreshThrottle`, and holds one lock over the whole table because this endpoint is called a handful of times per person in a lifetime and an indivisible "expire, decide, record, clear out" is worth more than concurrency here. The refusal is `429` with `Retry-After` and a fixed sentence naming no count, no window and no business. `Inventory.Application.Onboarding.IBusinessApplicationAudit`, emitted by `InventoryApi.Adapters.Onboarding.LoggingBusinessApplicationAudit` as one structured `ILogger` event with the request's correlation id, records one committed application: the actor's `(tid, oid)` pair, the new business id and the instant — and structurally **no business name, contact address, ABN, GST registration, display name or email address**, because the entry type has no field for any of them. A refused submission and a resubmission are audited as nothing, since neither created a business.

**What this slice does not do.** Approving or rejecting an application (#509) and the application form itself (#543 now calls this route from the form at `/apply`; see [Business application form](#business-application-form-issue-543)), email notifications, billing and tenant switching are all out of scope. It changes no existing business, no membership but the applicant's own new one, and no schema.

**What proves this slice.** `BusinessApplicationPolicyTests` (the delegation to the settings policy including its own length bound, the resubmission comparison over validated values, and the refusal wording for every account state — none of which names a business, a role or a member), `ApplyForBusinessTests` (the decisions over fakes with the real write guard: the flag checked before anything is read or validated, validation before an allowance is spent, the creation happening inside the transaction in the order `begin → eligibility read → create → commit`, the application instant sampled after the write lock was granted, one audit event after the commit, every refusal and its sentence, the pending-business row missing or no longer `Pending` refused rather than reported back, and the rate limit refusing without reading or writing anything), `BusinessApplicationRateLimiterTests` (the window, its edge, the per-identity bucket including two GUID spellings of one identity, a clock that moved backwards, and the clear-out never resetting a live allowance), `EfBusinessApplicationStoreTests` (the relational adapter under the denied scope every application carries: the created columns and instants, the applicant's display values stored and absent ones left absent, no Nayax connection and no business data created, the existing business untouched, the filtered one-active-membership index still refusing, both central enforcers refusing and storing nothing, the read reporting a business that never applied and an undeclared status exactly as stored, and the denied context still reading and writing no business data), `BusinessApplicationConcurrencyTests` (two real writers on a real SQLite file through the shared `MembershipWriteRaceHarness`: an invite and an application by one identity leaving exactly one active membership with the loser leaving nothing behind, the same race for a revoked identity, two applications by one identity creating exactly one business whichever way they interleave — with every attempt answered either by that one application or by the membership conflict, and the conflicting interleaving itself proved deterministically by an application whose eligibility read missed a committed one, which is refused and leaves no business row behind — two applications by two identities both succeeding, and the sequential resubmission changing nothing), `BusinessApplicationApiTests` (the whole pipeline on a host with the flag on: the first-sign-in workflow end to end with the account state before and after, the response naming no business id or contact detail, the applicant's own display values on the new membership, every validation rule answering `400` and writing nothing, the same unbindable bodies still answering `[ApiController]`'s `400` (and `401`/`403` without authentication or scope) with the flag on, each refusal with its sentence and the existing member keeping their own access, the released and the rejected applicant both admitted with the rejected application kept, the resubmission answered with the waiting application and the differing one refused, `401`, the missing-scope `403`, the same business-less caller refused by every other endpoint, a pending applicant refused by every normal endpoint, the `429` with `Retry-After`, and the audit event carrying no name or email address while a refusal and a resubmission are audited as nothing), `BusinessApplicationDisabledApiTests` (the shipped default on its own host: the generic `404` for a well-formed, a malformed and an ineligible submission alike, and for every body MVC cannot bind — truncated JSON, a wrongly typed field, an empty body and one with no media type — with nothing written, authentication and the scope still required and still `401`/`403` for those unbindable bodies, `onboardingEnabled` reported as `false`, and the existing business unaffected) and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests`/`MembershipNotRequiredEndpointAllowlistTests` (the reviewed allowlist entry and the marker's own rules).

### Platform diagnostics (issue #336)

The tenant boundary above fails closed, and that is exactly why it is hard to investigate a problem *in* it: a row assigned to the wrong business, or a child row whose parent is in another business, is invisible to the only caller who would notice. Issue #336 adds one explicitly authorized, read-only, audited path for that investigation, and nothing else. It is the single documented exception to "no cross-business *query* path", and every sentence below is part of the boundary rather than a description of it. The platform administrator's other surface, the business directory and the two decisions of issue #544, is a separate and much narrower one — a fixed set of columns and two status writes, not a statement — and is documented in [Super Admin businesses API](#super-admin-businesses-api-issue-544).

**Who. A separately configured identity, held outside the data.** Authority is an Entra `(tid, oid)` pair in configuration (`PlatformAdmin:DirectoryTenantId`, `PlatformAdmin:ObjectId`), resolved once at startup through the same `ActorIdentity.TryCreate` normalisation the membership lookup uses, so every spelling of a GUID matches and a malformed or half-filled setting identifies nobody. It is deliberately **not** a `BusinessMembership` row, a business role, an email address or a display name: the point is that this authority cannot be created, moved or destroyed by the rows it exists to investigate, and that it is not reachable from any request input. **Both values empty is the shipped state and means nobody is a platform administrator** — the policy then denies every caller, including a legitimate business member.

**How it is enforced. Twice, independently.** `PlatformAdminAuthorizationHandler` answers the named `PlatformDiagnostics` policy from `IAuthenticatedActorAccessor` — the same single `(tid, oid)` parse the membership path uses, so there is one answer to "who is calling" rather than two that could disagree. `[Authorize(Policy = PlatformAdminPolicy.Name)]` on `AdminDiagnosticsController` has the authorization middleware evaluate it before any action runs, and `BusinessScopeMiddleware` then re-evaluates the same policy itself before letting the request past the `BusinessMembership` requirement. The second check is not redundancy for its own sake: a membership bypass that rested on the authorization middleware having run earlier in the pipeline would be one pipeline edit away from applying to a caller nobody authorised. Eligibility for the bypass is marked by `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute`, which grants nothing on its own — the marker decides *which* endpoints may ask, and the policy decides the answer.

**What the bypass is, and is not.** It is a bypass of the membership requirement only. A bypassed request carries a **denied** `BusinessScope`, so the tenant query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` are fully in force for it and it reads nothing whatsoever through `AppDbContext`. Every other endpoint keeps the behaviour it had: the configured platform administrator, who has no membership, still receives `403` from `/api/products` and every other business route, and an ordinary member's access is unchanged.

**The two endpoints.**

```text
GET  /api/admin/diagnostics/access   capability signal: { authorized, crossBusinessScope, limits }
POST /api/admin/diagnostics/query    { sql } -> a bounded, truncation-flagged result
```

`access` exists for the UI in issue #335 and exposes no tenant data at all — reaching it *is* the signal, and the body carries only the server's limits. `query` takes one statement and nothing else: no page size, no row count, no timeout and no business identifier, so there is no request input that could widen or loosen anything. `crossBusinessScope` is `true` in both contracts because this path reads across every business by design, and saying so in the contract is what keeps it from being a surprise.

**The super-admin page (issue #335, moved under its own top-level group in issue #546).** `/super-admin/diagnostics` is the Angular page in front of those two endpoints, and it is presentation only: it adds no authority, no limit and no second access rule. `/admin/diagnostics` is its old address and now only redirects there. The sidebar's top-level `Super Admin` group offers its link only while `GET /api/admin/diagnostics/access` has confirmed the signed-in actor, and the route itself carries `platformAdminGuard`, which asks the same probe and sends a refusal to the dashboard; the page then asks the same endpoint again on arrival and renders a refusal instead of the query form when it is refused — but **neither guard nor page is the boundary, and the design depends on that rather than on hiding the link**. Entering either URL directly reaches the page (through the redirect for the old one), and reaches nothing else: the policy on `POST /api/admin/diagnostics/query` re-decides authority on every single request regardless of what the frontend guard or page decided. There is deliberately no frontend role, claim, flag or cached verdict that could grant access and then diverge from the configured Entra `(tid, oid)` identity: `PlatformDiagnosticsAccessService` asks the API, treats a refusal, a failure, an unanswered probe and a body that does not confirm access all as "no", and never reports a capability the API did not confirm. Unlike every business route, `/super-admin/diagnostics` carries no `accountStateGuard`: platform-admin authority has nothing to do with business membership, so a refusal belongs on the dashboard, never on a membership-handling destination.

**The cached probe belongs to one signed-in identity (issue #605).** `PlatformDiagnosticsAccessService` coalesces **one** `GET /api/admin/diagnostics/access` per current identity — the sidebar and the guard share it however often they ask — and that answer is bound to the identity it was asked as, because a browser outlives a session: one memoised probe for the service's lifetime would carry the administrator's grant onto the next person who signs in, and an ordinary member's refusal onto the administrator. The cache is dropped on sign-in, sign-out and an MSAL active-account change, observed from MSAL's own account events and from `inProgress$` settling together — the same two signals [`AccessService`](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528) watches, deliberately not read through it, because this answer has nothing to do with membership or capabilities — and acted on only when the identity the answer was asked for actually changed, so a duplicate notification costs nothing. The two members say what each consumer needs:

| Member | Answers | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `granted$` | `false` until the current identity's own probe confirms access, and `false` again the moment the identity changes | The sidebar's `Super Admin` group, so a previous identity's granted group is gone on the switch itself |
| `isGranted()` | Once, with the answer for whoever is signed in when it is asked, waiting for that identity's probe | `platformAdminGuard`, which must not refuse the administrator over an answer that has not arrived yet |

**A superseded probe decides nothing.** Every invalidation bumps a generation: an answer that arrives for an identity that is already gone is discarded instead of published, and a probe whose request has not been sent yet — one still waiting for a sign-in interaction to settle — is never sent at all. Neither an A → B → C switch nor a sign-out during a pending probe can therefore restore an earlier grant. Nobody signed in is an *answer* (`false`) rather than a request, so no protected probe is issued while signed out or while sign-in is in progress, and a refused or failed probe stays the same quiet `false` it always was: unreported, unlogged and never retried behind the operator's back. None of this is a boundary either — it decides which menu entry and which route redirect an identity is shown, while the policy on both endpoints re-decides authority per request.

The page says what it is before it knows who is asking: cross-business scope, read-only, repair out of scope, every query audited. It publishes the server's own limits — the 5-second ceiling, the 500-row cap, the 1 MiB response cap and the 16 KiB SQL cap — from the `access` body rather than restating them, lists the permitted table/column surface as help text while saying the server is what decides, and offers only read-only examples. Every outcome the contract can report has its own visible state: a complete result, a timeout, a refusal with its denial reason, a provider failure, and a truncated read labelled **incomplete** with the cap that stopped it — the row cap and the response-byte cap separately, because a byte cap reached before 500 rows is exactly the case a row count alone would misrepresent. Result values and server messages are rendered through Angular interpolation only, never as markup. The statement and its results live in component state while the page is open and nowhere else: no `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, cookie, URL, toast or console, because they describe data across every business. The query-shape fingerprint the response carries is shown so a result on screen can be matched to its audit entry without the statement appearing in either. Per [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) the routed `PlatformDiagnosticsComponent` resolves the capability and composes `PlatformDiagnosticsQueryComponent`, which owns the statement, the submission and every outcome.

**The permitted data surface.** `Inventory.Application.PlatformDiagnostics.PlatformDiagnosticsDataSurface` is an allowlist of table *and column* pairs, with no wildcard over current or future columns. The physical names are verified against the mappings on `develop` — `Purchase` is mapped to `Receipts` and `PurchaseItem` to `ReceiptItems`, and `PurchaseItem.ReceiptId` / `StockAdjustment.ReceiptItemId` keep their legacy names:

```text
Businesses(Id)
Categories(Id, BusinessId)
Suppliers(Id, BusinessId)
Products(Id, BusinessId, CategoryId)
Receipts(Id, BusinessId, SupplierId)
ReceiptItems(Id, BusinessId, ReceiptId, ProductId)
StockAdjustments(Id, BusinessId, ProductId, ReceiptItemId)
```

Every entry is an identity or foreign-key column, which is what an orphan or cross-business ownership investigation needs and all it needs. No name, note, amount, quantity, timestamp or free-text column is on it; `Businesses` exposes only `Id`, not the trading name. `BusinessMemberships` (Entra identity data), the `Nayax*` and `Imported*` tables (raw remote payloads, and where issue #327's token configuration would land), SQLite's own schema tables and everything else are absent. **A new table, or a new column on a listed table, is denied automatically** until a separately reviewed change adds it here. `Products.SupplierId` was on this list until issue #787 dropped the column; the allowlist names *physical* columns, so a column that leaves the schema leaves the surface with it — narrowing needs no review, only widening does.

**How the surface is enforced: inside SQLite, not by reading the SQL.** `Inventory.Infrastructure.PlatformDiagnostics.SqliteDiagnosticsQueryExecutor` opens its own connection to the same configured data source and puts four independent barriers in front of the statement:

1. `Mode=ReadOnly`, so the database file is never opened for writing;
2. `PRAGMA query_only`, so the connection refuses to start a write transaction even if it had been;
3. `SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED = 0`, so `ATTACH` cannot reach another database file — including the live one, opened writable;
4. `SqliteDiagnosticsAuthorizer`, installed through `sqlite3_set_authorizer` and consulted during `sqlite3_prepare` for every table, column, function and operation the statement actually reaches.

The authorizer is why the acceptance criterion "do not rely on regex rejection alone" is met structurally. It sees the *resolved* statement, not its text: a column reached through a join, an alias, a correlated subquery, an `IN` list, a `CASE` expression, an `ORDER BY`, a `HAVING` clause or a `WITH` clause arrives as the same `SQLITE_READ` on the same physical column as a direct reference, so there is no spelling of a forbidden read that gets past it. Everything not explicitly permitted is denied: writes, DDL, `PRAGMA`, `ATTACH`/`DETACH`, transaction control, schema metadata, and every SQL function outside a small documented set of aggregates and null handling — which is what keeps `load_extension`, `readfile`/`writefile`, `zeroblob`/`randomblob` and the `sqlite_version` introspection family out. A denial fails preparation with `SQLITE_AUTH` rather than returning `SQLITE_IGNORE`, because substituting `NULL` for a forbidden column would silently answer a different question than the one asked. Nothing is permitted by *name*, which is why the rowid spellings `rowid`, `oid` and `_rowid_` are not special-cased: SQLite resolves them against the table's declared columns first, so they mean the internal row identifier only while no real column carries that name, and a migration adding one (`ALTER TABLE Products ADD COLUMN oid TEXT`) would otherwise turn the spelling into a way to read a brand-new unlisted column. When such a reference really is the internal row identifier, SQLite reports it to the callback under the name of the table's `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` — `Id` on every table of this surface — so an ordinary `SELECT rowid FROM Products` is allowed on the surface's own terms and a shadowing column is denied like any other new one. `Pooling=false` means no connection — and so no residual callback or interrupted-statement state — is ever reused.

`DiagnosticsSqlShape` adds the one thing a callback inside SQLite cannot answer: that *one* statement was submitted, and that it was submitted as a read. It is a character walk that tracks string literals, quoted identifiers and comments, so a semicolon inside a literal and a keyword inside an identifier are read as data and a name rather than as structure. It is explicitly not the access boundary and is not trusted as one.

**The limits, all server-side and none raisable by a caller.** 5 seconds for preparation, execution and result reading together; 500 result rows; 1 MiB for the complete serialized response body, counted as JSON bytes while rows are read; 16 KiB of submitted UTF-8 SQL, rejected before preparation. `PlatformDiagnosticsQueryLimits.Create` clamps with `Math.Min`, so configuration and the test suite can make them *tighter* and nothing can make them looser. Reading stops at the row or byte cap and the response reports `truncated` with the reason, because a prefix must never be presented as the complete answer.

**Timeout and cancellation interrupt SQLite, not the HTTP wait.** A progress handler is installed for the life of the query and aborts the virtual machine when the deadline passes or the caller's token trips, and the token additionally calls `sqlite3_interrupt`. Both reach into the running statement, which is what makes an expensive query that never produces a first row interruptible — a plain `await` timeout would return while SQLite kept stepping, and `CommandTimeout` alone only bounds lock waiting. The reader and the connection are disposed on every path, so an interrupted query leaves nothing holding the database and the next query opens cleanly.

**Audit: one structured log event per query, and no table.** `LoggingPlatformDiagnosticsAudit` writes one `ILogger` `Information` event for every query — including a refused one, which is precisely what an investigation into misuse would look for, and including one whose execution threw instead of returning an outcome, which `RunDiagnosticsQuery` audits as `Failed` before letting the exception propagate — carrying the actor's `(tid, oid)`, the timestamp, the request/correlation id, a SHA-256 fingerprint of the *normalized query shape*, the duration, the row count, the cross-business scope flag and the outcome. It never carries the raw SQL, a result row, a column value, a business name or any credential. There is deliberately **no audit table and no migration**: an audit row written into the same database the query reads would be evidence kept inside the thing it is evidence about, would need an owner for a non-tenant-owned table, and would make a read-only request a write. **The log destination and retention period are platform configuration — Application Insights when `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` is set, the App Service log stream otherwise — and they are set on that resource, not in this repository. The application therefore cannot assert that its audit trail is durable, and does not: a human must verify the destination and retention before relying on this API's audit trail.**

**Repair is out of scope, and must stay a separate, named operation.** This API is read-only and is not an execution path for anything else. Any future data repair must be a separately reviewed, named maintenance operation with a preview/dry-run step and explicit verification — the shape [`bootstrap-business`](#tenant-ownership-issue-64), [`migrate-documents`](#document-storage) and `InventoryCostRepair` already use: explicit, auditable, idempotent or safely restartable, and covered by regression tests. A repair must never be reachable by submitting SQL. Issue #62's [Historical GST Preview/Apply](#historical-gst-classification-preview-and-apply-issue-433) and issue #472's [Nayax sale timestamp repair](#nayax-sale-timestamp-repair-preview-then-apply-issue-472) are separate, business-scoped maintenance workflows and neither depends on this API.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/PlatformDiagnostics` covers the surface contract, the shape check, the limits and their clamping, and the use case's audit behaviour. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/PlatformDiagnostics/SqliteDiagnosticsQueryExecutorTests` runs against a real migrated SQLite file: permitted reads across two businesses, forbidden columns and tables through joins, subqueries, aliases and expressions, forbidden functions, every write and DDL shape refused with the row counts proving nothing changed, `PRAGMA`/`ATTACH`/transaction control refused, the row and byte caps, a costly permitted query interrupted at its deadline with the next query still working, request cancellation, and a column added to a permitted table after the fact staying inaccessible — including one named `rowid`, `oid` or `_rowid_`, which must be refused rather than mistaken for the internal row identifier. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/PlatformAdminAuthorizationTests`, `PlatformAdminCompositionTests`, `PlatformDiagnosticsResponseSizeTests` and `BusinessScopeMiddlewarePlatformDiagnosticsTests` cover the HTTP boundary, the shipped unconfigured state, the serialized-byte cap, and the middleware's independent policy re-check.

### Super Admin businesses API (issue #544)

Until this slice the platform administrator could only *look* (the read-only diagnostics API above), and nobody could decide a business application at all: issue #541 creates a `Pending` business and leaves it waiting. Issue #544, one slice of #509 under #328, is the first write-capable platform-admin path — the Super Admin sees every business and approves or refuses an application — and the whole design is about keeping "write-capable" from meaning "unrestricted".

**What this surface writes, and what it deliberately does not.** A business's lifecycle status, one of its memberships' activation, and — on an approval alone — that business's own copies of the enabled supplier presets. The business's *plan* is **not** on this surface and `IPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` was not widened to write one: the manual plan grant a Super Admin may decide (issue #982) is its own controller, its own narrow port and its own reviewed write, described in [Super Admin sets a business's plan](#super-admin-sets-a-businesss-plan-issue-982).

**Who, and how it is enforced. Exactly the diagnostics surface's answer, reused rather than re-invented.** `SuperAdminBusinessesController` carries `[Authorize]`, `[Authorize(Policy = PlatformAdminPolicy.Name)]`, `[RequiredScope("access_as_user")]` and `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute`. That is class 2 of the four [endpoint authorization classes](#capability-authorization-issue-525) — **not** a fifth class and **not** a second marker, which is the point: a platform surface that writes must not also be a new mechanism to review. Authority is the separately configured Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, held outside the database, and both values empty — the shipped state — means nobody reaches this controller at all. An Owner holds the strongest business role there is and is refused here exactly as any other member is, because this controller declares no capability any role could satisfy. Both policies are enforced, and both attributes are needed: the named policy *replaces* the default one rather than adding to it, so a controller with only `[Authorize(Policy = …)]` would leave the delegated scope undemanded — platform authority is an additional requirement on a delegated API call, never a replacement for one.

**The four endpoints.**

```text
GET  /api/super-admin/businesses                        every business, pending applications first
GET  /api/super-admin/businesses/pending-count          { pendingCount }
POST /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/approve   Pending -> Active, + DecidedAtUtc,
                                                        and the enabled supplier presets copied in
                                                        (issue #849)
POST /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/reject    Pending -> Rejected, + reason, + DecidedAtUtc,
                                                        and the applicant's membership released
```

**The business id in a route is the subject of a decision, not a tenancy scope.** Every other endpoint in this application resolves its business from the authenticated actor's membership and accepts no owner from a request ([Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)). A platform decision has to name the application it is about, so these two routes carry the id — and that is the whole of what it does: it resolves no business for the request, which still runs with a **denied** `BusinessScope`; it is never stamped on a row; it cannot reach a tenant-owned table; and it is checked against the stored rows on every call, so an unknown id is `404` and an already-decided one is `409`. The directory response carries the id for the same reason, and it is the only response in the application that carries a tenant key. Neither shape may be copied onto a business endpoint.

**A deliberately tiny persistence surface — this is what bounds the write.** `IPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` (`Inventory.Application/PlatformAdmin/`) is nine methods — five for this slice, four more for the lifecycle transitions of [#545](#deactivating-reactivating-and-releasing-members-issue-545), and none added by [#550](#support-sessions-the-store-and-the-control-endpoints-issue-550), which reuses this port's existing read rather than opening a second one, or by [#983](#the-businesss-nayax-connection-status-issue-983), which adds one field to the record `ListAsync` already returned — and `EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` is the whole of what a platform administrator can reach of a *business* through `AppDbContext`: a fixed set of `Businesses` columns, the count of active `BusinessMemberships` per business, a yes/no for whether a `BusinessNayaxConnection` row exists and the status stored on it (issue #983), the memberships of one named business, and writes that reach nothing but the business's `Status`/`DecidedAtUtc`/`RejectionReason` and one membership's `IsActive`/`StatusChangedAtUtc`. No method takes a table name, a predicate, a column list, a filter, a page or a statement, and the list deliberately takes no caller-supplied filter, sort or search at all: a caller-supplied predicate over a cross-business read is how a fixed list stops being a list and becomes a query engine. Nothing tenant-owned is readable or writable through it — an adapter test asserts that the same denied context still reads no `Products` or `Categories` row and still has a tenant-owned write refused with `CrossBusinessAccessException`. Both writes go through `SaveChanges` on tracked entities on purpose, so `BusinessStatusEnforcer`, `BusinessTimeZoneEnforcer`, `BusinessAbnEnforcer` and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` all run; a set-based `ExecuteUpdate` would write past all four.

**The one bypass, and why it is two columns.** The Nayax connection is the only fact here that lives on a tenant-owned table, so under the denied scope the central filter `!TenantFilteringEnabled || e.BusinessId == CurrentBusinessId` hides every row of it. The adapter therefore makes exactly one `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement, projecting `BusinessId` — the ownership key itself, which is not business data — and `Status`, the stored connection status that issue #983 widened this projection by under the repository owner's approval, and nothing else. The credential columns are not in the projection, are not materialised and do not appear in the generated SQL; no operator id, key id, credential revision, last-tested instant or ciphertext can reach a response. The rejected alternatives are recorded in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The unrestricted-context rule. A second `IgnoreQueryFilters`, a further widened projection or any predicate over a tenant-owned table in this adapter is a boundary change needing its own reviewed issue.

**What the directory reports, and what it deliberately does not.** Twelve fields per business: `businessId`, `name`, `status`, `createdAtUtc`, `appliedAtUtc`, `decidedAtUtc`, `contactEmail`, `abn`, `state`, `activeMemberCount`, `nayaxConfigured`, `nayaxConnectionStatus`. `nayaxConnectionStatus` is the stored `NayaxConnectionStatus` name (issue #983, `NotConfigured` for a business with no connection row) — see [The business's Nayax connection status](#the-businesss-nayax-connection-status-issue-983). `state` is the Australian state or territory the business recorded (issue #933, `null` for one that recorded none), added so an application can be reviewed with it; it is one more column of the same fixed set of the business's own published details, not a new kind of read — no predicate, no second table and nothing tenant-owned came with it (see [The business's state or territory](#the-businesss-state-or-territory-issue-933)). No sale, stock, cost, purchase, product, machine, site, document or report value — nothing tenant-owned — and no member's display name, email address or Entra identifier. `contactEmail` is the business's own published detail as its application recorded it, not a member's personal address. `activeMemberCount` counts the memberships that are currently active, which is the question the directory answers — how many people can reach this business now — so a refused application reads `0` because its rejection released the applicant. `status` is the published `BusinessStatus` name rather than a number a renumbering would silently change, and a stored value this code does not declare is reported as it is rather than presented as something decidable.

**Only a `Pending` business may be decided.** `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessDecisionPolicy` is the rule, and the deny direction is the default: an already-active business, an already-refused one, a deactivated one and an undeclared stored value are each refused with one sentence that names no status. Approving an Active business and reviving a Rejected one are not operations at all; deactivating, reactivating and releasing members are [#545's](#deactivating-reactivating-and-releasing-members-issue-545), under their own rules and their own refusals. The rejection reason is validated there too — trimmed, at most 500 characters, and a blank reason stored as `null`, which is the single representation of "no reason"; an over-long reason refuses the decision before anything is read or written rather than being truncated into the applicant's own explanation. A rejection with no reason is still a rejection.

**The authoritative read, the comparison and the mutation are one operation.** Both decisions run inside issue #522's shared [`MembershipWriteGuard`](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522) transaction — SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so the write lock is held before anything is decided — and `BusinessApplicationDecisionWriter` re-reads the business and its applicant **inside** it. The read the use case takes before the transaction opens decides nothing: it exists to answer "no such business" with a `404`, to refuse a stale view before a write lock is taken on the caller's behalf, and to supply the immutable fact the eligibility re-check needs. A simultaneous approve and reject therefore resolves to one recorded decision and one `409`, never to two writes — which would otherwise leave a trading tenant whose applicant has been released, or a refused application whose applicant is still a member of it. A relational race test over two connections to one real SQLite file asserts exactly that, and asserts the resulting state rather than which decision won.

**Approving is a membership gain, so `MembershipEligibility` is re-checked — with the applicant's own membership excluded.** The applicant is already the `Pending` business's active Owner (that is what makes the application theirs), but approval makes it a membership in a *trading* business, and a person belongs to one business at a time. The check therefore runs with `MembershipWriteIntent.ExcludedMembershipId` set to that membership: without the exclusion the applicant's own row would count against them and **no application could ever be approved**. The exclusion is sound because the in-transaction read refuses unless the applicant is still the very membership it names — an exclusion granted for one membership key is never spent on another. An applicant who can no longer be approved — their membership in the application is inactive, the business has no single identifiable applicant, or the stored Entra pair is not a usable identity — is refused with one sentence that describes the application rather than the person. Rejecting activates nothing, so it runs no eligibility check and requires no active Owner afterwards: a refused application is not a business that has to stay reachable.

**Rejecting releases the applicant, and that is what lets them apply again.** While they hold an active membership anywhere, `MembershipEligibility` refuses them a second one, so a rejection that left the membership active would refuse the applicant their own next application and leave them attached to a business nobody can reach. The rejected business row is kept rather than deleted; `GET /api/me/account-state` reports `ApplicationRejected` with the stored reason, to that applicant's own identity and nobody else's. A membership that is already inactive is left exactly as it is, state-change instant included — rewriting it would claim a transition that never happened.

**Audit: one structured log event per committed decision, and no table.** `LoggingPlatformBusinessDecisionAudit` writes one `ILogger` `Information` event carrying the deciding administrator's `(tid, oid)`, the business id, the old → new status, whether a reason was recorded, the instant and the request/correlation id. It never carries the business name, the contact address, the ABN, the applicant's identity or the rejection reason's *text* — `PlatformBusinessDecisionAuditEntry` has no field for any of them, so even a sink that printed the whole entry could not emit one. A refused decision is not audited, because nothing happened. There is deliberately no audit table and no migration, for the reasons the diagnostics audit has none; **the log destination and retention period are platform configuration a human must verify**, exactly as for that one.

**No schema change in this slice.** Issue #540's lifecycle status, `DecidedAtUtc` and `RejectionReason` are the columns #544 writes; nothing is added, and there is no migration in it. Issue #849 later added one nullable column to `Businesses` and one more thing an approval writes — see [Supplier presets copied into an approved business](#supplier-presets-copied-into-an-approved-business-issue-849).

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Tenancy/BusinessDecisionPolicyTests` covers the decidable statuses, the reason bounds and the refusal wording. `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/PlatformAdmin/BusinessApplicationDecisionTests` runs both decisions over the real `MembershipWriteGuard`: the exclusion that makes an approval possible, the refusals for an applicant who joined elsewhere or cannot be identified, the status and applicant changing while the write lock is awaited, and what each refusal leaves unwritten and unaudited. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStoreTests` is the relational half over two businesses and a denied scope: the cross-business list, the active-member counts, the Nayax flag and the stored connection status beside the proof that the ordinary read of that table still sees nothing, the tenant-owned read and write still refused, and a membership of another business that cannot be released by a decision on this one. `PlatformBusinessDecisionConcurrencyTests` is the race. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/SuperAdminBusinessesApiTests` is the HTTP boundary: every endpoint refused for an Owner, a Manager, the applicant, a stranger, an anonymous caller and a caller without the delegated scope; the administrator still refused by every business endpoint; the applicant reaching their own business only once it is approved; the response carrying exactly the twelve declared properties - the recorded state included, and `null` for a business with none - and neither a product name, an operator id, an encryption key id nor a token ciphertext; and the unconfigured host refusing everyone. `BusinessScopeCompositionTests` pins the store's registration and dependencies, and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` pins all thirteen platform-admin endpoints — the two diagnostics ones, these eight, and the three support-session ones of #550 — as class 2 with no capability.

#### Deactivating, reactivating and releasing members (issue #545)

The slice above decides whether a business may *start*. This one, the second slice of #509 under #328, is how one that has already traded is switched off and on again — and how somebody attached to a business that is off can be freed to join another one. It adds four endpoints to the same controller, under the same policy and the same marker, and **no schema change**: the columns it writes are issue #540's lifecycle status and issue #522's `StatusChangedAtUtc`.

```text
POST /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/deactivate   Active -> Deactivated, + its live invites cancelled
POST /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/reactivate    Deactivated -> Active, needs an active Owner
GET  /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/members       while Deactivated only
POST /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/members/{membershipId}/release   while Deactivated only
```

**Each transition starts from exactly one status, and the deny direction is the default.** `Inventory.Domain.Tenancy.BusinessLifecyclePolicy` is the rule: only an `Active` business may be deactivated, only a `Deactivated` one may be reactivated, and the members of a business may be listed or released only while it is `Deactivated`. A `Pending` application, a `Rejected` one and a stored value this code does not declare are refused in every direction, so a business whose state nobody decided is never the subject of a transition. Unlike `BusinessDecisionPolicy`'s refusals these sentences may name the state the business is in: those are read back by an *applicant* through their account state, while these reach the platform administrator alone, whose own directory already reports every business's status.

**Deactivating is one transaction: the status, the invites, and the hook.** `Businesses.Status` becomes `Deactivated`, which is not `Active`, so `BusinessMembershipResolutionPolicy` resolves nothing and every member of the business gets the ordinary `403` on their very next request — membership resolution is memoised per request only, so there is no cache to wait for and no sign-out to force. **No data is deleted and no membership is touched**, flag and `StatusChangedAtUtc` alike: the members are refused because the business no longer resolves, not because their rows were changed, which is exactly what lets a reactivation put the business back. In the same transaction every invite of that business that is still live is cancelled permanently through issue #531's `IMemberInviteStore.CancelAllLiveAsync` — a deactivated business whose outstanding links still worked would be a way back in after the door was closed, and an invite cancelled by a deactivation that then rolled back would have been withdrawn for nothing. Already-used, already-cancelled and expired invites are left exactly as they are, which also makes a repeated deactivation idempotent, and the response reports how many were cancelled because that is the one part of the transition the business row does not show afterwards. That cancellation is the **one statement this feature makes outside its own port**: `MemberInvite` is one of the five structural non-tenant-owned tables, and `BusinessLifecycleWriter` passes it the business id of the row it has just read *inside* the transaction, never the route value. A second implementation of the same cancellation in the platform store would be two statements that could drift apart.

**And no Owner write can land after it (issue #680).** Cancelling the invites that exist when this transaction runs is only half of "deactivation cancels pending invites permanently": the other half is that none appears afterwards. Because this transition and the Owner's invite creation, settings save and member changes now all run inside the same `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` write path, and each of those three re-reads the business's status inside it, an Owner request already in flight when this commits is refused rather than committed onto a business that has been switched off. The consequence the follow-up review found was specific: a `Pending` seven-day invite created a moment after a deactivation is redeemable again the instant the business is reactivated. A reactivation still revives nothing by itself — no membership, no invite, no session — so what the pair of rules guarantees together is that a deactivation followed by a reactivation leaves no redeemable invite at all. See [One active membership per identity](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522) for the re-check, and `OwnerWriteDuringDeactivationTests` for the relational proof over all three writes.

**The hook point was declared here, and issue #550 is what is behind it (the fourth criterion).** `IBusinessDeactivationHook` is called last inside the deactivation's transaction, after the status and the invites. It exists because issue #512's support sessions have to end when the business they are inside is deactivated, and the only safe place for that is inside this transaction: a session ended by a deactivation that rolled back would have been ended for nothing, and a session left running by a deactivation that committed would be exactly the access the deactivation exists to stop. A hook that throws therefore refuses the whole deactivation rather than leaving a half-finished one. The composition root registers exactly one implementation: #545 shipped a no-op, and [#550](#support-sessions-the-store-and-the-control-endpoints-issue-550) replaced that single line with `EndSupportSessionsOnBusinessDeactivation` rather than editing this transition — **no session logic is in this transition**, then or now.

**Reactivating requires an active Owner, and that refusal is part of the write.** The rule is `BusinessOwnerRetention`'s — the same one the member management of #533 is bound by — re-read inside the transaction over the memberships the business actually holds, so a released Owner, a Manager who is active and a stored role this code cannot read are all "not an Owner" here exactly as they are everywhere else. A business that fails it is refused with `409` and `BusinessLifecyclePolicy.NoActiveOwnerMessage`, having changed nothing. The message is deliberately **not** `BusinessOwnerRetention.LastActiveOwnerMessage`: that one tells the reader to give another member the Owner role first, which only an Owner inside the business can do, and a business that is still deactivated has no reachable Owner at all. Only an Owner may manage members, roles, the integration and the business record, so a trading business without one cannot be administered by anybody inside it and has no repair path short of a human editing the database — which is why this is checked as part of the write rather than reported afterwards. **A reactivation restores only the business**: a membership released while it was off, or revoked by its Owner before that, stays inactive, and a cancelled invite stays cancelled. Both are deliberate decisions about a person, and a business returning is not a reason to undo one — a released person may by now hold an active membership somewhere else, and reviving their old one would deny them *both* businesses (`MembershipEligibility`).

**Releasing a member is the gap this slice exists for, and the last-Owner rule deliberately does not apply to it.** A person belongs to one business at a time, and a membership in a deactivated business still occupies that one slot — `MembershipEligibility` never reads the owning business's state. Releasing a membership is normally the Owner's doing, but a deactivated business does not resolve, so its Owner can act on nothing: without this endpoint a member of a business that was switched off could never join anywhere else, which is precisely what `MemberInviteRedemptionPolicy.ReleaseRequiredMessage` already tells them to come here for. `BusinessOwnerRetention` protects a *trading* business from losing the only person who can administer it; a business nobody can reach has no such access to protect, and applying the rule here would leave its last Owner permanently attached to it. What keeps that from being a hole is the pair of rules around it: a release is refused unless the business is still `Deactivated`, and the reactivation above refuses to bring a business back while it has no active Owner. The release writes one membership's `IsActive` and `StatusChangedAtUtc` together, and releasing a membership that is already inactive changes nothing and is audited as nothing — re-stamping its instant would claim a transition that never happened (issue #522).

**The members list is the one read in this application that reports another business's members, and it is bounded in every direction.** Only while that business is `Deactivated`, and only four fields per membership: `membershipId`, `displayName`, `role` and `isActive`. No email address, no Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, and nothing tenant-owned. The display name is there because choosing which membership to release is impossible from a column of keys, and it is the same display-only value an Owner's own members list reports (issue #524) — never an identifier. A trading business's membership list stays its own Owner's business (issue #533), and both the list and the release answer `409` for any other status. Like the business directory beside it, the list opens no transaction and emits no audit event: it is a read, and the status gate is the whole of what decides whether it may answer.

**The authoritative read, the comparison and the mutation are one operation.** All three actions run inside issue #522's shared [`MembershipWriteGuard`](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522) transaction — SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so the write lock is held before anything is decided — and `BusinessLifecycleWriter` re-reads the business and its memberships **inside** it. The read before the transaction opens decides nothing: it answers "no such business" with a `404` and refuses a stale view before a write lock is taken on the caller's behalf. A status that changes while a deactivation waits for the lock refuses it, and an Owner released while a reactivation waits refuses that. None of the three activates a membership, so none runs `MembershipEligibility`'s check, and the guard's own "keep an active Owner" check is deliberately not asked for either — a release must not be subject to it, and a reactivation's Owner rule is about the business it is about to start trading rather than about a membership row it changed.

**Audit: one structured log event per committed action, and no table.** `LoggingPlatformBusinessLifecycleAudit` writes one `ILogger` `Information` event carrying the acting administrator's `(tid, oid)`, the business id, which action it was, the old → new status, the membership id where one applies, how many invites were cancelled where that applies, the instant and the request/correlation id. It never carries the business name, the released member's display name or email address, or their Entra identity — `PlatformBusinessLifecycleAuditEntry` has no field for a name of any kind, so even a sink that printed the whole entry could not emit one. A refused action is not audited, and neither is one that changed nothing. It is a separate port from the decision audit because a lifecycle action records a membership id and an invite count and has no rejection reason; **the log destination and retention period are platform configuration a human must verify**, exactly as for the other two platform trails.
