**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Tenancy/BusinessLifecyclePolicyTests` covers the three status gates, including `0` and an undeclared value, and the refusal wording. `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/PlatformAdmin/BusinessLifecycleTests` runs all four over the real `MembershipWriteGuard`: the order the status write, the invite cancellation and the hook happen in inside one transaction, a hook that refuses rolling the whole deactivation back, the status and the Owner list changing while the write lock is awaited, releasing the last active Owner succeeding while the reactivation that follows is refused, the release asking neither of the guard's two questions, and what each refusal leaves unwritten and unaudited. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStoreTests` is the relational half: the lifecycle read's memberships, each write touching only its own column, and another business's membership that cannot be released by naming its key here. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/SuperAdminBusinessLifecycleApiTests` is the HTTP boundary over the real migration history: the members of a deactivated business refused by their own endpoints while nothing in their rows changed, the live invite cancelled and the closed ones untouched, the reactivation restoring only still-active memberships, every Owner released then the reactivation refused, the members list carrying exactly the four declared properties and neither an email address nor an Entra id, and — end to end — a released person redeeming an invite into another business and staying released when their original business comes back, with `GET /api/me/account-state` reporting `Member` of the new one. `SuperAdminBusinessesApiTests` calls all eleven endpoints of the platform-admin business surface — the eight on this controller and the three support-session ones of #550 — for every caller who is not the configured administrator.

#### Super Admin Businesses page (issue #547)

The two slices above are the API; this one, one slice of [#510](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/510) under #328, is the Angular page in front of it — `/super-admin/businesses`, reached from the sidebar's `Businesses` link beside `Platform Diagnostics` (see [Application shell and navigation](#application-shell-and-navigation-issue-391) above) and guarded exactly like it: `platformAdminGuard`, no capability, no `accountStateGuard`, because platform-admin authority is independent of business role or membership, and because entering the URL directly is safe either way — the eight endpoints decide authority on every request regardless of what the guard or the page did.

**It is presentation only, and the routed page is a thin composition boundary** per [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191): `SuperAdminBusinessesComponent` owns the table, the status filter and the three single-call confirmations (approve, deactivate, reactivate) behind the shared `ConfirmationDialogComponent` — the same shape `ProductListComponent` already uses for a single-call confirmation — while Reject (its own reason text and submission state) and Members (its own load, release confirmation and error) are dedicated feature components, `BusinessRejectDialogComponent` and `BusinessMembersDialogComponent`, composed through `[businessId]`/`[businessName]` and their own outputs. Every refusal the page shows is the API's own sentence, verbatim, including reactivate's "no active Owner" one (`BusinessLifecyclePolicy.NoActiveOwnerMessage`) — the page duplicates no rule.

**The table shows exactly the directory's fields, minus the one instant the page has no use for.** Name, status, applied date, contact email, state, ABN, active member count, whether Nayax is configured and — as a coloured dot beside the name, with its own words (issue #983, see [The business's Nayax connection status](#the-businesss-nayax-connection-status-issue-983) below) — the stored Nayax connection status; `decidedAtUtc` is read by the API but not rendered, because issue #547's acceptance criteria named only the first seven, and `state` was added with the column itself (issue #933) so an application is reviewed with the state it recorded; a business that recorded none shows an em dash, never a guess. Pending applications sort first because the directory read already returns them that way; the status filter narrows the same ordered list rather than requesting a different one, since the list endpoint takes no server-side filter at all (see [Super Admin businesses API](#super-admin-businesses-api-issue-544) above). Approve and Reject are offered only for a `Pending` business, Deactivate and **View as this business** only for `Active`, and Reactivate and Members only for `Deactivated` — the same `BusinessDecisionPolicy`/`BusinessLifecyclePolicy` gates the API itself enforces, mirrored here only to decide which buttons to show, never to decide whether an action succeeds.

**The pending-count badge (on the sidebar's `Super Admin` group and its `Businesses` link) is re-read after every action, not cached state the page pushes to it.** `SuperAdminBusinessesService.notifyChanged()` is a plain `Subject<void>` notification with no payload, called once a mutating call — approve, reject, deactivate, reactivate or release — has itself completed, and also when approve, deactivate or reactivate is refused with `409` or `404` (issue #681), because that refusal means the business changed or disappeared elsewhere and the page reloads its table for the same reason; `SidebarNavComponent` is the one subscriber, and on each notification (while platform-admin access is granted) it re-reads `GET .../pending-count` itself rather than trusting a number the mutating caller computed. The badge is `null` — rendered as no badge at all — until access is granted and a first read returns, and it is cleared the moment access is lost, the same rule issue #605 already gives the group itself. **A refused read reaches that same stable `null` and asks for nothing further** (issue #673): `GET .../pending-count` is classified `platform-admin`, so its `403` refreshes neither member cache, and it was the capability refresh — not the badge — that used to bring the read straight back round. See [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528) for the classification and the loop.

**"View as this business" (issue #553, one slice of #513) is the one action here that does not stay on this page.** `ViewAsBusinessDialogComponent`, composed the same way Reject and Members already are, starts a support session through `SupportSessionService`; see [Support session banner and the in-memory session id](#support-session-banner-and-the-in-memory-session-id-issue-553) for what that does next. No backend change came with it: the dialog calls the one endpoint #550 already shipped (`POST /api/super-admin/support-sessions/{businessId}`), unchanged. Hiding write controls and support-view messages once inside the session is issue #554's separate follow-up.

**What proves it.** `super-admin-businesses.service.spec.ts` covers the eight HTTP calls, including the trimmed/blank/absent reason on reject and the `changed$` notification. `business-reject-dialog.component.spec.ts` and `business-members-dialog.component.spec.ts` cover each dedicated workflow's own load, confirmation, success and API-refusal-shown-verbatim paths; `view-as-business-dialog.component.spec.ts` is the same shape for the required-reason dialog issue #553 added. `super-admin-businesses.component.spec.ts` covers the status filter, which actions each status offers (including **View as this business** for `Active` alone), each confirmation, the reactivate no-active-Owner refusal shown verbatim, and that a reload (and a badge notification) follows every completed action and every `409`/`404` refusal, but not any other failure. `sidebar-nav.component.spec.ts` covers the badge itself: hidden until access is granted, hidden again at zero, shown on both the group and the `Businesses` link once a count is read, re-read on a `changed$` notification, cleared the moment access is lost, and — composed with the real `AccessService`, the real `SuperAdminBusinessesService` and the production `403` chain (issue #673) — settling on a persistent refusal instead of looping, with the badge `null`, the group still offered and no toast. `navigation.spec.ts` and `app.routes.spec.ts` cover the real `Businesses` `NavLink` replacing issue #546's placeholder and the route's guards.

#### The business's Nayax connection status (issue #983)

The directory above reported a Nayax **yes/no**, which cannot tell a business whose token was verified from one whose token was saved and never tried, or from one whose last test failed. Each business already stores exactly that answer — `Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionStatus`, written only by a credential save or by a permission test result applied for the revision it was produced for (see [Per-business Nayax connection](#per-business-nayax-connection-issue-518)) — so this slice publishes **that stored value** and nothing else.

**It is a widening of the platform directory store, and it was an owner decision.** AGENTS.md § Super Admin businesses API limited that store to "a yes/no for whether a `BusinessNayaxConnection` row exists" and said not to widen it; the repository owner approved widening it by exactly the stored connection status on 29 October 2026, and AGENTS.md, this document and the README record that together. What the widening is, in full: `PlatformBusinessSummary` gains `NayaxConnectionStatus`, `SuperAdminBusinessResponse` gains `nayaxConnectionStatus` as the published name, and `EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore`'s one `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement projects `Status` beside `BusinessId`. The existing `nayaxConfigured` stays exactly as it is — nothing was removed from the contract, and nothing else was added to it: not the operator id, not the encryption key id, not the credential revision, not the instant of the last test, not whether the machine checks were left unverified, not any Nayax error text, and under no circumstances any part of the token.

**It is the stored result, never a live check.** Listing businesses reads rows and makes no Nayax call, resolves no credential and decrypts no token — which is also the only thing it *could* do, since a platform-admin request carries a denied `BusinessScope` and `NayaxRequestCredentialProvider` resolves credentials from the caller's own resolved business. Nothing here tests or re-tests a connection, and nothing here writes a status: how a status is set is unchanged and belongs to [Saving a tested connection and re-testing it](#saving-a-tested-connection-and-re-testing-it-issue-537). A business with **no connection row** reads `NotConfigured`, which is exactly what the absence of that row means, so "nothing stored" and "stored but unusable" stay apart here as they do on the row.

**Three colours, four states, four sentences.** On the Businesses page a dot sits beside each business's name: **green** (`bg-rr-ok-text`) for `Ready`, **orange** (`bg-rr-warn-text`) for `PendingPermissions` *and* `NeedsAttention`, and **red** (`bg-rr-danger-text`) for `NotConfigured`. The two orange states share a colour because neither is a working connection and neither is nothing at all, and they are told apart by **words**: `NAYAX_STATUS_PRESENTATION` in `SuperAdminBusinessesComponent` gives each of the four its own sentence — `Ready` "Nayax verified at last test", `PendingPermissions` "Nayax token saved, not tested yet", `NeedsAttention` "Nayax last test failed", `NotConfigured` "Nayax not set up" — rendered as the dot's `title` **and** as an `sr-only` label in the same cell, with the dot itself `aria-hidden`. Colour is therefore never the only signal, the status is announced once rather than twice, and a status name this code does not declare is shown as a neutral dot and "Nayax status unknown" rather than presented as one of the four. The page maps and formats; it decides nothing.

**Who sees it.** Only the platform administrator, through the existing `PlatformAdminPolicy` and `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute` on the unchanged `SuperAdminBusinessesController` — class 2, no new endpoint, no new policy and no new marker. No business-facing response, capability or page changed: a business's own members still read their connection state through `GET /api/settings/nayax-connection/status` exactly as before, and an Owner, Manager or Operator still receives `403` from every endpoint of this surface.

**What proves it.** `SuperAdminBusinessesApiTests` covers the four statuses over real HTTP, the stored row left untouched by the read (status, revision and last-tested instant unchanged), the response carrying exactly the twelve declared properties, no operator id, encryption key id, last-tested month or token ciphertext anywhere in the body, and an Operator of a trading business refused every endpoint of the surface beside the Owner, Manager, applicant and stranger the theory already covered. `EfPlatformBusinessDirectoryStoreTests` is the relational half under the denied scope: the stored status for each value, `NotConfigured` for a business with no row, and the ordinary read of that table still seeing nothing through the very same context. `super-admin-businesses.component.spec.ts` covers each dot colour, each distinct tooltip and screen-reader label, and that the dot carries no text of its own.

#### Super Admin supplier presets (issue #848)

The surfaces above decide things about a *business*. This one, child B of [#835](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/835), decides nothing about any business at all: it is the platform's own list of suggested suppliers that child C copies into each newly approved business. **This slice does not do the copying**, deliberately, so the list exists and is editable before anything depends on it; the copying is [Supplier presets copied into an approved business](#supplier-presets-copied-into-an-approved-business-issue-849) below. Issue [#931](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/931) then made the same list the **supplier master for price checks** — see [The supplier-master fields](#the-supplier-master-fields-issue-931) below — and the shipped list is nine records rather than the original four.

**The table is the one *platform* table in the schema, which is a classification of its own.** `SupplierPreset` is not `IBusinessOwned` and has no `BusinessId` — see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) for why that is a different thing from the five structurally non-tenant-owned tables and for the one-time seed semantics. What bounds it is authorization, not ownership.

**Authorization is the three surfaces above, unchanged: class 2, one marker, one policy.** `SuperAdminSupplierPresetsController` carries `[Authorize]`, `[Authorize(Policy = PlatformAdminPolicy.Name)]`, `[RequiredScope("access_as_user")]` and `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute`, and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` lists its three endpoints by name beside the diagnostics, businesses and support-session ones. It is not a fifth endpoint class and not a second marker. An Owner is refused like any other member, an anonymous request is `401`, and `RolePreviewMiddleware` refuses the two writes as read-only with `read_only_role_preview` — the rule that holds on every endpoint rather than per controller. A previewed **read** is unaffected, for the reason it is unaffected on the businesses surface: this controller declares no capability for a preview to narrow, and the administrator's own authority is not a business role. The `X-Support-Session` header is not acted on here at all, because `BusinessScopeMiddleware` decides a marked endpoint before it resolves a session; a member who sets it is still an ordinary member, and the administrator reaches this surface as themselves — writes included — exactly as they reach the businesses one. Both of those answers are pinned by tests of their own (`A_role_preview_read_is_unaffected`, `The_administrator_holding_a_live_support_session_still_reaches_this_surface`), because issue #848's acceptance criterion reads "support sessions and role preview get `403`" without distinguishing the caller or the method, and refusing *this* surface because its caller holds a session, or refusing a previewed read only here, would be a per-surface refusal rule contradicting [Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) and [Super Admin role preview](#super-admin-role-preview-issue-720). Changing either answer is therefore a deliberate design decision for a human, not an implementation detail.

**One narrow port over one table.** `ISupplierPresetStore` (Application) offers a list with no filter at all, a normalised-name existence check that can exclude one row, an add, an update and `IsDuplicateName`. No method takes a predicate, a column list, a page, a sort or a statement, and nothing tenant-owned is reachable: `EfSupplierPresetStore` touches `SupplierPresets` and no other table — `Suppliers` in particular — makes no `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement, and runs on the request's own denied-scope `AppDbContext`. `ListSupplierPresets`, `CreateSupplierPreset` and `UpdateSupplierPreset` hold the rules; the controller binds, invokes and maps.

**`GET`, `POST` and `PUT`, and deliberately no `DELETE`.** A preset that should stop being suggested is disabled, which is reversible and leaves whatever a business already copied from it untouched; a delete would be the one action on this surface with no way back. Enabling and disabling is the `PUT` rather than a separate toggle, because the mutable fields are what a preset *is* and a second write path over one row would be a second race to reason about. Since #931 every field arriving together is also what makes the supplier-master rules decidable: whether nationwide conflicts with a state list, and whether the connector key belongs to the connector, are questions about a whole submission rather than about one field. Disabled presets stay in the list: one nobody can see is one nobody can re-enable.

**The name rule is this feature's; the website rule is [#847](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/847)'s, reused rather than restated.** `Inventory.Domain.Suppliers.SupplierPresetPolicy` owns the name (required, trimmed, at most 200 characters) and the normalised comparison key. The optional website is `Inventory.Application.Suppliers.SupplierUrlPolicy` — the one supplier-website rule there is, documented at [A supplier's optional website (issue #847)](#a-suppliers-optional-website-issue-847): absolute `http`/`https` with a host, at most 2048 characters measured after trimming, blank normalising to `null` rather than to an empty string, and only those two schemes because the value is rendered as a link a person clicks. Nothing fetches, resolves or verifies the address.

#848 was implemented while #847 was still open and briefly carried its own copy of that rule in `Inventory.Domain.Suppliers`; the copy is gone. Two policies of one name was the duplication this feature's own criterion forbids — and when #847 merged (PR #858) the pair also made `AppDbContext`'s single unqualified reference ambiguous and broke the build (`CS0104`). The deeper reason there may only ever be one is the copying ahead: child C turns a preset into an ordinary `Supplier` row, so an address the preset rule accepted and the supplier rule refused would be a copy that fails. The preset use cases call the Application rule, which reports a field-level message, and raise it as the `DomainValidationException` this surface already answers every refusal with — so presets keep their `400`-with-a-sentence shape while a business's own supplier write keeps #847's `ValidationProblemDetails` against `url`. `SupplierUrlRuleSingleSourceOfTruthTests` refuses a second policy of that name in any backend layer, and asserts the preset policy holds no website rule of its own.

**The audit trail is the two platform-business ones' shape, minus the content.** `ISupplierPresetAudit`, implemented at the InventoryApi boundary over `ILogger`, records one event per **committed** create or edit with the actor `(tid, oid)`, the preset's key, which change it was, whether the preset is suggested afterwards, the instant and the correlation id. `SupplierPresetAuditEntry` has no field for the preset's name or its URL, so neither can reach the trail by a sink's discretion — the same restraint the decision and lifecycle audits show about a business's name, contact address and rejection text. A refused write is audited as nothing.

**The page** is `/super-admin/supplier-presets`, in the sidebar's `Super Admin` group behind `platformAdminGuard`, exactly like the two routes beside it. Per [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) `SuperAdminSupplierPresetsComponent` owns the table and the enable/disable confirmation behind the shared `ConfirmationDialogComponent`, while Add and Edit — their own form values, field validation and submission state — are `SupplierPresetDialogComponent`, composed through `[preset]` and its `(saved)`/`(canceled)` outputs. Field validation mirrors the server's rules and sentences so a mistyped address is reported in the field; the server stays the authority, and its refusals — the duplicate-name `409` above all, which only it can decide — are shown verbatim. The website half of that is not a second mirror: the dialog and the list both use `components/suppliers/supplier-url.ts`, the one browser-side copy of #847's rule, so the presets form and the Suppliers form refuse the same addresses in the same words. A website is rendered with `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"` **only when that helper still accepts the stored value** — anything else shows as plain text, so a value that reached the table without passing the server rule is never clickable. `super-admin/supplier-presets` is also in `classifyMemberRequest`'s platform-admin prefix list, so a `403` from it drives no capability re-read and no member message, and neither the role-preview nor the support-session header is attached to it.

##### The supplier-master fields (issue #931)

[#931](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/931), the first task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), turned this list into the **supplier master a price check reads**: one record per store, saying which states it serves, whether the prices it publishes include GST, and how those prices are collected. **No price collection, catalogue or comparison work is here** — that is #817's later children — and nothing about a *business* changed: the table is still about no business, and issue #849's copy still carries the name and the website and nothing else.

**Five additive columns on `SupplierPresets`.** `ServesNationwide` (bool) and `ServedStates` (the declared state codes, comma-separated in the policy's own order, empty for a nationwide record) are the market; `PricesIncludeGst` (bool) is the tax basis of the published price list; `PriceConnector` (nullable enum) and `PriceConnectorKey` (nullable text) are the collection route and what it needs to know which retailer it is for. The market is two columns because the two claims differ: "serves everywhere" is not "serves these eight", and collapsing the one into the other would lose the distinction the next territory to be declared would need. The state list is one column rather than a child table because the vocabulary is closed at eight values, a market is read and written whole, and nothing joins to a state; the canonical order is what makes one market have exactly one stored spelling.

**`Inventory.Domain.Suppliers.SupplierPresetMasterPolicy` is the one rule, beside `SupplierPresetPolicy` rather than inside it.** That one owns what a preset is *called*; this one owns what it *claims*, and every rule here is about the consistency of the three claims with each other. Nationwide and a state list are mutually exclusive and one of them is required — "nationwide *and* NSW" has no meaning a price check could act on, and neither would be a supplier that serves nowhere while looking configured. The connector key is required for `Varnmill`, which serves several retailers through one service, and must be empty for every other route **and for no route at all**, because a key nothing reads is a value that looks meaningful and is not. Both vocabularies are **closed and checked**, on the rule [an enum is a compile-time constraint and not a validation](#purchase-gst-classification-issue-429) states: a connector arrives as an arbitrary JSON number and a served state as arbitrary text, and a value outside the declared set is `400` rather than stored. A read is deliberately more tolerant than a write — `ReadServedStates` drops a code only a direct database edit could have produced — so a preset in that condition reads as serving nowhere, which is visible on the page and refused the moment it is edited.

**Whether prices include GST is a stored fact and is never inferred**, the same restraint [a supplier's GST default](#product-and-supplier-gst-rules-issue-430) is held to: the supermarkets, Kmart and BIG W publish GST-inclusive prices and JB Metro publishes ex-GST ones, and nothing derives that from a name, a connector or an amount. The policy holds no amount at all and calculates no GST; the field says what a collected price *means*, which is what stops a later comparison putting an inclusive price beside an exclusive one. It is marked `JsonRequired` on both writes for that reason: a `bool` omitted from a body would bind `false` indistinguishably from an explicit `false` and record the price list as ex-GST, silently, on a field AGENTS.md treats as financial data.

**The connector names a route, not a service.** `Varnmill`, `Kmart`, `BigW` and `JbMetro`, numbered from 1 so no stored number is read as the first route by accident, and `null` — nothing collects this supplier's prices — is a real state and the one Costco is in. `BigW` is **one** value even though [#926](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/926) reaches a BIG W price by name search with a direct SKU lookup behind it: a preset says which route to take, and which calls that route makes is the collector's business. The names are settled here and consumed by the collector work of [#924](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/924). For a JB Metro record the site the route talks to is the record's existing `Url`, which is why **a new JB Metro site is a new record and not new code**.

**`AddSupplierPresetMasterFields` adds the columns, sets the four existing rows and inserts five records — once.** It is a one-off `INSERT` in the migration, never `HasData` and never a startup seed, for the reason the one-time seed exists at all ([Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)): production applies migrations at startup, so anything that re-applies itself would quietly undo an edit or re-enable a deliberately disabled preset at the next deployment. The four rows #848 shipped are recognised **by normalised name** and given their values — Coles, Woolworths, Big W and Costco are all nationwide and all GST-inclusive, with Coles and Woolworths on the Varnmill route (keys `coles` and `woolworths`), Big W on its own, and Costco with no connector until the owner decides otherwise. ALDI, Kmart and three JB Metro records (NSW; South Coast & ACT; SA & NT, each with its own site as its `Url`) are inserted. **A row that was renamed or removed matches nothing and is left entirely alone**, keeping the column defaults rather than being guessed at; a disabled row is given its values without being re-enabled; and the `CreatedAtUtc`/`UpdatedAtUtc` of the existing rows are untouched, because this migration gave them columns they never had and did not make an edit on anybody's behalf.

**Each of those five inserts is skipped when the name is already taken, and that is what keeps the upgrade applicable.** The Super Admin surface has accepted any name since #848, so a database being upgraded may already hold an `ALDI`, a `KMART` or a JB Metro record somebody created by hand. `NormalisedName` is unique, so an unconditional insert would fail with `UNIQUE constraint failed: SupplierPresets.NormalisedName` — and because **production applies migrations at startup and fails closed**, that would be a deployment that does not start rather than a row that does not arrive. Every insert is therefore `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS` over that normalised name. The record that is already there is kept **exactly as it is** — name, website, enabled state and both instants — and is *not* given the values above either: its new columns take the fail-closed defaults, so it reads as "no market recorded" until a Super Admin completes it. A migration may not declare somebody else's record GST-inclusive or point it at a collection route on their behalf, which is the same restraint that leaves a renamed row alone.

**`Down` removes the records this migration created and nothing else.** The five rows it inserts carry a fixed literal `CreatedAtUtc` (`2026-10-27 00:00:00`), and a preset a person created carries the clock instant of the moment they created it, so that literal is a provenance stamp: the delete matches one of the five normalised names **and** that instant. Deleting by name alone would destroy the very record `Up` was careful not to touch, and a delete is not recoverable by reversing anything. A record somebody renamed in between matches no name and stays, as above; the values set on the four rows that already existed go with the columns that held them, which is what reversing an additive migration means.

**The defaults fail closed.** `ServesNationwide` and `PricesIncludeGst` default to `0` and `ServedStates` to the empty string, so a row the migration did not recognise reads as "no market recorded" — an unconfigured preset the page reports as *Not set* and the policy refuses on the next edit. Defaulting to nationwide would have been the migration inventing a claim about where a supplier sells, and defaulting the GST flag to `1` would have been it inventing a tax basis.

**The audit trail carries the new fields, including the connector key.** What a preset claims about its market, its price basis and its collection route is configuration a Super Admin chose, and "who switched this supplier to ex-GST prices" is exactly what this trail is for; `SupplierPresetAuditEntry.For` builds the event from the preset **as it was stored**, so a submitted value the Domain trimmed, folded or re-ordered is not what is recorded. The preset's name and its website stay absent, as before: the connector key names which retailer a shared route is for and is nobody's name, address or business data.

**On the page**, the dialog offers the market (one *Australia nationwide* switch, and the eight state checkboxes while it is off), the *Prices include GST* switch, and the connector with its key; the table shows all three, with *Not set* for a record with no recorded market and *Not collected* for one nothing collects. Two of the server's refusals are made **unreachable** rather than mirrored, which is the stronger kind of agreement with a rule: the state checkboxes exist only while nationwide is off and are cleared when it is switched back on, and the key field exists only for the route that reads it and is cleared when another is chosen. The list's **Disable/Enable** confirmation re-sends the row's own supplier-master values, because the endpoint is a `PUT` of the whole resource — sending the form's defaults instead would move a JB Metro record to nationwide, GST-inclusive prices as a side effect of a button that says *Disable*.

**What proves it.** `SupplierPresetPolicyTests` covers the name rule, its boundary and the case-insensitive key, and that this policy holds no website rule of its own; #847's `SupplierUrlPolicyTests` covers the website rule the preset surface reuses, and `SupplierUrlRuleSingleSourceOfTruthTests` holds it to one home. `SuperAdminSupplierPresetsApiTests` asserts the two website refusals against `SupplierUrlPolicy.InvalidMessage` and `.TooLongMessage` themselves, so a preset that started accepting an address a business's own supplier would not would fail. `AddSupplierPresetsMigrationTests` covers the table, the four seeded rows, the unique index, the absent business column, the `Down`, and — the criterion the design exists for — that an edited and disabled seeded row survives a second migrate and restart with nothing re-inserted or re-enabled. `SupplierPresetMasterPolicyTests` covers #931's rules: the closed state vocabulary, the canonical stored order, the mutual exclusion and the "at least one" half of it, the tolerant read, every connector/key combination including a key with no route at all, and an undeclared connector number. `AddSupplierPresetMasterFieldsMigrationTests` covers the five columns, their fail-closed defaults, the nine records with their values, the seeded connector numbers asserted against the enum itself (the migration writes them as literals), the canonical seeded state lists, and — over a database that was renamed, disabled and given a website *first* — that a renamed row is left entirely alone, a disabled one is updated without being re-enabled, the instants are untouched, nothing is re-inserted on a second migrate, and the `Down` removes the five records and the columns. It also covers the upgrade state that made the insert conditional: a database where a Super Admin had **already** created presets under three of the five names — one enabled with a website, one typed in lower case and then disabled, one JB Metro site pointed elsewhere — upgrades successfully, keeps all three unchanged (including their instants) with the fail-closed defaults in their new columns, duplicates nothing, still inserts the two records whose names were free, and on `Down` keeps those three while removing the two the migration created. The database's own refusal of a second row under a seeded normalised name is asserted beside them, because that refusal is why the skip exists. `EfSupplierPresetStoreTests` adds the adapter's round trip of the new fields and reads the seeded master list back through the real projection, and `EfBusinessSupplierProvisioningStoreTests` asserts that none of the new fields reaches a business's copy — on the schema as well as on the values, because `Suppliers` holds no such column. `EfSupplierPresetStoreTests` covers the adapter under a denied scope and stages the pre-check/index race deterministically, so "a conflict, never a `500`" is proved for the create and the edit alike without depending on two threads interleaving. `SupplierPresetConcurrencyTests` then races it for real — a SQLite **file**, two service scopes with their own `AppDbContext` and connection, both released from a barrier *after* both pre-checks have answered "no such name" — and asserts one created preset, one `DomainConflictException` carrying the duplicate sentence (the `409` the surface answers with), one row and exactly one audit event. `SuperAdminSupplierPresetsApiTests` covers the whole surface over HTTP: `403` for an Owner, a Manager, an applicant, a stranger, a member presenting a support-session id and the administrator without the delegated scope, `401` anonymous, `read_only_role_preview` on both writes with nothing stored, the two answers the issue's `403` criterion does not distinguish (a previewed read, and the administrator holding a live support session), the list's fields and ordering, each create and edit refusal, the duplicate `409`, the audit event's contents and absences, and that `/api/suppliers` is unchanged in both directions. `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` hold the two classifications. On the frontend, `super-admin-supplier-presets.service.spec.ts`, `supplier-preset-dialog.component.spec.ts`, `super-admin-supplier-presets.component.spec.ts`, #847's `components/suppliers/supplier-url.spec.ts`, `navigation.spec.ts`, `sidebar-nav.component.spec.ts`, `breadcrumb-routes.spec.ts`, `app.routes.spec.ts` and `member-endpoint.spec.ts` cover the client, the list, the form, the validation, the confirmation, the navigation, the breadcrumb, the guarded route and the `403` classification.

#### Supplier presets copied into an approved business (issue #849)

Child C of [#835](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/835) is the other half of the list above: a business that has just been approved starts with **its own copies of the enabled presets** rather than with an empty supplier list. The presets stay platform configuration, and what lands in the business is an ordinary tenant-owned `Supplier` row it owns.

Issue [#934](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/934) then made each copy **stay linked** to the master row it came from, under the owner's decision of 27 October 2026 on [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817) — see [The link, the lock and the "Not used" switch](#the-link-the-lock-and-the-not-used-switch-issue-934) below. A copy is therefore no longer a row the business owns *outright*: its name, its website and the link are the master's, it cannot be deleted, and the contact details and the supplier GST defaults are still its own.

Issue [#935](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/935) then made **which** records a business receives a question about where it trades: the approval copies only the enabled records that are nationwide or serve the business's own recorded state, and the ones it is not entitled to at approval time reach it later only because somebody asks for them. The state rule, the top-up a state change makes and the "Available to add" list are all in [Supplier records by business state, and "Available to add"](#supplier-records-by-business-state-and-available-to-add-issue-935) below; what the rest of this section describes — when the copy happens, the marker, what is copied, what never copies, and the provisioning exception — is unchanged by it.

**Copy at approval, inside the approval's own transaction.** Not at application time: an application may be refused, and a refused business must not be left holding suppliers. `BusinessApplicationDecisionWriter`, on the approval branch and immediately after `IPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore.ApproveAsync`, calls `IBusinessSupplierProvisioningStore.CopyEnabledSupplierPresetsAsync` with the **decision instant** and with **`current.BusinessId`** — the key of the business row that transaction read, never the route value the request carried, exactly as the deactivation's invite cancellation hands over the id it read ([Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)). Both writes are inside issue #522's shared `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, so it is **all or nothing**: a copy that fails rolls the status change back with it, the business is still `Pending`, it holds no supplier, its marker is still `NULL`, and no audit event is emitted — a refused decision is not audited, because nothing happened. The audit event itself is unchanged and says nothing about suppliers: `PlatformBusinessDecisionAuditEntry` has no field for a count or a name, and adding one would be a change to what that trail may carry.

**The marker is the whole of the idempotency rule.** `Business.SupplierPresetsCopiedAtUtc` is an additive nullable column (`AddBusinessSupplierPresetsCopiedAt`); the copy happens only while it is `NULL`, and the copy sets it in the same `SaveChanges` as the suppliers. Supplier **names** are deliberately never consulted *by the copying*: a business may add and delete its own suppliers the moment it starts trading, so a name is not evidence about whether a copy was made, and a name-based rule would duplicate the list for a business that had tidied it. Zero enabled presets still sets the marker — the copy *was* made and what it contained was nothing — because leaving it `NULL` would turn a later attempt into a second copy. The one place in the application that does consult a name is issue #934's **one-time link backfill**, which creates nothing and is described below.

**What is copied, and what is not.** One `Supplier` per `IsEnabled` preset **that serves the business's own recorded state** (issue #935), read in **one snapshot** inside the transaction, with `Name`, `Url` and — since issue #934 — the preset's `Id` copied, and the supplier-master fields deliberately **not** copied: a `Supplier` has no served states, no price basis and no connector, what a preset claims about those is platform configuration for price checks, and giving a business's own supplier row one of them would be a separate decision ([The supplier-master fields](#the-supplier-master-fields-issue-931)). Contact fields stay `null`, because the platform knows no contact for a suggested supplier, and all three GST defaults keep `GstRules.None`, because a supplier GST default is explicit configuration a business makes about a supplier it buys from and is never inferred from a name or a website ([Product and supplier GST rules](#product-and-supplier-gst-rules-issue-430)). `IsHidden` starts `false`: a business receives every enabled suggestion in use, and "Not used" is its own later decision. Disabled presets are not copied. Nothing is written back to `SupplierPresets`: editing, renaming or disabling a preset afterwards changes no existing copy and does not break the link (the id is what the copy holds, not the name), editing a copy changes no preset and no other business's copy, and a business's copies are subject to the ordinary supplier permissions — and, since issue #934, to the lock rules below — from the first request.

**Nothing else copies, ever.** A rejection, a deactivation, a reactivation (`BusinessLifecycleWriter.ReactivateAsync`), a second approval attempt, `bootstrap-business` and `E2ETestFixture` all leave both the suppliers and the marker alone — the first five because only the approval branch calls the port, the last two because they create a business that is already `Active` and has no application to approve. **Existing businesses are never given suppliers**: `AddBusinessSupplierPresetsCopiedAt` stamps nothing and inserts nothing, so every business that predates the column reads `NULL` and keeps the suppliers it has. Issue #934's migration does not change that — it **links** some of the rows a business already had and creates, renames, hides and deletes nothing. An application that is still `Pending` when this ships *does* get its copies when it is approved, because it is a new business.

**The write is a provisioning path, and it is the one reviewed exception to "a denied scope writes nothing tenant-owned".** The design of that exception — the one entity type, the one state, the one business, the one save, the `internal` lease, the `Denied`-only precondition, and the fact that nothing becomes readable and no `IgnoreQueryFilters` over `Suppliers` exists — is in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The one reviewed provisioning write. `IBusinessSupplierProvisioningStore` is a separate one-method Application port rather than a method on `IPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` on purpose: that port's stated boundary is that no method on it reaches a tenant-owned row, and widening it would make the sentence that bounds it untrue. The new port takes no predicate, no filter, no supplier field and no preset id, is registered scoped with the request's own `AppDbContext` as its only dependency, and is reachable from the approval and from nowhere else.

**What proves it.** `BusinessApplicationDecisionTests` (unit) covers the hand-off: the copy is made once, inside the transaction and before the commit, with the in-transaction business id and the decision instant; a rejection provisions nothing; a refused approval provisions nothing; and a failed copy refuses the approval with nothing audited. `EfBusinessSupplierProvisioningStoreTests` is the relational half over two businesses and a denied scope: only enabled presets, the website carried across, contacts null and GST defaults `None`, the marker, the second call writing nothing even after the business renamed its copy, a business whose marker is already set receiving nothing, the copies invisible to the other business, preset and copy edits not reaching each other, an unknown business writing nothing, and — the boundary itself — the same denied context still refusing a product insert, a supplier insert of its own outside the lease and every other tenant-owned write, plus a resolved scope and a support session being unable to provision at all. `PlatformBusinessDecisionConcurrencyTests` races it: approve/approve leaves exactly one set of copies and one marker, approve/reject leaves the copies only if the approval won, and an injected copy failure rolls the whole approval back. `SuperAdminBusinessesApiTests` is the HTTP boundary: the copies and the marker after an approval, zero enabled presets, a rejection copying nothing, deactivate/reactivate copying nothing for either business, the copies being that business's own suppliers the new Owner lists through `/api/suppliers` — under issue #934's lock rules, which that test now pins too — while another business's Owner sees none of them, and a preset edited afterwards leaving the copies alone. `AddBusinessSupplierPresetsCopiedAtMigrationTests` is the upgrade from the previous schema: the column arrives `NULL` for every existing business, no supplier is invented, and the seeded presets are untouched. `BusinessBootstrapTests` and `E2ETestAuthenticationTests` prove the two paths that must not copy, and `BusinessScopeCompositionTests` pins the adapter's registration and its single dependency.

#### The link, the lock and the "Not used" switch (issue #934)

The copies of #849 were ordinary rows the business owned outright: it could rename one, point it at another website, or delete it, and nothing recorded which suggestion a row came from. That is what issue #934 fixes, as the second task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817) and under the owner's decisions of 27 October 2026. A copy **stays linked** to its master row, so its identity cannot drift and a later price comparison that reads the master can rely on the link. The link is also what issue [#935](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/935) counts: "this business already has that record" is the link and nothing else — see [Supplier records by business state, and "Available to add"](#supplier-records-by-business-state-and-available-to-add-issue-935) below.

**Two columns on `Suppliers`, and the link is the whole of the rule.** `SupplierPresetId` is nullable — `null` for a supplier the business created itself, which is still refused nothing at all — and `IsHidden` is the business's "Not used" switch, `false` by default. The schema half of the decision (the `Restrict` key to the platform table, the absence of a navigation property, and the filtered unique index on `(BusinessId, SupplierPresetId)`) is in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64); the behaviour half is one Domain policy, `Inventory.Domain.Suppliers.SupplierPresetLinkPolicy`, which reads exactly one fact:

| On a supplier | Linked copy | The business's own row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rename | refused `400` | allowed, as before |
| Set, change or clear the website | refused `400` | allowed, as before |
| Delete | refused `400` | allowed, as before |
| Contact name, phone, email, address | allowed | allowed |
| Supplier GST defaults (#430) | allowed | allowed |
| "Not used" | allowed, and reversible | refused `400` — delete it instead |

The contact details and the GST defaults are deliberately editable: they are the business's own accounting settings about a supplier it buys from, and the link locks the supplier's *identity*, not what the business records about its invoices. "Not used" is refused on an unlinked supplier because it is what a linked copy has *instead of* a delete, and a supplier the business can simply delete has no use for a second, quieter way out of the pickers.

**Only a change is refused, and the read, the comparison and the write are one operation.** The supplier form submits the whole record, so an operator correcting a phone number sends the stored name and website back unchanged; refusing that would make a linked copy's contact details uneditable. `EfSupplierStore` therefore applies the policy to the **row it loaded**, inside the same unit of work as the write, comparing ordinally — a different capitalisation or a trailing space is a different name and is refused rather than quietly stored — and a refused update writes nothing at all, not even the contact fields that would have been allowed on their own. The URL is normalised by issue #847's `SupplierUrlPolicy` *before* the comparison, so a blank submission means "no website" on both sides.

**One policy answers both the refusals and what a client may offer.** The `/api/suppliers` list and detail publish `isLinked`, `isHidden`, `canRename` and `canDelete` on `SupplierDetailResponse`, all four from that same policy. They are **eligibility, never authorization**: the endpoints refuse a linked copy's rename, website change and delete whatever a client renders. The response is a new type rather than four fields on `SupplierResponse`, because that record is schema-identical to the legacy `Supplier` component every nested `supplier` object in a purchase, a supplier order and an operating expense references — widening it would have changed three unrelated contracts to carry a lock state about the Suppliers page. The four fields are additive, so a client reading the seven it already knew is unaffected.

**Hidden means "not offered", never "removed".** `GET /api/suppliers` leaves the hidden suppliers out **by default**, and only `?includeHidden=true` returns them. That direction is the fail-safe one: every picker — a purchase, a supplier order, a product's order dialog — gets the right list by asking for nothing, so a client that forgot a parameter cannot offer a supplier the business has taken out of use, and the Suppliers page is the single caller that asks for the hidden ones, because switching one back off requires seeing the row. Nothing is deleted or detached: `GET /api/suppliers/{id}` still answers for a hidden supplier, and a purchase, supplier order or operating expense that already names it still resolves and displays it through its own relationship.

**The switch is its own resource.** `PUT /api/suppliers/{id}/not-used` takes `{ "isHidden": true|false }` and writes that one column. It is not a field on the supplier update body, so correcting a phone number on a stale form cannot put a supplier back into the pickers as a side effect. It declares **no capability of its own**: the controller's existing `Purchasing.Operate` is the supplier-write capability, and hiding a supplier is a purchasing decision about who this business buys from rather than accounting configuration like the GST defaults. In a read-only support session it is refused like every other non-`GET` request, by the method rule in `SupportSessionAccessPolicy` and not by anything written on this controller — and the Suppliers page hides the switch there for the same reason it already hides Create and Delete ([Extending write-control hiding to Purchases and Suppliers](#extending-write-control-hiding-to-purchases-and-suppliers-issue-657)).

**The backfill consults a name exactly once, and links rather than creates.** `AddSupplierPresetLink` adds the two columns, links the suppliers businesses already have, and only then adds the unique index. #849's rule that supplier names are never consulted is unchanged **for the copying**; this is the one deliberate exception the owner decided on, and it is narrower in every direction: it runs once, it reads a name only to decide a *link*, and it creates, renames, hides and deletes nothing. A supplier is linked when its trimmed, upper-cased name equals a preset's `NormalisedName` **and** no other supplier of the same business normalises to that value. Two rows that both match one preset — `Coles` and ` COLES ` in one business — are therefore **both left unlinked**, because the migration cannot know which one the business actually buys from and the index would make a guess permanent; another business's single `Coles` is linked as normal, since the rule is per business exactly as the index is. A name matching no preset is left unlinked. Enabled and disabled presets are matched alike: the link says where a row came from, not whether the suggestion is still offered.

**Which is what makes the index safe to add in the same migration.** The unique index comes *after* the backfill, over data the backfill has already made acceptable to it, so the upgrade cannot fail on an existing database and no row ever has to be deleted, unlinked or merged to make an index fit — which matters because **Production applies migrations at startup and fails closed** ([Database and migrations](#database-and-migrations)). The comparison is SQLite's `UPPER(TRIM(Name))`, which agrees with .NET's `Trim().ToUpperInvariant()` on every name either side holds today and differs only outside ASCII; where they would disagree the row simply does not match and is left unlinked, which is the fail-closed direction. Re-implementing invariant upper-casing in SQL would have been a second normalising rule free to drift from the one the presets are indexed by.

**What proves it.** `SupplierPresetLinkPolicyTests` (unit) is the policy itself, including that an unlinked supplier is refused nothing, that re-submitting the stored name and website is allowed, that the website is refused when set, changed *and* cleared, and that the four refusal sentences are four different sentences. `SupplierUseCaseTests` and `SuppliersControllerTests` are the use cases and the HTTP boundary: the refusals and which field each is reported against, the contact details and the GST defaults still saving, the hide and unhide, the default list leaving the hidden suppliers out, and the link state published on both the list and the detail. `EfSupplierStoreTests` is the relational half — a refused update writing nothing at all, the selectable list, the restricted key refusing to delete a preset a business holds a copy of, and the filtered unique index allowing one copy per business and any number of unlinked rows. `EfBusinessSupplierProvisioningStoreTests` proves the copies carry their preset and arrive visible, and that a master edited afterwards keeps the link. `AddSupplierPresetLinkMigrationTests` is the upgrade, seeded on purpose with the same-name duplicates: the exact single match linked, no match and both duplicates left unlinked, another business's single match linked, no other column changed, and the index and key created on that very database. `SupportSessionRequestApiTests` covers the read-only refusal, `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` the one tenant-to-platform key and the index, and the Suppliers page's own specs the lock state, the locked inputs, the switch and the refusal sentences.

#### Supplier records by business state, and "Available to add" (issue #935)

The third task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817) answers a question the first two left open: *which* of the platform's supplier records a business is entitled to. A Canberra business has no use for a Perth wholesaler, and JB Metro South Coast & ACT is exactly the record it does want. Under the owner's decisions of 27 October 2026 there are three answers and they are deliberately different from each other.

| When | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| The application is approved | The enabled records that are **nationwide or serve the business's state** are copied, linked (#934), inside #849's existing provisioning write |
| The Owner changes the business's state | Every enabled record that **now** matches and has no copy here is added, in the settings save's own transaction, as an ordinary write in the Owner's own scope |
| The platform adds or enables a record later | **Nothing is pushed.** It appears on each served business's Suppliers page under "Available to add", and one click adds it |

**One rule decides all three.** `Inventory.Domain.Suppliers.SupplierPresetMarketPolicy` compares what a record claims — `ServesNationwide`, or the stored `ServedStates` list read back through #931's `SupplierPresetMasterPolicy.ReadServedStates` — against `Business.State` (#933), and answers `IsOfferedTo` only when the record is **also** still enabled. A **business with no recorded state** receives the nationwide records alone: every business that predates #933's column has none, nothing backfills them, and a state is never inferred from a time zone (which cannot tell NSW from the ACT), an address or an ABN. A **record with no recorded market** — the fail-closed default a row #931's migration did not recognise carries — serves nobody; it reads as *Not set* on the Super Admin's page and is corrected by editing it there. An unrecognised stored code matches nothing, because the tolerant read drops it. The comparison happens in memory, not in SQL: a market is one comma-separated list of codes and a `LIKE` over it would match a code inside another's text.

**Nothing is ever taken away.** A copy a business holds is never removed, hidden, relinked or edited because the business changed state or the platform disabled the record — a purchase may already name it, and a business that moves has still bought what it bought. The top-up and the add only ever insert. Removing or relinking copies is explicitly out of scope of this issue.

**The approval's copy is unchanged except for which records it takes.** `EfBusinessSupplierProvisioningStore` reads the state from the very business row it already loaded to check `SupplierPresetsCopiedAtUtc` — the row the approval's own transaction read, never a route value — filters the snapshot through the policy, and inserts the rest exactly as before. The lease, the one entity type, the one business, the one save, the marker and the `Denied`-only precondition are all as [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The one reviewed provisioning write describes them; a business that no enabled record serves is approved normally with no supplier and **still gets the marker**, because the copy was made and what served it was nothing.

**The state change's top-up is an ordinary write, deliberately not the provisioning exception.** `UpdateBusinessSettings` runs `AddMatchingSupplierPresets` inside the `MembershipWriteGuard` transaction it already opens (#680), immediately **after** the save, so what the rule matches against is the state that was just stored and the new state and its suppliers commit together or not at all. Its list is a *candidate* list: each copy judges its own eligibility inside the write lock, as the add's does, so a record that stopped being offered is skipped rather than written or reported — the top-up normally runs where nothing can commit between the list and the copies at all, and the per-copy check is what keeps the rule true when it does not. It runs **only when the state actually changed** (`BusinessSettingsField.State` is in the save's own change set): an Owner correcting an ABN must not acquire suppliers as a side effect, and a record enabled since the business was approved must not arrive by the back door — that is what "Available to add" is for. The write goes through the central ownership stamp in the Owner's resolved scope, which is why no widening of #849's exception was needed: that exception exists only because an approval has a *denied* scope and no other way to equip the business it is approving.

**"Available to add" is a member-facing read of a platform table, and it is the second one in the application.** `GET /api/suppliers/available-presets` publishes the **id, name and website** of the enabled records that serve this business and that it holds no copy of — no served states, no price basis, no connector, no business id, and no filter, search, page or sort for a caller to supply. Why that is a reviewed tenancy decision, and what bounds it, is in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64). Only the **link** hides a record from the list: a supplier the business typed in itself under the same name is not a copy of anything and never suppresses the offer, which is the same rule #934's backfill applied when it left same-name duplicates unlinked.

**`POST /api/suppliers/available-presets/{presetId}` adds one, and carries nothing else.** No body, no name, no website, no business: the name, the website and the link are read from the record by the adapter, and the business is the caller's own. It declares **no capability of its own** — the controller's existing `Purchasing.Operate` is the supplier-write capability, exactly as it is for #934's "Not used" switch, because deciding that this business buys from a suggested supplier is purchasing work rather than accounting configuration. A read-only support session and a role preview are refused by their own method rules (`SupportSessionAccessPolicy`, `RolePreviewPolicy`), not by anything written on this controller, and the Suppliers page hides the action in both states for the same reason it already hides Create and Delete. A record that does not exist, is no longer suggested, or does not serve this business is one answer — `404` — so a member learns nothing about the platform's list beyond what the list told them.

**Eligibility is decided by the copy, in the same operation as the insert.** `EfAvailableSupplierPresetStore.CopyAsync` opens the `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction of `SqliteWriteLockTransaction` — the same write lock the machine delete and the membership write path take — and then, with the lock held, reads the three facts the rule is made of: the record's `IsEnabled` flag, its served states, and the business's own `Business.State`. It inserts inside that transaction. Nothing can commit in that window, so a Super Admin disabling the record or re-pointing its market, and an Owner changing the business's state, either land before the lock and are seen or wait behind it. A deferred transaction would not be enough — it takes the write lock at the first *write*, which is after the reads the decision was made from, which is exactly how a check and a write that share a transaction can still disagree. There is deliberately **no** "is this available?" method beside it: an answer given before the write is a stale read, and acting on one is how a business acquires a record nothing entitles it to. So a record that stopped being offered in that window is `404` for the add and a skip for the top-up, and never an exception: the only read that stands on its own is the list, which is a page's contents and decides nothing.

**One copy per business per record, and the index is the backstop under that.** The filtered unique index #934 added on `(BusinessId, SupplierPresetId)` is what makes the rule true against a writer this process did not serialise with — another process, or a row written by hand — and its violation is translated into the *same* answer the in-lock read gives: `409` with `SupplierPresetMarketPolicy.AlreadyAddedMessage` for the add, and a skip for the top-up, which carries on with the rest rather than failing an Owner's state change over a supplier they now have. Either way there is exactly one copy and never a `500`. The adapter recognises that one constraint and nothing else, so an unrelated database failure stays a database failure.

**What proves it.** `SupplierPresetMarketPolicyTests` (unit) is the rule: nationwide, a matching state, a non-matching state, a business with no recorded state, a record with no recorded market, an unrecognised stored code, and the enabled/serving halves varied separately. `BusinessSettingsUseCaseTests` covers the top-up's conditions — added on a state change inside the committed transaction with the business from the membership, nothing added when the state did not change, nothing added when the save is refused, a record copied in between skipped while the save still commits, and a record the platform *disabled* between the candidate list and the copy skipped the same way. `SuppliersControllerTests` covers the HTTP shapes: the three published fields, the `201` with the linked copy, the one `404` for all three "not offered" cases, the `409` on a second add, and the same `409` when the unique index refuses a copy the in-lock read could not see. `EfAvailableSupplierPresetStoreTests` is the relational half over three businesses — the ACT one, the WA one and a legacy one with no state: what each is offered, that an unlinked same-name supplier hides nothing, the copy's own fields and that the other business receives none of it, both businesses holding their own copy of one record, a record that serves elsewhere unaddable by id, the real index refusing a second linked copy with the adapter recognising that refusal, the top-up adding only what is missing while a hidden copy, a stale copy and the business's own supplier are all left exactly as they were, the top-up's idempotence, and the whole chain through the real `UpdateBusinessSettings`. Its *Eligibility that changed* tests are the ones that hold the atomicity above: a record disabled, a record re-pointed at other states and the business itself moved, each between the list the caller is looking at and the add, all answered "not available" with nothing written and nothing thrown; a copy created in that window answered "already added" with the existing copy (its "Not used" flag included) untouched; and the authoritative copy asked for each of the three directly, which is the regression test — before this it threw an unhandled `InvalidOperationException` for the disabled record and *copied* the other two. `EfBusinessSupplierProvisioningStoreTests` covers the approval's copy by state, including a business with no state and one no record serves still getting the marker. `PlatformBusinessDecisionConcurrencyTests` counts the copies a racing approval makes through the same rule. `SuperAdminBusinessesApiTests` is the end-to-end: a `QLD` application approved with the Queensland record and not the Western Australian one, and then a record added afterwards being offered to that business, added with one request, refused as already added on a second, and reaching no other business. `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests`, `SupportSessionRequestApiTests` and `RolePreviewApiTests` pin the capability and the two read-only refusals. On the frontend, `supplier.service.spec.ts` covers the two requests and `supplier-list.component.spec.ts` the section, the safe website link, the add, the reload, and the action being hidden in a support session and in a role preview.

#### Support sessions: the store and the control endpoints (issue #550)

The two slices above decide whether a business may trade and whether it is switched on. This one, the first slice of [#512](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/512) under #328, is how the Super Admin gets to *look at* one: a business reports an error nobody can reproduce from the outside, and the administrator opens a time-limited, audited, read-only **support session** on it. The session is the record that the access was granted, and this slice is that record plus the three endpoints that manage it; what a request then *does* with one is [#551](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**What this slice deliberately did not do, and why that order.** #550 shipped the record before anything acted on it: it resolved no business from a session, and [#551](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) is what added the reading of the `X-Support-Session` header, the `SupportReadOnly` scope state, the read-only enforcement and the Nayax block (#552 then degraded the dashboard summary, below). Building the audited record first was the fail-closed order: the alternative would have been a slice where access existed and the record of it was still being designed. What survives from it is the narrower claim an API test still pins — *holding* a session grants nothing, because a request that does not present the id runs as the administrator's own (non-existent) membership.

```text
POST /api/super-admin/support-sessions/{businessId}   { "reason": "..." } (required) -> the session id, name, expiry
GET  /api/super-admin/support-sessions/active         the caller's own session, or 204
POST /api/super-admin/support-sessions/active/end     ends it, or 204 when there is none
```

**Class 2, the same marker and the same policy, and no header.** `SuperAdminSupportSessionsController` carries `[Authorize]`, `[Authorize(Policy = PlatformAdminPolicy.Name)]`, `[RequiredScope("access_as_user")]` and `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute` — the diagnostics surface's authorization, reused rather than re-invented, and class 2 of the four [endpoint authorization classes](#capability-authorization-issue-525). These three endpoints are the *control* surface and are reached as the administrator themselves, so they neither need nor accept the support-session header: the session they act on is the one belonging to the authenticated actor, found server-side. An Owner is refused here exactly as any other member is, and with no administrator configured — the shipped state — nobody reaches the controller at all.

**The business id in the route is the subject of the session, not a tenancy scope.** It is the same reviewed shape as the lifecycle routes above: the request still carries a **denied** `BusinessScope`, the id resolves no business for it, nothing is stamped with it, it cannot reach a tenant-owned table, and it is checked against the stored rows on every call (`404` for an unknown business, `409` for one that is not `Active`). It is in the route rather than in a body because no DTO in this application carries a business id inwards.

**What a session is, as a row.** `SupportSessions` is an additive table and the **fifth** structural non-tenant-owned one ([Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)): the business id, the administrator's Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, the reason, the started and expiry instants, a nullable ended instant, and the session id's hash. The structural reason for the exemption is who writes it — every request that reaches this table is a platform-admin request, and a platform administrator is a member of no business, so the request resolves nothing: a tenant query filter would match none of its rows and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`'s stamp would have no business to stamp. The boundary is instead the business id, or the actor pair, named in every statement of `EfSupportSessionStore` — and both only ever come from the server's own side of the operation.

**The session id is a credential, and is stored only as a hash.** It is `SupportSessionId.EntropyBytes` (32) bytes from the platform's cryptographic generator, rendered URL-safe, and returned **once** — in the response to the start that created it. The row holds `SupportSessionId.Hash`'s SHA-256 digest, so a copy of the database yields no usable session id; the active-session read deliberately does not re-issue it, and no log or audit event carries it in either form. A lost id means starting a new session, which is audited like the first. The uniqueness of that hash is global rather than per business, which is the deliberate opposite of the invite token's constraint and is explained in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § Tenant-scoped uniqueness.

**Sixty minutes, fixed by the server.** `SupportSessionPolicy.Lifetime` is both the default and the maximum, and the start request carries **no duration at all**: a caller-supplied one — even a capped one — would make "how long was this business readable?" a property of the request instead of a fact about the feature. The only way to hold access open longer is to start another session, which is audited as a new one.

**A session is active until it is ended or it expires, and expiry is derived.** `SupportSessionPolicy.IsActive` is the one rule — not ended, and `nowUtc < ExpiresAtUtc`, inclusive of the expiry instant exactly as an invite's is — so a session stops being usable at the instant it runs out, on every path at once, with no sweep to run and no row left claiming otherwise. `EndedAtUtc` therefore means "somebody decided to end this" and never "this is over": an expired session keeps it null for the rest of its row's life, and nothing reads that column to mean "still usable".

**Three ways a session ends.** *Expiry*, as above. *The administrator's own end call*, which takes no session id — the session is the authenticated actor's, so there is nothing a request could present and no way to end somebody else's — and which is a success that writes and audits nothing when there is nothing active, including for a session that had already expired. And *the caller no longer passing `PlatformAdminPolicy`*: authority is the configured Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, every read and write of a session names the actor pair it belongs to, and a session is only ever visible, usable and endable by that one actor. Change the configured administrator and the previous pair cannot reach any of these endpoints at all while the new pair's own reads never see the old row — so the session it granted is unreachable to everybody, and #551's middleware re-evaluates the same policy on every request that presents a session id.

**One active session per administrator.** A second start while one is still active is `409` and writes nothing; the first session is untouched. The reason is attribution: two live sessions make "which business was this administrator reading?" unanswerable for every request that names neither, and they double the data readable at one moment for no case anybody asked for. Ending the first is a single call. There is deliberately **no filtered unique index** behind this rule, because "active" is partly derived from the clock and an index cannot express it — an expired session would otherwise occupy the slot forever. What makes the rule hold instead is the write lock: the check and the insert are one operation inside the transaction below.

**The authoritative read, both rules and the write are one operation.** The start runs inside issue #522's shared [`MembershipWriteGuard`](#one-active-membership-per-identity-issue-522) transaction — SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so the write lock is held before anything is decided — and re-reads the business's status and the administrator's active session **inside** it. A deactivation that commits while a start waits for the lock refuses that start, and two simultaneous starts resolve to one session and one `409`. The read before the transaction opens decides nothing: it answers "no such business" with a `404` and refuses a stale view before a write lock is taken on the caller's behalf. The explicit end runs in the same transaction for the same reason, and both store methods are a read followed by one conditional statement over the same "only while active" predicate, so the rows they return are the rows they wrote. Neither asks the guard its membership questions — a session grants no membership — so the intent handed to it is the empty one.

**A business deactivation ends every session for that business, in the same transaction.** This is what [#545's](#deactivating-reactivating-and-releasing-members-issue-545) `IBusinessDeactivationHook` was declared for: `EndSupportSessionsOnBusinessDeactivation` is the single registration that replaces its shipped no-op, it is called last inside the deactivation's own write transaction, and it ends every session of the business the transition read — never a value from the request — at the instant the deactivation recorded. A session that survived the business being switched off would be exactly the access the deactivation exists to stop, and a session ended by a deactivation that then rolled back would have been cut off for nothing. **A reactivation does not revive one**: the ended instant is never rewritten, so a business coming back is not a reason to restore somebody else's access to it, and an administrator who still needs to look starts a new session. Another business's session is untouched, and an already-ended or expired one is left exactly as it is, which is what makes a repeated deactivation idempotent.

**Audit: one structured log event per session started and per session ended, and no table.** `LoggingSupportSessionAudit` writes one `ILogger` `Information` event carrying the administrator's `(tid, oid)`, the business id, the session row's own key (so a start and its end read as one session), which event it is, **the reason**, both instants, and for an end the ended instant and why it ended — `EndedByAdministrator` or `BusinessDeactivated`. The reason is the one free-text value any platform trail here carries, and it is the point: a support session is somebody outside a business reading its data, so "why" is what makes the access reviewable. It never carries the session id in either form — a trail is read by more people than a response is — nor the business's name, nor anybody else's identity; `SupportSessionAuditEntry` has no field for any of them. A refused start is not audited, and neither is an end that closed nothing. There is deliberately no audit table, and **the log destination and retention period are platform configuration a human must verify**, exactly as for the three platform trails beside it.

**The one place an event is not strictly post-commit, stated plainly.** Every other platform audit event in this application is emitted after its transaction commits. The ends a *deactivation* causes are emitted inside that transaction, because the hook has no post-commit callback — the only step left after it is the commit itself — and the alternative, a deactivation that ended somebody's access and recorded nothing about whose, is the worse gap. A failed commit therefore leaves an event about an end that did not happen, in a request that also failed: the business is still active, the session is still live, and the administrator sees the error rather than a silent partial result. The start and the explicit end are both audited after their commit as usual.

**Expiry is not an event.** Nothing happens when a session runs out — the rule simply stops answering "active" — so there is no end event to emit and nothing that could claim one. When the session would have ended is already in the trail: the start event carries the expiry instant.
