**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Tenancy/SupportSessionPolicyTests` covers the fixed lifetime, the status gate including `0` and an undeclared value, the inclusive expiry boundary, the reason's bounds and the id hash's two properties. `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/SupportSessions/SupportSessionTests` runs the three use cases and the hook over the real `MembershipWriteGuard`: the order the reads, the write, the commit and the audit event happen in; the refusals for a non-active business, a second session and a missing or over-long reason, and what each leaves unwritten; a status or a session that changes while the write lock is awaited; another administrator's session being neither read nor ended; and — through #545's real `DeactivateBusiness` with this hook registered — the session ending inside the deactivation's transaction, a refused deactivation leaving it running, and a reactivation not reviving it. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfSupportSessionStoreTests` is the relational half over two businesses and two administrators under a denied scope: what a start stores, the per-actor read, the derived expiry with nothing written, each end naming one column and nobody else's rows, the globally unique hash the database enforces, and the proof that the same denied context still reads no `Products` row and still has a tenant-owned write refused. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/SuperAdminSupportSessionsApiTests` is the HTTP boundary over the real migration history: the stored row and the audit event a start produces (and what neither contains), every refusal, the active read never re-issuing the id, the end and its idempotent repeat, and the deactivation ending two administrators' sessions with one audited end each while another business's keeps running. What a started session then *grants* is [#551's](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) half, proved separately. `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` pins the fifth structural exemption, the absent query filter and the index shape; `BusinessScopeCompositionTests` pins the store's registration and dependencies and that the deactivation hook is this one; and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` pins the three endpoints as class 2 with no capability.

#### Support sessions in the request pipeline (issue #551)

Issue #550 made a support session a stored, audited fact and deliberately gave it no effect. Issue
#551 — the other half of the same slice of #512, under #328 — is what a session now *does*: a
request presents its id, resolves the chosen business, reads that business and nothing else, and
cannot change anything or touch its Nayax account.

**How a request joins a session.** `InventoryApi.Auth.RequestSupportSessionAccessor` is the only
thing in the application that reads the value of the `X-Support-Session` header. It is the boundary
implementation of one narrow Application port, `ISupportSessionAccessor`, so the inner layers get the
answer — which business, its name, when the session runs out, and the session row's key — and never
the header. It is registered per request and memoised: the capability authorization handler asks
before the endpoint is chosen, `BusinessScopeMiddleware` asks to publish the scope, and the use cases
ask again through `CurrentCapabilities` and `GET /api/me/access`, and all of them get one answer from
one lookup.

Both halves are required and both are this request's own. `PlatformAdminPolicy` is re-evaluated here,
on this request, rather than inferred from the fact that the authorization middleware ran earlier —
the same reasoning as the diagnostics membership bypass of [#336](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336),
and for the same reason: an access decision that depended on pipeline position would be one edit away
from applying to somebody nobody authorised. Then the presented id is hashed with
`SupportSessionId.Hash` and matched by `ISupportSessionStore.FindActiveForActorByIdHashAsync`, the one
lookup #551 adds to that port. The actor pair is part of the `WHERE` clause beside the hash, so a
leaked id is not a session somebody else is *refused* — it is a session they cannot find. "Still
active" is in the clause too (`SupportSessionPolicy.IsActive`), so an ended or expired row is not
something the store can hand back and somebody then has to remember to reject. Finally the business
row is read **now** rather than trusted from when the session started, and must still be
`Active` by the same `SupportSessionPolicy.CanStartFor` rule a start is judged by: a business a
session could not have been started for is not one it may go on reading.

**Fail closed, with one code and one sentence.** Four things make a presented session unusable — it
was never this caller's, it was ended, it expired, or its business is no longer active — and all four
answer `403` with `support_session_ended`. The differences between them are facts about somebody
else's session or about a business this caller is no longer entitled to anything about; which one it
was is logged for an operator and never returned. The refusal happens in two places because the
pipeline notices it in two places: the capability authorization handler runs before
`BusinessScopeMiddleware`, so it refuses there first for an endpoint that declares a capability, and
the middleware refuses for the rest — the same code, the same sentence, the same shape, so a client
sees one answer wherever it was decided. Neither falls back to the administrator's own membership.
They have none, and a silent fallback would turn "your session ended" into "you are not a member of
anything".

**A request that presents nothing is untouched, and so is a member who presents something.** No
header means the ordinary membership path, unchanged. A caller the platform-admin policy refuses has
the value not read at all, which is what keeps a member who sets the header an ordinary member: it
can still only do the one thing it has done since [#524](#member-display-name-and-email-issue-524) —
suppress the cosmetic profile refresh.

**The scope it publishes.** `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly` is the third state a request can
carry (after `Denied` and `Resolved`; `Unscoped` is not a request state at all). For every
tenant-owned read it is exactly `Resolved`: `AppDbContext`'s global filters compare against the same
`CurrentBusinessId`, so a support request sees the chosen business and nothing else, by the existing
central mechanism rather than a second one. The business id is the one stored on the matched session
row, which the start transaction took from the business row it read — never a request value. The
request's business time zone is published from that same business, so business dates are derived in
*its* calendar (issue #499) rather than in anything belonging to the administrator, who has none.
`ICurrentBusinessProvider.RequireBusinessIdAsync` answers with it too, so a use case that has to hand
a business id to a port acts in the business its reads are already filtered to; `ResolveAsync` and
`RequireRoleAsync` deliberately keep failing closed, because a support session is not a membership
and the administrator holds no role.

**Read-only is enforced three times, in three layers, and none of them is per controller.** That
repetition is the design, not redundancy: the first layer decides what a request may *ask for*, and
the other two decide what the database and the filesystem will *accept*.

1. **The capability handler.** `BusinessCapabilityAuthorizationHandler`, in `SupportReadOnly`,
   succeeds only when the capability is in the support set **and** the method is `GET` or `HEAD`. The
   method rule is checked first and independently, so a write is refused as a write — `403` with
   `read_only_support_session`, whatever capability it carried — rather than as a missing capability,
   which is the difference a support banner has to be able to show. It is an allowlist of two
   methods, so a verb nobody thought of is refused by construction. ASP.NET Core's default answer to
   a failed policy is a bare `403` with no body, which is right for a capability refusal and wrong
   for these two, so `SupportSessionAuthorizationResultHandler` gives *only* the failures carrying
   one of these codes an RFC 7807 body and leaves every other authorization failure exactly as it
   was.
2. **The persistence boundary.** `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` refuses every `SaveChanges` in
   `SupportReadOnly` with `SupportSessionReadOnlyException`, before its stamping and ownership rules
   are even considered. It covers every entity rather than only the tenant-owned ones, because in
   this state there is no write this application wants: not a tenant-owned row, not a membership, not
   an invite, not a business. A `SaveChanges` with nothing tracked is not a write and is left alone.
3. **Document storage.** `SupportSessionReadOnlyDocumentStorage` wraps whichever provider is
   configured and refuses every save and delete in this state. A document's bytes live outside the
   database, so a transaction that never commits does not un-write a file — and a deleted receipt is
   not recoverable by rolling one back. Reads pass straight through: a supporter looking at a
   purchase is looking at its receipt too.

**Nayax is blocked in the same change, in the provider.** `NayaxRequestCredentialProvider` refuses in
`SupportReadOnly` before it reads the connection and before any token could be decrypted, so every
ordinary Nayax call — read and write alike — fails with `403` and code
`unavailable_in_support_view`, and no request leaves the API. It is there rather than in each of the
~27 consumers for the reason the status gate is: a per-controller check is a check somebody forgets
to add to the next controller. The reason it exists at all is that the operator id and token are the
*business's* credential: nobody outside the business has agreed to its Nayax account being used on
their behalf, and a call made in a support view would be indistinguishable, at Nayax, from one the
business made itself. Every Nayax-backed screen therefore fails closed with this code in a support
view, which is the accepted outcome rather than a defect — except the home dashboard, which issue
#552 degraded instead, below.

**The dashboard degrades rather than fails (issue #552).** `GET /api/dashboard/summary` is the
landing page of the application, and its refill and ordering cards are the only part of it that needs
the live fleet; the week's sales, the catalogue, the storage units and the valuation are reads of the
business's own database. So in a support view it is answered `200` with
`Inventory.Application.Dashboard.SupportViewDashboardSummaryDto`: every local section exactly as a
member of that business is given it, and `needsRefill` and `needsOrdering` replaced by
`{ "available": false, "reason": "SupportView" }`. The whole section is replaced rather than
zeroed or nulled, because `machinesNeedingRefill: 0` reads as a fact about the business's machines.
That is the same shape issue #329 publishes with `reason: "NayaxNotConnected"` for a business whose
connection is unusable, and deliberately one shape rather than two: a client maps a stable reason
code to its own wording, and the reason is never a sentence to display. Mapping it to a message - and
hiding the write controls a read-only session cannot use - is issue #554's work, not this one's.

**And the fleet read is not attempted.** `GetDashboardSummary` branches on
`IBusinessScope.State == SupportReadOnly` and never calls `CalculateReorderNeeds` at all, so there is
no refused Nayax call, no resolved credential and nothing to swallow — which is why the decision is
taken from the published scope rather than from a second rule about who the caller is: it is the very
state `NayaxRequestCredentialProvider` refuses in, so "the dashboard degrades" and "Nayax is blocked"
cannot come to mean different things. The week's figures are in the response because the support set
grants `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, and that capability is still read through `CurrentCapabilities` on
the request rather than assumed, which is why there is one support-view shape and not a redacted pair
(see [Dashboard financial redaction](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527) for the member
shapes). No other degraded screen is part of #552; the rest are #329's.

**The capability set is written out, not derived.** `Inventory.Application.Access.SupportSessionAccessPolicy`
holds exactly thirteen capabilities — `Dashboard.View`, `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, `PickList.View`,
`Inventory.Operate`, `Purchasing.Operate`, `Expenses.Manage`, `Reports.View`, `Imports.Run`,
`SiteCommissions.Manage`, `Integration.Manage`, `Data.Repair`, `Roles.View`, `Business.Manage` — and
records the two it excludes beside them with their reasons: `Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults` guards
nothing but an edit, which is already refused, so granting it would be a grant with no effect; and
`Members.Manage` is the one capability whose *reads* are themselves private, because the members list
carries people's names and email addresses, which a supporter from outside the business does not see
in v1. It is deliberately not "every capability minus two": a capability a later deployment declares
must be added here by somebody who decided it belonged, rather than granted to a reader from outside
the business on the day it is invented. `CurrentCapabilities` is the one place that chooses between
this set and `RoleCapabilities`, so the capability an endpoint enforces, the one the dashboard decides
its shape from, and the list `GET /api/me/access` reports cannot come from different tables.

**What the caller is told.** `GET /api/me/access` in a session reports that set, a `null` role — the
administrator holds none, and reporting one would describe access nobody granted — and
`supportSession: { businessName, expiresAtUtc, readOnly: true }`. `readOnly` is stated rather than
implied so a client never has to infer that a support session means a read-only one, and the block
carries no session id, no business id and no actor. For an ordinary member the field is an explicit
`null`, so the shape is stable.

**One audit event per request, including the refused ones (issue #672).**
`InventoryApi.Auth.SupportSessionAuditMiddleware` emits a structured `ILogger` event for every
request made in a session, carrying the route **template**, the method, the status it was answered
with, the business id and the session row's own key — so a trail of requests reads as one session,
tied to the start event #550 recorded under that same key, which is where the administrator's
identity and their stated reason are. The template rather than the path is the point:
`api/Products/{id}` says which endpoint was reached without recording which record. It carries no
response body, no count, no query string and never the session id in either form. As for the three
platform trails beside it, **the log destination and retention period are platform configuration a
human must verify**.

**Coverage and final-outcome timing are both decided by where that middleware sits**, and it is the
outermost one in `Program.cs`: `SupportSessionAuditMiddleware` → `UseExceptionHandler` → `UseCors` →
`UseAuthentication` → `UseAuthorization` → `BusinessScopeMiddleware` → the endpoint. #551 emitted the
event from `BusinessScopeMiddleware`, and that position could answer neither half of what the trail
is for. A request the authorization middleware refuses — a capability the session's set does not
hold, or any method that is not a read — is refused *above* that middleware and never reached it, so
the attempts a support trail most needs to show were precisely the ones missing from it. And a
request whose endpoint throws unwinds *past* it before `UseExceptionHandler` maps the exception, so
the event recorded the `200` the response still held rather than the `403` or `500` the caller got —
a Nayax-backed read in a support view, which is a refusal by construction, was recorded as a success.
From the outermost position both are the same fact read once: every refusal is downstream, and by the
time `_next` returns the status is the one that was written. The event is still written in a
`finally`, so a request that failed outright is recorded rather than quietly left out, and there is
exactly one emitter, so exactly one event per request. A handled exception clears the endpoint before
the exception handlers run, so the route template is taken from the exception-handler feature on that
path rather than lost.

**Attribution is the resolved session and never the header.** The header's *presence* decides only
whether the question is worth asking — every ordinary request leaves this middleware on one
dictionary lookup — and the business id and session key come from `ISupportSessionAccessor`'s
verified answer: the presented id hashed and matched against an active, unexpired session of that
same caller's, for a business that is still `Active`. It is the same memoised answer the capability
handler and the published scope acted on, so what was authorised, what was read and what is recorded
cannot disagree. A presented session that is no longer usable and an ordinary member who sets the
header therefore record **nothing at all**: there is nothing verified to attribute the request to,
naming the business the caller *presented* would be trusting the header as evidence of itself, and
neither falls back to anybody's ordinary membership. Why such a session was refused is logged by the
accessor, for an operator, and the caller's own answer is the `403` above. Recording happens after
the caller has been answered and so can never change a response: a failure to record is logged as the
operational problem it is — a request missing from the trail — and is not turned into a second
failure for a caller who was already served.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/Access/SupportSessionAccessPolicyTests` pins the
thirteen capabilities literally from the agreed list, the two exclusions as exclusions, that the two
lists together are the whole vocabulary — so a capability declared later fails until somebody decides
which list it belongs in — and the read-method allowlist including a blank and an unknown verb.
`CurrentBusinessProviderTests` covers the support branch: the business answered without a membership
lookup, no resolution and no role, and a member's own resolution unchanged.
`NayaxRequestCredentialProviderTests` covers the block with the connection in each usable status, and
asserts the connection was never read at all. `GetCurrentAccessTests` covers the reported set, the
absent role and the session block. `GetDashboardSummaryRedactionTests` covers the financial figures
being decided from the support set rather than from a role, and
`GetDashboardSummarySupportViewTests` the degraded shape of issue #552: the two sections reported
unavailable with their reason, not one fleet call attempted, the local sections identical to the ones
a member of that business is given, a member's own request still reading the fleet and keeping its
shape, and a denied scope refused rather than degraded.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/BusinessScopeMiddlewareSupportSessionTests` is the middleware's own
decision: the published read-only scope and the supported business's time zone, the refusal with its
code before any business is resolved, the refusal *despite* a usable membership, a presented-nothing
request resolving its own membership, the refusal body naming nothing, and no profile refresh
scheduled. `BusinessCapabilityAuthorizationHandlerTests` is the complete per-capability matrix,
including the capabilities no endpoint declares yet: a read succeeding for each of the thirteen, both
exclusions refused even for a read, every non-read method refused with `read_only_support_session`,
`HEAD` allowed, a dead session refused with `support_session_ended` without touching the caller's own
membership, and a member's own decisions unchanged.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/SupportSessionReadOnlyPersistenceTests` is the
relational half over two businesses: the chosen business's rows and only those, another business's row
unreachable by its key, an insert, an update and a delete of the business's *own* data all refused, a
non-tenant-owned write refused too, an empty `SaveChanges` left alone, and a member's write
unaffected. `EfSupportSessionStoreTests` covers the new lookup: the caller's own active session found,
and nothing found for another administrator holding the same id, after expiry, after an end, for an id
nothing issued, or for a blank hash.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/Documents/SupportSessionReadOnlyDocumentStorageTests`
covers the document guard in both directions and under every other scope.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/SupportSessionRequestApiTests` is the HTTP boundary over the
real migration history, with two businesses and a Nayax client that resolves credentials before
recording a call — which is what makes "no Nayax call" mean something: only the chosen business
visible in both directions, every read in the set answered `200`, every write `403` with
`read_only_support_session`, both exclusions refused for a read with no member's name or address in
the body, the Nayax-backed reads `403` with `unavailable_in_support_view` and zero calls *beside* the
control that the same endpoints really do call Nayax for a member, the dashboard summary's degraded
shape asserted as its exact property sets with zero calls, its local sections still describing the
supported business, and the same summary keeping its normal shape and its real fleet call for that
business's Owner, an expired/ended/unknown/another
administrator's id refused, a deactivation mid-session closing the next request, the no-header request
falling to the administrator's own (absent) membership, a member unaffected with and without the
header, no membership written, the `/api/me/access` contract, and the audit event's fields and
absences — including, for issue #672, the refused attempts the trail has to carry and the status
each of them was actually answered with: a read outside the capability set and a refused write each
recorded once with their `403`, a Nayax-backed read recorded with the `403` its mapped exception
produced rather than a `200`, a read that found nothing recorded with its `404`, and an expired
session and a member who merely set the header each recorded as no session at all.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/SupportSessionAuditMiddlewareTests` is that middleware's own
decision, which only it can be asked directly: the status read after the rest of the pipeline has
finished with the response, the route template taken from the exception-handler feature once a
handled exception has cleared the endpoint, a request that threw recorded without the exception being
swallowed, an unusable session and a `NotRequested` one recording nothing, a request with no header
not asking the accessor at all, and a failure to record leaving the request untouched.
`DocumentStorageProviderSelectionTests` pins that both providers are reached through the
guard.

#### Super Admin role preview (issue #720)

A support session answers "what does this business's data look like?". This slice of
[#719](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/719), under #328, answers the other
question a Super Admin gets asked: "what does an Operator *see*?" A request carries
`X-Role-Preview: Owner`, `Manager` or `Operator`, and is answered exactly as that role would be
answered — the same pages refused, the same financial figures withheld.

**Who may send it, and how that is decided.** `InventoryApi.Auth.RequestRolePreviewAccessor` is the
only thing in the application that reads the header's value. It is the boundary implementation of one
narrow Application port, `IRolePreviewAccessor`, so the inner layers get the answer — which role —
and never the header. A preview is honoured only when `PlatformAdminPolicy` succeeds, re-evaluated on
**this** request rather than inferred from the fact that the authorization middleware ran, for the
same reason the support-session accessor and the diagnostics membership bypass re-evaluate theirs. It
is registered per request and memoised, so the middleware, the capability handler through
`CurrentCapabilities`, the use cases and the response projections all narrow by one answer and the
policy is evaluated once.

**It narrows by intersection, which is the whole safety argument.** `CurrentCapabilities` resolves
what the request would have been allowed — the caller's own role's capabilities, or the support
session's fixed set — and then applies `RolePreviewPolicy.Narrow`, an intersection with the previewed
role's own set. So a Manager previewing an Owner is still answered a Manager's capabilities; a
previewed request in a support session is answered the support set minus whatever the role lacks, and
`Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults` stays absent under a `Manager` preview because the support set never
held it; and a platform administrator with no usable membership and no session gets the refusal they
get without the header, because the base is resolved **before** the narrowing. `X-Role-Preview` never
takes part in resolving a business: there are still exactly three ways that happens (see
[Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)), and a preview is not one of them.

**It is read-only, at the HTTP boundary, on every endpoint.** `InventoryApi.Auth.RolePreviewMiddleware`
sits after `UseAuthentication()` and before `UseAuthorization()` and `BusinessScopeMiddleware`, and
refuses every previewed request whose method is not `GET` or `HEAD` with `403` and
`read_only_role_preview`. It is a middleware rather than a rule in the capability handler because the
rule has to hold on the endpoints that declare no capability too — the three membership-not-required
ones and the Super Admin's own write surface — and a rule added per endpoint class is a rule somebody
forgets to add to the next class. Its position is what makes "nothing is written" true of a refusal:
the endpoint never runs, no business is resolved, and issue #524's profile refresh is never even
scheduled. The method list is an allowlist of two, so a verb nobody thought of is refused by
construction. Every request without the header leaves this middleware on one dictionary lookup.

**Three refusals, in one precedence.** `role_preview_not_permitted` (`403`) first: the caller is not
the platform administrator, so the header means nothing on their request. Then `invalid_role_preview`
(`400`): the value is not exactly one of the three published role names — a different case, a stored
value like `20`, `Viewer`, a blank value, or the header sent twice — so the preview cannot be read.
Then a support session's own refusals, `support_session_ended` and `read_only_support_session`, which
are about a credential rather than a view and are made where they already were; the middleware steps
aside for exactly the requests they answer, which is a request that presented a session on an endpoint
where a session is honoured. Then `read_only_role_preview`, the one refusal that says the preview
itself was fine. Each body is RFC 7807 with the same `code`/`message` extensions the application's
other handled refusals carry, and names no business, actor, capability or presented value.

**Why a refusal and not a silent ignore.** The support-session header's value is deliberately *not
read* for a caller the platform-admin policy refuses: it is a credential, and reading it for an
ordinary member would let a session rule refuse a request that has nothing to do with sessions. This
header is the opposite shape — its only effect is to take access away — so ignoring it would answer a
client that believes it is previewing an Operator with everything an Owner may see. The same
reasoning makes `CurrentCapabilities` grant **nothing** for a preview state the boundary refused: that
path is unreachable behind the middleware, and its direction is what matters. An *unauthenticated*
request is left alone, so it keeps its ordinary `401` and the anonymous health probes are unaffected —
the same choice `BusinessScopeMiddleware` makes, and for the same reason: turning a `401` into a `403`
would hide the difference between "you are not signed in" and "you may not preview a role".

**Why it is server-side rather than built from `role-definitions.ts`.** The financial figures an
Operator must not see are withheld by the API, inside responses every role may request (see
[Operator-readable financial disclosure](#operator-readable-financial-disclosure-issue-700)), so a
preview assembled in the browser would still have received them. And `docs/architecture.md`'s own rule
for [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528)
and [The Roles page](#the-roles-page-issue-530) is that the frontend must not become a second role
source for a navigation or authorization decision. Deciding the preview once, in
`CurrentCapabilities`, means the capability policies, the reported list and the redaction follow it
together or not at all. The Angular half — the menu, the banner, the interceptor and the wording — is
the sibling task #721.

**Why there is no audit event and no persistence-level layer.** A preview grants nothing: every
previewed request is one the caller's own membership or support session already permitted, narrowed.
There is therefore nothing to record that the existing trails do not already cover — a previewed
request inside a support session is audited by `SupportSessionAuditMiddleware` exactly as any other
request in that session is. And the read-only rule is a safety rail rather than a security boundary,
because the administrator's own membership genuinely permits those writes; adding a
`SaveChanges`-level refusal for previews would imply a boundary that is not there. Both are recorded
decisions of #720, not omissions.

**No configuration, and one deployment note.** No migration, no data change and no new setting: the
header is honoured only for the `(tid, oid)` pair that is already configured. The API's CORS policy
(`Program.cs`) allows any request header, so no change was needed there; a reverse proxy or gateway
in front of the API that enumerates allowed headers must allow `X-Role-Preview` the same way it
allows `X-Support-Session`, which is deployed configuration outside this repository.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/Access/RolePreviewPolicyTests` pins the parse
(each exact name, and every rejected shape: wrong case, a stored value, an undeclared role, blank,
padded and comma-joined), the read-method allowlist including a blank and an unknown verb, the three
previewable roles, and the intersection over every base/preview pair there is — never adding a
capability the base lacked, never adding one the role lacks, and keeping the published order.
`CurrentCapabilitiesRolePreviewTests` is the narrowing itself: each preview role from an Owner base, a
preview of a *wider* role granting no more than the caller's own, both support-session bases, `Allows`
agreeing with the reported list for every capability, no header changing nothing, an unresolved
membership still refused with the header, an unusable preview granting nothing, and the one memoised
lookup. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Auth/RequestRolePreviewAccessorTests` is the boundary decision,
including the empty header value an HTTP client will not send, the header sent twice (with two roles
and with one), the policy asked before the value is read, an unauthenticated request asking for
nothing without evaluating the policy, no request at all, and the memoisation.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/RolePreviewApiTests` is the pipeline: `/api/me/access` under
each role with the stored role unchanged, a bare `403` for a capability the previewed role lacks
beside the same endpoints unrefused without the header, every non-read method refused with
`read_only_role_preview` on a capability endpoint, both membership-not-required writes and three
Super Admin writes — with the pending business still pending and the expense never recorded, beside
the control that the same write succeeds without the header — an ordinary Owner, Manager and stranger
refused with `role_preview_not_permitted` and no data served and no membership changed, every
undeclared value refused with `invalid_role_preview`, both precedence pairs, an unauthenticated
request's `401`, an administrator whose membership was deactivated refused identically with and
without the header, and the support-session composition in four directions including a write refused
as the session's own and a dead session still refused as ended.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/RolePreviewFinancialRedactionApiTests` is the figures: on the
dashboard summary, the machine list, the site list and the global stock history, a previewed Operator
is answered byte-for-byte what a **real** Operator of that business is answered and not what the
administrator is answered without the header, each surface's withheld fields are absent or `null`
rather than `0`, none of the four seeded amounts appears anywhere in a previewed body, and a `Manager`
preview is still given the figures.

### Switchable Admin option visibility (issue #873)

**One option, one shared answer, and it is about what is *offered* rather than about what anybody may do.** Historical GST Classification (see [Historical GST classification: Preview and Apply](#historical-gst-classification-preview-and-apply-issue-433)) is an occasional maintenance tool: once a business's historical purchase components have been classified, it is a page nobody needs again. Issue #873 lets a Super Admin stop offering it to everybody else while keeping it themselves.

**Who owns the setting.** The platform, not a business. It is one row of `PlatformOptionVisibility`, the **second platform table** in this schema (the first is `SupplierPreset`, issue #848): the answer is shared by the whole application, so there is no business whose key the row could carry, no query filter to apply and no ownership stamp to make. It is declared in `PlatformEntities` in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` beside the supplier presets, never in `DeliberatelyGlobalEntities`; see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64).

**Persistence and the default.** The row's key is the fixed constant `PlatformOptionVisibility.SingletonId` and the database assigns nothing, so two writes that both find no row collide on the primary key and `EfOptionVisibilityStore` resolves that into the update it should have been — one row, never two answers. **No row at all is the shipped state and means every option is offered**, which is why `AddPlatformOptionVisibility` creates the table and inserts nothing: every existing installation keeps exactly the visibility it has today until a Super Admin switches something off, and there is nothing to backfill. `Inventory.Application.PlatformOptions.OptionVisibilitySettings.Default` is the one statement of that default, applied by `GetOptionVisibility` alone — the adapter reports the absence of the row as `null`, because "nothing stored" and "this is the answer" are different facts.

**Who may change it.** Only the platform administrator. `PUT /api/super-admin/option-visibility` sits behind `PlatformAdminPolicy` and the `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute` marker — class 2 of the [endpoint authorization classes](#capability-authorization), the same as the diagnostics, Super Admin businesses, support-session and supplier-preset surfaces — and keeps `[Authorize]` and the `access_as_user` scope. The authority is the configured Entra `(tid, oid)` pair and nothing else: an Owner is refused exactly as any other member is, a member who presents an `X-Support-Session` id is still an ordinary member, and the shipped state (no administrator configured) means nobody can reach it at all. A role preview is refused by `RolePreviewMiddleware`, like every other write. The request carries a **denied** `BusinessScope`, so nothing tenant-owned is reachable; the write passes `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` because the entity is not `IBusinessOwned`, not because anything was relaxed. Each committed change emits one structured `ILogger` audit event with the acting administrator's `(tid, oid)`, the resulting state and the instant — and nothing about a business, a member or anybody's data, because the setting is about none of them. A refused write is not audited, because nothing happened.

**Who may read it, and the one boundary decision in this feature.** Every signed-in caller, through `GET /api/me/access`, which now reports `historicalGstClassificationVisible` beside the capability set. That is the **one documented exception** to "only the platform-admin surface reaches a platform table": an option the application has switched off has to stop being offered to the people it was switched off for, and the shell builds one menu from one read. It is as narrow as the exception can be — one boolean, one column, no caller-supplied input, read through the one-method `IOptionVisibilityStore` — and it publishes nothing about any business, any member or the supplier presets beside it. The invariant is recorded in AGENTS.md § Tenant ownership and data isolation; a second platform-table read from a member-facing endpoint is a boundary change needing its own reviewed issue.

**It is not a permission, and nothing about the tool's authorization changed.** `POST /api/admin/historical-gst-classification/preview` and `.../apply` keep requiring `Data.Repair` in both states, with the Preview-then-Apply fingerprint contract untouched, so the route entered directly still resolves and still refuses exactly whom it refused before. The reported capability set is byte-for-byte identical in both states. The switch therefore **hides a page rather than protecting one**, which is the same thing a capability-hidden menu entry has always done (see [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528)), and switching the option back on restores the entry only to members whose capabilities already allowed it — it grants nothing.

**What the frontend does with it.** `AccessService` carries the answer as `MemberAccess.optionVisibility` (`access/option-visibility.ts`), so it is invalidated and re-read on exactly the triggers the capability set is. `navigationFor` applies it in the same pass as the capability set: the one destination `switchableOptionRoute` names is left out while the setting says it is switched off and the viewer is not the platform administrator, and `optionSwitchedOff` is the one rule both the sidebar and the Admin hub render from. A Super Admin keeps the entry in both states, with a pill reading exactly **`Off`** immediately after `Historical GST Classification` and the sentence a screen reader is given beside it, in the sidebar and on the hub's card alike. An **unread or unreported** answer hides nothing and shows no pill — the fail-open rule an unreadable capability set already follows. A role preview withholds the administrator's own treatment, exactly as it withholds the `Super Admin` menu group (issue #721): what a preview shows is what the previewed role sees.

**The switch itself** is `HistoricalGstVisibilityToggleComponent`, composed into the Admin hub beside that card and offered to a Super Admin alone. It is a button rather than a checkbox on purpose: a checkbox carries its own state, which the browser flips on the click, so a refused save would leave it reading as the new setting while the server still holds the old one. What it displays is the state the server reported; a successful save reports the **server's** answer to the hub; a refused save changes nothing on screen, keeps the `Off` pill and the menu as the stored setting has them, and says that the change was not saved.

**The save and the re-read are one lifecycle, and nothing inside it invents an answer.** The two are not simultaneous: the `PUT` answers for the signed-in identity straight away, and the `GET /api/me/access` that publishes the new setting to every other surface takes a moment, keeps the previous answer published while it runs (a same-identity re-read does, by design — see [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528)), and may fail outright. `AdminComponent` therefore **holds the answer the save confirmed** and re-reads in the same step: the held answer is what the hub states — the card, the `Off` pill and the switch's own label all render from it — until the read carries one of its own, at which point the hub drops its copy; and it is dropped with the published answer when an identity change or a sign-out republishes `unread`, because a setting one administrator stored is not the next identity's answer. A read that could not answer leaves the held answer standing, says that the menus may still show the previous state, and offers reading the setting again. The **unknown** answers are rendered as themselves: the switch is offered only for `on` and `off`, and an `unread` or `unavailable` setting is described as being read or as unreadable, with no control offering to change it — the opposite of a value nothing reported is not what an administrator asked for. The navigation's fail-open rule is unchanged and is a different statement: leaving an entry in place over an unknown answer is the state the application was in before the setting existed, while telling the administrator the option is definitely `On` would be a claim nobody made. The pill and the withheld card still come from `optionSwitchedOff` alone, over that one resolved answer, so the two cannot disagree.

**Tests.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/PlatformOptions/OptionVisibilityTests` is the default rule and the write: nothing stored reads as offered and writes nothing, a stored answer is reported in both directions, a switch stores what was asked and audits it once with the actor's own identity, switching to the state already held is still one ordinary write, and an unidentifiable actor is denied with nothing written. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Controllers/SuperAdminOptionVisibilityApiTests` is the pipeline: the default with no row at all, the administrator switching it off and on with every member read reporting the stored answer from a separate request, an Owner, a Manager, an applicant and a stranger each refused without mutation, a refusal leaving an already-switched-off setting switched off, the unauthenticated `401` and the scope-less `403`, the support-session header refused as an ordinary member's, the audit event and the absence of one for a refused write — and that switching the option off leaves the Owner's own `POST .../preview` answering `200`, which is the test that fails if this switch ever starts restricting the tool. The frontend specs are `layout/navigation.spec.ts`, `layout/sidebar-nav.component.spec.ts`, `components/admin/admin.component.spec.ts`, `components/admin/historical-gst-classification/historical-gst-visibility-toggle.component.spec.ts`, `services/option-visibility.service.spec.ts` and `access/access.service.spec.ts`. The save-and-re-read lifecycle has its own block in the hub's spec — a stored `Off` kept accurate while the re-read has not answered and after it has failed, with the next switch asking for `on`; the hub handing the answer back to the shared read once it carries it; the held answer dropped when the published answer goes back to `unread`; and an unreadable or unread setting offering no switch and claiming nothing — and the toggle's own spec covers the four displayed states, the refused re-read's message and that applying an unknown setting submits nothing.

### Business subscriptions and plan entitlements (issue #966)

**One business, one plan, and a plan is not a role and not a provider connection.** Issue #966 — a child of #965 — defines the business-owned subscription state, the authoritative Free/Starter/Pro catalogue and the single effective-entitlement rule the enforcement (#967, #977), billing (#969), quota (#968) and frontend (#970, #979) tasks consume. It publishes that answer and **withholds nothing**: with the rollout setting off, which is the shipped state, every business is unrestricted and behaves exactly as it did before plans existed. What *does* withhold a feature once that setting is on is issue #967, which reuses this slice's one rule and adds no record of its own — see [Plan enforcement on reports and Nayax operations](#plan-enforcement-on-reports-and-nayax-operations-issue-967).

**The catalogue is compiled, priced in minor units, and stated once.** `Inventory.Domain.Subscriptions.PlanCatalogue` holds the three rows agreed on #965 — Free A$0 with 1 GB of attachments, Starter A$7 with 20 GB, Pro A$15 with 20 GB, five included connected machines and A$2 per additional one — where **1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes**, the decimal gigabyte issue #968's quota decision of 29 October 2026 fixed (the catalogue counted 2^30 until that decision; nothing had been enforced or charged against it, and the allowance and its enforcement had to count the same multiple) — each as an integer count of minor units with an explicit `AUD` currency beside it, because a price that reaches a payment provider, an invoice and a page must have exactly one representation and a binary floating-point price cannot be compared for equality. It is a compiled table rather than configuration or a row: a price change is a commercial decision with a deployment behind it, and a table a setting could edit is a table that can disagree with what a customer was charged. Whether the advertised prices include GST is an **open launch decision** on #965; the catalogue records the advertised amount and claims nothing about its tax treatment. Being above the included machine allowance is **billed, never blocked** — `AdditionalConnectedMachinePriceMinorUnits` is a price and no code may read it as a limit. `SubscriptionPlan` declares no `0`, for the reason `BusinessStatus` declares none, and `SubscriptionPlans.IsDeclared` is what every reader asks before treating a stored value as a plan.

**Two records per business, and neither ever writes the other.** `BusinessBillingSubscription` is the paid record, written **only** by verified billing events (#969) — this slice reads it and offers no write at all, so `IBillingSubscriptionStore` has one method. `BusinessPlanGrant` is the manual record, written **only** by a Super Admin (#982) or by the grandfathering step below, which is why `IManualPlanGrantStore`'s one write is "add the grandfathered grant unless this business already holds one". Both are ordinary **tenant-owned** tables — filtered, stamped and enforced centrally with nothing added — and the business is never a parameter on either port: it is whichever business the request or the command's own scope resolved, so no route, query, body, header or command line can choose whose plan is read or written. Keeping them apart is the decision of 29 October 2026: a Super Admin granting Pro must not be able to look like a paying customer, and a refund must not silently revoke a grant somebody gave for a reason. One "current plan" column could not keep those two facts apart. At most one subscription per business, and at most one *grandfathered* grant per business, are the database's rules — a unique index and a filtered unique index led by `BusinessId` — because the complimentary grants of #982 are legitimately a list.

**One rule, as a pure Domain function.** `Inventory.Domain.Subscriptions.EffectiveEntitlementPolicy.Decide` takes the rollout switch, the grandfathering marker, the business's grants, its subscription and the current instant, and returns what it may use. Nothing else decides it, and the order of the rules is the design:

1. the rollout setting **off** → unrestricted, whatever either record says, and nothing about the business is read at all;
2. on, but **no grandfathering completion marker** → still unrestricted, because enforcement cannot start before the businesses that were already trading hold their grant;
3. otherwise the effective plan is **the higher of** the active manual grant and the active paid plan (`SubscriptionPlans.Higher`);
4. nothing active → **Free** for paid features. Free's own local features are never locked, so failing closed here withholds nothing a business was doing before plans existed.

An **expired** period, a **cancelled** subscription, a **missing** record and a record this code cannot read all land on rule 4. "Cannot read" is specific and never guessed: a plan or status value this deployment does not declare, and a period whose end is at or before its start, make that record unusable — the policy drops it and reads the other one rather than substituting the nearest plan it knows or treating a malformed period as open-ended. A row that cannot be *interpreted* is Free; a database that cannot be *reached* is an error, exactly as it is for every other part of the access response, because answering Free over a transport failure would lock a paying business out of what it bought. Times are **UTC instants** and every period is **half-open** (`EntitlementPeriod`): it applies from its start instant inclusive and stops at its end instant exclusive, which is the convention the provider coverage ranges of issue #730 use and is what makes a renewal's new period neither overlap the old one nor leave a gap. When both records are active at the same plan the one that entitles for **longer** is reported, so `endsAtUtc` is the truth about when the plan is lost — a grandfathered Pro grant with no end date beside a Pro subscription ending next month keeps Pro after next month — and a genuine tie reports the record the business is paying for.

**The rollout switch is a startup decision, and off is the fail-closed direction.** `Subscriptions:EnforcementEnabled` is read once at startup by `ConfiguredSubscriptionEnforcementFlag` and published as `ISubscriptionEnforcementFlag`, exactly as `SelfServiceOnboarding:Enabled` is: only the composition root reads configuration, while the decision lives in the Application layer where the entitlement read and every later enforcement check consume it. An absent section, a blank value and an unparseable one are all **off**, because the answer that must never come from a mistyped setting is "start withholding features the business is using today". Nothing reads the setting any other way.

**Enforcement cannot start early, and the API says so.** While the setting is on and no completion marker exists, the policy treats every business as unrestricted *and* `SubscriptionEnforcementStartup` logs a startup **error** naming the missing `grandfather-business-plans` command and saying that nothing is enforced. It reports rather than refuses to start: the rule already fails safe, so what is missing in that state is visibility, and an API that stopped serving a working business over a plan rollout that has not begun would be the wrong trade.

**The grandfathering step is human-run, idempotent and restartable.** `grandfather-business-plans` (`InventoryApi/Bootstrap/BusinessPlanGrandfatheringCommand`, with the data half in `BusinessPlanGrandfatherer`) is the sixth human-invoked command, on the terms the others follow: a dry run writes **nothing at all** — not a grant, not the cutoff — `--apply` must be typed explicitly, and the command line takes no cutoff, plan, date or business, because one that could name a business would be a way to grant Pro to one that was not entitled to it. Its first apply records a **fixed cutoff** from the clock in the one-row `SubscriptionGrandfatherings` table; every later run reads that instant back and grants by it, and nothing in the adapter can move it. Eligibility is `GrandfatheringEligibilityPolicy`'s, from four stored facts: created before the cutoff, status `Active` or `Deactivated` at it, and **not decided at or after it** — that last clause is what makes "a pending application approved later starts on Free" survive a rerun, because by then its status is `Active` and its creation predates the cutoff. Each grant is one transaction that inserts only if that business holds no grandfathered grant, with the filtered unique index underneath it; the **completion marker is written last**, so an interrupted run leaves some businesses granted, the cutoff fixed and *nothing enforced*, and running it again finishes the rest by the same cutoff. A run after completion changes nothing and reports that. It grants and never revokes: there is no path that deletes, ends or rewrites a grant, so an end date an owner sets later survives a rerun untouched, and it writes no business's status and no subscription. It is deliberately **not** an unrestricted context (AGENTS.md § Tenant ownership and data isolation): `Businesses` and the grandfathering row carry no tenant query filter, so a **denied** scope reads both, and every grant is written through a context scoped to the one business it belongs to.

**The answer is published by extending `GET /api/me/access`, and by nothing else.** `GetEffectiveEntitlement` is a scoped use case that takes no identifier; `CurrentAccess.Entitlement` carries it and `MeAccessResponse.entitlement` publishes `enforced`, `plan` (the published name, or an explicit `null` while nothing is enforced), `source`, `endsAtUtc`, `attachmentStorage` (since issue #968) and `connectedMachines` (since issue #978). There is **no separate read endpoint and no caller-supplied business id**: the business is the one the request already resolved, so inside a [support session](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) the plan reported is the **viewed** business's own — that falls out of the resolution rather than being coded for — and a [role preview](#super-admin-role-preview-in-the-angular-app-issue-721) narrows role capabilities only and cannot reach the plan at all. It is computed per request with **no server cache**, so a grant that ends or a subscription that is cancelled applies on the next request; and while nothing is enforced the use case reads nothing about the business at all, so a deployment that has switched nothing on makes no extra query. The response carries no price — that is the catalogue's, published separately by `GET /api/me/plan-catalogue` and shown by the Plan page (see [The Plan page](#the-plan-page-issue-970)). It does carry one storage figure, added by issue #968: `entitlement.attachmentStorage`, which is this business's attachment usage, its plan's allowance and the warning state those two produce, and is an explicit `null` while nothing is enforced (see [Attachment storage quotas](#attachment-storage-quotas-issue-968)). That is reported here rather than from an endpoint of its own for the reason the plan itself is: a page that warns at 80% and explains a refused upload at 100% must read the figures and the plan in one answer. It also carries the **connected-machine allowance and count** since issue #978, because what a business is billed for above its allowance depends on a figure only the server can date; see [Counting connected machines](#counting-connected-machines-issue-978), and note that an allowance there is an amount to bill against and never a limit. `Plan` is `null` rather than `Pro` or `Free` while nothing is enforced: "unrestricted" is not a plan anybody is on, and reporting `Free` would lock a business nothing is enforcing anything for. **It is not a capability and implies none**: the capability set is identical whatever the plan says, and the frontend reads it as `MemberAccess.entitlement` (`access/entitlement.ts`) on exactly the triggers the capability set is re-read on, with an absent field read as "not known", which withholds nothing.

**The tenancy cost, stated plainly.** One platform table is added — `SubscriptionGrandfathering`, the **eleventh** entry in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests.PlatformEntities` — and two tenant-owned ones, `BusinessBillingSubscriptions` and `BusinessPlanGrants`, which are asserted as owned. The per-request read of the completion marker is the **fifth** member-facing read of a platform table and is bounded by this issue's own review: one question, through the one-method-per-question `ISubscriptionGrandfatheringStore`, no caller-supplied input of any kind, and what reaches the response is the single boolean `entitlement.enforced` — never the cutoff instant, the completion instant or the count of grandfathered businesses. Nothing cross-business is read: there is no `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement, no unscoped context and no raw SQL anywhere in this slice. The migration `AddBusinessSubscriptions` is additive, creates **no grant** and downgrades **no business**.

**Tests.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Subscriptions/EffectiveEntitlementPolicyTests` is the entitlement table row by row: the switch off and on, the grandfathering gate, each record alone, both together in either order, the equal-plan and tie rules, the half-open boundaries at the exact instant and one tick either side, and every way a record fails to entitle anything — expired, not started, cancelled, missing, malformed and undeclared. `PlanCatalogueTests` pins every price and limit literally; `GrandfatheringEligibilityPolicyTests` is the eligibility table, including the cutoff instant itself and the approved-after-the-cutoff case. `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/Subscriptions/GetEffectiveEntitlementTests` proves the use case reads nothing while nothing is enforced, and `Application/Access/GetCurrentAccessTests` that the plan travels with the capability set without changing it and that a role preview leaves it alone. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfSubscriptionStoreTests` is the relational half with two businesses: the fixed cutoff, the single completion, one grant written and a rerun writing nothing, an owner's end date surviving a rerun, a complimentary grant neither satisfying nor being changed by the step, and a denied scope and a support session each reading and writing nothing they should not. `AddBusinessSubscriptionsMigrationTests` is the upgrade: three empty tables, an untouched business, the two uniqueness rules read from the schema and the business column present on two tables and absent from the third. `Bootstrap/BusinessPlanGrandfatheringTests` is the command: the arguments, a dry run that writes nothing, the first apply, a rerun after completion, an interrupted run resumed after a new business has arrived and a pending one has been approved, and the printed report. `Bootstrap/SubscriptionEnforcementStartupTests` is the startup error, and `Adapters/Subscriptions/ConfiguredSubscriptionEnforcementFlagTests` the blank/unparseable/absent-is-off rule. `Controllers/MeAccessEntitlementApiTests` is the published contract over HTTP against a host with the setting **on** — the gate, Free, each record, the higher of the two, the cross-tenant case, the support session reporting the viewed business's plan and the role preview leaving it alone — while `Controllers/MeAccessApiTests` asserts the shipped state, where the field is present and reports that nothing is enforced.

### Counting connected machines (issue #978)

**A connected machine is a machine on the business's Nayax account, and the count is dated evidence rather than a live figure.** Issue #978 — a child of #965, after #966 — records how many machines each counted business's Nayax account holds, once per UTC day, so the extra-machine billing of #969 has something dated to charge from and the plan screens of #970 have something to show. The decision of 29 October 2026 is that a connected machine is a machine on the account **whether or not it is linked in this application**, because Nayax imports sales for every machine on the account either way; a manual machine has no provider id, is never in a fleet read, and can never be counted. Nothing is blocked or unlinked by any of this, and while the rollout setting of #966 is off — the shipped state — snapshots may be recorded but nothing is shown or billed.

**The source is the existing fleet read, and every machine it returns is counted.** `Inventory.Domain.ConnectedMachines.ConnectedMachineFleetRead` is the one place a fleet answer becomes a count: ids distinct, positive and ascending, so the same fleet always produces the same stored evidence. The read is `INayaxLynxClient.GetMachinesFreshAsync` — the whole-fleet Lynx call the machine list already makes, which passes no `ResultsLimit` and so returns the whole fleet — authenticated with the business's own stored credentials through `INayaxRequestCredentialProvider`, with the status gate and the support-session refusal applied exactly where every other ordinary Nayax call applies them (see [Per-business Nayax credentials](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520)). **The documented `MachineStatusBit` is deliberately not read.** The Lynx fleet contract (`GET /v1/machines`) declares it only as "a bit field indicating the status of the machine"; the one place the Nayax developer portal gives it a meaning is the create-machine guide, as a *request* value ("1 for active, 2 for inactive"), and nothing documents what a read returns for a machine that was removed. #978's criterion permits excluding an inactive or removed machine "only after confirming from the actual fleet endpoint's response and the Nayax docs that the field is returned and what it means", and that confirmation is not available for a read — so the application does not deserialise the field at all and counts every machine returned (AGENTS.md § Nayax contract verification). Excluding one later is a change in its own right with the then-confirmed contract behind it.

**The account series is what a count belongs to, and it is never a credential.** `BusinessNayaxConnection.AccountSeries` starts at `1` for the first account a business stores credentials for and moves to the next value only when a **different** operator id is saved, with `AccountSeriesChangedAtUtc` recording when. It is deliberately not `CredentialRevision`, which counts every save: a rotated token for the same account is the same fleet, and billing evidence must not be split by an operator pasting a fresh token. It is deliberately not the operator id either, so a snapshot can name the account it belongs to while carrying no part of a credential. The comparison and the write are **one `UPDATE`** in `EfNayaxConnectionStore.SaveCredentialAsync`, evaluated against the row being replaced, so "is this the same Nayax account?" is answered by the stored row rather than by a value the process read earlier. A permission test or re-test changes the status and never the series. The additive migration gives every existing connection series `1` with no changed instant, so the account a business is already on is its first series.

**One snapshot per business, UTC day and series, and the claim is the database's.** `BusinessConnectedMachineSnapshots` is an ordinary **tenant-owned** table — filtered, stamped and enforced centrally with nothing added — holding the UTC date, the series, the count, the provider machine ids counted, when the read was taken and whether it was complete. The unique index on `(BusinessId, SnapshotDateUtc, AccountSeries)` is the whole mechanism: the app's refresh path and the daily job both record through one insert-if-absent operation (`IConnectedMachineSnapshotStore.TryRecordAsync`, one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction with that index underneath it), so when two complete reads race the first to commit wins and the other **discards its snapshot without an error and without a retry**. The rows are **append-only**: the port offers no update or delete, and `ConnectedMachineSnapshotEnforcer` refuses every modified or deleted row on `SaveChanges`, because #969 charges from these rows and a count that can change after it was charged is not evidence. A correction is a later day's row. `ReadWasComplete` is always `true` on a stored row — an incomplete read stores nothing — and is recorded rather than assumed so a future decision to keep partial evidence could not be made invisibly.

**An account change keeps both accounts' evidence.** When the series moves, the previous series' snapshots are untouched and the new series may record its own snapshot the same day, so one day can hold one row per series. `ConnectedMachineSnapshotPolicy.Latest` is the one place "the day's count is the **later series'** snapshot" lives — later date wins, and on one date the later series wins — and both the entitlement read and #969 are meant to read it rather than write that rule a second time.

**A snapshot is stamped with the account that authenticated the fleet read it came from, and the series travels out of that request rather than being looked up again.** An Owner can save a different Nayax account while a fleet request is in flight, so "which account is stored now" and "which account authenticated this request" are two different facts, and only the second one attributes evidence. The series is therefore read in the **same statement** as the status, the operator id, the ciphertext and the revision (`EfNayaxConnectionStore.FindForOperationCoreAsync`), carried on `NayaxConnectionSnapshot.AccountSeries` and `NayaxRequestCredential.AccountSeries` — non-secret, never the operator id or any part of a token — and handed back with the fleet by `INayaxFleetProvenanceClient.ReadFleetFreshAsync`, which `NayaxLynxClient` and `CachingNayaxLynxClient` both implement. It is the same shape, and the same reasoning, as `INayaxLynxCachedReadClient`: one credential resolution per call decides the request *and* the thing derived from it, so the count of connection reads per Nayax call is unchanged at one (`NayaxParallelCredentialAccessTests`). `ConnectedMachineFleetRead.AccountSeries` then carries it into the Application layer, and `RecordConnectedMachineSnapshot` will stamp a row with nothing else. Three consequences follow, and together they are the whole guarantee: a superseded in-flight answer is recorded as **its own** account's evidence, which is what it truthfully is; it can **never** claim the replacement account's day, because the claim it makes names its own series — so there is no superseded-response discard to make atomic, the claim and the provenance being one value; and a later valid read of the new account therefore still records its own snapshot that same day. A read whose provenance is unknown records **nothing** (`ConnectedMachineSnapshotOutcome.AccountUnknown`): evidence that cannot name its account is not evidence, and in this application only the end-to-end testing stub, which reaches no Nayax account at all, answers without one. Do not reintroduce a second connection read as the source of a snapshot's series on either path.

**Two ways in, one writer.** `Inventory.Application.ConnectedMachines.RecordConnectedMachineSnapshot` is the only writer, takes no business, date, series or count from a caller, and decides every skip before anything expensive happens: the connection first — which answers "may this business's fleet be read at all?", and **only** that, never "which series would this belong to?" — then the day's existing claim for the read's own series, then the plan records. On the job's path the series that gate returns is used for one more thing, the cheap "already counted today?" skip that decides whether to spend a call at all, and it is replaced by the read's own series the moment the fleet answers. The **refresh path** is `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.ConnectedMachineCountingNayaxLynxClient`, the decorator the composition root puts outside the machine-list cache of [issue #840](#the-machine-list-cache-issue-840): a complete *fresh* fleet read any feature makes becomes the day's evidence, which is why the count costs **no extra Nayax call on a page load** and why a feature that reads the whole fleet tomorrow is counted without being changed. A **cached** machine list is not recorded — an answer up to ten minutes old is not a read of the account — and a snapshot that cannot be written is logged and abandoned rather than failing the caller's sales sync or dashboard refresh. That decorator asks the client it wraps for the fleet **and** its account series and hands both to the recorder; it reads no connection itself, because it has no second opinion about the account to give. The **job path** reads the fleet itself through `IConnectedMachineFleetReader`, implemented over the *inner* typed client so the job's read is not recorded twice over and there is no resolution cycle; the refusals are identical, because they belong to the credential provider rather than to either decorator, and that adapter carries the request's own series out in the same way.

**Which businesses are counted, with the rollout gates set aside.** `ConnectedMachineSnapshotPolicy.PlanOnRecord` asks `EffectiveEntitlementPolicy.Decide` itself what the business's records support — so "the higher of the active grant and the active paid plan", the half-open periods and every way a record fails to entitle anything stay in one place — and sets aside only the rollout switch and the grandfathering marker, because evidence has to accrue **before** enforcement is switched on. `RecordsSnapshots` then asks for at least `Pro`, the one plan with a Nayax connection and an included allowance. It grants nothing and withholds nothing: no feature is offered or refused on the strength of that answer.

**The daily job is a CLI mode, scheduled by a human.** `snapshot-connected-machines` (`InventoryApi/Bootstrap/ConnectedMachineSnapshotCommand`, with the data half in `ConnectedMachineSnapshotJob`) is the eighth human- or scheduler-invoked command, on the terms [Implementing a background workload under the current decision](#implementing-a-background-workload-under-the-current-decision) states for scheduled work: the work is an Application use case, the adapter is thin, and the schedule is the App Service WebJob mechanism of issue #333 rather than a second host. It takes **no arguments at all** — no business, date, series, count or cap — considers only `Active` businesses in business-id order, refuses to run against a schema with pending migrations, makes at most `ConnectedMachineSnapshotRunLimits.MaxFleetReadsPerRun` (100) fleet reads and **logs** reaching that bound, and catches each business's failure on its own so one outage is one business's outage. There is no retry beyond the Nayax client's own bounded resilience. Its failure-recovery mode is **self-healing**: a missed run leaves yesterday's count as a stale figure until the next successful one, and a second run on the same day records nothing because a business already counted today costs no call. It is deliberately **not** an unrestricted context (AGENTS.md § Tenant ownership and data isolation): `Businesses` carries no tenant query filter, so the enumeration reads it under a **denied** scope, and every snapshot is recorded — and every credential resolved — through a scope resolved to the one business it belongs to. **Putting it on a schedule is an operator step and is not part of this change.**

**What `GET /api/me/access` publishes.** `EffectiveEntitlement.ConnectedMachines` carries `includedByPlan`, `purchasedAdditional`, `allowance`, `count`, `asOfDateUtc`, `ageInDays`, `state`, `unavailableReason` and `machinesOverAllowance`, and is `null` while nothing is enforced — in that state nothing about the business is read at all, which is #966's rule. `ConnectedMachineCountPolicy` is the one rule behind every one of those fields: an unusable connection (`NotConfigured`, `NeedsAttention`) is `Unavailable` with its reason and makes no call; a snapshot of a superseded series is `AccountNotYetCounted` rather than this account's count; today's snapshot is `Current` and an older one stays the count as `Stale` with its age; and `count` and `machinesOverAllowance` are **`null`, never `0`**, when there is no count, because "none over" and "not known" are different answers. The allowance is `PlanCatalogue`'s `IncludedConnectedMachines` plus the extras the business bought — `0` until #969 records a purchase, since an unrecorded purchase is none rather than a guess — and `machinesOverAllowance` is **an amount to bill, never a limit**: nothing reads it to refuse linking, importing, a report or the pick list. The frontend type (`access/entitlement.ts`) carries the field so the contract is stated once; the Plan page is what now displays it (see [The Plan page](#the-plan-page-issue-970)).

**The tenancy and contract cost, stated plainly.** One tenant-owned table is added and asserted as owned — no platform table, no `IgnoreQueryFilters`, no unscoped context, no raw SQL in any adapter of this slice — and two columns are added to an existing tenant-owned one. The migration `AddConnectedMachineSnapshots` is additive, creates no snapshot (nothing is counted by a migration) and changes no credential, status or revision. The only API change is the additive `entitlement.connectedMachines` object on an endpoint that already existed.

**Tests.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/ConnectedMachines/ConnectedMachineFleetReadTests` pins what is counted — every machine returned, each one once, in one stored order, nothing for an entry that identifies no machine, and the stored id form round-tripping — and `ConnectedMachineCountPolicyTests` and `ConnectedMachineSnapshotPolicyTests` are the two decision tables row by row, including the two-series day, the superseded series, the stale age, the allowance with purchased extras and the status gate. `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/ConnectedMachines/RecordConnectedMachineSnapshotTests` is the writer: what is stored, the incomplete read that stores nothing, every skip happening before the Nayax call, the day already claimed reading no plan, and the lost race discarded without an error. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfConnectedMachineSnapshotStoreTests` is the relational half with two businesses — the claim, the unique constraint refusing a second row, one day holding two series, the latest-day read, the denied scope and the support session each writing nothing, and the append-only refusals; `AddConnectedMachineSnapshotsMigrationTests` is the upgrade, including an existing connection landing on series 1 with every credential fact untouched; `EfNayaxConnectionStoreTests` covers the series itself (same account keeps it, a different account moves it and records when, a status result leaves it alone). `Infrastructure/Nayax/ConnectedMachineCountingNayaxLynxClientTests` is the refresh path — a fresh read recorded, a cached list not, a failure to record leaving the caller unaffected, and each read offered under the account that authenticated it — and `Bootstrap/ConnectedMachineSnapshotJobTests` the job's bounds, its active-only enumeration, its per-business failure isolation and its refusal against a pending schema. **The account attribution has its own deterministic regressions on both paths.** `RecordConnectedMachineSnapshotTests` switches the stored account from either side of a read and asserts the series the row lands under, that the other account's day stays free, that a token rotation starts no new series, and that a read with no provenance records nothing; `Infrastructure/Nayax/ConnectedMachineSnapshotAccountSwitchTests` is the same thing end to end over relational SQLite with the real connection store, credential provider, AES-GCM decryption, Lynx client, machine-list cache and daily claim — an HTTP handler **pauses** the fleet response, a second simulated request saves a different Nayax account, and only then does the answer arrive, with the bearer header asserted so the test says which account each request really used. `EfNayaxConnectionStoreTests` covers the series on the per-operation read itself (the same statement as the status and token, kept across a token rotation, moved by a different account, and still reported beside a refused status that decrypts nothing), `CachingNayaxLynxClientTests` that a fresh fleet read reports the series of the one credential it resolved, and `NayaxRequestCredentialProviderTests` that the series travels out with the credential. `Controllers/MeAccessEntitlementApiTests` is the published contract over HTTP, and `Controllers/MeAccessApiTests` asserts that the shipped state publishes the field as `null`.

### Super Admin sets a business's plan (issue #982)

**One record, one decision, and no billing.** Issue #982 — a child of #965, after #966 — is how the
platform owner gives a business Starter or Pro **without charging it**: grandfathering, a trial, a
pilot site, a complimentary plan. It writes the business's **manual grant** of #966 and nothing else.
No payment, price, billing status or subscription field is on this surface at all, the business's
`BusinessBillingSubscription` is neither read to validate a grant nor written, and
`EffectiveEntitlementPolicy` remains the one rule that reads both records — so a granted plan can
never look like a paid one, and a refund can never revoke a grant somebody gave for a reason
(the decision of 29 October 2026 on #965).

**This is an owner-approved amendment of the platform-admin write rule, recorded in AGENTS.md § Super
Admin businesses API.** Before it, the platform-admin surface wrote a business's lifecycle status,
one membership's activation and an approval's supplier copies, "and nothing else". The amendment is
exactly the manual-grant write described here: one tenant-owned record of one business, through its
**own** narrow port, with the directory store left exactly as it was.

```text
GET  /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/plan-grant       the grant and the revision to present
PUT  /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/plan-grant       { plan, endsOnUtc?, reason, revision }
POST /api/super-admin/businesses/{businessId}/plan-grant/end   { reason, revision }
```

**Authorisation is the other Super Admin surfaces', unchanged.** `SuperAdminPlanGrantsController`
carries `[Authorize]`, `[Authorize(Policy = PlatformAdminPolicy.Name)]`,
`[RequiredScope("access_as_user")]` and `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute` — class 2 of the five
ways an endpoint may declare its authorization, with both halves required and no new class and no new
marker. A business Owner, Manager or Operator is refused exactly as any other member is, because a
business role is not platform authority; a **role preview** is refused by `RolePreviewMiddleware` like
every other write, with `read_only_role_preview`; and a member who presents an `X-Support-Session`
header is still an ordinary member and is refused by the platform-admin policy. A **support session**
therefore cannot change a grant from either direction: the administrator reaches this surface as
themselves, and a session grants read-only access to a business rather than authority over it.

**Its own port, deliberately.** `Inventory.Application.PlatformPlans.IPlatformPlanGrantStore` has
four methods over exactly two tables — `BusinessPlanGrants` and `BusinessPlanGrantAudits` — and
`IPlatformBusinessDirectoryStore` is untouched: that store reaches a business's lifecycle status and
its memberships and no tenant-owned row, and widening it to write one would have made the directory
the thing that writes a business's own data. No method takes a predicate, a column list, a page, a
sort, or a plan applied to several businesses at once, and `ManageBusinessPlanGrant` is the one use
case over it.
