**The authoritative read, the revision comparison and the write are one operation.** Each decision
opens `EfPlatformPlanGrantStore`'s `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, re-reads the **business row** and
its grant inside it, compares the revision the caller presented with the stored one, writes the grant
and its audit row in one `SaveChanges`, and commits. The read before the transaction decides nothing
— it exists to answer `404` without taking a write lock on the caller's behalf. `BusinessPlanGrant`
gains one additive column, `Revision`, which starts at `0` for every row written before this surface
existed (the grandfathered grant included); a write presents the revision it read, and anything else
is `409` with `ManualPlanGrantPolicy.StaleRevisionMessage` — so two Super Admin tabs cannot overwrite
each other, and the later one is told to reload rather than silently winning. Because the comparison
happens under the write lock, a grant committed between the caller's read and their write makes them
stale too.

**The grant and the record of who gave it commit together.** `BusinessPlanGrantAudits` is an additive,
append-only tenant-owned table written in the **same** `SaveChanges` as the grant: the actor's Entra
`(tid, oid)`, the business, which kind of decision it was, the plan it moved from and to, the end
instant, the revision, the reason as typed and the instant. There is no update and no delete path. One
structured `ILogger` event is emitted beside it, after the commit, as every platform-admin action
emits one — and `PlatformPlanGrantAuditEntry` has **no field for a reason or a name of any kind**, so
the administrator's prose cannot reach a log pipeline even from a sink that printed the whole entry.
A refused decision writes neither row and logs nothing, because nothing happened.

**What the rules are, and where they live.** `Inventory.Domain.Subscriptions.ManualPlanGrantPolicy` is
the whole of them: Starter and Pro are grantable and **Free is not** (a business with no record is
already on Free, so a Free grant would be a row that entitles nothing); a reason is required and is
stored; and the end **date** an administrator chooses is converted once, here, into the exclusive end
instant a half-open `EntitlementPeriod` stores — a grant ending on 31 December covers every moment of
it — with the same rule read backwards to show the date again. A date already over is `400`, because
it would entitle nothing at any instant. A plan arrives as its published **name** and
`SubscriptionPlans.TryParse` refuses a number, for the reason `BusinessRoles.TryParse` does: a caller
names a plan and never supplies a stored representation. Deliberately **not** invented here: any rule
about the business's lifecycle status. A grant may be decided for any business that exists, because
the issue states none and a platform-admin surface is not the place to invent one.

**Ending a grant deletes nothing.** It records the end instant on the row, keeping the plan, the start
and the reason it was granted for, and records the ending reason on the audit row — so the trail of
what was granted and why survives, and the business falls back to whatever else entitles it, its paid
subscription or Free, on its members' next read of `GET /api/me/access`. Ending a grant the business
does not hold, or one that has already ended, is `409` rather than a second write that would move an
end instant that already happened.

**The tenancy cost, stated plainly.** A platform-admin request carries a **denied**
`BusinessScope`, and a manual grant is tenant-owned, so this surface needs two narrow, reviewed
openings and has exactly two:

- **One `IgnoreQueryFilters` path**, the **fourth** in the application (see [the reviewed paths
  above](#tenant-ownership-issue-64), now four). `EfPlatformPlanGrantStore` reads
  `BusinessPlanGrants` through one `IQueryable` pinned to the single business id the route named
  *and* to `ManualPlanGrantSource.Complimentary`, projecting the plan, the period, the reason, the
  revision and the instant. The grandfathered grant is excluded by that predicate, so it is not
  readable, not comparable against and not writable here. The alternatives are the ones issue #544
  already rejected: an unscoped context in a request path hands one adapter every tenant-owned table
  at once, and resolving each business into the request scope makes a platform decision impersonate a
  tenant.
- **One write lease**, the **third** denied-scope write exception after issue #849's supplier
  provisioning and issue #941's collector matching, and narrower than the rule rather than a way
  around it.
  `AppDbContext.BeginPlanGrantWrite(businessId)` is `internal`, its only caller is that adapter, it
  may be taken only while the scope is `Denied` (so no member's request and no support session can
  open one), only one may be open at a time and never beside a provisioning or matching lease, and
  while it is open `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` accepts
  **two entity types for one business** — an insert or update of that business's `BusinessPlanGrant`
  and an insert of its `BusinessPlanGrantAudit` — and refuses every other tenant-owned write, every
  delete and every other business exactly as it does without a lease. The business id is the key of
  the row the decision's own transaction read, never the route value. Nothing becomes *readable*
  through the lease: the query filters do not consult it.

What the business's own members then read is unchanged by all of this: the grant is an ordinary
tenant-owned row, `IManualPlanGrantStore` reads it through the central filters, and
`GET /api/me/access` reports the effective plan exactly as #966 defines it.

**Tests.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Subscriptions/ManualPlanGrantPolicyTests` is the rule table —
the grantable plans, Free and an undeclared value refused, the reason, and the end-date conversion at
the day boundary and one tick either side; `PlanCatalogueTests` covers the name parsing, including
that a number is refused. `Inventory.UnitTests/Application/PlatformPlans/ManageBusinessPlanGrantTests`
is the use case with a fake port: what a create, a change and an end write and audit, the
re-read-inside-the-transaction order, every refusal writing nothing and committing nothing, a grant
committed between the two reads making the caller stale, and a decision touching only the business it
names. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfPlatformPlanGrantStoreTests` is the
relational half with two businesses: the grant and its audit row committed together and neither
surviving an uncommitted transaction, the grandfathered grant invisible, another tenant-owned row
refused while the lease is open, another business's grant row refused, a denied scope without a lease
refused, a member's and a support session's scope unable to open one at all, and the business's own
members reading what the platform wrote through the ordinary path.
`AddPlanGrantRevisionAndAuditMigrationTests` is the upgrade: the audit table arrives empty and the
grant that already existed keeps everything and gains revision `0`.
`Controllers/SuperAdminPlanGrantsApiTests` is the published contract over HTTP: every business role,
an anonymous caller, the administrator without the delegated scope, a member presenting a session id
and the administrator in a role preview each refused on all three endpoints with nothing written; the
grant, the change, the end, the end-date boundary, the stale revision `409`, the `400`s, the unknown
business `404`; the audit row committed with the grant and the log entry carrying no reason; and the
granted business reading its new plan through `GET /api/me/access` while the other business still
reads Free.

### Attachment storage quotas (issue #968)

**The problem this solves is that a file and a row cannot be written in one transaction.** A purchase document and an expense attachment live in document storage — the filesystem, or Azure Blob — and the record that refers to it lives in SQLite, so a crash between the two leaves either a file nothing refers to or a row pointing at bytes that were never written. Issue #968 — a child of #965, depending on #966 and #976 — measures a business's attachment storage against its plan's allowance across that gap, and does it without ever preventing a transaction from being recorded.

**Usage is derived from records, never counted in a column.** A business's usage is the **stored bytes of the attachments its active purchase and expense rows refer to, plus its unexpired upload reservations** (decided 29 October 2026 on #965). `AttachmentStorageUsageQuery` is the one statement of that — two `SUM`s over `Receipts.FileSizeBytes` and `OperatingExpenses.AttachmentFileSizeBytes` where a stored name is present, and one over the reservations that have not expired — and both halves run through the ordinary tenant query filters, so there is no business parameter anywhere on the path. Deriving it has a consequence worth stating: deleting a purchase, an expense or an attachment **releases its bytes when that change commits**, with nothing to decrement, nothing to drift and nothing to repair if a decrement were ever missed. Two things are deliberately **not** charged to a business: a physical file no record refers to (an orphan, which the business can neither see nor delete, so billing it would be a bill it cannot settle) and an attachment whose size was never recorded (counting a number nobody measured would be a guess). The reconciliation command below is what reports both.

**What an upload costs is one Domain rule.** `Inventory.Domain.Attachments.AttachmentStorageQuotaPolicy` owns every decision: the chargeable bytes, whether they fit, the warning state and the reservation lifetime. A **new** attachment costs its whole size; a **replacement** costs only its net increase, `max(0, new − old)`, because the old file's bytes stop counting in the same transaction that points the row at the new one. The limit is **inclusive** — an upload that lands exactly on the allowance succeeds and the next byte does not — and an upload that costs **nothing always fits**, whatever the business already uses, which is what keeps a same-size-or-smaller replacement working at or over capacity. The allowance itself is the effective plan's `AttachmentStorageLimitBytes` from the #966 catalogue, reached through the one translation `AttachmentStorageAllowance.For`; nothing restates a number. The warning state is `Normal` under 80%, `Warning` from 80% and `Full` at or over the allowance, decided by cross-multiplication rather than by a computed percentage so it turns on the exact byte at every plan limit.

**The reservation protocol is what makes the gap safe.** Before a single byte is written, `AttachmentQuotaGuard` — the one place every upload path asks for room — reads the allowance and asks `IAttachmentQuotaStore` to reserve the chargeable bytes. `EfAttachmentQuotaStore` does that inside one `SqliteWriteLockTransaction` (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`): the usage read, the comparison with the allowance and the reservation's insert are one operation, so **two concurrent uploads cannot both pass a check only one of them fits** — the second waits, reads the first one's committed reservation and is refused. A refused reservation writes nothing at all. On success the reservation is handed to the write, which **consumes it in the same transaction as the row** (`AttachmentQuotaCommit`), so the reserved bytes become the attachment's own recorded size atomically and a rollback leaves both exactly as they were. Whenever the row does not end up referring to the file — a refusal, a conflict, a failure, an unknown record — the use case removes the bytes it wrote **and** releases the reservation.

**Reservations expire, which is the crash recovery.** A reservation stops counting 30 minutes after it was taken (`AttachmentStorageQuotaPolicy.ReservationLifetime`), and expiry is **read rather than swept**, so a process that died between writing a file and recording the row stops holding the business's storage on its own; reserving also tidies that business's expired rows away, which changes no answer. An expired reservation is never committed on trust: the commit re-validates the quota **inside its own transaction**, from the upload's own size and the attachment's **current** size — the full size for a new attachment, the recomputed net increase for a replacement. Still fits: the row commits normally. No longer fits: the write is refused with `AttachmentStorageQuotaExceededException`, nothing about the row changes, and the caller removes the file it had written (a failed removal is left for reconciliation rather than hiding the failure that produced it).

**Two replacements of one attachment cannot both take credit for the old file.** The operating-expense update is the one path that replaces an attachment — a purchase's document is attach-only-if-empty (issue #976), decided with the write lock held — so `OperatingExpenses.AttachmentVersion` exists for exactly that race. A replacement's reservation records the version (and the size) it was computed against; the commit points the row at the new file **only while the expense is still at that version**, read inside the same `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, and increments it. The loser is refused with `AttachmentReplacementConflictException` → `409` with a stable sentence, its row change is not made, its reservation is released and its file is removed, so exactly one replacement wins and the final usage is the winning file's size alone. The column is read by nothing else: it is not a row version for the expense's other fields, which are last-write-wins exactly as they were.

**Every upload path checks, and only the document is ever refused.** The four are purchase create (`UploadPurchase`), "add a document later" (`AttachPurchaseDocument`, issue #976), and the operating-expense multipart create and update. A refusal is about the *attachment*: a purchase or an expense can always be recorded without one, so the API answers `400` with a sentence that says so and the record is still savable. At or over capacity — including after a **downgrade** that leaves a business above its new allowance — viewing, downloading and deleting attachments, and creating and editing records without uploads, all keep working, and **nothing is ever deleted automatically**. While no plan is enforced (the rollout setting off, or the grandfathering step not completed, which is the shipped state) the guard reserves nothing, writes nothing and refuses nothing, so every upload behaves exactly as it did before quotas existed.

**The scoped quota contract.** `GET /api/me/access` reports `entitlement.attachmentStorage` — `usedBytes`, `limitBytes` and the published `warningLevel` name — for the business the request already resolved, and `null` while nothing is enforced, because then there is no allowance to be a percentage of and no aggregate runs at all. There is no separate read endpoint, no caller-supplied business id and no cache. Inside a [support session](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) the figures are the **viewed** business's own, which falls out of the resolution; that session can read them and can upload nothing, because every write is already refused in that state. The new `AttachmentStorageReservations` table is ordinary **tenant-owned** data — stamped, filtered and enforced centrally with nothing added — so a reservation is invisible and unreleasable from any other business. `RecordId` on it is deliberately **not** a foreign key: the record it names may never come into existence, and one that is deleted while an upload is in progress must stay deletable.

**Reconciliation is human-run, idempotent and never deletes.** `reconcile-attachment-storage` (`InventoryApi/Bootstrap/AttachmentStorageReconciliationCommand`, with the engine in `Inventory.Infrastructure.Documents.Reconciliation.AttachmentStorageReconciler`) is the seventh human-invoked command and insists on `--dry-run` or `--apply`, as `migrate-documents` does. It reports, **per business**, the records whose file is missing, the records whose size was never recorded, and the stored files no record refers to; an apply writes **one** thing — a size filled in from the stored file itself — and nothing else. An orphan file is reported, never removed: deleting a business's receipt is not recoverable by rolling a transaction back, and automatic orphan deletion is explicitly out of this issue's scope. A size that cannot be read from storage stays unknown and is reported as a missing file rather than guessed at. It reads what storage holds through `IAttachmentFileInventory`, which is deliberately **not** part of `IDocumentStorage` — that port is one document, by the stored name on a tenant-owned record, inside the business a request resolved, while this is every file across businesses — and which has no write or delete method at all, so "the reconciliation never deletes" is a property of the seam rather than a promise. Blob storage is per business by prefix, so it attributes an orphan to a business; the filesystem layout is one folder per category for every business, so its orphans are reported separately rather than charged to a business that may not own them. The command takes the unrestricted scope explicitly (AGENTS.md § Tenant ownership and data isolation), because a file is an orphan only if **no** business refers to it.

**Tests.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Attachments/AttachmentStorageQuotaPolicyTests` is the arithmetic row by row: a new attachment's full size, a replacement's net increase in both directions, the exact-limit boundary and the byte past it, the zero-cost upload at and over capacity, the 80% threshold at a real plan limit, and the expiry instant itself. `Application/Attachments/GetAttachmentStorageStatusTests` is the reported contract — nothing read while nothing is enforced, each plan's own allowance, the three warning states and the over-allowance case reported as it is rather than clamped — and `AttachmentQuotaUploadPathTests` is each upload path's composition: refused before anything reaches storage, the record still recordable without a document, the reservation reaching the write, and the bytes and the room both released on a refusal, a conflict, an expired-reservation refusal and a failure. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/AttachmentStorageQuotaPersistenceTests` is the relational half with two businesses: usage from the records, an unrecorded size charged as nothing, an unexpired reservation counted and an expired one not, the exact-limit reservation, the replacement credit, the over-allowance replacement, expired rows tidied, cross-business invisibility, the reservation consumed with the row, the expired reservation that still fits and the one that no longer does, the stale-version conflict, and a delete releasing its bytes. `AttachmentStorageQuotaConcurrencyTests` is the two races against a real database file with one connection each — two uploads where only one fits, and the **regression test this issue asks for by name**: two replacements of one attachment at full storage, exactly one committing, the loser refused with a conflict and the final usage equal to the winning file's size. `Infrastructure/Documents/AttachmentStorageReconcilerTests` is the command's engine: a clean business, the three disagreements per business, an apply that fills sizes and a rerun that finds nothing, an unknown size whose file is missing left unknown, and the unattributable orphan. `AddAttachmentStorageQuotaMigrationTests` is the upgrade from the migration before it (`AddConnectedMachineSnapshots` since issue #978), the preserved attachments, the version starting at `0`, and the rollback. `Controllers/MeAccessEntitlementApiTests` is the published contract over HTTP, including the cross-tenant case and each warning state, and `Controllers/MeAccessApiTests` asserts the shipped state, where the field is present and `null`.

### Plan enforcement on reports and Nayax operations (issue #967)

**One table of plan requirements, two enforcement points, and nothing stored is ever removed.** Issue #967 — a child of #965, after #966 — is what makes a plan withhold anything. It adds no table, no migration and no new read of a business's records beyond the one #966 already defined: it reuses that slice's `GetEffectiveEntitlement` and asks one more question of it. **While the rollout setting is off, which is the shipped state, nothing changes for any business**: `PlanFeaturePolicy.Allows` is `true` for every feature on an unenforced entitlement, so every call site behaves exactly as it did before plans existed and no extra query is made.

**Which plan a feature needs is `Inventory.Domain.Subscriptions.PlanFeaturePolicy`, and nowhere else.** `PlanFeature` is the whole vocabulary — `SalesProviderIntegration`, `BookkeepingAndGstReports`, `ProviderSalesReports`, `SiteCommissions`, `SalesFileImport`, and `ObservedSupplierPrices` since issue #977 ([Plan enforcement on supplier price data](#plan-enforcement-on-supplier-price-data-issue-977)) — and `RequiredPlan` is the one table: the two reports that need no sales provider and the observed supplier prices are **Starter**, and everything behind the provider, plus the uploaded Nayax sales file, is **Pro** (decided on #965 and its review of 29 October 2026). An endpoint declares a **feature**, never a plan, for the reason a controller declares a capability and never a role: a price or a plan restated at a call site is one that can disagree with the catalogue. No feature is Free, which is asserted: Free's own features are not plan features at all, so a `Free` requirement would be a feature nothing could ever withhold. `Allows` fails closed in the one direction that matters — an entitlement that is enforced and carries no plan, or a plan this deployment does not declare, includes nothing that is not free — and refuses an undeclared `PlanFeature` outright rather than letting the unenforced branch pass it.

**The Application asks through one memoised read.** `Inventory.Application.Subscriptions.CurrentPlan` is the Application-layer companion to `CurrentCapabilities`: it takes no identifier and no plan, only a `PlanFeature`, and it memoises the one entitlement read per request. That memoisation is what keeps a bounded Nayax fan-out from turning one plan question into one database read per machine — the fan-outs resolve credentials once per call, deliberately and still do, and the first asker's read is the one every other asker awaits, concurrent ones included. A failed read is not retried: a database that cannot be reached is an error for every asker, exactly as it is for `GET /api/me/access`, because answering "not included" over a transport failure would lock a paying business out of what it bought.

**The first enforcement point is the credential gate, and it covers every mixed surface at once.** `NayaxRequestCredentialProvider` asks the plan question immediately after the support-session refusal and **before the stored connection is read** — so a downgraded business with perfectly valid saved credentials makes no Nayax request at all and no token is decrypted. It raises the same `NayaxNotConnectedException` every consumer already handles, carrying `RequiredPlan` instead of a connection `Status`, which is what makes the issue's central result fall out of one check rather than out of twenty-four endpoints: the dashboard withholds its fleet card, the machine reads and the Pick List matrix answer their existing `409`, reorder answers in `StorageOnly` mode, the site-commission report comes out unavailable, the inventory-cost transition previews, the catalogue review and Sync Restock degrade as they already do without a connection, and manual pick-list entry, purchasing, inventory and expenses are untouched. **Being here rather than in each consumer is the whole point**: a per-controller check is a check somebody can forget to add to the next controller. The one surface the gate cannot cover is the Sync Restock *reminder*, which makes no Nayax call at all — it reads the stored connection status directly — so `GetMachineRestockSyncReminder` asks the same question itself, before that read, and is withheld with the same reason.

**Each refusal carries the distinct plan reason, and the existing one is unchanged.** Every per-feature availability vocabulary gains a `PlanRequired` member beside `NayaxNotConnected` and `PermissionNotGranted`, spelled identically in all of them — `MachineNeedUnavailableReasons` (the dashboard's withheld section and the reorder listing's response headers), `MachineLatestSalesUnavailableReasons`, `SiteCommissionUnavailableReasons` and `MachineRestockSyncReminderHiddenReasons` — and the HTTP boundary publishes `nayaxUnavailableReason` and `requiredPlan` beside the **unchanged** `409` and the **unchanged** `nayax_not_connected` code. Keeping the status code and the code itself is deliberate: every surface that degrades to its no-usable-provider behaviour does so on that exact answer, so moving a plan refusal to `403` would turn a Pick List that opens manual entry into a Pick List that shows an error. A client that has not learnt about plans therefore degrades exactly as it does today, and one that has can say "needs Pro" instead of "connect Nayax" (issue #979). A plan refusal reports **no** connection status, because no connection was read to have one; a Pro business without a usable connection keeps today's status and reports no required plan.

**The second enforcement point is the endpoint, for what a plan refuses outright.** `InventoryApi.Auth.RequirePlanAttribute` declares the feature an endpoint needs and is an **MVC authorization filter, not an authorization policy**. That is the design rather than a detail: a second `AuthorizeAttribute` would be evaluated together with the capability policy by one middleware in no defined order, and a caller holding neither could be told about the plan instead of simply being refused. An MVC filter runs after the authorization middleware has finished, so **a role refusal stays exactly the bodiless `403` it is today**, a plan is only ever asked about for a caller the role already allowed, and the check happens before model binding and before the action — which is what makes "a refused save leaves the stored credentials unchanged" and "a refused import stores nothing" properties of the pipeline rather than of a use case. A plan never grants a role more access: every endpoint that declares a plan requirement still declares its capability, which an architecture test asserts. The refusal is one shape everywhere, `InventoryApi.Auth.PlanRequirement`: `403` with the stable code `plan_required`, the plan the business would need and the feature, and nothing about the caller, their role, the capability or a price.

**The endpoint requirements, as the issue decides them** (issue #977 adds one more to the Starter row, `POST /api/cheapest-suppliers/summary`). Starter and Pro: `GET /api/reports/bookkeeping` and `/gst`. Pro: `/daily`, `/transactions`, `/reconciliation`, `/machine-profitability`, `/product-profitability`, `/dashboard`, the whole of Site Commissions (the report, the agreements and the payments — a site is known only from the live fleet read, so commission is a provider feature throughout), `POST /api/imports/nayax-sales`, and the three Owner credential actions `POST /api/settings/nayax-connection/test`, `.../save` and `.../retest` — the only Nayax calls in the application that do not go through the ordinary credential provider, which is exactly why they declare the requirement themselves. **`GET /api/settings/nayax-connection/status` deliberately carries none** and stays available on every plan to every role that sees it today: it makes no Nayax call, and it is what tells a downgraded business that its saved credentials and their status are still there. So does the reimbursement XML import, whose figures feed the two reports a Starter business includes.

**A report and its own export cannot need different plans.** `GET /api/reports/{report}/export` is one endpoint serving every report family, so its requirement cannot be a constant: it declares `[RequirePlanPerReport]` and resolves the feature through `Inventory.Domain.Subscriptions.ReportPlanRequirements`, the same table the report actions' declared features are asserted against. A report name this application does not recognise resolves to the **most restricted** feature, because the export's own row builder falls through to product profitability for one — so misspelling a URL is not a way to download a Pro report.

**Every endpoint is accounted for.** `EndpointPlanRequirementTests` (`backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Architecture/`) is the plan half of what `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` does for roles: one maintained list of every controller action and one of four kinds — a declared feature, per report, **via the provider gate** (nothing declared, because the sales-provider behaviour is behind the Application's own plan check and degrades rather than refusing), or **none** (every plan includes it). A new endpoint fails the build until somebody decides, and the test also checks each entry against what the endpoint actually declares, in both directions. Like issue #700's financial-disclosure test it is honest about its limit: the gate/none boundary is an allow-list of *decisions* and no reflection rule can prove at build time that an endpoint's Nayax use all goes through the gate. What it does prove is that nobody added an endpoint without that decision being made.

**Nothing is deleted, altered or migrated.** A plan change writes nothing: no sale, cost, link, history row, credential, connection status, agreement, payment or attachment is touched, and a feature becomes readable again the moment the plan includes it. There is no migration in this slice, no new table, no new port and no cross-business read.

### Plan enforcement on supplier price data (issue #977)

**One feature decides both halves: who may read supplier price data, and whose products the shared collector is sent out for.** Issue #977 — a child of #965, after #966 and #967 — is the plan half of the supplier price catalogue. It adds a sixth `PlanFeature`, `ObservedSupplierPrices`, whose required plan is **Starter** (the issue's own first criterion: "shown only to Starter and Pro businesses"), and no table, no migration and no new port. `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.PriceCollectionEligibilityPolicy` is the one place that names that feature for collection, so the endpoint that serves the prices and the collection that produces them cannot drift apart: nothing is searched for at a supplier on behalf of a business that would be refused the answer, and nothing a business is entitled to see goes uncollected.

**Price data is served by one endpoint, and that endpoint declares the requirement.** `POST /api/cheapest-suppliers/summary` ([The cheapest-supplier summary](#the-cheapest-supplier-summary-and-the-cheapest-supplier-column-issue-930)) carries `[RequirePlan(PlanFeature.ObservedSupplierPrices)]` on the controller, so a business whose effective plan is Free is refused with the one shape issue #967 defined — `403`, the stable `plan_required` code, the plan it would need and the feature — after the capability check and **before** the action, so nothing is read. No other endpoint embeds a supplier price: the summary's DTOs are the only API contract that carries one, which `SupplierPriceObservationBoundaryTests` holds as a declared list of every production file that may name an observed price at all. The page around the call keeps working, because the Cheapest supplier column has always had an answer for a read that did not land ("Unavailable", with the rest of the page and the purchase-cost columns untouched); the inline lock that names the plan instead is issue [#979](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/979).

**The tracking switch is deliberately on every plan.** `PUT /api/products/{id}/price-tracking` and the two reads beside it ([Tracking supplier prices on a product](#tracking-supplier-prices-on-a-product-issue-938)) carry **no** plan requirement: which of its own products a business wants priced is its own record, not the price data. A Free business switches tracking on and off exactly as before, the mapping is kept through a downgrade — nothing deletes it, and the collector simply stops being issued work for it — and it takes effect again the moment the plan includes the prices. The matched master product's name and size that read publishes is not a price and stays readable, which is what lets a downgraded business see where its own request stood.

**Collection eligibility is decided per business and applied per product description.** `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` reads the businesses' plan records, asks `EffectiveEntitlementPolicy` (the same rule `GET /api/me/access` reports) which of them include the feature, and restricts its two mapping statements to those businesses. The issue's criteria then fall out of the deduplication the work list already does:

- a **matched** product is issued while at least one entitled business tracks it, because the matched read takes the distinct master products the reachable mappings name;
- a **waiting key** is issued while at least one entitled business's product folds to it, and the spelling sent is one of those businesses' own;
- a product tracked by a **Free and an entitled** business is still collected, and still once — the Free business's mapping neither adds a second search nor withholds the first;
- a product only Free businesses track is not collected, and **nothing about it is removed**: the mapping, the master product, the listings and every observation stay exactly as they are (the shared catalogue is about suppliers' shelves and is never a business's to delete).

Why the eligibility is decided *behind* the work-list port rather than in front of it is the tenancy argument, not a convenience: anything deciding it outside the adapter would have to hand the port a set of business ids, and the whole of what makes that cross-business read safe is that no business id — nor a count of businesses — crosses the boundary. It is the fifth reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` read, bounded in the same directions as the four before it, and is described in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64).

**A run already issued completes unchanged.** The results path of [#937](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/937) judges a submitted row against the work item the run issued and asks no plan question at all, so a price read for a product whose only entitled business downgraded mid-run is still accepted, recorded and published to the businesses that are entitled. Eligibility applies **from the next issued run**, which is the natural consequence of it being evaluated when a run is issued.

**And until enforcement is switched on, nothing changes for any business.** With the rollout setting off, or with the grandfathering step not completed, `PlanFeaturePolicy.Allows` is `true` for the feature, the endpoint refuses nobody, and the work list reads **no plan record at all** — both mapping statements are exactly the ones issue #923 shipped.

**What proves it.** `PriceCollectionEligibilityPolicyTests` pins the feature, its Starter requirement, the plan-by-plan answer, both unenforced states and the fail-closed direction; `PlanFeaturePolicyTests` gains the new feature in the declared vocabulary, the required-plan table and the plan × feature matrix. `EndpointPlanRequirementTests` records the endpoint's declared feature, asserts it is the **same** feature the collection gate names, and keeps the three tracking endpoints in the "included in every plan" list. `PlanEnforcementApiTests` covers the whole pipeline over real HTTP: the summary served or refused plan by plan with the refusal naming Starter and the feature, a Free business switching tracking on and off and reading its own state, a downgrade keeping the mapping while the prices are refused and an upgrade restoring them, and — with the rollout setting off — the summary served to a business with no plan record at all. `PriceCollectorPlanEligibilityTests` is the relational half over two businesses and the denied scope a collector carries: a matched product only a Free business tracks not issued with the mapping, master product and listing all still there, the same product issued on Starter and on Pro, a product a Free and an entitled business both track issued once, a paid subscription deciding it the same way a grant does and a cancelled one not, an ended grant stopping it, a waiting key issued only while an entitled business folds to it, a mixed-plan work list carrying no business id or name, both unenforced states collecting for everybody, and a run issued before a grant ended still being completed afterwards while the next run omits the product. On the frontend, `cheapest-suppliers.component.spec.ts` covers the refused read leaving the rest of the page working.

### The Plan page (issue #970)

**The page reads only the #966 entitlement, beside the catalogue it reads separately — and adds nothing to the backend's subscription or billing model.** Issue #970 — a child of #965, after #966, #968 and #978 — is the first screen that shows any of the entitlement answer `GET /api/me/access` has published since #966: the effective plan and its source, the attachment storage figures of #968 and the connected-machine answer of #978. It invents no status the server does not already publish (#965's "Launch decisions to settle" and the owner decision of 30 October 2026, recorded on the issue, superseded an earlier request for pending/past-due/cancelled/grace states and a separate complimentary/grandfathered split — none of those exist in `EntitlementSource` or `BillingSubscriptionStatus` today, and this page does not infer them from dates or add a placeholder value).

**One small, additive read makes the comparison table possible: `GET /api/me/plan-catalogue`.** `MeAccessResponse.entitlement` deliberately carries no price, storage limit or machine allowance (see [Business subscriptions and plan entitlements](#business-subscriptions-and-plan-entitlements-issue-966)) — repeating them on every access read would be a second place a figure could disagree with the catalogue. The new endpoint is a thin `MeController` action over one narrow Application use case, `Inventory.Application.Subscriptions.GetPlanCatalogue`, which returns `Inventory.Domain.Subscriptions.PlanCatalogue.All` and which the action maps into `MePlanCatalogueResponse`/`MePlanCatalogueEntryResponse`: no store, no migration and no change to any existing contract — `GET /api/me/access` is untouched. **The use case is there because the controller does not read the Domain directly**, whatever the read costs: a controller binds transport input, invokes a use case and maps its result (AGENTS.md § Architecture rules), and a read that looks trivial today is exactly the one a page would otherwise grow logic into. It takes no identifier, reads no row and holds no state — the catalogue is a compiled table, identical for every caller — so it is registered as a **singleton** in `Inventory.Application.DependencyInjection`, unlike the scoped `GetEffectiveEntitlement` beside it, which belongs to one request's resolved business. It declares `[RequireCapability(Capability.DashboardView)]`, the one capability every role and a support session hold, because the catalogue is visible to everybody rather than gated by what a role may do; `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` and `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` cover it the same way every other capability endpoint is covered, and `Controllers/MePlanCatalogueApiTests` pins the body against `PlanCatalogue.All` directly and asserts it names no business and is identical for every role.

**The Angular page composes the two reads and nothing else.** `PlanComponent` (`components/plan/plan.component.ts`) subscribes to `AccessService.access$` throughout its life rather than reading it once, so a support session starting or ending and a role preview changing both reach it for free through the `AccessService.refresh()` calls `SupportSessionService` and `RolePreviewService` already make — there is no re-read trigger of its own to get wrong. `PlanCatalogueService` (`access/plan-catalogue.service.ts`) reads the static catalogue once; it is identical for every caller, so there is nothing about it to cache per identity or invalidate on those transitions. **One figure is composed from both reads: the current plan's own monthly price**, taken from the catalogue row whose published plan name matches `entitlement.plan`. When the catalogue read failed, or carries no row for that name — a plan a newer deployment publishes — the card says the price is unavailable; there is no price in Angular to fall back to and none is guessed, which is the same rule the comparison table follows. Prices, the storage figures and the plan's own name/source are shown to every member; the catalogue's per-extra-machine rate is the one figure gated by `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, because it is a billing amount beyond the plan price in the sense [Business subscriptions and plan entitlements](#business-subscriptions-and-plan-entitlements-issue-966) already draws that line at. An Owner sees a "coming soon" upgrade/manage-billing message (no checkout or success state exists until #969), every other role is told to ask their Owner, and the whole action area is withheld — never merely disabled — inside a support session or a role preview, because neither is a context a write or billing action belongs in. The route `/plan` needs only `Dashboard.View` and sits as its own top-level link under the sidebar's `Settings` heading (`layout/navigation.ts`), beside rather than inside the `Admin` group, because every role reaches it while `Admin`'s own route needs a stronger capability no Operator holds.

**What proves it.** `Controllers/MePlanCatalogueApiTests` is the catalogue endpoint's own contract and `Application/Subscriptions/GetPlanCatalogueTests` is the use case behind it, pinning that it hands the one definition back unchanged and in its own order; `plan-catalogue.service.spec.ts` is the frontend read. `plan.component.spec.ts` covers every published `entitlement.source` value and an unrecognised one falling back to its raw name rather than a guessed label, the enforced/unenforced states, the current plan's own monthly price and the three states in which it is reported unavailable rather than guessed (catalogue read failed, no catalogue row for the plan, nothing enforced), the 80%/100% storage states and the accessible progress bar's reported percentage, the connected-machine current/stale/unavailable states and the never-a-zero rule, the Owner-versus-other-role action text, the action withheld in a support session and in a role preview, and the financial-capability gate on the one priced column the comparison table conditionally shows. Two further cases are the structural half of the issue's 390px and keyboard evidence, which a jsdom test can state and a browser screenshot is needed to show: the comparison table — five columns wide for a role with `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` — sits in the same `overflow-x-auto` scroll container every other wide table in the application uses, so a narrow viewport scrolls the table rather than the page; and the page renders **no interactive control at all** in any of its states, so it has no focus order, focus trap or keyboard-only action to get wrong. `navigation.spec.ts` and `sidebar-nav.component.spec.ts` cover the new top-level link's capability and position, including that it is the one entry that keeps the `Settings` heading open for an Operator who has no `Admin` group at all.

### Per-business Nayax connection (issue #518)

Issue #518 — a slice of #500, under the contract of #328 — added the **storage** a per-business
connection needs, and nothing else: when it shipped, the Nayax integration was still configured once
for the whole application (`NayaxLynx:OperatorId` and a configured bearer token), no consumer read
the new record, and application behaviour was unchanged. Issue #520 is what made the client read it;
this section describes the storage, and
[Per-business Nayax credentials](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520) describes its use.

**One row per business, owned centrally.** `BusinessNayaxConnection` (`Inventory.Infrastructure/Models`)
holds the operator id, the encrypted access token, the id of the key that encrypted it, the
connection status, the credential revision, whether the last completed check left the machine checks
unverified (`MachineChecksPending`, added additively by issue #537 — see
[Save and re-test](#saving-a-tested-connection-and-re-testing-it-issue-537)), and the last-tested
and updated instants. It implements
`IBusinessOwned`, so it is filtered, indexed and stamped by the same mechanisms as every other
tenant-owned entity, with no predicate of its own anywhere; the additive
`AddBusinessNayaxConnections` migration creates the table and a **unique index on `BusinessId`**, so
"one connection per business" is a schema guarantee rather than an adapter convention. The migration
stores and infers nothing — moving the existing configured credential is the human-run
`migrate-nayax-connection` command of issue #519, described in
[Migrating the Nayax connection](#migrating-the-nayax-connection-issue-519) — so every business
starts with no row at all, which is what `NotConfigured` means.
`BusinessNayaxConnections` is deliberately **not** on the [platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336)
allow-list and must not be added to it.

**Storing the credential also records the business's sales provider** (issue #759).
`SaveCredentialAsync` claims `Business.SalesProvider = Nayax` while that column is empty, in the same
transaction as the credential, and refuses the save when the business already sells through a
different provider — a business has one sales provider, and switching it is a separate design (#761).
That belongs to this one port rather than to each of its callers, so no path can store credentials
without recording the provider they belong to. See
[Provider identity on the local row](#provider-identity-on-the-local-row-issues-732-759-and-735).

**Encryption lives in Infrastructure, behind `INayaxTokenProtector`.** `AesGcmNayaxTokenProtector`
encrypts with AES-256-GCM, a fresh random nonce per encryption, and stores
`v2:base64(nonce || tag || ciphertext)` with the key id in its own column. Authenticated encryption is
the point: a tampered ciphertext fails its tag check and throws rather than decrypting to a
different token that would then be sent to Nayax, and a per-save nonce means the column cannot
reveal that two businesses configured the same credential. The key id travels with the ciphertext so
a key can be rotated without re-encrypting every row at once — new ciphertext uses
`NayaxTokenProtection:ActiveKeyId`, older ciphertext keeps naming the key that produced it, and
removing a key from configuration is what retires it and makes anything still naming it
undecryptable on purpose. Every failure refuses: an unknown key id, a malformed value and a failed
tag check all raise `NayaxTokenProtectionException`, and no message or log event ever carries a
token, a ciphertext or key material. `Inventory.Application` and `Inventory.Domain` know none of
this — the composition root reads the key configuration and calls `AddNayaxTokenProtection`, exactly
as it does for the Nayax HTTP client's options — so Key Vault stays out of the inner layers. An
environment with no key configured gets the fail-closed `UnconfiguredNayaxTokenProtector`: the API
starts and runs normally, and only storing or reading a per-business token fails, because
provisioning the key is a human step (see README.md § Configuration and secrets). Since issue #520
that is what every Nayax call does, so in an environment that uses Nayax a missing key means the
Nayax features fail closed until a human provisions one — and nothing else does.

**The ciphertext is bound to its business, and that is authenticated rather than merely stored**
(issue #681). Both members of `INayaxTokenProtector` take a `BusinessId`, and the owning business's
key is the AES-GCM *associated data*, so the authentication tag covers it: a value encrypted for
business 4 fails its tag check the moment it is presented as business 9's, whatever the key. Before
this, encryption on its own answered "is this a genuine ciphertext?" and said nothing about *whose* —
so a value copied between rows by a hand-written `UPDATE`, a restored backup or a mistaken repair
decrypted perfectly, and the other business then authenticated to Nayax with it. The business id is
not a secret and does not have to be; the property wanted is that it cannot be changed without
invalidating the tag. The adapters resolve it from the context's own tenancy scope — the same scope
whose query filter selected the row — so it is never a value a request supplied, and both
`EfNayaxConnectionStore` and `EfNayaxConnectionTestDraftStore` bind it the same way.

**Two stored formats, and the format is self-describing.** A value written since issue #681 carries
the `v2:` marker and is business-bound. A value written before it is bare base64, is decrypted with
no associated data, and therefore still decrypts — existing rows keep working across the deployment
with no migration and no re-encryption step. The marker is unambiguous because base64 contains no
`:`, so neither format can be mistaken for the other. A legacy row is consequently **not**
business-bound: re-encrypting one happens when an Owner saves their connection again, or through the
human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command, and never as an automatic rewrite — AGENTS.md
§ Database and migrations forbids a startup data operation, and the protector holds no database to
do one with. A deployment that wants every row bound re-saves each business's connection
deliberately, and the marker is how an operator tells a bound row from one still to do.

**`CredentialRevision` is what makes a status write safe.** The Application port is
`Inventory.Application.Nayax.INayaxConnectionStore`, implemented by
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfNayaxConnectionStore`. A credential save increments the
revision in the database, resets the status to `PendingPermissions`, and clears the last-tested
instant and the pending-machine-checks flag, so a newly stored token can never inherit the previous
token's test result; the first save creates the row at revision 1. A save is atomic, and it takes part in a transaction its caller has
already begun on the same context instead of committing on its own, which is what lets
`migrate-nayax-connection` make the save and the status write that follows it one change (see
[Migrating the Nayax connection](#migrating-the-nayax-connection-issue-519)); with no transaction in
progress a save still gets its own. A permission test result carries the revision it was produced for,
and applying it is **one conditional statement** — `UPDATE … WHERE BusinessId = @b AND
CredentialRevision = @r`, where the business predicate is contributed by the central query filter
and the revision predicate by the caller's expected value. Zero rows matched means an operator saved
different credentials while the test was running: the result is discarded, not written, and one
structured `ILogger` warning records it with the business id and the two revisions and nothing else.
A status result that also knows about the machine checks writes `MachineChecksPending` in that same
statement, and one that does not — the `401` an ordinary Nayax call reports, which never ran those
checks — leaves that column exactly as it is rather than claiming they passed (issue #537).
That is also why this adapter refuses to run without a single resolved business —
`ExecuteUpdate` executes in the database without passing through `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`, so an
unscoped context would be the one way such a statement could carry no business predicate at all.

**Reading the secret is a separate call.** `FindAsync` returns a `NayaxConnection` that cannot hold
a token, which is what every status read uses; only `FindCredentialAsync` decrypts, and it returns
`NayaxConnectionCredential`, deliberately a class with a redacting `ToString` rather than a record,
because a record's generated `ToString` would put the token into the first log line or assertion
message that rendered it. An undecryptable credential throws rather than reading as absent or
empty.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/Nayax/NayaxTokenProtectorTests`
covers the round trip and key id, ciphertext that differs from the plaintext and from a second save
of the same token, tampered and malformed values, an unknown key id, rotation across two keys, the
unconfigured protector and the startup validation of the key section.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Adapters/Persistence/EfNayaxConnectionStoreTests` runs on relational
SQLite: revision 1 on first save, the increment and cleared test result on a later save, the applied
and the discarded status result with the log event's exact properties, the statement shape itself,
two-business isolation for reading, decrypting, saving and status writes, two overlapping saves
leaving the last committed credentials, a save inside a caller's transaction landing only when that
caller commits, a retired key and a tampered ciphertext failing closed, a
denied and an unscoped context writing nothing, and the unique index refusing a second row.
`AddBusinessNayaxConnectionsMigrationTests` is the upgrade test from the previous migration.

### Migrating the Nayax connection (issue #519)

The record #518 added starts empty, and the credential it is for is live in production
configuration. `migrate-nayax-connection` is the human-run command that moves it: the fourth
early-command branch in `Program.cs`, alongside `bootstrap-business`, `migrate-database` and
`migrate-documents`, so starting the API and moving a credential can never be the same action. The
operator procedure, the cutover window around issue #520 and when the global settings may be
removed are in `docs/tenant-rollout.md` § Migrating the Nayax connection into the business; what
follows is why it is built this way.

**It reads the same configuration the client reads, and writes only through #518's store.**
`NayaxConnectionMigrationCommand` binds `NayaxLynxOptions` and resolves the token through
`NayaxLynxConfiguration.ResolveAccessToken`, the same function the composition root uses, so the
command cannot hold a second opinion about where the live credential lives. It then hands the
plaintext token to `INayaxConnectionStore.SaveCredentialAsync` exactly once. Encryption, the key id
and the credential revision stay entirely inside the #518 adapter; nothing here knows a cipher.

**It uses no unrestricted context** — see [the unrestricted-context rule](#tenant-ownership-issue-64).
`NayaxConnectionMigrator` resolves and verifies the business through a *denied* context, which can
read `Businesses`, `BusinessMemberships` and `BusinessBackfillAudits` because those are the
deliberately global tenancy tables, and reaches no tenant-owned row at all. The credential is then
read and written through a context scoped to that one resolved business, so the central query
filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` are in force for every statement, and the adapter's own
refusal to run without a single resolved business is satisfied honestly rather than bypassed.

**A dry run writes nothing, rather than writing and rolling back.** `bootstrap-business` measures by
doing the work inside a transaction and rolling it back, because its numbers are counts across every
owned table. Here the whole change is two values and a status, so it can be reported exactly without
writing: a dry run opens no transaction on the credential table and the status it reports for
"after" is declared as a prediction.

**`Ready`, not `PendingPermissions`, on the credential it stores — and the command never calls
Nayax.** Every save through the store lands on `PendingPermissions` — a freshly stored token is
never assumed to work — so the command applies a status result for the exact revision it just
wrote, through the same conditional `TryApplyStatusResultAsync` path a real permission test uses.
The evidence is production use rather than a live test, which is also why the instant recorded is
when that was adopted. A revision that moved in between discards the result rather than describing
credentials it was not produced for, and the command reports that rather than claiming success.
**That reasoning reaches exactly as far as the credential this run stored** (issue #675): over a
credential that was already there it writes no status at all, because "the configured token is the
one in production use" says nothing about a verdict something else already reached on it.

**An apply is one transaction, so a partial state is not something it can leave.** Storing the
credential and marking the connection `Ready` are two statements, and a command that committed the
first and then failed the second would leave a credential whose status was never written while
reporting a failure — the database changed by a run that says it refused. `NayaxConnectionMigrator`
therefore opens one transaction on the business-scoped context and does everything inside it: the
authoritative read of what the business holds, the comparison against the configured credential, the
save, the `Ready` status write and the read-back. It commits only once a credential it stored is
actually `Ready` — a run that stores nothing has nothing to commit either. A refusal, a status
result the revision guard discarded, and a failed read or write all
roll it back, so a run that reports anything other than success has written nothing at all, and
recovering from one is simply running the command again rather than repairing a half-finished
change. Putting the read inside that transaction is also what makes the "never replace a credential
I did not recognise" refusal a decision about the state the write lands on, rather than about a
state that may have been superseded since; the conditional status write still carries the revision
it was produced for as well. The one ending the transaction cannot decide is a commit that itself
fails: the database then holds the whole change or none of it, and the result says exactly that
(`CommitFailed`, reported as an unknown database state) instead of claiming either. Every result
carries a `DatabaseState` of `Unchanged`, `Changed` or `Unknown`, and the printed report states it
in words on success and failure alike, so a refusal can never be read as a partial write.

**Refusals, and what makes a re-run a true no-op.** It refuses when the configuration holds no
operator id or token; when the schema has pending migrations; when tenant ownership is not
bootstrapped — which is where "more than one business exists" lands, since `TenantOwnershipReadiness`
requires exactly one active business with a usable membership and no unassigned rows; when no
`BusinessBackfillAudit` row names that business, so it is not demonstrably the one
`bootstrap-business` adopted; when a *different* operator id or token is already stored, because
replacing a credential something else stored is a human decision; and when the token cannot be
encrypted or the stored ciphertext cannot be decrypted, which fails closed rather than overwriting
a credential nothing could read. **A business already holding exactly the configured pair is left
completely untouched, whatever its status says** (issue #675) — the row is not rewritten, so not
even the ciphertext changes, and the revision, the status, the last-tested instant and the
machine-check flag all stay exactly as they were. The dry run and the apply agree on that: the dry
run predicts the stored status rather than `Ready`, and the apply attempts no write at all, not
even the conditional status write. This is what keeps a re-run from reviving a connection a Nayax
`401` moved to `NeedsAttention`: that verdict came from Nayax, this command never calls Nayax, and
only a connection test — the Owner's re-test on Admin → Integrations — can conclude a new status.
A matching pair stored but not yet `Ready` is therefore left on `PendingPermissions` as well, and
is also a re-test rather than a re-run.

**The token never leaves the ciphertext column.** It is in no result member, no message, no
exception and no printed line — not as a length, a prefix or a hash. The operator id is printed,
because it is a remote identity an operator has to be able to confirm, and whether the stored token
matches the configured one is printed as a plain yes/no.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Bootstrap/NayaxConnectionMigrationTests` asserts that directly: it
sweeps every reachable outcome's message, record `ToString`, printed report and captured log entries
for both the configured and a second token, and sweeps every column of the credential table for the
plaintext. Its fixture is built by running the real `BusinessBootstrapper`, because "bootstrapped"
means that command's outcome — a migrated-but-unbootstrapped database is not merely empty, since a
migration seeds a `NayaxProcessingFeeRate` with no owner.

The same tests pin the atomicity, with the credential replaced between the save and the `Ready`
write: the apply leaves no row at all, a status write that fails outright takes the save back with
it, the apply that follows a rolled-back one stores the credential at revision 1 as a first apply
would, and every ending reports its database state — only a failed commit is allowed to report
`Unknown`, and no refusal may claim a write it did not make. They pin the re-run contract the same
way: a matching credential in `Ready`, `PendingPermissions` and `NeedsAttention` alike comes out of
both a dry run and an apply with its status, revision, ciphertext, last-tested instant and
machine-check flag unchanged, and a store double that throws on either write proves the apply
attempts none rather than merely leaving the row looking the same.

### Per-business Nayax credentials (issue #520)

Issue #520 — the last slice of #500, under the contract of #328 — is what makes the record of #518
the thing every Nayax call authenticates with. Before it, `AddNayaxLynxClient` registered one typed
`HttpClient` with the globally configured operator id and bearer token baked in at construction, and
about 27 non-test files depended on the resulting `INayaxLynxClient`. After it, **the only global
Nayax setting left is `NayaxLynx:BaseUrl`**, and there is no fallback to a global credential or to
another business's: a business either has its own usable connection or its Nayax features fail
closed. Since issue #967 the same provider also refuses a business whose **plan** does not include
the sales provider, before the stored connection is read and with its own distinct reason, which is
how one check covers every ordinary Nayax call in the application — see
[Plan enforcement on reports and Nayax operations](#plan-enforcement-on-reports-and-nayax-operations-issue-967).

**The credential is resolved per call, centrally, and no consumer learns that.** `INayaxLynxClient`
was unchanged by this issue, so none of those ~27 consumers changed either (issues #840 and #842 later
added one machine-list and one machine-products member to that port and put a caching decorator in
front of the client — see [The machine-list cache](#the-machine-list-cache-issue-840) and
[The machine-products cache](#the-machine-products-cache-issue-842) — and the credential resolution
described here is exactly what that decorator runs before every answer it gives). What changed is one
step inside `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxLynxClient`: every operation starts by resolving
`Inventory.Application.Nayax.INayaxRequestCredentialProvider`, and applies the result to *that
request* — one resolution per operation, still, for the cached reads whose caller resolves it a
layer up (see [The machine-list cache](#the-machine-list-cache-issue-840)) as much as for the other
twenty-odd — the `Authorization: Bearer` header Nayax documents
([Security & Token](https://devzone.nayax.com/docs/manage-data-operations/lynx-api/security)) and the
`OperatorID` path parameter of the operator endpoints, which are built from the same resolved
credential so the token and the operator id can never belong to different businesses. Nothing
credential-shaped is held on the shared `HttpClient`, in the container, or in the client's own
fields, which is what makes the boundary structural rather than careful: there is no place for one
business's token to outlive its request. `NayaxLynxClient` queries no EF Core; the provider
(`NayaxRequestCredentialProvider`, in `Inventory.Application`, scoped per request) reads #518's
`INayaxConnectionStore`, which reads the business the `AppDbContext` tenant filters already resolved.
A caller with no resolved business reads nothing and therefore calls nothing.

**A Nayax call therefore touches the request's persistence, and the store owns that context (issue
#667).** The credential read is a real `SELECT`, and a `401` is a real `UPDATE`, on the one scoped
`AppDbContext` of the request that made the call — not on a context of the Nayax client's own. That
is the right ownership (a second context would be a second tenant scope, which
[Concurrency inside one request](#concurrency-inside-one-request-the-scoped-ef-context-issue-313)
rules out), but it means the bounded parallel Nayax fan-outs — the reorder and Pick List fan-outs,
the per-site machine reads, the catalogue import, the cost-transition preview — put several
credential reads, and sometimes several `401` writes, on a context that supports exactly one
operation at a time. **`EfNayaxConnectionStore` admits one operation at a time**, with a gate that is
per request (the adapter is scoped beside the context it guards), is held for the database work only,
and is never re-entered: its `SaveCredentialAsync` reads back through the private core rather than
through its own public `FindAsync`. What that does *not* change is as important as what it does:

- **The fan-out stays parallel.** Only the database statement is serialized, so the remote requests
  still overlap and the bound on them is still the fan-out's own
  `MaxConcurrentMachineRequests`. Cancellation is honoured while waiting for a turn, so a cancelled
  caller stops rather than queuing.
- **Waiting is not caching.** Every call still resolves its own snapshot when its turn comes, so the
  status gate still closes mid-fan-out: a call whose turn arrives after a `401` has been recorded
  reads `NeedsAttention` and fails closed instead of being handed a credential the request resolved
  earlier. The status, operator id, token and revision of each snapshot still come from one statement,
  and a refused status still never reaches the ciphertext.
- **Which `401` wins is still decided by the revision, not by the order of arrival.** The conditional
  `UPDATE ... WHERE CredentialRevision = @r` is evaluated against the row as it stands when the
  statement runs, so a whole fan-out of results produced for a superseded revision is discarded, one
  structured "stale Nayax status result discarded" event each, and the replacement credentials keep
  their own `PendingPermissions`.
- **The use case still may not overlap *other* scoped persistence with a Nayax call.** The gate makes
  the credential path safe against itself, not against the rest of the request;
  `GetNayaxCatalogReconciliation` and `GetSiteSummaries` await their remote reads before the local
  ones for that reason.
- **A support session resolves nothing**, before any of this: the refusal below is taken in the
  provider, before the store is reached at all.

**And a support session resolves nothing at all** (issue #551). The provider's first act is to refuse
when the request carries `BusinessScopeState.SupportReadOnly`: before the connection is read, before
the gate is applied and before any token could be decrypted, with `403` and the stable code
`unavailable_in_support_view`. A support session is somebody from outside the business reading its
data to help with a problem, and the operator id and token are the *business's* own credential —
nobody outside it has agreed to its Nayax account being spent on their behalf, and a call made in a
support view would be indistinguishable, at Nayax, from one the business made itself. Being in the
provider is what makes it hold for every Nayax read and write at once, for the same reason the status
gate is there rather than in each of the ~27 consumers. See
[Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**The status gate is a Domain rule, and it is an allow-list.**
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionStatusGate.AllowsOrdinaryOperations` is the one place that
decides: `Ready` and `PendingPermissions` may run ordinary operations, `NotConfigured` and
`NeedsAttention` may not, and a status value outside the declared vocabulary — which is what a cast
integer or a hand-edited row can produce — is refused rather than assumed usable. `PendingPermissions`
is deliberately allowed: the credentials are stored and may well work, and refusing every call until
something had tested them would make a freshly connected business look broken. The provider caches
nothing, so the call after a status change sees the new status.

**The status, the operator id, the token and the revision come from one snapshot of the row.** The
gate decides, and the 403 classification below depends on the status *the sent token is stored
with* — so resolving the two separately would be wrong, not merely untidy: a credential save
committing between a status read and a token read hands the caller the previous status beside the new
token, a pair the record never held, and a connection disabled between those reads would still have
its credential sent under the status the earlier read saw. `INayaxConnectionStore.FindForOperationAsync`
is therefore the one read an ordinary call resolves its credentials through, and
`EfNayaxConnectionStoreTests.The_operation_read_resolves_the_status_and_the_credential_in_one_statement`
pins it to a single `SELECT`. The gate travels *into* that read as the predicate that decides whether
the token may be decrypted, which keeps both properties at once: the rule stays the single Domain
allow-list the Application layer owns, and **a refused status never decrypts the token at all** — the
adapter stops before the ciphertext, so the gate is still a decision taken before the risky step
rather than after it. `NayaxRequestCredentialProvider` then applies the same gate to the snapshot's
own status to refuse and report the operation. `FindAsync` and `FindCredentialAsync` remain for the
callers that genuinely want one or the other: a token-free status read, and the gate-free re-test
read below.

**A refusal is a stable error the frontend can show.** `NayaxNotConnectedException` (Application)
carries the fixed sentence of `NayaxNotConnectedException.StableMessage`, the stable code
`nayax_not_connected`, and the connection's own status;
`InventoryApi.Http.NayaxConnectionExceptionHandler` maps it, and
`NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException`/`nayax_permission_not_granted`, to `409 Conflict`
`application/problem+json` with `detail`, the `message` extension the existing frontend error
handling reads, the `code`, and — for a connection failure — `nayaxConnectionStatus`. **Neither
becomes `401` or `403`**: those statuses describe the *caller's* Entra token and business membership,
and a signed-in member whose business has not connected Nayax is perfectly entitled to the feature.
Neither is a `502` either — Nayax answered correctly, or was never called, and retrying would not
help. Each is logged once at `Warning` with the error code, the status or refused operation, and the
request's method, path and trace id; the operator id, the token and the upstream body appear in
neither the response nor the log. Making each individual Nayax screen degrade gracefully around this
error is issue #329 and is deliberately not part of this change.

**401 and 403 mean different things, because Nayax documents them differently**
([App tokens troubleshooting](https://devzone.nayax.com/docs/manage-data-operations/lynx-api/app-tokens)):

- **401 — the token is invalid or has expired.** That is a verdict on the stored credentials, so the
  connection moves to `NeedsAttention` through #518's conditional update, and the caller gets the
  stable "not connected" error because that is now the connection's state. The revision written is
  **the one read when the call started**, never whatever is stored when the answer arrives: a 401
  answering a call that used revision N, arriving after revision N+1 was saved, matches no row and is
  discarded (with the store's structured "stale Nayax status result discarded" event) rather than
  marking a token an operator has just fixed as broken. The recorded instant becomes the connection's
  last test result, because a 401 in production traffic is exactly a test of those credentials.
- **403 — the token's scopes do not cover this resource or action.** That is a verdict on one
  feature, not on the credentials, so **nothing writes a status**. While the credentials have not been
  tested since they were saved (`PendingPermissions` in the same snapshot the request's token came
  from, never a status read separately from it), it surfaces as the per-feature "Nayax hasn't
  granted permission for this" error, which is what lets the rest of the integration keep working. A
  403 against credentials that were tested and worked stays the ordinary upstream failure it was
  before this change: the issue defines the per-feature error for the unverified state, and widening
  it would change an established mapping without an issue asking for it.

Every other non-success status is unchanged: one log line with safe fields and
`NayaxUpstreamException` for the HTTP boundary's controlled `502` (see
[External integration errors](#external-integration-errors)), caller cancellation stays cancellation
and writes no status, and the resilience handler underneath is untouched — a 401 or 403 was never
retryable and still is not.

**The re-test read is a separate port, and that is enforced.** Issue #506's Owner-only re-test has to
be able to test credentials the gate refuses — otherwise `NeedsAttention` would be unrecoverable, as
nothing could ever check the stored token again — so `INayaxConnectionRetestCredentialProvider`
decrypts regardless of status and returns the revision it read, for the result to be applied back to
the exact credentials it tested. It is a **separate interface** rather than a second method on the
gated provider, because an ordinary consumer that could reach it would have a way to use credentials
the gate refuses. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Architecture/NayaxRetestCredentialBoundaryTests` pins
that against the compiled assemblies: only the port, its implementation and the registration may name
it, the gated port's surface is frozen at its two members, `NayaxLynxClient` depends on the gated
port, and one test proves the dependency rule can actually see a dependent. #506's endpoint adds
itself to that allow-list as a reviewed edit.

**Startup needs no credential.** `NayaxLynxConfiguration.ValidateNonSecretFields` no longer requires
an operator id, and `NayaxLynxConfiguration.BuildBaseAddress` is what `AddNayaxLynxClient` validates
and configures the typed client's base address from, so an API with no Nayax credential in
configuration at all starts and serves every non-Nayax feature normally. The global
`NayaxLynx:OperatorId`/`AccessToken` (and the legacy `Nayax:Token`) are read by exactly one thing
now, the human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command of
[issue #519](#migrating-the-nayax-connection-issue-519); removing them from an environment is the
human step described in `docs/tenant-rollout.md`. **Deploying this change makes Nayax unavailable
for a business whose credential has not been moved into its record**, scheduled syncs included, which
is why that command is run around the deploy rather than later.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Nayax/NayaxConnectionStatusGateTests` covers every
declared status, undeclared values, and that a new status cannot be added without a decision here.
`Inventory.UnitTests/Application/Nayax/NayaxRequestCredentialProviderTests` covers each status
through the gate, that a refused status never decrypts the token, a missing record, a credential that
disappears mid-call, an undecryptable credential propagating rather than reading as "not connected",
the 401 write and its discarded stale-revision case, two businesses resolving their own credentials,
and that rendering a resolved credential never prints the token;
`NayaxConnectionRetestCredentialProviderTests` covers the gate-free read at every status.
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/Nayax/NayaxLynxClientConnectionGateTests` covers the
client's side: no HTTP call at all for a refused connection, the bearer token and operator path
parameter, the 401 report and its revision, the 403 split, that no 401/403 response body or token
reaches an exception or a log, and cancellation. `NayaxLynxClientPerBusinessCredentialTests` runs the
real client over the real provider, the real store and real AES-GCM encryption on relational SQLite
with two businesses: each business's own operator id and token on the wire, a business with no record
failing closed while the other is connected, a denied caller calling nothing, each status deciding
whether a call happens, a 401 marking only the calling business's row, the call after a 401 being
refused by the gate, a 403 leaving the row byte-for-byte unchanged, a credential replaced *while the
request is in flight* leaving the new revision's status alone, and an existing consumer
(`NayaxCatalogSnapshotProvider`) working unchanged. `NayaxParallelCredentialAccessTests` runs the same
real stack through the real fan-out use cases with the EF command recorder attached (issue #667): a
bounded reorder fan-out that keeps its remote requests concurrent while one operation at a time
reaches the context and resolves one credential read per call, concurrent `401`s all answering with
the stable not-connected error and leaving one `NeedsAttention` row, a whole fan-out of `401`s from a
superseded revision discarded with the replacement credentials untouched, two businesses each using
their own credentials and their own status row, and the catalog reconciliation and site dashboard
keeping their local reads off the context while their remote reads run.
`NayaxConnectionExceptionHandlerTests` pins the `409` contract and its log;
`NayaxLynxClientDependencyInjectionTests` pins the base address, that registration needs no credential
and registers none, and that the registered client is built from the provider.

### The machine-list cache (issue #840)

Issue #840 — step 1 of #839 — is the one Nayax read this application holds on to. `GET /v1/machines`
("[Get All Machine Basic Info](https://devzone.nayax.com/docs/manage-data-operations/lynx-api/machines/retrieve-machine-information)",
the endpoint `INayaxLynxClient.GetMachinesAsync` is) is called by twelve use cases, and nothing
