cached it: **one Dashboard visit spent five requests on it** — the dashboard summary, low stock, the
sales sync, the sites read and the machine list — several of them at the same moment. Machine ids,
names and site `CustomerID`s change rarely, so those repeats bought nothing.

**The port says which read a caller wants, and the composition root decides what that costs.**
`INayaxLynxClient` has two machine-list members: `GetMachinesAsync`, which may answer with a list up
to ten minutes old, and `GetMachinesFreshAsync`, which always reads Nayax and replaces what is held.
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.CachingNayaxLynxClient` is what `AddNayaxLynxClient`
registers the port as; it wraps the typed `NayaxLynxClient` (still registered under its own type,
still named after the port for its base address and its resilience pipeline) and holds the lists in
the one singleton `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxMachineListCache`, whose mechanism is the
shared `NayaxReadCache<TKey, TValue>` described under
[the machine-products cache](#the-machine-products-cache-issue-842). `NayaxLynxClient` itself
caches nothing, so for it the two members are the same request — which is what keeps the connection
test outside all of this. No cache type exists in `Inventory.Application`: a use case states the
requirement it has, never where the answer comes from.

**Ten minutes, decided by the repository owner on 23 October 2026.** A machine added in Nayax can
take up to ten minutes to appear on the pages that read through the cache. It is in memory rather
than in a column, like `NayaxSalesSyncRateLimiter`'s window and `MemberProfileRefreshThrottle`: which
machines Nayax reported ten minutes ago is not part of the business's record, and a restart simply
reads the list again. On a single instance
([SQLite operating assumptions](#sqlite-operating-assumptions-and-scale-strategy-issue-53))
that is the whole truth; a second instance would mean one cached list per instance, which is still
bounded and still correct. A distributed or persisted cache is explicitly out of scope.

**The key is the business id and the credential revision.** The business id is in the key because a
process-wide list would be the one place in this application where one business could be served
another's data, and it comes from the request's resolved `IBusinessScope` — never from anything a
caller passed in. The credential revision is in the key because replacing a connection may point the
same business at a different Nayax operator account: saving a connection raises the revision, which
is a new key, so the next read goes to Nayax rather than answering from a list the previous
credentials fetched. A scope with no resolved business caches nothing at all rather than sharing a
key. Keys are forgotten once more than `NayaxMachineListCache.MaxTrackedKeys` are remembered, and
only the ones holding nothing usable, so the clean-up is about memory and never changes an answer.

**And the key names the credentials the request actually carried.** One credential is resolved per
machine-list call and *that* credential is what the upstream request is sent with: the decorator hands
it down through `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.INayaxLynxCachedReadClient.ReadMachinesAsync`, which
is `NayaxLynxClient`'s ordinary `GET /v1/machines` — same endpoint, same operation name in logs, same
`401` and `403` classification — with the resolution step skipped because it has already happened.
Resolving once for the key and letting the client resolve again for the request would leave a window,
because the credential provider caches nothing on purpose: a connection saved between the two reads
would have put the new credentials' fleet under the old revision's key. The extra member lives in
`Inventory.Infrastructure` for the same reason the cache does — nothing in `Inventory.Application`
knows that a credential revision or a cache key exists.

**Every refusal still happens, before every answer.** The cache is not an authorization boundary and
must never become one. The decorator resolves
[`INayaxRequestCredentialProvider.GetForOperationAsync`](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520)
first on every machine-list call — the stored connection, `NayaxConnectionStatusGate` and the
support-session refusal of [issue #551](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) — so a
business whose connection is now `NotConfigured` or `NeedsAttention`, and a platform administrator
reading in a support session, get today's refusal even while a list for that key is in memory. A
cache that answered before that check would be a way to read a business's Nayax data after its
connection stopped allowing it.

**Simultaneous readers share one request, and share its failure.** The Dashboard's five reads start
before any of them finishes, so a cache that only stored finished answers would let all five miss.
The first caller's read is published for the key and the others join it; each gets its own `List` over
the same machines, so a caller that sorts or trims what it was handed cannot change what the next one
reads. The shared read runs under the cancellation token of the caller that started it, and a caller
that joined may still leave early on its own token. **Nothing failed is ever held**: a `401`, a `403`,
any other upstream status and a cancellation all reach the callers unchanged and leave the entry as it
was, because a cached failure would turn one bad moment into ten minutes of refusals.

**Ordering is explicit, because results arrive out of order.** Every read takes a sequence number
before it starts, and a result is stored only while no later read has stored one, no fresh read has
begun and no invalidation has happened since. So a slow read that started before a fresh read cannot
store its older list over the fresher one it finished after — the slow caller still receives the
answer it was given, it simply does not become what the next caller sees. The fence is taken when the
fresh read *begins*, not when it succeeds: a fresh read that fails or is cancelled has nothing to
store, and the older read beside it must not become the answer by default. Letting a cached list
expire is an invalidation too, taken under the same lock that would otherwise hand it out.

**An invalidation also unpublishes the read that is still running.** Forgetting the held list and
barring older results from being stored is not enough on its own: a caller arriving while a read that
started before the invalidation is still open would otherwise join it and be handed exactly the
pre-invalidation list — for the expiry path a list already too old to serve, and after a credential
change the previous connection's fleet. So that read stops being joinable, its own callers still
receive what they asked for, and the next caller starts its own read. A fresh read is deliberately
the other way round: it bars the in-flight read from being stored but leaves it joinable, because it
is a live read of the same key from seconds ago and refusing to share it would cost the extra Nayax
request this cache exists to remove.

**Five callers always read fresh, and the connection test is outside the cache entirely.**
`ReviewProviderMachines` and `ApplyProviderMachineLinks` (a provider machine becoming a local machine,
and a link refused for a machine outside the fleet), `SyncLatestNayaxSales` (it records business-wide
sales coverage under issue #730, so a machine missing from an old list would be claimed as covered
without being read), `InventoryCostTransitionPreviewBuilder` (its
opening machine stock becomes a costing baseline) and `NayaxSaleTimestampRepairProjection` (its
evidence is the live rolling window of every machine) all call `GetMachinesFreshAsync` and replace the
entry for their business and credential revision. Every other caller — the dashboard summary and low
stock, the sites read and site products, reorder, the pick list, the machine list, the machine
products listing's site lookup (issue #846, below), the site commission report, the transaction
report's live site names and the catalogue snapshot — reads through the cache.
`NayaxConnectionCheckRunner` neither reads from nor writes to it, structurally: it builds its own
`NayaxLynxClient` over the candidate credentials an Owner pasted and is constructed from an
`HttpClient` and a logger and nothing else, so it never resolves the decorated port. That matters
because the pasted pair may belong to a different Nayax operator account, whose fleet is not the
business's fleet. Nothing else was cached by this change: machine products — cached since
[issue #842](#the-machine-products-cache-issue-842), under their own key and their own sixty seconds —
machine stock, last sales, alerts, one machine, the product catalogue, the product groups, the devices
and the machine-product write all reached the client every time.

**The machine products listing takes the machine's site from that list** (issue #846, step 2 of
#839). Opening a machine loads `GET api/machines/{id}` and `GET api/machines/{id}/products` together,
and both used to read the machine from Nayax — the listing only ever wanted one field of it, the
`CustomerID` that `Inventory.Application.Products.ResolveMachineProductPricing` prices each slot's
site commission by. So `Inventory.Application.Machines.ListMachineProducts` reads that `CustomerID`
from the machine list instead, which the same page has just read through this cache, and **opening a
machine makes one Nayax machine read across both requests** rather than two. A machine the list does
not hold — one
added in Nayax within the last ten minutes, or one Nayax does not know — falls back to the single
machine read exactly as before, and still before the machine products are read, so an unknown
machine still answers with today's controlled `502`. A listed machine with no `CustomerID` is at no
site and is priced with none: that is the list's answer, not a reason to ask again.

**The saving did not buy a new permission.** A Nayax account may grant `GET machines/{id}` and
`GET machines/{id}/machineProducts` while refusing `GET machines`, and that is precisely the account
whose connection the test of issue #536 concludes `PendingPermissions` for — which is what makes its
`403` the classified per-feature `NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException` rather than an upstream
failure. So a `NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException` on the fleet read falls back to the single-machine
read, and the listing answers exactly as it did before issue #846 instead of refusing an endpoint
that worked. That one classified refusal is the **only** thing the fallback catches. A
`NayaxNotConnectedException` (nothing stored, `NotConfigured`, or the `NeedsAttention` the status
gate refuses) refuses the single-machine read in the same breath; a support session resolves no Nayax
credentials at all (issue #551); a cancellation is the caller's own; and a transport or `5xx` failure
is an outage. All four propagate untouched, because retrying them against another endpoint would
either spend a request to reach the same answer slower or report a working site where there is an
outage. A `403` on a connection that is already `Ready` stays what it is everywhere else in this
application — an upstream failure, and so a `502` — because `NayaxUpstreamException` is an
Infrastructure type and `Inventory.Application` classifies availability by the two exceptions of
issue #726 and nothing else; a `Ready` connection is in any case one whose own `Machines` check
passed.

**Which means site pricing can be up to ten minutes stale after a site move**, the cost the
repository owner accepted with the lifetime on 23 October 2026. When a machine moves from site A to
site B in Nayax, its products page keeps suggesting site A's commission until the cached list
expires, and prices with site B's on the first load after that. Nothing else about the listing goes
stale: the slots, their machine prices, their MDB codes and their stock all still come from that
machine's own live `GET .../machineProducts` read, and the machine dashboard beside it still reads
the machine itself. `GetMachineDashboard` is deliberately not changed to read the list — it is the
read that remains, it needs the whole machine record rather than one field, and a machine page whose
header came from a ten-minute-old list would be a second, staler answer to what the page is about.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/Nayax/NayaxMachineListCacheTests`
covers the mechanism over a scripted read whose every call is counted and can be held open: a hit
inside ten minutes, a per-caller list, expiry exactly at ten minutes on a fake clock, five
simultaneous readers making one request, each of the three Nayax failures and a cancellation reaching
every caller and being held by none, two keys never crossing, a fresh read ignoring and replacing what
is held, a failed fresh read leaving it alone, an older in-flight read overwriting neither a newer
fresh read nor an invalidation — in either completion order, and including a fresh read that fails —
a caller after an invalidation not joining the read that was already running, and expired keys being
forgotten while a live one keeps its list. `CachingNayaxLynxClientTests` covers the
decorator for both caches (see [the machine-products cache](#the-machine-products-cache-issue-842)):
a second read answering from memory, each of the three refusals still happening with a warm
cache, two businesses never receiving each other's list, new credentials sending the next read to
Nayax, one credential resolved per call and the read carrying it, the key naming the credentials the
request really carried — over the real `NayaxLynxClient` and a handler that answers each
request with its own payload, with the stored connection replaced between two calls — a fresh read
reaching Nayax with a warm cache, nothing but those two reads being cached, and a scope with no
business caching nothing.
`NayaxConnectionCheckRunnerTests` pins the connection test's structural isolation, and
`NayaxLynxClientDependencyInjectionTests` pins that the port resolves to the decorator over the one
HTTP client with one process-wide cache behind it. Each fresh caller's own suite refuses the cached
read outright, so a use case that stopped reading fresh fails loudly. Issue #846's own staleness is
proved through this whole composition rather than a stand-in for it:
`Inventory.IntegrationTests/Application/Machines/MachineProductsSitePricingStalenessTests` runs
`ListMachineProducts` over the real decorator, the real machine-list and machine-products caches
and a fake clock while the fake Nayax moves the machine from site A to site B — site A's
suggestions, site A's again a second before the lifetime, site B's on the first load after it, two
list reads for three loads and no machine read at all — plus the fallback machine read happening on every load for a machine the list does not hold,
the unchanged upstream failure for a machine Nayax does not know, and nothing but the site-based
suggestions differing across the expiry. It covers the permission answers through the same
composition: an account refused the fleet list is priced by the machine's own read on every load
(the cache holds no refusal), and an unusable connection still refuses the listing without the
machine being read at all. `ListMachineProductsTests` pins the same choices against a mocked port —
the listing being identical whichever read the site came from, including after a fleet-permission
refusal; both reads refused still refusing; and the not-connected, support-session, cancellation and
upstream fleet failures reaching the caller with neither the machine nor its products read.

### The machine-products cache (issue #842)

Issue #842 — step 2 of #839 — is the second Nayax read this application holds on to, and the one that
repeated most. `GET /v1/machines/{MachineID}/machineProducts`
("[Get Machine Products](https://devzone.nayax.com/reference/lynx/machine-products/get-machine-products)",
the endpoint `INayaxLynxClient.GetMachineProductsAsync` is) was read **three times per machine on one
Dashboard visit**, largely at the same moment: `GET api/dashboard/summary` and
`GET api/products/alerts/low-stock` (both `CalculateReorderNeeds`) and `GET api/sites`
(`GetSiteSummaries`). With ten machines that is thirty requests where ten would do.

**Sixty seconds, not ten minutes, and that difference is the whole design.** The decision is the
repository owner's, on 23 October 2026. The fleet list changes rarely; this payload carries the
machine's **live stock levels** — `PAR`, `MissingStockByMDB` and `VendOutAlertThreshold`, each a
nullable `int32` in the authoritative Lynx contract — and an operator reads those to decide what to
restock. So a read-only page may show a figure up to a minute old, and everything that plans a
refill, records a count or establishes a costing baseline reads fresh instead. Like the machine list
it is in memory rather than in a column, and a restart simply reads it again; a distributed or
persisted cache is explicitly out of scope.

**One mechanism, two caches.** `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxReadCache<TKey, TValue>` is the
single-flight, explicitly ordered, expiring cache both reads use, and
`NayaxMachineListCache` and `NayaxMachineProductsCache` are what state each read's key and lifetime
over it (both registered as singletons by `AddNayaxLynxClient`, both held by the one
`CachingNayaxLynxClient` the port resolves to). Everything the machine-list section above describes
about the mechanism — simultaneous readers sharing one request and its failure, nothing failed ever
held, expiry taken under the lock that would otherwise hand the entry out, the sequence-numbered
ordering between an older read, a newer fresh read and an invalidation, an invalidation also
unpublishing the read still running, and keys being forgotten only while they hold nothing usable —
is therefore the same code and the same guarantees here, at sixty seconds. It was written twice in
neither place on purpose: a divergence between two copies of that reasoning would show up as a stale
stock figure rather than as a compile error.

**The key is the business id, the credential revision and the machine id.** The first two for exactly
the reasons the machine list has them — one business must never be served another's stock figures, and
new credentials may name a different Nayax operator account — and the machine id because this read is
per machine: one entry per machine is what turns three requests per machine into one. All three come
from the server's own side of the request: the resolved `IBusinessScope`, the credential snapshot that
was just gated, and the machine the caller is reading. A scope with no resolved business caches nothing
at all rather than sharing a key. And the key names the credentials the request actually carried: one
credential is resolved per call and handed down through
`INayaxLynxCachedReadClient.ReadMachineProductsAsync`, which is `NayaxLynxClient`'s ordinary
per-machine `GET` with the resolution step skipped because it has already happened — same endpoint,
same operation name in logs, same `401` and `403` classification, and still exactly one connection
read per Nayax call.

**Every refusal still happens, before every answer.** The decorator resolves
[`INayaxRequestCredentialProvider.GetForOperationAsync`](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520)
first on every machine-products call — the stored connection, `NayaxConnectionStatusGate` and the
support-session refusal of [issue #551](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551) — so a
business whose connection is now `NotConfigured` or `NeedsAttention`, and a platform administrator
reading in a support session, get today's refusal even while a list for that key is in memory. The
cache is not an authorization boundary and must never become one.

**A successful write forgets that machine's entry.** `CreateMachineProductsAsync` replaces selections
in Nayax, so what is held for that machine is no longer what the machine has: the write goes through
`INayaxLynxCachedReadClient.WriteMachineProductsAsync` with the same already-gated credential — which
is what makes the invalidated key the one belonging to the credentials the write really carried — and
the entry is invalidated after it, and only when it succeeded. A failed write changed nothing in
Nayax, leaves the held entry alone, and raises the same exception to the caller as before. No other
machine's entry is touched, because the write said nothing about any other machine.

**Four callers always read fresh, and the connection test is outside the cache entirely.** `GetPickList`
(what an operator loads a van from), `SyncMachineStockFromNayax` (the machine + MDB mapping decides
which product a stock adjustment is recorded against), `NayaxMachineStockObservationSource` (the
machine-stock ledger and the operator's stock counts, where a minute-old figure would move a reported
shrinkage — see [Machine stock ledger and shrinkage reconciliation](#machine-stock-ledger-and-shrinkage-reconciliation-issue-56))
and `InventoryCostTransitionPreviewBuilder` (its opening machine stock becomes a costing baseline) all
call `GetMachineProductsFreshAsync` and replace the entry for their business, credential revision and
machine. The cached callers are exactly `CalculateReorderNeeds`, `GetSiteSummaries`, `GetSiteProducts`
and `ListMachineProducts` — the read-only Dashboard, Sites and machine pages this cache exists for.
`NayaxConnectionCheckRunner` neither reads from nor writes to it, structurally, for the same reason it
stays outside the machine-list cache: it builds its own `NayaxLynxClient` over the candidate
credentials an Owner pasted, and the machines of the account being considered are not this business's
machines.

**What proves it.** `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/Nayax/NayaxMachineProductsCacheTests`
covers the mechanism at this key and this lifetime over a scripted read whose every call is counted and
can be held open: a hit inside sixty seconds and expiry exactly at sixty on a fake clock, a per-caller
list, three simultaneous readers making one request, each of the three Nayax failures and a
cancellation reaching every caller and being held by none, another machine/business/credential revision
being another key, a fresh read ignoring and replacing what is held, a failed fresh read leaving it
alone, an older in-flight read overwriting neither a newer fresh read nor an invalidation in either
completion order, a caller after an invalidation not joining the read that was already running, and
expired keys being forgotten while a live one keeps its list. `CachingNayaxLynxClientTests` covers the
decorator: a second read of a machine answering from memory, every refusal still happening with a warm
cache (for the cached read, the fresh read and the write), two businesses never receiving each other's
selections, each machine having its own entry, new credentials sending the next read to Nayax, the
fresh read reaching Nayax and replacing what is held, a successful write forgetting that machine's
entry and no other's, a failed write leaving it alone, one credential resolved per call with the read
and the write carrying it, and nothing but the two cached reads being cached.
`DashboardMachineProductsFanOutTests` measures the outcome on the shape that caused the issue: the
Dashboard's three requests, over the real `CalculateReorderNeeds` and `GetSiteSummaries`, each with its
own decorator and credentials and all three sharing the process-wide caches, with every upstream read
held open until all three have asked for every machine — one `machineProducts` request per machine, and
one fleet read for the three requests. Each fresh caller's own suite refuses the cached read outright,
so a use case that stopped reading fresh fails loudly.

### Nayax connection checks and the Test endpoint (issue #536)

Issue #536 — one slice of #506, under the contract of #328 — is how an Owner finds out whether a
Nayax token works *before* it becomes the business's connection. The problem it solves is specific:
new Lynx app tokens frequently authenticate perfectly and lack one or more of the permissions this
application needs, and until now the only way to discover that was for a feature to fail in
production. So the server runs the reads the application actually makes, reports each one on its own
line, and holds the tested credentials as a short-lived **encrypted draft** that nothing has
accepted yet.

Since issue #967 this endpoint — and the save and re-test beside it — additionally requires the
**Pro** plan, declared at the endpoint rather than in the credential gate, because these are the only
Nayax calls in the application that do not go through that gate: the test authenticates with the
pasted pair and the save and re-test run the checks themselves. The requirement is evaluated after the
Owner capability and before the action, so a refused request makes no Nayax request, writes no draft
and leaves the stored credentials exactly as they were. Reading the connection *status* carries no
plan requirement at all. See
[Plan enforcement on reports and Nayax operations](#plan-enforcement-on-reports-and-nayax-operations-issue-967).

**The checks are the endpoints the application already calls, and they are all reads.**
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionCheck` is the complete, declared list, and there is one check
per endpoint rather than one per feature — a token missing one permission is the ordinary case, and
collapsing two endpoints into one line would hide which of them was refused:

| Check | Endpoint | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SignIn` | `GET devices` | Proves the token authenticates at all |
| `Machines` | `GET machines` | Also decides whether the machine checks run |
| `Machine` | `GET machines/{id}` | Machine-scoped |
| `ProductCatalogue` | `GET operators/{operatorId}/products` | Operator-scoped |
| `ProductGroups` | `GET operators/{operatorId}/productGroups` | Operator-scoped |
| `MachineProducts` | `GET machines/{id}/machineProducts` | Machine-scoped |
| `MachineLastSales` | `GET machines/{id}/lastSales` | Machine-scoped |
| `MachineLastAlerts` | `GET machines/{id}/lastAlerts` | Machine-scoped |

**`POST machines/{id}/machineProducts` is never called**, and it is absent from the vocabulary rather
than merely unused: testing a connection must not change an operator's Nayax data.
`NayaxConnectionCheckRunnerTests.No_check_ever_makes_a_write_call` asserts that over the wire for a
success, a `401`, a `403` and a `5xx` alike.

**With no machines, the machine lines read `NotChecked`.** A business connecting Nayax before its
first machine exists has nothing to run `GET machines/{id}` against, and the same is true when the
machine list itself could not be read. That is reported as its own status — never as a pass, because
an untested permission must not look like a granted one, and never as a failure, because the
credentials did nothing wrong. `NayaxConnectionCheckReport.NothingFailed` is therefore `true` while
the only non-passing lines are unchecked ones, so the wizard of #538 can let such a business finish.
The machine checks also run against the **first** machine only: a token either carries the machine
permissions or it does not, and walking the estate would turn a connection test into a load test of
somebody else's API.

**What a Nayax answer means is one Domain table.**
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionCheckPolicy.Classify` is the only place it is decided, for the
same reason `NayaxConnectionStatusGate` is: "lacks a permission" and "token expired" need completely
different actions from an operator, and a second opinion written inline in an adapter is how the
wrong one ends up on somebody's screen. The mapping is Nayax's own documented vocabulary
([App tokens troubleshooting](https://devzone.nayax.com/docs/manage-data-operations/lynx-api/app-tokens)):

- **`401` → `InvalidOrExpiredToken`.** The documented "token is invalid or has expired".
- **`403` → `PermissionNotGranted`.** The documented "Insufficient permissions to perform this
  action" — a verdict on one endpoint, not on the token.
- **`404` on an operator-scoped check → `OperatorIdMismatch`.** Only `.../operators/{operatorId}/...`
  carries the submitted operator id, so only those two checks can answer "that operator is not one
  this token covers". A `404` anywhere else is **not** reported as a mismatch: it would send an
  operator to re-check a correct operator id.
- **`5xx`, a timeout, a dropped connection or an open circuit → `NayaxUnavailable`.** Nothing was
  learned about the credentials, so nothing is concluded about them.
- **Anything else → `UnexpectedResponse`.** A `400`, the documented `429` rate limit, a `404` on a
  check that carries no operator id, or a body that is not the documented shape. An answer nobody
  has interpreted is never presented as one that has been.

**The checks go through `NayaxLynxClient`, with the one thing that differs swapped.** That client is
the single place a Nayax request is built, authenticated, sent and then accepted or rejected, and the
runner needs exactly that — the same relative endpoints, the same `Authorization: Bearer` header, the
same operator-id path parameter built from the same credential, the same rule that an upstream body
is never read or logged. What differs is **only** where the credential comes from, so only the
credential provider differs: `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxConnectionCheckRunner` constructs
the client over a private `INayaxRequestCredentialProvider` that answers with the pasted pair. Its
status is `PendingPermissions` — the truth about a token nothing has stored or tested, and what makes
the client report a `403` as the per-feature permission answer the test needs per line — and its
`ReportUnauthorizedAsync` is a **no-op**: a `401` here is a verdict on credentials that have never
been stored, so there is no revision it belongs to and no row it may touch. **A test of a bad token
therefore cannot move a working stored connection to `NeedsAttention`**, and cannot change its
operator id, status, revision or last-tested instant either. It gets its own `HttpClient` from the
same base address with the same `NayaxResilienceHandler`, because "Nayax is unavailable" has to mean
the same thing on a test as on a sync. This is **not** the gate-free re-test read of
[issue #520](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520): nothing here reads the stored connection at
all.

**The draft: encrypted, tenant-owned, actor-bound, one per business, fifteen minutes.**
`POST /api/settings/nayax-connection/test` takes `{ operatorId, token }`, runs the checks, and stores
the pair in the additive `NayaxConnectionTestDrafts` table through
`Inventory.Application.Nayax.INayaxConnectionTestDraftStore`. It is deliberately **not**
`BusinessNayaxConnections`: a draft holds credentials nothing has accepted, no Nayax call may resolve
one, it carries no `NayaxConnectionStatus` and no credential revision, and promoting one into the
connection is issue #537's separate, reviewed step.

- **The token is stored only as ciphertext**, through #518's `INayaxTokenProtector`, with the key id
  beside it. Holding a plaintext token for fifteen minutes to achieve a pre-flight check would defeat
  the point of the check. The response body carries the operator id's draft but never the token, and
  neither do the stored results, a log line or an exception.
- **It is tenant-owned by the central mechanism.** The entity implements `IBusinessOwned`, so the
  `AppDbContext` query filters scope every read and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` stamps the insert; the
  adapter adds no business predicate of its own and refuses to run at all without a single resolved
  business, because the replacing `DELETE` executes in the database without passing through
  `SaveChanges`.
- **It is bound to the Owner who created it**, by the validated Entra `(tid, oid)` pair. A draft id
  naming another business's draft, another member's draft, or an expired one all read as *there is no
  such draft*: distinguishing them would tell a caller that somebody else's draft exists.
- **One draft per business, replaced by the next test.** A unique index on the ownership column makes
  that a schema guarantee rather than a convention, so a second decryptable token cannot exist for a
  business however the write path is called, and a superseded ciphertext is not left behind. The
  delete and the insert are one transaction, so a failed replacement leaves the previous draft in
  place rather than leaving the business with none.
- **It expires after fifteen minutes** (`TestNayaxConnection.DraftLifetime`) — long enough to read
  eight result lines and decide, short enough that an abandoned browser tab does not leave a
  decryptable token in the database for the rest of the day. Expiry is a **read** rule, not a sweep:
  past the instant the draft stops existing for every caller, and the row goes when the next test
  replaces it.
- **The returned `draftId` is opaque.** A random GUID carrying nothing about the business, the actor
  or the credentials.
- **It is excluded from platform diagnostics**, like `BusinessNayaxConnections` and for the same
  reason. `PlatformDiagnosticsDataSurface` is an allow-list of table/column pairs, so a new table is
  denied automatically until a separately reviewed change adds it — and this one must never be added.

**Owner only, through the ordinary capability mechanism.** `NayaxConnectionController` declares
`[RequireCapability(Capability.IntegrationManage)]`, which #328's table grants to an Owner alone, the
same capability `api/settings/nayax-processing-fee-rates` carries and for the same reason. The action
is a `POST`: it submits a secret in a body rather than a URL, it calls out to Nayax, it writes the
draft, and a cached `GET` response would hand a caller a verdict about credentials it never tested.

**The rate limit is per business, and spent before anything is sent.**
`Inventory.Application.Nayax.NayaxConnectionTestRateLimiter` allows five runs per business per rolling
ten minutes. The bucket is the **business**, not the actor: one run is eight calls against somebody
else's API, a Test button is trivially clickable in a loop, and rate-limiting the actor would let a
second Owner start again from zero against the same operator account. The window **slides**, because
a fixed ten-minute bucket would allow five runs at the end of one and five at the start of the next.
The allowance is claimed *before* the runner, so a refused request makes no Nayax call and stores
nothing, and a failing run is not refunded — a failing test is exactly the run that gets repeated.
The refusal is `429` with a `Retry-After` in seconds and a fixed sentence that names neither the
count, the window nor the token. The window lives in memory rather than in a column, like
`MemberProfileRefreshThrottle`'s hour: what the record of a connection holds is the connection, not
how often somebody pressed Test, and on a single instance
([SQLite operating assumptions](#sqlite-operating-assumptions-and-scale-strategy-issue-53)) in-process
state is the whole truth.

**The allowance is the business's, and clearing out memory never changes it** (issue #606). The
limiter remembers one claim history per business and, once more than `MaxTrackedBusinesses` (256) are
remembered, each granted claim also clears out what has gone stale. That housekeeping is bounded by
one rule: it expires the attempts that have **left** the window and forgets only a business left with
none of them. A business whose oldest attempt has expired while later ones are still live keeps those
live attempts and so keeps exactly the slots they have freed — dropping its history wholesale would
restart its window and let five more runs reach Nayax inside the same ten minutes, which is the
regression issue #606 fixed and `NayaxConnectionTestRateLimiterTests` now pins with a deterministic
one-attempt-then-four sequence. The threshold is therefore a hint about memory, never a cap: crossing
it neither grants, denies nor resets any business's allowance, and a business that really has been
quiet for a whole window is still forgotten. Expiring, counting and recording a claim are one
operation on the history that business is tracked by, so a claim racing the clear-out is still counted
against the window rather than landing in a forgotten history — test and re-test share that one
history, so the pair of them is five runs per business per rolling ten minutes in any mix.

**Nothing is logged that should not be.** The runner logs nothing itself; the underlying client's one
`Error` line for an ordinary upstream failure carries the operation, method, relative endpoint and
status code and never the token, the authorization header or the upstream body, exactly as before.
`NayaxConnectionCheckRunnerTests.The_token_and_the_upstream_body_never_reach_the_report_or_a_log`
sweeps both for a success and for each refusal.

**What is deliberately not here.** The connection banners (#539), the permanent credential store and
provider (#500's own slices), and anything that creates a Nayax token or requests a permission
automatically. Saving a draft and re-testing the stored credentials arrived with issue #537,
immediately below, and the Owner-facing wizard over all of it with issue #538 — see
[The Nayax connection wizard](#the-nayax-connection-wizard-issue-538).

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Nayax/NayaxConnectionCheckPolicyTests` — every
documented status on every check, the two `404` readings, no answer at all, and the vocabulary itself,
so a check, status or cause added later has to make a decision there.
`Inventory.UnitTests/Application/Nayax/NayaxConnectionTestRateLimiterTests` — the fifth run allowed
and the sixth refused, the sliding boundary and its `Retry-After`, a clock that moved backwards not
reopening a slot, one business not spending another's allowance, and, above the tracking threshold
(issue #606), clearing out keeping a mixed history's live attempts over repeated passes, forgetting a
fully idle business, leaving an unrelated business's allowance alone, and a coordinated race of claims
against clearing out granting the five runs exactly once.
`TestNayaxConnectionTests` — the submitted credentials reaching the runner, pasted whitespace trimmed,
a blank field refused before any call or allowance, no token in the result or the stored results,
the fifteen-minute expiry, the opaque id, replacement, actor binding, and a rate-limited request
calling Nayax not at all. `Inventory.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/Nayax/NayaxConnectionCheckRunnerTests`
— the eight endpoints called once each with the submitted bearer token, no write call ever, each
status mapping over a fake handler, zero machines, the first machine only, a transport failure, an
unreadable body, caller cancellation, and the token/body log sweep.
`Adapters/Persistence/EfNayaxConnectionTestDraftStoreTests` — relational SQLite with two businesses:
ciphertext at rest and no plaintext in any column, replacement, expiry, actor binding, cross-business
isolation in both directions, an unscoped write refused, and a protector that cannot encrypt leaving
the previous draft alone. `Adapters/Persistence/AddNayaxConnectionTestDraftsMigrationTests` — the
table and its unique index arrive, a second draft per business is refused by SQLite, the stored
connection is byte-for-byte unchanged, and nothing is backfilled.
`Controllers/NayaxConnectionTestApiTests` — the published response shape through the real pipeline and
the real migration history, the token never echoed, the draft encrypted and bound, a second test
replacing the first, the stored connection untouched, `400` for a missing field, and the `429` with
its `Retry-After`. `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` and
`EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` carry the endpoint's capability row.

### Saving a tested connection and re-testing it (issue #537)

Issue #537 — the next slice of #506, under the contract of #328 — is what turns a completed test into
the business's connection, and what lets an Owner run those checks again later against the token the
business is actually using. It adds three endpoints to `NayaxConnectionController` and one additive
column, and nothing else: no banners (#539). The Owner-facing wizard that drives these endpoints
arrived separately with issue #538 — see
[The Nayax connection wizard](#the-nayax-connection-wizard-issue-538).

| Endpoint | Capability | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST api/settings/nayax-connection/save` | `Integration.Manage` | Promotes one draft into the connection and deletes it |
| `POST api/settings/nayax-connection/retest` | `Integration.Manage` | Runs the same checks with the **stored** token and writes what they concluded |
| `GET api/settings/nayax-connection/status` | `Dashboard.View` | Reports the status and whether the machine checks are still pending |

**Save takes a draft id and never a token.** That is the whole point of the two-step shape: the
credentials being stored are exactly the ones the server tested, so one token's successful test can
never be presented as evidence for another, and a request cannot store a credential nothing has
tried. `NayaxConnectionSaveRequest` is one nullable `Guid` and **must never gain** an operator id, a
token, a status, a check result or a business id. The operator id, the token and the results all come
out of the claimed draft; the business comes from the caller's membership and the actor from the
validated Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, so another business's draft and another member's draft are not
saveable.

**Claiming the draft and writing the credential are one transaction.** `Inventory.Application.Nayax.SaveNayaxConnection`
opens it through the narrow `INayaxConnectionSaveTransactions` port — named for this one operation
because the transaction spans *both* Nayax connection ports, so putting it on either would imply the
other's writes were outside it — and `EfNayaxConnectionSaveTransactions` opens it on the request's own
`AppDbContext`, the scoped unit of work both EF adapters are constructed with. It asks SQLite for
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, the second place in the application to do so and for the same reason as
`EfBusinessMembershipWriteStore` (see [Membership roles and capabilities](#membership-roles-and-capabilities-issue-521)):
a deferred transaction takes its write lock at the first write, which is *after* the read the claim is
decided on, so two simultaneous saves would meet each other at their deletes — where one is already
waiting to commit and SQLite can only answer "busy". With the lock taken at `BEGIN`, the second
caller waits and then reads the first one's committed state, and the refusal is the deliberate `409`.
Inside it:

- **The claim is a conditional delete that must remove exactly one row.**
  `INayaxConnectionTestDraftStore.TryClaimAsync` reads the row (id, owning business from the central
  query filter, creating actor, `ExpiresAt > @now`), decrypts the token, and then deletes under that
  same predicate; the claim succeeds only when the `DELETE` removed one row. The delete — not the
  read — is what the caller branches on, because a test-then-delete would leave exactly the race this
  is for open. Decryption happens *before* the delete so a key-configuration failure consumes
  nothing.
- **Two saves of one draft therefore end as one save and one refusal**, with `CredentialRevision`
  increased exactly once. The refusal is `409` with the fixed sentence *"This test result was already
  used or has expired. Run the test again."* — the same answer for an unknown id, an expired draft,
  another business's, another member's, and one a previous save already claimed, because
  distinguishing them would tell a caller that somebody else's draft exists.
- **A refusal commits nothing.** The transaction is simply not committed, so a save refused for a
  failed sign-in, or one whose credential write fails, puts the claimed draft back rather than
  destroying a tested token the Owner can no longer save.

**The status comes from that draft's own results, through one Domain rule.**
`Inventory.Domain.Nayax.NayaxConnectionCheckOutcomePolicy` is the only place a completed run is
interpreted, beside `NayaxConnectionCheckPolicy` and `NayaxConnectionStatusGate` and for the same
reason: "this token works", "this token is missing a permission" and "this token is dead" need
completely different actions from an operator. It takes the three facts it needs — the sign-in line's
status, its failure cause, and whether any other executed check failed — so the Domain keeps no
dependency on the Application layer's report type; the projection lives on
`NayaxConnectionCheckReport.Outcome`.

| Run | Outcome | Status it concludes | May be saved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Every executed check passed | `Ready` | `Ready` | ✔ |
| Sign-in passed, another executed check failed | `PendingPermissions` | `PendingPermissions` | ✔ |
| Sign-in refused with `401` | `TokenRejected` | `NeedsAttention` | ✘ |
| Sign-in did not pass and gave no verdict | `Inconclusive` | *(none — status unchanged)* | ✘ |

**Only a `401` is a verdict on the token.** That is Nayax's own documented meaning — "the token is
invalid or has expired", against a `403`'s "Insufficient permissions to perform this action", a
verdict on one endpoint's scope
([App tokens](https://devzone.nayax.com/docs/manage-data-operations/lynx-api/app-tokens), confirmed
for this change). Every other way a sign-in can fail to pass — Nayax unavailable, an answer nobody
has interpreted, the sign-in endpoint itself refused for lack of a scope, a line never checked —
concludes **nothing**: the issue spells out the `401` and the `5xx` cases, and this is the fail-closed
reading of the rest, because concluding anything from an answer nobody interpreted would either break
a working connection or bless a dead one. A save is refused whenever the sign-in did not pass (`400`,
*"The tested token did not sign in to Nayax, so it was not saved…"*): a token that has never been
shown to authenticate must not replace what the business is using today.

**"Not checked" machine lines do not block `Ready`, and the saved connection records them.** A
business connecting Nayax before its first machine exists has nothing to run `GET machines/{id}`
against, which is a fact about the account and not a fault of the credentials. The save stores
`Ready` and sets `MachineChecksPending`, computed from the report as "the machine list was read,
and a machine-scoped line was still never checked" — which checks need a machine stays
`NayaxConnectionCheckPolicy.RequiresMachine`'s answer. A machine list that was itself refused or
never checked leaves the flag unset (issue #681): those lines are unchecked for want of the list,
not of a machine, the refused line already records `PendingPermissions` (or the sign-in's own
verdict), and "re-test once your machines are set up" would send an Owner who has machines to the
wrong fix. A later re-test that reaches them clears it. `false` is therefore both "the machine checks
passed" and "no check has ever run", deliberately: the flag exists to ask an Owner to re-test once
their machines are set up, so the additive migration backfills nothing and the connection the
human-run `migrate-nayax-connection` command stored — which has been authenticating in production —
reports "not pending" rather than being made to look incomplete.

**Re-test is the one ordinary consumer of the gate-free credential read.**
`Inventory.Application.Nayax.RetestNayaxConnection` resolves the stored token through
`INayaxConnectionRetestCredentialProvider` ([issue #520](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520)),
which deliberately ignores `NayaxConnectionStatusGate` — a connection in `NeedsAttention` is exactly
the one an operator has to recover, and the gate that refuses ordinary calls in that state would make
recovery impossible. It is listed in `NayaxRetestCredentialBoundaryTests`' allow-list as the reviewed
exception that boundary always anticipated, and nothing else may join it. It runs the same read-only
checks through the same `INayaxConnectionCheckRunner`, so a re-test makes exactly the same eight
`GET`s and no write.

**Every result is bound to the revision it tested — whatever it concluded — and a run that learned
nothing writes nothing.** The credential read reports the revision the token was read at. A concluded
status is written by #518's conditional `UPDATE … WHERE CredentialRevision = @r`, and a run that
concluded nothing compares that revision with the stored one before its report is accepted
([issue #607](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/607)). An Owner who saves a
replacement token while a re-test is in flight therefore keeps the replacement's own status in both
cases: the older run describes credentials that no longer exist, so its result is discarded — never
returned beside the replacement's summary — and the caller gets `409` with the fixed sentence *"The
connection changed while testing. Run the test again."* A connection that has been removed by then is
the same answer as a replaced one. When the sign-in produced no verdict at all — a `5xx`, a timeout,
an open circuit — **nothing is written** either way, not even a last-tested instant that would claim
the current credentials had been checked: at the tested revision the response is `200` with
`statusUpdated: false`, the stored status read back from the row, and the lines that say Nayax was
unavailable; at any other revision it is the `409` above, with no completed stale report and the
replacement's status, token, revision, last-tested instant and machine-check flag all untouched. That
comparison and the summary returned with it come from **one** read of the row
(`INayaxConnectionStore.FindAsync`, one statement), for the same reason #520's snapshot exists: two
reads could pair the old run's report with the new credentials' state. A business with no stored
credentials has nothing to re-test and gets the stable `nayax_not_connected` `409`.

**Test and re-test share one per-business allowance.** A re-test is the same eight calls against the
same upstream, so it claims from the same `NayaxConnectionTestRateLimiter` singleton, before the
runner, and the two count together: five runs per business per rolling ten minutes in any mix, then
`429` with a `Retry-After` and no Nayax call at all.

**The status read is for every member, and answers two things.** The banners of #539 are shown to a
Manager and an Operator, who cannot open the Owner-only integration settings at all, so
`GET …/status` carries `Dashboard.View` and returns the status name and `machineChecksPending` and
**nothing else** — no operator id, no credential revision, no last-tested instant, no check lines. It
never decrypts the stored token. A business with no row reads `NotConfigured`, which is also what a
caller whose business does not resolve reads. Because capability requirements accumulate down an
endpoint, the capability is declared **per action** on `NayaxConnectionController` rather than on the
controller: a controller-level `Integration.Manage` would mean this read required both and so be
Owner-only (issues #525 and #526).

**What proves it.** `Inventory.UnitTests/Domain/Nayax/NayaxConnectionCheckOutcomePolicyTests` — every
row of the table above, each unstated sign-in failure concluding nothing, a failed sign-in deciding
the outcome whatever else failed, and an undeclared status or outcome refused rather than defaulted.
`Inventory.UnitTests/Application/Nayax/SaveNayaxConnectionTests` — the status from the draft's own
results, the stored credentials being the tested ones, unchecked machine lines saved `Ready` with the
flag set, a failed sign-in refused with nothing stored and nothing committed, a draft saved only once
with the revision increased once, expiry and actor binding refused identically, and a missing draft id
refused before a transaction is begun. `RetestNayaxConnectionTests` — each outcome from each of
`Ready`, `PendingPermissions` and `NeedsAttention`, an unavailable Nayax leaving the row
byte-for-byte, the revision the checks ran with, the pending machine checks recorded and then
cleared, a replacement saved mid-run keeping its own status for a concluded *and* for an inconclusive
run (each cause that concludes nothing, plus a connection removed mid-run), an unchanged revision
comparing and reporting from one read, no stored credentials, and the shared allowance.
`GetNayaxConnectionStatusTests` — the two fields, `NotConfigured`, and no token decrypted.
`Adapters/Persistence/NayaxConnectionSaveTransactionTests` — relational SQLite over a database
*file*, so two saves of one draft are genuinely concurrent: exactly one succeeds, the other is the
`409`, the revision increases once, and the draft is consumed once; plus a refused save and a failed
credential write both leaving the draft in place.
`Adapters/Persistence/EfNayaxConnectionTestDraftStoreTests` — the claim returning the decrypted
credential and deleting the row, a second claim finding nothing, a draft that disappears between the
read and the delete claiming nothing, cross-business and unscoped claims refused, and an
undecryptable token failing closed without consuming the draft.
`Adapters/Persistence/EfNayaxConnectionStoreTests` — the machine-checks column written only by a
result that states it, and cleared by a credential save.
`Adapters/Persistence/AddNayaxConnectionMachineChecksPendingMigrationTests` — the column arrives, no
other column or index changes, the existing connection is byte-for-byte unchanged and reads "not
pending", and nothing is backfilled. `Controllers/NayaxConnectionSaveRetestApiTests` — the whole flow
through the real pipeline and the real migration history: test then save, the token as ciphertext and
never echoed, every refusal's status and sentence, the re-test outcomes including the recovery from
`NeedsAttention` and both the concluded and the inconclusive re-test overtaken by a save — the `409`,
its exact sentence and the replacement's row byte-for-byte unchanged — the shared `429`, the status
read for each role with exactly two fields, and a non-Owner neither saving nor re-testing.
`CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` and `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` carry the three
endpoints' capability rows.

### The Nayax connection wizard (issue #538)

Issue #538 — the Owner-facing slice of #506, under #328 — is the screen over the endpoints above: a
six-step wizard on Admin → Integrations (called Nayax Settings until issue #729), beside the
processing-fee editor it did not replace. It is
**frontend only**: it adds no endpoint, changes no contract and holds no rule of its own.

`NayaxConnectionWizardComponent` and the presentational `NayaxConnectionChecklistComponent`
(`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/admin/nayax-settings/`) are composed by the routed
`NayaxSettingsComponent` per [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191): the
steps, the token field, the checklist, the support request and the save/re-test lifecycle belong to
the wizard, not to the page. `NayaxConnectionService` is the one client for the four endpoints.

**The token field is write-only, and that is the point of the whole shape.** Step 3's input is bound
to no component state — no `ngModel`, no signal, no field — because a component property holding a
Lynx token is exactly what must not exist. It is read from the DOM when Test is pressed, passed once
to `POST …/test`, and cleared the instant that call returns, on a success, a refusal and a transport
failure alike. Nothing writes it to `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, a cookie, the URL or a toast,
and nothing re-sends it: Save carries the server's own opaque draft id, so the credentials stored are
the ones the server tested (see
[Saving a tested connection and re-testing it](#saving-a-tested-connection-and-re-testing-it-issue-537)).
`NayaxConnectionWizardComponent`'s spec asserts the absence - the token in no own property, in
neither storage, and the field emptied on both paths - because "we do not keep it" is a claim only a
test can keep true.

**It concludes nothing about the connection.** Every check line, cause sentence, machine count and
status on screen is the server's own finding, read through the one area/cause vocabulary the
checklist and the support request share. A `NotChecked` line is rendered as neither a pass nor a
failure, and it says *why* from the machine count: zero machines reads "no machines in this Nayax
account yet", while no count at all reads "the machine list could not be read" — a business that has
machines must not be sent to set them up. The checklist also states that the restock write call is
never tested and is checked on first real use, because a connection test must not change an
operator's Nayax data.

**Step 5 exists because the fix is usually Nayax's to make.** When any line failed, the wizard
composes a ready-to-copy request naming the operator id that was tested — captured with the result,
not read from the field an Owner may have edited since — and every area refused for lack of a
permission (`PermissionNotGranted`) with its cause, links the Nayax support portal
(`https://nayax.service-now.com/csm`) and offers `integration-support@nayax.com` as the secondary
contact. The request names no token. A line refused for any other cause is not a permission Nayax
could grant, so it is left out of the request and gets its own advice instead (issue #681): an
invalid or expired token asks for a new token, an operator id mismatch asks the Owner to check the
operator id, an unavailable Nayax asks for another try, and an answer nobody interpreted asks for a
re-test before anyone is asked about it. Step 5 is skipped entirely when the server reported nothing
failed.

**Save and re-test say what the server said.** Save is not offered for a run whose sign-in did not
pass, or whose draft has expired — the server refuses both, and this only avoids spending a request
on a known refusal. A consumed or refused draft is withdrawn from the screen, so a second save is
impossible here as well as refused. The stored-connection panel reads `GET …/status` on arrival,
shows the status, prompts "Re-test once your machines are set up" while the machine checks are
pending, and offers Re-test in every status including `NeedsAttention`. A re-test that concluded
nothing says the stored status is left exactly as it was; a `409` shows the server's own *"The
connection changed while testing. Run the test again."*, and the component carries that sentence
itself for a refusal that arrives with no body.

**Owner only in three places, authoritative in neither of the first two.** The route requires
`Integration.Manage` (`app.routes.ts`), the wizard hides itself and refuses its own actions without
that capability, and each endpoint checks it and refuses the request regardless. The capability read
starts granted, so an unanswered read leaves the wizard as it was before roles were rendered.

**What is deliberately not here.** The connection banners on other screens (#539) and any backend
change.

### Nayax connection status banners (issue #539)

Issue #539 — the last slice of #506, under #328 — is the explanation every other Nayax-dependent
screen was missing: Machines (`MachineListComponent`, `MachineDetailComponent`), Sites
(`SiteListComponent`, `SiteProductsComponent`), Pick List (`PickListComponent`, until it was removed
there - see below) and the Sync Restock workflow (`MachineRestockSyncComponent`) all read a live Nayax projection through
`INayaxLynxClient` (`ListMachineDashboard`, `ListMachineProducts`, `GetSiteSummaries`,
`GetSiteProducts`, the Pick List projection and `SyncMachineStockFromNayax`), so each of them now
composes the one shared `NayaxStatusBannerComponent`
(`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/shared/nayax-status-banner/`) just under its page header
(and, on `MachineRestockSyncComponent`, inside its own card beside the Sync Restock button, since
that is the workflow a Manager or Operator actually triggers). It is **frontend only**: it adds no
endpoint and decides no rule of its own.

**It reads the same status the wizard reads, once, and adds nothing to it.** The status comes from
`GET …/nayax-connection/status` (issue #537, `Dashboard.View` - every role) and the banner shows
nothing until that answer is known. It is hidden while the status is `Ready` and while the read could
not be answered at all - a page's own data load already reports its own failure, and a banner built
on a probe nobody could answer would only add a second, possibly wrong, explanation beside it - and
shown for every other published status (`NotConfigured`, `PendingPermissions`, `NeedsAttention`).
Since issue #728 the banner takes that answer from the application-wide
`ProviderAvailabilityService` rather than calling `NayaxConnectionService.status()` itself, so the
three or four banners a screen can hold, and the filters and fields beside them, state one answer
from one read - see [Shared provider availability and error-versus-empty
states](#shared-provider-availability-and-error-versus-empty-states-issue-728). Its displayed
behaviour is unchanged.

**Who sees the setup link is `Integration.Manage`, not a role string.** That capability is the one
`RoleCapabilities` grants to an Owner alone, so the banner reads it through
`AccessService.allows('Integration.Manage')` exactly as `NayaxConnectionWizardComponent` does, and
with the same fail-open default (`canManage` starts `true`) so an unanswered capability read never
hides a link an Owner's role would show once the identity is known. An Owner sees "Nayax isn't fully
connected for this business." with a link to the wizard (`/admin/nayax-settings`, independently
guarded by the same capability); a Manager or Operator sees the fixed sentence "Nayax isn't fully
connected for this business. Ask a business Owner to finish the Nayax connection." with no link at
all - never a derived "ask your admin" message, because this is the one sentence #328 agreed on.

**The Pick List no longer composes it.** At the owner's request the banner was taken off
`PickListComponent`: on the Pick List it showed for a connection that still works
(`PendingPermissions` passes the status gate), and the page already says in its own words when Nayax
actually refuses it (`calculatedUnavailableReason`, which falls back to manual entry). Its spec now
proves the banner is absent there even for a non-`Ready` status. Every other screen listed above
still shows it.

**What is deliberately not here.** The wizard itself (#538) and making these screens usable without
Nayax at all, which is #329's release-gated work - the banner only explains the failure these
screens already have; it does not give any of them a working degraded mode.

**What proves it.** `NayaxStatusBannerComponent`'s own spec - every published status for an Owner
and for a non-Owner, hidden on `Ready`, hidden while unread and while the status call fails, the
Owner's link target, and the Manager/Operator sentence verbatim. Each remaining host component's own spec
proves the banner is composed and reacts to the same `NotConfigured`/`Ready` stub the banner's own
spec already covers in full, rather than re-asserting that matrix five more times.

### Document storage

Uploaded business documents reach storage through one Application port,
`Inventory.Application.Documents.IDocumentStorage` (issue #39, checkpoint 1). It takes a
`DocumentCategory` — `PurchaseDocument` or `ExpenseAttachment` — and the server-generated stored
file name already held on the tenant-owned purchase or operating-expense record, and offers
`SaveAsync`, `OpenReadAsync` and `DeleteAsync`. It exposes no filesystem path, no container or
URL, no `IWebHostEnvironment`, and no business identifier: ownership is resolved before a call
reaches the port, by loading the parent record through the tenant-filtered `AppDbContext`, so the
#64 boundary is what decides whether a document may be touched at all.
`Inventory.Application.Purchases.UploadPurchase`/`AttachPurchaseDocument`/`DeletePurchase` (issues
#281 and #976) and, since the operating-expenses slice (issue #50),
`Inventory.Application.Expenses.CreateOperatingExpense`/`UpdateOperatingExpense`/`DeleteOperatingExpense`
compose `SaveAsync` and `DeleteAsync` around their own database work to replace a document, which
is what keeps cleanup-on-failure ordering visible at the call site rather than hidden in storage.
A purchase may have **no** document at all since issue #976, and then it reaches this port not at
all: `SaveAsync` is called only when there is something to store, and the purchase's four document
values are stored as `NULL` together (see
[A purchase's document is optional](#a-purchases-document-is-optional-issue-976)).

`Inventory.Infrastructure.Documents.FileSystemDocumentStorage` writes new documents to
`{ContentRoot}/protected-files/{category}/`, reads them back from there or, failing that, from
the legacy `{WebRoot}/{category}/` location, and refuses to overwrite an existing document or to
leave a partially written one behind. Category folders keep their legacy names (`receipts`,
`expenses`) because persisted metadata refers to documents by stored file name alone.

`Inventory.Infrastructure.Documents.AzureBlobDocumentStorage` (issue #39, checkpoint 2) is the
second implementation. It keys every document by the business that owns it:

```text
tenants/{businessId}/purchases/{storedFileName}
tenants/{businessId}/expenses/{storedFileName}
```

The `businessId` is read from `IBusinessScope` — the trusted per-request scope issue #64
publishes from the authenticated actor's membership — and never from a route, query, form,
header, JSON body or file name; `IDocumentStorage` deliberately has no parameter that could
carry one. A denied scope and the deliberate `Unscoped` opt-out both refuse: a document belongs
to exactly one business, so there is no prefix that could stand in for "all of them", and
cross-business maintenance work needs its own explicit path rather than a mode of the request
path. `BlobDocumentPath` reduces an untrusted stored name to its last path segment before it can
reach the service, because the Blob service canonicalises nothing and a `..` in a name would
otherwise be a real blob under a different prefix. Uploads use `overwrite: false`, so the
service itself refuses to replace an existing document; a blob is readable only once its upload
is committed, so a failed upload leaves nothing behind and the adapter deliberately does not
delete on failure. The container is private and no SAS or public URL is generated.

The SDK sits behind a small seam, `IDocumentBlobContainer`, implemented by `AzureBlobContainer`.
That is what lets the adapter's rules — tenant-scoped names, no overwrite, missing blob means
`null` — be tested without Azure credentials or a network.

**Migrating documents to Blob storage.** `migrate-documents`
(`InventoryApi/Bootstrap/DocumentMigrationCommand`) copies the documents already on disk into the
Blob container, as a human-invoked command run with `--dry-run` to inspect and `--apply` to copy.
Exactly one of the two must be given: unlike the other commands, a bare invocation is refused
rather than treated as a dry run. The web host never performs it.

Ownership comes from the database and nowhere else: each document's business is read from the
persisted purchase or operating-expense record that owns it, never from a folder name, a file
name, a blob name or the command line. A record whose `BusinessId` is unusable is reported and
left alone rather than filed under a default. The command therefore reads through
`UnscopedBusinessScope.Instance` — it must see every business at once — but it is emphatically
not a request: it uses `IDocumentMigrationDestination`, a separate Infrastructure abstraction
that takes an explicit `BusinessId`, rather than `IDocumentStorage`, which has no such parameter
and whose Azure adapter correctly refuses to run unscoped. Keys are built with the same
`BlobDocumentPath` the running application uses, so a migrated document lands where the API will
later look for it.

Sources are resolved exactly as a live download resolves them — protected storage first, then the
legacy web root — by reusing `FileSystemDocumentStorage`. Each document is fingerprinted by
streaming SHA-256 and size: an absent destination is written create-if-absent and then read back
and verified before it counts as `Migrated`; a destination already holding the same bytes is
`AlreadyPresent`, which is what makes a rerun safe; a destination holding *different* bytes is a
`Collision`, never overwritten, renamed or deleted. Missing sources, unusable business ids and
failed verifications are reported per document with the record type, id, business, stored name
and reason — and nothing about the document's contents. The command requires
`DocumentStorage:Provider=AzureBlob` and refuses to run against the filesystem default, which
would otherwise copy every document from the filesystem back to the filesystem and report
success. It exits `0` when nothing is unresolved (a dry run's pending work is not a problem) and
`1` when any document is missing, collided, unowned or failed, so an apply can be gated on a
clean dry run.

A failure reaching the destination — container missing, authorization refused, account disabled,
service unavailable — aborts the whole run rather than becoming a few documents' `Failed`. Those
failures are about the destination rather than the document being copied, and reporting them per
item would print the most misleading summary the command could produce. Recovery is to fix the
destination and run again, which is safe because the migration is idempotent. A document's
`Failed` therefore always means something narrower and specific to it: its copy could not be read
back, or did not match its source.

It never deletes or modifies a source document, and never writes to the database: the stored file
name is the link between record and document, and moving bytes is not a reason to change it.
Retiring the filesystem copies and the legacy fallback is a separate human decision, after a
verified migration. [docs/document-storage-rollout.md](document-storage-rollout.md) is the
operational runbook for the whole rollout — prerequisites, the dry-run review gate, verification,
the separate runtime switch, and the rollback.

**Configuration and provider selection.** `Program.cs` binds the non-secret `DocumentStorage`
section and passes it, with the host's content and web roots, to
`AddDocumentStorage`:

```text
DocumentStorage__Provider=AzureBlob
DocumentStorage__BlobServiceUri=https://<storage-account>.blob.core.windows.net
DocumentStorage__ContainerName=business-documents        # business-documents-dev for development
```

An absent provider means `FileSystem`, which is what every environment ran before the setting
existed. An unrecognised provider, or an `AzureBlob` provider with a missing, non-absolute or
plaintext endpoint, a missing container, or an endpoint carrying a query string or credentials
(what a SAS token or an embedded key looks like), throws while the container is being built.
There is deliberately no fallback from `AzureBlob` to the filesystem: an application that could
not reach its configured storage would otherwise look healthy while writing business documents
to a local disk nobody backs up. Authentication is `DefaultAzureCredential` throughout — the App
Service's system-assigned managed identity in Azure, the developer's own Azure sign-in locally —
so no account key, SAS token, client secret or storage connection string is ever configured.
`FileSystemDocumentStorage` stays registered as a concrete type under either provider, because
switching the provider does not move the documents already on disk.

### API documentation policy

`Swashbuckle.AspNetCore` (`AddSwaggerGen`/`UseSwagger`/`UseSwaggerUI` in `Program.cs`) is intentionally retained to give local developers an interactive view of the API surface. It is registered only behind `app.Environment.IsDevelopment()`, so it never runs, and never exposes `/swagger`, outside the Development environment; its `SwaggerDoc` metadata carries only a title, version, and description, with no authentication scheme or configuration values. `dotnet-tools.json` keeps the matching `swashbuckle.aspnetcore.cli` local tool so a developer can export `swagger.json` manually with `dotnet swagger tofile` if needed.

No generated OpenAPI client is adopted (see [Runtime configuration and API contracts](#runtime-configuration-and-api-contracts)): the frontend uses manually maintained TypeScript contracts, and no `nswag.json` or `OpenApiReference` item exists anywhere in the repository. `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Client` and `NSwag.ApiDescription.Client` were unused package references with no consumer and have been removed; re-add them only alongside an issue that deliberately adopts a generated client.

### External integration errors

External service failures are represented by a typed integration exception rather than by a raw transport exception or a silently empty result. `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxLynxClient` validates every Nayax response in one place and throws `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxUpstreamException`, which carries only the operation name, HTTP method, relative endpoint, and upstream status code. The exception lives in Infrastructure, not alongside the `INayaxLynxClient` port in `Inventory.Application`, because it carries HTTP-specific diagnostics that `CleanArchitectureDependencyTests` forbids Application from depending on.

The HTTP boundary maps that exception centrally. `NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandler` is an `IExceptionHandler` registered with `AddProblemDetails()` and `UseExceptionHandler()`; it returns `502 Bad Gateway` as `application/problem+json` with the current trace ID, and returns `false` for every other exception so unrelated failures keep their normal pipeline behaviour. Controllers and services do not catch Nayax transport errors individually.

Not every Nayax failure is an upstream one. Since issue #520 two of them are statements about the *current business's own* Nayax connection rather than about the remote service — it has no usable credential, or Nayax refused one feature for lack of permission — and those are Application-owned exceptions mapped to `409 Conflict` by a second handler, `NayaxConnectionExceptionHandler`. They are deliberately neither `502` (Nayax answered correctly, or was never called) nor `401`/`403` (which describe the caller's own token and membership). See [Per-business Nayax credentials](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520) for the complete contract.

Tokens, authorization headers, and raw upstream response bodies must never be logged or returned. A failed call logs the operation, method, endpoint, and numeric upstream status only; the public response carries a fixed title and detail and no exception information. An upstream failure must never be disguised as an empty collection, and caller cancellation must stay cancellation rather than becoming a `502`.

Issue #165 made that log entry explicit at the HTTP boundary: an unreachable or refusing Nayax is an infrastructure failure an operator has to be able to find in retained telemetry, so `NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandler` logs each claimed exception exactly once at `Error` with the structured `NayaxOperation`, `UpstreamMethod`, `NayaxEndpoint` and `UpstreamStatus` properties the exception was designed to carry, plus the request's own `Method`, `Path` and `TraceId`. **The exception object is deliberately not attached to that entry.** `NayaxUpstreamException`'s own message is safe, but its inner exception is whatever the transport threw, and a transport exception's message is text this application did not compose: it can repeat a request header or an upstream response body verbatim. Logging only composed fields is what makes the "never log a token, an authorization header, or a sensitive upstream payload" rule structural rather than a review habit, and the operation name already identifies the call site exactly, so little diagnostic value is given up. An exception this handler does not claim is not logged here either — it belongs to whichever handler does claim it, and double logging would double the telemetry cost.

#### HTTP resilience policy

`Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxResilienceHandler` (issue #48) is a `DelegatingHandler` registered by `AddNayaxLynxClient` (`.AddHttpMessageHandler<NayaxResilienceHandler>()`), so every call `NayaxLynxClient` makes through its `HttpClient` passes through it first. It sits entirely below `NayaxLynxClient`, which is unchanged: `NayaxLynxClient` still inspects the final `HttpResponseMessage` exactly as before and has no knowledge that some calls were retried underneath it, and retry/timeout/circuit-breaker types (`Polly.*`) never appear in `INayaxLynxClient` or any other Application-facing contract.

It composes three bounded Polly v8 strategies, built once per handler instance (`NayaxResilienceOptions` holds the tunables - fixed engineering constants, not environment configuration, so there is nothing here for `appsettings.json`/README to document):

- **Timeout** (innermost): each individual HTTP attempt is bounded (10 seconds by default). Polly's timeout strategy distinguishes an attempt that ran out of time from the caller cancelling: if the request's own `CancellationToken` (not the internal per-attempt one) is what fired, the original `OperationCanceledException` propagates unchanged and is never retried, never counted as a circuit-breaker failure, and never becomes a `502` - preserving the caller-cancellation rule above. An attempt that genuinely times out surfaces as `Polly.Timeout.TimeoutRejectedException`, which the retry/circuit-breaker layers above treat as transient.
- **Retry** (outermost, so each retried attempt is individually timed and circuit-broken): up to 3 retries with exponential, jittered backoff (250ms base), applied **only to idempotent requests** (`GET`/`HEAD`) - a request's `HttpMethod` decides this once, at the top of the handler. `CreateMachineProductsAsync`'s `POST` is never retried, because retrying an unsafe write without proven idempotency is exactly the failure mode this issue was written to avoid. A retryable outcome is a network failure (`HttpRequestException`), an attempt timeout (`TimeoutRejectedException`), or an upstream status of `408`, `429`, or any `5xx`; every other 4xx status (authentication, authorization, validation, not-found, conflict) is a terminal failure on the first attempt, and the caller's cancellation is excluded from all of this, per the timeout bullet above. A response that is abandoned in favour of a retry is disposed immediately so its connection is not leaked. A `429` is retried under the narrower budget below.
- **Circuit breaker** (middle): once at least 8 sampled outcomes in a rolling 30-second window are transient failures at a 50%+ ratio, the circuit opens for 15 seconds and every call in that window fails fast with `Polly.CircuitBreaker.BrokenCircuitException` without an upstream HTTP attempt at all - so a sustained Nayax outage is not retried into indefinitely. The breaker shares the same transient-failure definition as retry and observes both `GET` and `POST` traffic (it does not retry, so it carries no idempotency risk of its own), so a `429` still counts as a failure towards opening it.
