##### The rate-limited case: one retry, and the wait Nayax asked for (issue #844)

A `429 Too Many Requests` is the one transient status that says the remedy is *fewer* requests, so it is not retried like a `5xx`. The retry budget of one Nayax `GET` is therefore two rules at once, and no mix of failures can exceed either:

- **At most 3 retries in total** - 4 attempts - whatever combination of `408`, `429`, `5xx` and attempt timeouts the request meets.
- **At most 1 of those retries may follow a `429`.** A second `429` on the same request stops retrying at once, even when retries are still budgeted, because the upstream has now said twice that we are sending too many requests. A `429` never buys an extra attempt either: it spends one of the three already budgeted.

The per-request `429` count lives in the Polly resilience context's properties, so it is per request rather than per handler, and `SendAsync` resets it (and the honoured delay below) on every call, because the context is pooled.

`Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxRetryAfterPolicy` is the one place a `Retry-After` header becomes a decision, and the ceiling it honours is **10 seconds** (decided 23 October 2026): a page request must not hang while an upstream's own cool-off period is waited out, so a longer requested wait ends the request instead of being silently shortened - retrying sooner than Nayax asked is the one thing the policy must never do. The header is parsed strictly by RFC 9110 § 10.2.3, against the current instant from `Inventory.Application.Time.IClock` (injected into the handler, so an HTTP date is deterministic and testable rather than read from the host's clock):

| `Retry-After` value | Treated as |
| --- | --- |
| Whole number of seconds, 1 to 10 | Wait that long, then retry once |
| Whole number of seconds above 10 | Do not retry |
| HTTP date 1 to 10 seconds in the future | Wait until then, then retry once |
| HTTP date more than 10 seconds in the future | Do not retry |
| `0`, or an HTTP date now or in the past | Retry once after the existing base backoff (never with no delay) |
| Missing | Retry once after the existing base backoff |
| Malformed (negative, decimal, non-numeric text, unparseable date, several values) | Same as missing |

Three things about that table are deliberate. A value this application cannot read is the *same* as no value, never a wait invented from it and never an immediate retry. `0` and an elapsed instant still wait the ordinary jittered backoff, because a rate-limited upstream is the last place to send a request with no delay at all. And Nayax documents the `429` for Lynx but publishes neither a numeric rate limit nor a `Retry-After` contract ([Lynx app tokens § 429 Too Many Requests](https://devzone.nayax.com/docs/manage-data-operations/lynx-api/app-tokens#429-too-many-requests)), so the missing-header row is the expected case rather than an error, and nothing here assumes a header shape the provider has not published.

Every wait is a Polly retry delay, so caller cancellation during one is observed as cancellation, exactly as the timeout bullet above requires - never as a `502`. A `429` that is *not* retried (its single retry already used, a second `429`, or a `Retry-After` beyond the ceiling) is returned to `NayaxLynxClient` as it stands and becomes today's `NayaxUpstreamException`/`502`: this work changed when a request stops, never what the caller is told. The retry log line adds the delay actually waited to the attempt number, path and status it already carried, and still carries no token, header or response body.

None of these three strategies changes what a *successful* retry-exhausted or breaker-open call ultimately looks like to a caller: a final non-success `HttpResponseMessage` still reaches `NayaxLynxClient.EnsureNayaxSuccessAsync` unchanged and becomes `NayaxUpstreamException`/`502` exactly as before — except for the two statuses that describe the business's own connection rather than the remote service, which that method classifies instead (issue #520, [Per-business Nayax credentials](#per-business-nayax-credentials-issue-520)) and which were never retryable anyway; an unwrapped exception (`HttpRequestException`, `TimeoutRejectedException`, `BrokenCircuitException`) that survives retries still reaches `GlobalExceptionHandler` as a generic `500` with no Nayax-specific handling, the same place an untranslated provider SDK exception already lands per the exception-ownership table below. The retry-attempt and circuit-open/close log lines carry only the attempt number, the request's relative path, and the HTTP status/break duration - never a token, an authorization header, or a response body.

### Domain and application error mapping

Issue #59 replaced ad hoc, per-controller exception handling with a small typed strategy and two more centrally registered `IExceptionHandler`s, alongside the untouched Nayax handler above. Issue #163 then audited every custom exception in the backend and consolidated ownership so each one is defined in the layer that owns the failure it reports, never in `InventoryApi`.

#### Exception ownership table

| Layer | Owns | Examples | Escapes to the caller as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Inventory.Domain` (`Inventory.Domain.Exceptions`) | Domain invariants: a deliberate business-rule/input check, or a request that conflicts with the current state of the data | `DomainException` (abstract root), `DomainValidationException`, `DomainConflictException`, `InsufficientStockException` | `400`/`409` via `DomainExceptionHandler`, message verbatim |
| `Inventory.Application` | Use-case-specific failures that are not domain invariants: a feature's own request validation, an access-control refusal, or an integration the current business has not made usable | `Tenancy.BusinessAccessDeniedException`; `Nayax.NayaxNotConnectedException` and `Nayax.NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException` (issue #520) | The two Nayax connection failures become `409` via `NayaxConnectionExceptionHandler`, which publishes the fixed, caller-safe sentence each type declares as a constant. Anything else here is not claimed by a handler and propagates to `GlobalExceptionHandler` as a generic `500` unless a use case's controller catches it deliberately |
| `Inventory.Infrastructure` | Provider-specific failures (EF Core, Azure Blob, filesystem, HTTP, Nayax), translated to a plain answer or a narrow typed exception at that layer's own boundary so the provider SDK's exception type and message never cross it | `Nayax.NayaxUpstreamException`; `Documents.AzureBlobContainer` translates `Azure.RequestFailedException` by `ErrorCode` into a `bool`/`null` return and lets every other Azure failure propagate untranslated (never re-wrapped, never given a caller-safe message) | `502` via `NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandler` for Nayax; an untranslated provider failure (a missing container, a revoked role assignment) reaches `GlobalExceptionHandler` as a generic `500` with no SDK detail |
| `InventoryApi` | No business exceptions. Only `IExceptionHandler` implementations that translate an already-thrown exception to HTTP `ProblemDetails` | `DomainExceptionHandler`, `NayaxConnectionExceptionHandler`, `NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandler`, `GlobalExceptionHandler` | n/a - these are the translators, not the failures |

The allowed dependency direction is the same one enforced everywhere else in this document - `Inventory.Domain` ← `Inventory.Application` ← `Inventory.Infrastructure` ← `InventoryApi` - so a domain exception may be thrown from any layer, but only `Inventory.Domain` may *define* one, `Inventory.Application` may define a use-case-specific one without reaching into `Inventory.Domain`'s hierarchy, and a provider-specific exception must never leave `Inventory.Infrastructure` for `Inventory.Application`, `Inventory.Domain`, or `InventoryApi` to see its concrete type or raw message. `CleanArchitectureDependencyTests.No_new_business_exception_is_defined_in_InventoryApi` enforces the `InventoryApi` row: it freezes an explicit allow-list of exceptions that predate this rule and are intimately coupled to code that has not migrated out of `InventoryApi` yet (`Bootstrap.PendingMigrationsException`, `Bootstrap.DatabaseMigrationFailedException` (issue #201, added alongside the pending-migrations one for the same reason), and `Data.CrossBusinessAccessException`, all coupled to `AppDbContext`), and fails if any other exception type is added there. `InventoryCostDataQualityException`, a developer-facing `InvalidOperationException` subclass rather than a caller-safe type, was on that list until issue #296 moved it to `Inventory.Application.Costing` with the product cost rebuild use case that throws it; the HTTP boundary still does not map it.

`Inventory.Domain.Exceptions` defines a small, documented hierarchy with no ASP.NET Core reference, matching the Clean Architecture rule that a Domain failure must not know about HTTP: the abstract `DomainException` root (a deliberate business-rule failure, never a programming error, an infrastructure fault, or an unexpected condition), `DomainValidationException` for a deliberate business-rule/input check, `DomainConflictException` for a request that cannot proceed because of the current state of the data (an overlapping agreement, a concurrent change), and `InsufficientStockException`, which specializes `DomainConflictException` because the conflicting state it reports is a stock level rather than an overlapping record. Their messages are written for the caller and must never carry an internal path, identifier, or another actor's data. `DomainValidationException` and `InsufficientStockException` are sealed; `DomainConflictException` stays unsealed so a future specialization can join it the same way `InsufficientStockException` did.

`InventoryApi/Http/DomainExceptionHandler.cs` publishes an exception's own message to the caller, so it may only claim exception types whose contract guarantees that message is caller-safe. Exactly three qualify: `DomainValidationException` and `InsufficientStockException` become `400 Bad Request`, and `DomainConflictException` becomes `409 Conflict`. `InsufficientStockException` qualifies because its message is a fixed sentence plus an available-stock count the caller is already entitled to see; its arm in the handler's `Classify` switch must stay listed ahead of `DomainConflictException`'s, because a C# type-pattern switch matches in source order and `InsufficientStockException` is now a subclass of `DomainConflictException` - without that ordering (and a matching exclusion in the conflict-logging check) it would silently fall back to `DomainConflictException`'s `409`-and-log-a-warning behaviour instead of keeping its own established `400`, unlogged one. Every `ProblemDetails` response carries the current trace ID and a `message` extension equal to `detail`, kept for the existing frontend error handling that already reads `error.message` for this migration (see `machine-detail.component.ts`). A validation outcome is not logged; a conflict is logged once at `Warning` with the trace ID, because it may indicate a real race between two callers, but it is still an expected outcome rather than a server error - `InsufficientStockException` is excluded from that logging despite being a `DomainConflictException` by inheritance, because its established behaviour predates that inheritance.

**The handler must never claim a framework-wide base type such as `ArgumentException` or `InvalidOperationException`, and it must never claim a provider-specific infrastructure exception.** Because `UseExceptionHandler()` is registered ahead of the rest of the request pipeline, a type-based rule here applies to the whole application, not only to the controllers that were migrated. `ArgumentException` and `InvalidOperationException` are thrown throughout the BCL, EF Core, and this application's own infrastructure — `BusinessScope.Resolve`'s tenant-scope double-resolve guard, `BusinessId.From`, `EffectiveFinancialConfiguration.ResolveAgreement`, `GetReportExportRows`, `InventoryCostDataQualityException` — with messages written for a developer, not an API client. Claiming them would turn unrelated internal failures into public `400` responses that echo an internal message and are never logged, and would silently downgrade a tenant-isolation bug from a loud `500` to a quiet `400`. They therefore fall through to `GlobalExceptionHandler` as logged, generic `500`s, and `DomainExceptionHandlerTests` locks that in for `ArgumentException`, `ArgumentNullException`, `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, `InvalidOperationException`, and an `InvalidOperationException` subclass. A provider SDK exception (an Azure `RequestFailedException` `AzureBlobContainer` did not recognize, an EF Core `DbUpdateException`) that reaches this far is exactly the same case: it is neither claimed here nor given a caller-safe message anywhere, so it reaches `GlobalExceptionHandler` as a logged, generic `500` with no SDK type name, error code, or connection detail in the response body - the policy that keeps infrastructure-specific exceptions from ever escaping into the API's public contract.

The consequence for a throw site is explicit: **a check whose message is meant for the caller must throw `DomainValidationException` or `DomainConflictException` itself.** Migrating a controller to the centralized mapping therefore means converting the deliberate validation throws in the service behind it, not widening the handler. Anything else stays an ordinary framework exception and stays a generic `500`.

`InventoryApi/Http/GlobalExceptionHandler.cs` is the catch-all last resort, registered after the other two. Anything neither handler claims is logged exactly once at `Error` with the exception and the same trace ID returned to the client, and answers with a fixed, generic `500` `ProblemDetails` that carries no exception message, type name, or stack trace. Caller cancellation is excluded from that logging and left to ASP.NET Core's normal handling, mirroring the same principle already documented above for Nayax upstream cancellation.

That log entry names its request context as the structured `Method`, `Path` and `TraceId` properties (issue #165), so Azure Monitor exports them as queryable custom dimensions and an operator can start from the trace ID a caller quotes. The request context stops at the method and the path on purpose: the query string and the request headers are the two parts of a request that routinely carry a credential — a bearer token, a cookie — and retained telemetry is the worst place for either. See [Observability and error telemetry](#observability-and-error-telemetry-issue-165).

Not-found handling is unchanged by this work: controllers continue to return `NotFound()` directly for a missing resource, and this issue introduces no typed not-found exception.

Migrating a controller to the centralized mapping never changes its status code or message; the only observable difference is that the response body for a migrated action becomes a `ProblemDetails` object (`application/problem+json`) instead of a bare JSON string, which is why the `message` extension above exists. `StockController.Adjust`, `InventoryCostTransitionsController` (all four actions), and `SupplierOrdersController.Create` were migrated this way, and the deliberate validation throws in what was then `StockService.Adjust` (now `Inventory.Domain.Stock.ManualStockAdjustmentPolicy`, issue #282), what was then `InventoryCostTransitionService` (now `Inventory.Domain.Costing.InventoryCostTransitionPolicy` and the `Inventory.Application.Costing` transition use cases, issue #298), and `SupplierOrderService.Create` were converted from `ArgumentException`/`InvalidOperationException` to `DomainValidationException` so those actions keep the exact `400` and message they returned before. `SiteCommissionsController.SaveAgreement`'s overlapping-agreement check moved from returning `Conflict(...)` directly to throwing `DomainConflictException`, still producing `409` with the same message. `ProductsController.Update`, `PurchasesController`, and `ImportsController.ImportNayaxSales` still catch their own exceptions and were intentionally left for a later, separate change. `OperatingExpensesController` no longer catches anything itself: the operating-expenses slice (issue #50) moved its attachment save/cleanup-on-failure try/catch into `Inventory.Application.Expenses.CreateOperatingExpense`/`UpdateOperatingExpense` as a side effect of the Clean Architecture migration, which is exactly the "way to run that cleanup from outside the controller" this paragraph used to call out as still missing; its validation failures are returned as explicit result values rather than thrown, so the controller still needs no exception mapping to keep its `400 Bad Request` behavior.

### Observability and error telemetry (issue #165)

Error handling decides what the caller sees; observability decides what the operator can still find afterwards. The two are deliberately separate concerns here: the exception handlers above own translation and the log entry's content, and this section owns where that entry goes.

**One pipeline, registered in one place.** `InventoryApi/Observability/ObservabilityServiceCollectionExtensions.cs` is the only telemetry registration in the application. `Program.cs` calls `AddInventoryApiTelemetry(builder.Configuration)` before anything else is built, and it calls `AddOpenTelemetry().UseAzureMonitor(...)` from the Microsoft-supported `Azure.Monitor.OpenTelemetry.AspNetCore` distribution. The distribution brings incoming ASP.NET Core requests, outgoing `HttpClient` dependencies (which is how every Nayax Lynx call is recorded), the SQL dependencies its `SqlClient` instrumentation supports, runtime/HTTP metrics, and every `ILogger` log with its attached exception — all correlated by trace/operation ID. The classic `Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.AspNetCore` SDK is **not** referenced: two instrumentation pipelines in one process double the cost and emit duplicate requests, dependencies and exceptions that no longer correlate with each other. `TelemetryCompositionTests` asserts both the absence of that package reference and that nothing registers a `Microsoft.ApplicationInsights` service.

**The boundary.** Telemetry is composition-root infrastructure, not an application concern. `Inventory.Domain`, `Inventory.Application` and `Inventory.Infrastructure` know nothing about Application Insights, OpenTelemetry or a telemetry client; they log through `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger` and throw. Nothing in this application calls a telemetry client directly for an ordinary log, which is what lets telemetry be switched off, reconfigured or replaced by editing one file. Adding a direct telemetry-client call in a feature would reintroduce the coupling this boundary exists to prevent.

**Configuration-gated, and optional by design.** The connection string comes from the single App Service application setting `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING`; it is a secret, so no value for it exists anywhere in this repository, and the Application Insights resource itself is created and connected by a human in Azure rather than by repository automation. With that setting absent — or present but blank, which is what a cleared App Service setting looks like — nothing OpenTelemetry-related is registered at all and the API starts and serves requests exactly as it did before. That is a deliberate asymmetry with document storage, where an incomplete `AzureBlob` configuration fails startup: storage is a dependency the API needs in order to do its job, whereas telemetry is diagnostics, and an application that refuses to start because it cannot report on itself is worse than one that runs unreported. Local development and the whole automated test suite run with no connection string.

**Trace correlation flow.** `Activity.Current` is created by the ASP.NET Core instrumentation at the start of the request, so one identifier already ties the request, its dependencies, its logs and its exceptions together:

```text
request arrives -> ASP.NET Core instrumentation starts an Activity (W3C traceparent)
  -> use case logs through ILogger            -> exported with the Activity's trace ID
  -> Nayax HttpClient call                    -> child dependency span, same trace ID
  -> an exception escapes
       -> IExceptionHandler logs once at Error/Warning with TraceId = Activity.Current.Id
       -> ProblemDetails returns the same traceId to the caller
```

The identifier returned to the caller is `Activity.Current?.Id`, falling back to `HttpContext.TraceIdentifier` when no activity is running (which is what the unit tests exercise). A W3C `Activity.Id` is `00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-<flags>`, and Application Insights indexes the middle segment as `operation_Id` — so a caller's quoted `traceId` locates every record for that request, which is what the KQL queries in README.md § Observability and error diagnostics do. The response still carries no stack trace, exception type or unexpected exception message: the trace ID is the entire channel between the caller and the server-side detail.

**Logging levels are part of the design, not a preference.** Everything that passes the configured levels is exported and retained, so the levels decide both the bill and whether anything is findable. `backend/InventoryApi/appsettings.json` holds the deployed policy — application code at `Information`, framework and Azure SDK categories at `Warning`, the per-query EF Core `Database.Command` log suppressed, `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Migrations` and `Microsoft.Hosting.Lifetime` kept at `Information` because automatic Production migration (issue #201) and host start/stop are audit records — and `appsettings.Development.json` raises the suppressed categories again for local debugging, where nothing is exported. No category may sit below `Warning`; silencing a category's warnings and errors would hide a real failure from the only place anyone can look after the fact. `LoggingLevelPolicyTests` reads the committed files and enforces that, so a change to the deployed levels has to be deliberate.

**What must never reach a log.** The same rule as the public response, for the same reason, with retention added: a log entry may carry only context the application composed. No Nayax token, `Authorization` header, cookie, connection string, document content, customer record or sensitive business data, and therefore no request query string and no request headers — the handlers add the request method and path and nothing else. The Nayax handler additionally omits the exception object, for the reason given under [External integration errors](#external-integration-errors). `GlobalExceptionHandlerTests` and `NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandlerTests` assert this over the structured properties as well as the rendered message, because an exported custom dimension leaks just as well as a message does.

## Frontend architecture

The frontend is an application boundary in its own right. It owns navigation, interaction state, accessibility, presentation, and communication with the API. It does not own inventory or accounting truth.

### Current composition

| Area | Current responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `app.component.*` | Application shell: header with the sidebar collapse control and the signed-in user control, the sidebar, the routed page region, MSAL redirect/account handling, and the toast/loading hosts; a route marked with the public layout is rendered with none of that chrome (issue #954) |
| `public/` | The public layout boundary (also used by `/sign-in` since issue #957) and the Restockroo landing page (issue #954): `PUBLIC_LAYOUT_DATA`, `signedOutVisitorGuard`, and `landing/` (the page, its header and mobile menu, the static example dashboard, and its copy) — see [The public landing page](#the-public-landing-page-issue-954) |
| `layout/` | Primary navigation: `navigation.ts` (the navigation data, each destination's capability, and its pure active-route rules), `sidebar-nav.component.*`, `user-menu.component.ts` |
| `access/` | What the signed-in member may do (issue #528) and which account state they are in (issue #529): the capability vocabulary, the cached `GET /api/me/access` and `GET /api/me/account-state` reads, the two route guards, the "access not allowed" and "access unavailable" pages, and the interceptors that keep the caches current and show the global `403` notice |
| `provider/` | Whether this business's Nayax connection is usable: the published availability vocabulary and its wording (issue #727), the application-wide session-cached signal, the per-feature permission vocabulary and evidence, the shared `409 nayax_not_connected` handling path and the one machine/site list load (issue #728) |
| `app.routes.ts` | Product, stock, supplier, machine, site, purchase, report, expense, and administration routes, each with the capability its page needs |
| `components/` | Routed feature pages plus a small set of shared components |
| `services/` | Typed HTTP calls, runtime configuration, toast state, and feature-specific client behavior |
| `models/models.ts` | Shared inventory, purchase, site, and machine contracts |
| Report base/classes | Common report filters, loading/error state, financial-year presets, and export behavior |
| `assets/config.json`, `api-base-url.ts` | Deployed API base URL and the local-vs-deployed resolution rule applied before the application starts |
| `auth-config.ts`, `auth/auth-callback.component.ts` | MSAL configuration, delegated `access_as_user` scope, protected-resource map, and the public Entra redirect callback route |

The application currently uses component-local state and RxJS-backed singleton services. That is appropriate for its present size. Do not introduce a global state library merely to reorganize files. Add one only when there is demonstrated cross-feature state, cache invalidation, or event-coordination complexity that local state and focused services cannot handle clearly.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Route["Route"] --> Page["Feature page"]
    Page --> View["Feature/shared UI"]
    Page --> Client["Typed API client"]
    Config["ConfigService"] --> Client
    Client --> API["Backend API"]
```

### Application shell and navigation (issue #391)

The shell is a left sidebar plus a slim header, and it is the only navigation system in the
application: the former horizontal header menu and its `<details>` report dropdown are gone, and
`app.component.scss` (which still styled that header) was deleted with them. Three files own it,
and they are the first realized part of the target `layout/` folder described below:

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `layout/navigation.ts` | The navigation data (`primaryNavigation`) and the pure matching rules `navLinks`, `activeNavRoute`, `activeNavLink` and `activeNavGroup`, plus `navLockOf` (issue #729) |
| `layout/sidebar-nav.component.*` | Renders that data, owns which groups are expanded, and resolves the active entry from the router |
| `layout/user-menu.component.ts` | The top-right signed-in user control: the active account and a sign-out item, or a sign-in button |
| `layout/bottom-nav.component.ts` | The narrow layout's bottom bar (issue #972): shortcuts picked out of `navigationFor` by `shortcutsOf`, and the More control that opens the sidebar as a sheet |
| `app.component.*` | The shell layout, the sidebar open/collapsed state and its handlers, the narrow layout's top-bar opener, the wide-versus-narrow layout decision, the MSAL identity it passes to the user menu, and whether the sidebar offers the ordinary business navigation at all (issue #676) |

`primaryNavigation` is a `NavItem[]` of direct links (`Dashboard`, `Pick List`, `Expenses`, and the
live provider destinations `Machines`, `Sites` and `Site Commissions`), expandable groups
(`Inventory`, `Purchases`, `Reports`, `Admin`) and, since issue #729, one section heading over the
live provider destinations — see [Provider-locked
navigation](#provider-locked-navigation-issue-729) for the order, the renames and the lock states.
Each destination also declares the capability its own page needs, and the sidebar renders only the ones
the signed-in member holds — see [Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528)
below — while whether it renders any of them at all follows the authenticated account state the
shell passes it (issue #676, see [Account-state
routing](#account-state-routing-the-access-unavailable-page-and-the-global-403-handler-issue-529)):
a signed-out visitor and an account with no usable membership are offered no business menu. A group
heading is a `<button>` that toggles its children and is deliberately not a destination, so no
group needs an overview page. **Every `route` must be a real page already declared in
`app.routes.ts`**: `navigation.spec.ts` compares the two and fails on a destination invented ahead
of the page that serves it, which is how the navigation stays free of placeholder
Users/Roles/Audit/Settings/Profile entries. `/admin` itself keeps its own address
and its `AdminComponent` link hub — the sidebar is now the primary way into the dedicated Admin
pages (six at issue #391, joined by `Historical GST Classification` in issue #433 and
`Nayax Sale Timestamp Repair` in issue #487), and `/admin`
remains a valid bookmark that the home Dashboard's "Open Admin" action and each dedicated page's
"Back to Admin" link still reach.

**One conditional group (issue #335, given its own top-level group in issue #546).** `Super Admin`
is the only entry that is not in `primaryNavigation`: `navigationFor(hasPlatformDiagnosticsAccess)`
appends the whole group, last, and only `GET /api/admin/diagnostics/access` can say yes. It holds
`Platform Diagnostics` (`/super-admin/diagnostics`, moved out of the business `Admin` group, which
`/admin/diagnostics` now only redirects to) and, since issue #547 built the real page, `Businesses`
(`/super-admin/businesses`) — an ordinary `NavLink`, not the `NavPlaceholder` issue #546 gave it
while no page existed yet; see [Super Admin Businesses page](#super-admin-businesses-page-issue-547)
below. Neither child declares a capability, because no business role grants either. `SidebarNavComponent` starts from `navigationFor(false)`, follows
`PlatformDiagnosticsAccessService.granted$`, and re-resolves the active entry whenever that answer
changes; a refusal, a failure and an unanswered probe all leave the navigation everyone else gets,
silently, because a navigation menu is not the place to report that one capability could not be
checked. **The group follows the signed-in identity (issue #605):** that answer is cached per
identity, so changing the active account, signing out or signing in removes a granted `Super Admin`
group on the switch itself — not when some other identity's answer happens to arrive — and the
group comes back only if the new identity's own probe confirms access, with a late answer for a
superseded identity discarded (see [Platform diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336)). The
group is presentation and never a boundary — the route and both endpoints are independently
authorized, so a hidden group hides a page rather than protecting one (see [Platform
diagnostics](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336)). Everything else about the shell is unchanged: the
`primaryNavigation` groups, their order, the matching rules and the active-state behaviour below all
stay as issue #391 left them.

**Active state.** `activeNavRoute` resolves the current URL to the most specific matching entry,
rather than relying on `routerLinkActive`, because several destinations are prefixes of each other:
`/purchases` highlights `Purchases` while `/purchases/orders` highlights `Supplier Orders`, and a
detail URL such as `/machines/7`, `/sites/3/products` or `/products/12/edit` stays highlighted on
its list page. The active link carries `aria-current="page"`, and `activeNavGroup` keeps the owning
group expanded and visibly active. A URL outside the navigation (`/auth`) highlights nothing.

**Collapse and the narrow layout.** One `isSidebarOpen` flag drives both layouts, because the
control an operator reaches for is the same in each. `AppComponent` reads the same `lg`
(`min-width: 1024px`) breakpoint the Tailwind classes use through `window.matchMedia` and keeps
listening for changes:

- **Wide layout:** the sidebar is always part of the page. The toggle expands it to labels or
  collapses it to a compact icon rail, whose labels stay in the accessibility tree (`sr-only` plus
  a `title`) so the names are never lost. A collapsed rail has no room for a submenu, so a group
  heading then asks the shell to expand (`expandRequested`) instead of opening one invisibly.
- **Narrow layout:** the sidebar becomes a dismissible overlay drawer that is not rendered while
  closed, so it is never left off-screen but focusable. It is dismissed by its own close control,
  by the backdrop, by `Escape` (which returns focus to the top bar's opener), and by choosing a
  destination. It never falls back to a horizontal menu.

Crossing the breakpoint re-applies that default: a wide layout opens with labels, a narrow one
starts dismissed so the drawer never covers the page the operator asked for.

**Where the toggle is rendered (issue #456).** There is exactly one toggle at a time, and the
layout alone decides where it is. On a **wide** layout it is in the sidebar's own header row,
beside the app title, and reports back through `collapseToggled`; the shell's top bar renders no
toggle at all, so nothing floats detached above the menu. Collapsed to the rail that header row
drops the title and centres the control alone, with a negative horizontal margin that lets it reach
the 44x44 CSS-pixel minimum touch target inside a `w-16` rail whose padding would otherwise leave
40px — the sidebar can therefore always be reopened, by pointer or by keyboard. On a **narrow**
layout the sidebar is a drawer that is not on the page, so there is no header row to hold a
control and the opener stays in the shell's top bar; that is also the element `closeSidebar()`
returns focus to. The drawer's own close control is unchanged in behaviour and sized to the same
44x44 target. None of this moved state: `AppComponent` keeps the one `isSidebarOpen` flag,
`toggleSidebar`/`expandSidebar`/`closeSidebar`/`onSidebarNavigated` and the `Escape` handler, and
`SidebarNavComponent` still decides nothing about layout.

**Semantics.** Every control is a native `<button>` or `<a>`, so it is keyboard operable and picks
up the global `:focus-visible` outline defined in `styles.scss`; the sidebar toggle, the top-bar
opener and each group heading expose `aria-expanded` and (while their target is rendered)
`aria-controls`. The sidebar is a single `nav[aria-label="Primary"]` landmark, and that `<nav>`
carries the `primary-navigation` id both toggles point `aria-controls` at — the id is on the
navigation container itself rather than on the component's `display: contents` host. Each toggle's
accessible name states the action rather than the state (`Collapse navigation` / `Expand
navigation`, `Open navigation menu` / `Close navigation menu`). The routed page sits in a `<main>`
beside the sidebar with its own responsive width and padding, so nothing is hidden behind the
sidebar or the sticky header.

**Authentication is unchanged.** `AppComponent` still owns the MSAL redirect handling, active
account resolution and `loginRedirect`/`logoutRedirect` calls; `UserMenuComponent` is presentation
only and reports the two intents the application actually has. It invents no profile or account
destination. The public `/auth` callback route and `MsalGuard` on every other route are untouched.

**The shell follows the identity signed in now (issue #604).** `AppComponent` watches the shared
`signedInAccountMayHaveChanged` trigger (`access/signed-in-account.ts`) — MSAL's own account
events, `ACTIVE_ACCOUNT_CHANGED` among them, as well as `inProgress$` settling — rather than the
interaction status alone. A direct Microsoft active-account switch raises only the event, because
no interaction is involved and `inProgress$` never leaves `None`: a shell watching the interaction
status alone therefore kept the previous account's displayed name, `businessAccountKey` and
published business time zone for the rest of the session, and the new account-state answer could
not repair it because the lookup that would have read it had already completed. The identity is
compared through the same `activeAccountKey` the access caches key their answers on, so the shell
and they cannot disagree about who is signed in. When it has actually changed, the shell does all
of this in one step, before anything is read for the new account:

- shows the new account in the header;
- calls `BusinessService.reset()`, which drops the cached business and clears the published zone,
  so no date is rendered in the previous business's zone and none is rendered in a guessed one;
- cancels the lookup in flight for the previous account, including a retry still waiting;
- closes the routed-page gate (`isBusinessContextReady`), so the page waits again instead of
  rendering the new account's data against the previous business's calendar.

It then waits for the new identity's own account state and reads its business once — see
[Account-state routing](#account-state-routing-the-access-unavailable-page-and-the-global-403-handler-issue-529)
below. A superseded lookup answering late can neither publish a zone (`BusinessService`'s
generation check refuses it) nor open the gate (its subscription is gone); a further notification
for the identity already loaded reads nothing again and does not restart a settled context; a
sign-out clears the context with no authenticated call; and the MSAL listeners end with the
component. `app.component.spec.ts` covers a direct event-only switch between two business zones
(`Australia/Sydney` to `Europe/London`, against the real `BusinessService` and
`BusinessTimeZoneService`), the new identity answering `NoMembership`, an unreadable new state,
the previous account's response arriving after the switch, the sign-out event, a duplicate
notification, and the cleanup on destroy.

**And the shell follows the business in effect now (issue #671).** A changed *identity* is not the
only thing that changes which business a tab resolves: so does a support-session start, end or
expiry, and so does the account state turning the identity already signed in into a `Member`. The
shell reads `GET /api/business/current` again on each of those, publishes the zone it answers with,
and reports an unanswerable lookup explicitly with a retry rather than letting a page render blank
instants. See [Reloading the business time zone after a context
change](#reloading-the-business-time-zone-after-a-context-change-issue-671) for which trigger
withholds the routed page and which deliberately does not.

Adding a navigation entry is therefore a data change in `layout/navigation.ts` once the page and
its route exist — not a template change in the shell.

**Material styling (issue #413).** The shell's look follows the #410 tokens and the #411
`app-icon` component; none of the behaviour described above changed.

- **Sidebar.** `sidebar-nav.component.html` renders a white panel (`rounded-md-card`, `shadow-md`)
  that floats with a `1rem` margin from the viewport edge on a wide layout; the narrow drawer keeps
  the same panel without the margin. Its own top section shows the app name, and the collapse
  control beside it (issue #456), above a `border-md-gray-200` divider. Each top-level link and
  group heading declares a decorative icon name in `NavItem.icon` (`layout/navigation.ts`) —
  presentation data only, rendered through `<app-icon [name]="item.icon" variant="outlined">` — and
  items are `text-md-body text-md-gray-800` with a `hover:bg-md-gray-100` state. The active link
  gets the `bg-md-dark-gradient` background with white text and (because `app-icon` fills with
  `currentColor`) a white icon; its parent group heading stays expanded and keeps a
  `bg-md-gray-100` highlight while one of its pages is open. Collapsed to the icon-only rail, each
  label keeps its accessible name as `sr-only` text (the behaviour above), not a styling change.
- **Outlined navigation glyphs (issue #456).** The sidebar is the one caller that asks `app-icon`
  for the `outlined` variant, and it asks for it everywhere a glyph appears — each destination,
  each group heading, the collapse/expand control and the drawer's close control — so the expanded
  desktop sidebar, the collapsed rail and the mobile drawer all draw the same unfilled geometry.
  The glyphs are the official Material Icons Outlined files, not filled paths thinned with a CSS
  stroke (see [Icon component](#icon-component-issues-411-and-456)). Nothing outside the sidebar
  changed: a Dashboard stat card, a report control and an action button all still render the
  default Rounded set. The group disclosure markers stay the existing `▴`/`▾` text characters —
  they are not Material glyphs and are not part of this icon set.
- **Sidebar height fills the available viewport (issue #455).** The white panel's height is not
  driven by its menu content: `app.component.html`'s shell row (`flex flex-1 items-stretch`)
  stretches the sidebar to the full height of that row, which the surrounding `min-h-screen`
  flex column already sizes to the viewport height minus the header, so no component adds a
  second, unconditional `100vh`. `SidebarNavComponent`'s host renders as `display: contents`
  (`host: { class: 'contents' }`) so it contributes no box of its own between the shell and the
  visible `<nav>` panel — without that, the host's own block box would absorb the stretched
  height and leave the white panel sized to its content, which is the bug this fixed. The panel's
  own `overflow-y-auto` then scrolls the navigation list internally, inside the stretched height,
  whenever expanded groups or a short browser window make it taller than the available space, so
  every entry (including nested `Admin` children) stays reachable without growing the page.
- **Top bar and user menu.** `app.component.html`'s header has no background of its own, so it
  shows the `bg-md-gray-100` canvas the shell's root element sets; `user-menu.component.ts` renders
  its open panel as a compact dropdown (`rounded-md-card`, `shadow-md`). The main content wrapper
  carries the same canvas colour and the #410 page padding (`p-4 sm:p-6`) so a restyled page's cards
  sit on the light grey canvas.
- **Main content width (issue #454).** The main content wrapper has no `max-width` or centering of
  its own: it fills whatever space the flex row beside the sidebar leaves it, at any sidebar state
  (expanded, collapsed, or the narrow drawer) and at any desktop width, with only the #410 page
  padding as a gutter. A data-heavy page (Products, Dashboard, Purchases, Reconciliation,
  Transaction Sales) therefore uses the full main-area width; it does not reintroduce a capped,
  centered column.
- **Page content containers fill that width too (issue #478).** A routed page's own outer content
  container — the `.card` an edit or upload page wraps its form in — carries no `max-w-*` and no
  `mx-auto` either, so the page is as wide as the content area the shell leaves it. The short
  controls inside it are laid out in a responsive column grid (one column, two from `md`, three
  from `xl`, with a textarea spanning the row at `md`) rather than stretched across the whole page;
  `product-form.component.html`'s edit layout, `purchase-upload.component.html`,
  `purchase-edit/purchase-edit-page.component.html` and
  `stock-adjustment-form.component.html` are the worked examples. A form long enough to need
  grouping stops at **two** columns and puts them in titled sections instead, so related fields
  share a row rather than being dealt across three columns in field order — what
  `product-form.component.html` does on New Product since issue #892
  ([the action row's placement](#choosing-a-products-gst-rule-while-creating-it-issue-829)). A narrower `max-w-*` remains
  correct, and stays, on the things it genuinely serves: dialogs and modals, the sidebar, menus and
  dropdowns, toasts, a single filter control or table cell, a readable explanatory paragraph, and a
  report's label/value summary panel (`card-body max-w-xl`), where a full-width line would put the
  label and its figure at opposite ends of the screen. This is a page-level content choice in each
  template, not something the shell imposes or forbids.
- **Sign-in callback.** `auth-callback.component.ts` centres a `.card` on the canvas background
  instead of a bare paragraph; its logic is still just the static "Signing you in..." message.

### Support session banner and the in-memory session id (issue #553)

Issues #550 and #551 built the support-session API and its read-only enforcement with no frontend
at all - the endpoints were called, and the header sent, by hand. Issue #553 is the one slice of
#513 that gives the Super Admin a UI for it: the **View as this business** dialog on the
[Super Admin Businesses page](#super-admin-businesses-page-issue-547), the banner every other page
shows while a session is active, and the one service, `support-session/support-session.service.ts`
(`SupportSessionService`), that both own. Hiding write controls and support-view messages once
inside the session is issue #554's separate follow-up and is not part of this slice.

**The session id lives in this service's memory and nowhere else.** `SupportSessionService` is a
root singleton holding a private `sessionId: string | null` field, read back only by
`currentSessionId()` and by the request-context capture issue #669 added - both of them
`supportSessionInterceptor`'s own accessors, documented below - and never
written to `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, a query parameter or any other part of the URL. A page
reload therefore forgets it, which is what the next two paragraphs exist to handle; this is the
same trade-off issue #550 made in choosing to answer the start call with the id and no other read
with it (`SuperAdminStartedSupportSessionResponse` above) - a value that is never written down
cannot leak through a saved page, a shared link, a browser history entry or a crash dump.

**Every open tab shares the id over `BroadcastChannel`, not through anything persisted.** Starting a
session broadcasts `{ type: 'started', accountKey, sessionId, businessName, expiresAtUtc }` to every
other open tab of the same origin, so each of them can both show the banner and present the header on
its own requests; ending one - from the banner's own **End session**, from another tab, or because the
server answered `support_session_ended` on some unrelated call (below) - broadcasts (or, for the
tab that merely received the broadcast, locally applies) `{ type: 'ended', accountKey }` everywhere at
once. The `accountKey` and the field-by-field check of every received message are issue #670's
([Refreshing the visible business data on a support-context transition](#refreshing-the-visible-business-data-on-a-support-context-transition-issue-670)):
the channel is shared by every tab of the origin and these messages carry the one credential this
application holds, so a malformed message, or one naming another signed-in identity, is ignored
entirely rather than adopting a session or ending the one a tab is in. The
listener is attached once, in the constructor, so it is live for every open tab regardless of
whether anything has subscribed to the banner's state yet. `BroadcastChannel` does not exist in this
build's Jest environment (`jest-environment-jsdom`'s bundled jsdom predates it), so it is used only
behind a `typeof BroadcastChannel` check - the same feature-detection `AppComponent` already uses
for `window.matchMedia` - and the Jest suite supplies a same-process double that preserves the one
asymmetry that makes a multi-tab test mean anything: a channel never delivers its own posted message
back to itself.

**A tab that was never told the id this way still learns a session is running.** A freshly opened
or reloaded tab cannot have received a `BroadcastChannel` message for a session that started before
it existed, so instead it asks `GET /api/super-admin/support-sessions/active` once - the one read
issue #550 resolves from the authenticated actor rather than from a presented id. It learns the
business name and the expiry, and can still end the session (the end call is likewise resolved from
the actor, not from an id); it cannot itself present the header until another tab's `started`
broadcast reaches it, because the active read deliberately never answers the id either
(`SuperAdminActiveSupportSessionResponse` above). **Issue #553 published its banner for that tab
anyway, which is the defect issue #668 fixed**: such a tab is `unresolved`, not a support view, and
renders an explanation instead of a page -
[Failing closed in a tab that cannot present the session](#failing-closed-in-a-tab-that-cannot-present-the-session-issue-668)
below is the current behaviour of everything in this paragraph. The probe itself is asked once per
browser session and only for a caller `PlatformDiagnosticsAccessService.isGranted()` already
confirms is the configured platform administrator, the same cached check `platformAdminGuard` uses -
asking it unconditionally for every signed-in member would be wasted traffic for a surface that can
never apply to them.

**`classifyMemberRequest` treats the support-session control surface like the diagnostics probe
beside it** (`access/member-endpoint.ts`, issue #602's classification, extended here): both are
`platform-admin` kind, reached as the administrator and authorized the same class-2 way, never
inside a session, so a `403` from either is excluded from the capability cache's refresh trigger,
the account-state cache's refresh trigger and the global "you don't have access to this" notice -
exactly as a refusal of the diagnostics probe already was. Without that extension, an ordinary
member's browser asking `GET .../active` (or, for a platform administrator outside an eligible
window, the dialog's own start call) would have its expected `403` misread as a member refusal.
Issue #673 completed the set by classifying the Super Admin businesses surface the same way; see
[Member access](#member-access-capability-built-navigation-guards-and-hidden-actions-issue-528) for
the full classification table and for the request loop the missing third prefix caused.

**`supportSessionInterceptor` (`support-session/support-session.interceptor.ts`) is what a request
actually joins a session through.** For every request this build's own API - never the support-
session control surface itself, never a static asset - it attaches `X-Support-Session:
<currentSessionId()>` while a session is active, and nothing while one is not. On the way back it
does two things with one rule:

1. **Reacts to `support_session_ended` from any call made in the context that is still current.** A
   `403` carrying that code - the one `SupportSessionAuthorizationResultHandler` and
   `SupportSessionExceptionHandler` both use - calls
   `SupportSessionService.handleSessionEndedSignal()`, which clears the id, publishes the banner's
   inactive state, broadcasts the end to other tabs, and does the same three things start and end
   both do: forgets the cached business (`BusinessService.reset()`), re-reads the capabilities
   (`AccessService.refresh()`) and navigates to the dashboard. It is idempotent, so a second
   signal - or one for a tab that was never active - does nothing further.
2. **Discards a response sent in a business context that is no longer current.** Issue #553
   compared only the id the request carried, and ran the reaction above first;
   [Discarding answers from a superseded business context](#discarding-answers-from-a-superseded-business-context-issue-669)
   below is the current rule: every request captures a context generation as well as the id, the
   comparison happens **before** anything reacts to the answer, and a superseded answer leaves the
   caller with neither a value nor an error - exactly `EMPTY` would. A request made with no session
   active is covered by it too, which the id comparison alone could not be.

**Start, end and the `support_session_ended` signal all do the same three things**, and do them from
one place (`SupportSessionService`) rather than three: forget the cached business the shell reads
for every member, re-read the capabilities - the support set inside a session, the administrator's
own (none) outside one - and navigate to the dashboard, because neither the page that was on screen
before nor the one a stale capability set rendered belongs to the business now in view. Issue #670
made that one path **every** transition's path, and made reaching the dashboard actually replace
what is on it; see
[Refreshing the visible business data on a support-context transition](#refreshing-the-visible-business-data-on-a-support-context-transition-issue-670).

**Signing out, switching account, and an end nobody asked for (issue #681).** A session belongs to
the administrator it was granted to, so the shell's sign-out asks
`SupportSessionService.endBeforeSignOut()` first: it ends the caller's session on the server, forgets
it in this tab and broadcasts the end, and only then does `AppComponent.logout()` start MSAL's
sign-out redirect. It always completes and never errors, so a failed end cannot block a sign-out; a
failed end still forgets the session here - the id must not outlive the identity it was granted
to - but is not broadcast, because a sibling dropping a session the server still holds would be told
something false. It navigates nowhere, because the redirect replaces the page. A **change of
signed-in identity** in a tab that knows of a session forgets it the same way, without an end call
and without a broadcast: the identity signed in now can neither end another administrator's session
(the end is answered for the caller's own session only) nor send a message any tab still holding it
would accept, and the shell discards the previous identity's business context itself (issue #604).
An end the administrator did not make - the session's own expiry, or the server refusing a call
with `support_session_ended` - shows one `ToastService.warning` notice
(`SUPPORT_SESSION_ENDED_MESSAGE`) on top of the transition, so the return to their own dashboard is
explained; the banner's own **End session**, and an end received from another tab, show none. The
banner itself uses the design system's danger colours (`md-danger` at 15% behind `md-danger-text`),
because issue #513 asks for a prominent red banner and it had shipped amber.

**What proves it.** `support-session.service.spec.ts` covers starting a session, ending it, the
`support_session_ended` signal (idempotent, and inert for a tab that was never active), the id never
reaching `localStorage`/`sessionStorage`/the URL, a new or reloaded tab's own-session probe (asked
once, gated on platform-admin eligibility, and never answering the id), and the two `BroadcastChannel`
cases: a session shared to another open tab and an end applied in every other open tab.
`support-session.interceptor.spec.ts` covers the header being attached and withheld, every one of the
control surface, the diagnostics probe and (since issue #673) the Super Admin businesses surface
never receiving it, the `support_session_ended` reaction, and a stale response - successful or
refused - being discarded while an unchanged context is left alone (issue #669 added the superseded
-generation cases there, and `support-session-request-context.spec.ts` for the composed rule).
`member-endpoint.spec.ts` covers the
`platform-admin` classification of the support-session control surface and of the Super Admin
businesses surface. `view-as-business-dialog.component.spec.ts` and
`support-session-banner.component.spec.ts` are the two components' own behaviour, and
`super-admin-businesses.component.spec.ts` covers **View as this business** being offered only for
an `Active` business and composed the same way Reject and Members already are (see
[Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191)).

### Hiding write controls and support-view messages (issue #554)

Issue #553 gave the Super Admin a session and a banner with no effect on the business pages viewed
through it; this is the one slice of #513 that closes the two gaps that left open: a write control
that still rendered, and a refusal or a degraded card that said nothing about why.

**A support session's capabilities are the wrong signal for a write control, and this is why a new
one was needed.** `SupportSessionAccessPolicy` (issue #551) grants a session several capabilities
that gate a write elsewhere in the application - `InventoryOperate`, `PurchasingOperate`,
`BusinessManage` and the rest - because the method rule, not the capability set, is what makes the
session read-only. A page that hides a control on the same capability a member's own role uses
(`AccessService.allows`, issue #528) would therefore still render it inside a session; only
`Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults`, one of the two capabilities `SupportSessionAccessPolicy.Excluded`
withholds entirely, happens to hide itself this way already. `SupportSessionService.active$` - a
`distinctUntilChanged` projection of the banner's own `state$` - is the one flag every other write
control reads instead: presentation only, exactly as a capability-gated control already is, and the
backend's read-only enforcement is still what would refuse the write if this page failed to hide or
disable it. `ProductListComponent` (Delete and, since issue #825, Deactivate and New Product, hidden, and since
issue #900, Reactivate the same way; the Active/Inactive toggle, disabled) and
`ProductFormComponent` (Save, disabled) are this slice's representative pages; rolling the same
`active$` subscription out to every remaining write control across the application is tracked as
follow-up under #513 - issues #659, #658, #660 and #657 extend this to expenses and site
commissions, machines and stock, business administration, and Purchases, purchase details/forms
and Suppliers (below), and issue #661 closes the audit over everything those five left
([Auditing the remaining write actions](#auditing-the-remaining-write-actions-across-the-support-view-ui-issue-661)).
Each page's write method (`confirmDelete`, `confirmDeactivate`, `toggleActive`, `save`) also
checks the flag itself and returns before calling the API, the same belt-and-suspenders the
capability-gated controls already follow - the control actually becomes unavailable rather than
merely invisible.

**The two refusal messages are read from the response's own `code`, by one interceptor, for every
request at once.** `support-session/support-session-messages.ts` declares the two codes
`Inventory.Application.SupportSessions.SupportSessionErrorCodes` answers a refused request with -
`read_only_support_session` and `unavailable_in_support_view` - and the one sentence this
application shows for each. `supportSessionMessageInterceptor` reads a `403`'s `code` and shows the
matching sentence through the same `ToastService` every other failure uses; a write control this
build failed to hide or disable ahead of the request (a race with the session ending, a page this
slice has not yet reached) still resolves to the right sentence rather than the generic "you don't
have access to this" `memberForbiddenNoticeInterceptor` would otherwise show for any other
member-endpoint `403` - that interceptor excludes both codes for exactly this reason. It is
installed in `app.config.ts` beside `FORBIDDEN_INTERCEPTORS`, outer to
`supportSessionInterceptor`, so it never reports a response that one has already discarded as
stale.

**The Dashboard's two Nayax-fed cards show the same Nayax sentence, read from a flag rather than a
refusal.** Issue #552 answers a support session's `GET /api/dashboard/summary` with "Needs refill"
and "Needs ordering" each replaced by `UnavailableDashboardSectionDto`
(`{ "available": false, "reason": "SupportView" }`) rather than a blanked figure inside either
card - there was no error to catch, because the backend declined to read the live fleet at all.
`DashboardSummary.needsRefill`/`needsOrdering` (`models.ts`) are each typed as the real summary
shape or `UnavailableDashboardSection`, and `isDashboardSectionUnavailable` is the one type guard
every reader uses. `DashboardComponent`'s value and footer helpers (`refillValueDisplay`,
`refillFooterText`, and the ordering pair beside them) check it first: the big number reads
"Unavailable", on the same rule the sales and inventory cards already use for a figure this
caller was not given, and the footer carries the one sentence - `support-session-messages.ts`'s
`NAYAX_UNAVAILABLE_IN_SUPPORT_VIEW_MESSAGE`, the same constant the interceptor above shows for a
direct refusal, so the error and the degraded card are never two different sentences for the one
reason.

Issue #726 added a second and third `reason` to the same shape (`NayaxNotConnected`,
`PermissionNotGranted`) for a business without a usable provider, and did not touch the frontend, so
such a business briefly saw "Unavailable" with the support-view sentence - wrong wording for the
right state. Issue #727 fixed that: `refillFooterText`/`orderingFooterText` now branch on the
**reason**, not on `available` alone, and the support-view sentence is one of three answers rather
than the only one. The other two have their own wording in `provider/nayax-availability.ts`, and a
`NayaxNotConnected` refill card is not worded at all, because that card is not rendered for a
business with no provider - see [Provider-optional dashboard and Needs Ordering screens](#provider-optional-dashboard-and-needs-ordering-screens-issue-727).

**What proves it.** `support-session.service.spec.ts` covers `active$` publishing `true` once a
session starts and `false` again once it ends, with no duplicate for an unchanged state.
`product-list.component.spec.ts` and `product-form.component.spec.ts` cover Delete being hidden,
the status toggle and Save being disabled, and each write method refusing to call the API while a
session is active - and that both controls render normally while none is. `dashboard.component.spec.ts`
covers the Nayax sentence appearing for both cards' value and footer when the summary carries
`{ available: false, reason: "SupportView" }`, and the real figures being unaffected when it does
not. `support-session-message.interceptor.spec.ts` covers the two messages being shown for their
own code and nothing else, and `member-forbidden-notice.interceptor.spec.ts` covers the generic
message staying silent for both support-session codes.

### Extending hidden write controls to expenses and site commissions (issue #659)

Issue #554 rolled `SupportSessionService.active$` out to Products as the representative pages and
tracked every remaining write control as follow-up under #513. This slice closes that follow-up for
Operating Expenses and site commissions: `OperatingExpenseComponent`, `SiteCommissionAgreementsComponent`
and the commission payment control on `SiteCommissionsReportComponent`.

**The same wrong signal, for two more capabilities.** `SupportSessionAccessPolicy` grants a session
`Capability.ExpensesManage` and `Capability.SiteCommissionsManage` alongside the capabilities #554
already named, so a page that gates its own write controls on either of those - exactly as Products
gates on `InventoryOperate` - would still render them inside a session. `active$` is the same shared
flag these pages now read instead, for the same reason: it is presentation only, and the backend's
read-only method rule is still what would refuse the write if a page failed to hide or disable it.

**What each page hides or disables, and why hidden rather than disabled differs by control.**
`OperatingExpenseComponent` hides Add Expense (a page action, like the rest of this build's create
entry points) and each row's Edit/Delete (following `ProductListComponent`'s Delete), and disables
Save on the open edit form (following `ProductFormComponent`) - a session cannot open an edit form in
the first place once Edit is hidden, but Save still checks the flag so a form already open when a
session starts cannot submit. `SiteCommissionAgreementsComponent` disables its single Save agreement
button, the same pattern as `ProductFormComponent`'s Save. `SiteCommissionsReportComponent`'s Record
Payment control - the input group and the button together - hides rather than disables, since (like
Products' Delete) there is no mid-edit state the control being merely inert would protect. Every
guarded handler (`startCreate`, `startEdit`, `save`, `remove` on the expense page;
`saveCommissionAgreement`; `recordPayment`) also checks `sessionActive` itself and returns before
calling the API, the same belt-and-suspenders #554 established: the control becomes unavailable
rather than merely invisible or inert.

**Read-only listings and reports are unaffected.** The expense table, the current-agreements table
and the commission report's rows, details and Print details stay visible and interactive during a
session; only the controls that attempt a write are touched. Server-side enforcement - the method
rule behind `ExpensesManage` and `SiteCommissionsManage` alike - is unchanged.

**What proves it.** `operating-expense.component.spec.ts`, added by this slice, covers Add
Expense/Edit/Delete being hidden and Save being disabled while a session is active, each guarded
handler (`startCreate`, `startEdit`, `save`, `remove`) refusing to call the service when invoked
directly, and normal create/edit/delete behaviour while no session is active.
`site-commission-agreements.component.spec.ts` gained a session-active describe block covering Save
agreement being disabled and `saveCommissionAgreement` refusing to call the service while a session
is active, and both staying available while none is. `site-commissions-report.component.spec.ts`,
added by this slice, covers Record Payment being hidden and `recordPayment` refusing to call the
service while a session is active, and both working normally while none is.

### Extending the read-only support-view guard to machines and stock (issue #658)

Issue #554 established the pattern and covered Products as its representative pages; this slice
rolls the same `SupportSessionService.active$` subscription out to the next bounded area #513
named: machine restock, the machine-level Nayax Sync Restock reconciliation workflow, and the
manual stock-adjustment form shared by the Stock History page and the preserved
`/products/:id/stock` entry point. Sites, site products and the Sites list carry no write control
at all - every call those pages make is a `GET` - so nothing in that family needed a guard.

**`MachineDetailComponent`'s Restock control (quantity input and button) was hidden per row**, the
same `ProductListComponent.confirmDelete`/Delete-button shape issue #554 used: there is no
read-only value left in a quantity input nobody may submit, so hiding it rather than disabling it
was the right call, the same way Delete was hidden rather than disabled, and `restockProduct()` also
returned before calling `StockService.adjust` while a session is active. **Issue #744's machine-page
consolidation removed that control and `restockProduct()` entirely**, replacing it with the
**Record refill** link described in [Machine-page consolidation: the "Record refill" link](#machine-page-consolidation-the-record-refill-link-issue-744);
that link is hidden during a support session on the same reasoning, and the write it leads to is
`ManualPickListComponent.save`'s own existing support-session refusal (see [Manual pick-list entry
and mode selection](#manual-pick-list-entry-and-mode-selection-issue-744)), not a second guard
invented here.

**`MachineRestockSyncComponent`'s Sync Restock trigger is disabled, not hidden**, because unlike
Restock's bare input it is a single well-known action on an otherwise-informative panel - the same
shape `ProductFormComponent.save` used. It needed the guard for a sharper reason than the others,
though: `POST /api/machines/{id}/sync-restock` is itself a `POST`, so
`SupportSessionAccessPolicy.IsReadMethod` refuses even the *preview* fetch during a session, not
only the apply/resolve calls that follow it - there is no partial, read-only view of this dialog to
leave open. Every write-shaped method on the component (`syncRestock`, `applySelectedEvents`,
`resolveDuplicate`, `resolveSelectedAsAlreadyRecorded`) checks `sessionActive` and returns before
calling `MachineService`, and the dialog's own Apply/resolve buttons are disabled the same way as a
second line of defence for the rare case the dialog was already open when a session started.

**`StockAdjustmentFormComponent`'s Apply Adjustment button is disabled**, on the same reasoning as
Save: the rest of the form (reason, machine, notes) stays useful to read, only the write at its end
is refused. `adjust()` returns before calling `StockService.adjust` while a session is active. Since
the component is composed into both `StockHistoryPageComponent` and the machine-detail/stock pages
behind it, this one guard covers every place a manual adjustment can be submitted from.

**What proves it.** The machine-detail page's own per-product Restock action was removed by issue
#744's machine-page consolidation (see [Machine-page consolidation: the "Record refill" link](#machine-page-consolidation-the-record-refill-link-issue-744));
`machine-detail.component.spec.ts` now covers its replacement, the **Record refill** link, being
hidden the same way while a session is active. `machine-restock-sync.component.spec.ts` covers Sync
Restock being disabled in both states and every one of the four write-shaped methods refusing to call `MachineService` directly
while a session is active, including the preview fetch. `stock-adjustment-form.component.spec.ts`
covers Apply Adjustment being disabled in both states and `adjust()` refusing to call
`StockService.adjust` directly while a session is active. `stock-history-page.component.spec.ts`
provides `SupportSessionService` for the embedded form so its own existing coverage keeps rendering
the composed page.

### Disabling business administration write controls in support view (issue #660)

Issue #554 rolled `SupportSessionService.active$` out to Products as the two representative pages;
this is the next slice of #513's follow-up, carrying the same `active$` subscription to the three
named business-admin mutation families the parent issue called out - Business Settings, Nayax
Settings, and members/users/invitations - each judged by the same question: does this page's route
capability stay granted inside a session?

**Business Settings and Integrations needed the guard, because their capabilities are granted.**
`Business.Manage` and `Integration.Manage` are both in `SupportSessionAccessPolicy.Capabilities`
(see [Hiding write controls and support-view messages](#hiding-write-controls-and-support-view-messages-issue-554)
for why a granted capability is the wrong signal for a write control), so a Super Admin's support
session reaches both routes with the page rendered exactly as an Owner sees it. `active$` is the
flag each page's write method checks instead, the same belt-and-suspenders `ProductListComponent`
and `ProductFormComponent` already follow:

- `BusinessSettingsFormComponent` disables Save and its `submit()`/`save()` both return before
  validating or calling `BusinessSettingsService.save()` - `save()` is checked a second time
  because `confirmTimeZoneChange()` reaches it without going through `submit()`'s own guard, which
  only covers a session that was already active when the form was submitted.
- `NayaxSettingsComponent` disables Save rate and `saveFeeRate()` returns before calling
  `NayaxSettingsService.saveRate()`.
- `NayaxConnectionWizardComponent` disables Test connection, Save connection and Re-test, and
  `runTest()`, `saveConnection()` and `retest()` each return before calling the matching
  `NayaxConnectionService` method - `canSave` folds the session flag in beside `canManage`, the
  existing `Integration.Manage` read, exactly as it already folds in `busy`.

Every one of these pages keeps its read-only information on screen - the stored fee-rate history,
the stored Nayax connection's status and checklist, the legacy-settings prompt - because only the
mutating action itself is disabled, never the page.

**Members, Invites and the rest of Admin Users needed no frontend change, because `Members.Manage`
is excluded.** `SupportSessionAccessPolicy.Excluded` deliberately withholds `MembersManage` from a
support session (the member list's names and emails are private even from a supporter - see
[Hiding write controls and support-view messages](#hiding-write-controls-and-support-view-messages-issue-554)),
and `admin/users`'s route requires exactly that capability (`app.routes.ts`). `requireCapability`
therefore redirects a session's request to `access-not-allowed` before `MemberManagementComponent`
or `MemberInvitesComponent` ever mounts, so role change, revoke, reinstate, invite creation and
invite cancellation are unreachable by construction rather than by a flag either component reads.
Teaching either component `active$` as well would be an assertion this build can never exercise
honestly, because the capability that would have to flip for the route to admit a session request
is the one `SupportSessionAccessPolicy.Excluded` pins shut; the backend side of that is proved by
`SupportSessionAccessPolicyTests`, and the route guard's generic redirect-on-denial behaviour is
proved by `capability.guard.spec.ts`, so this slice adds no redundant frontend test for a path that
cannot be reached.

**What proves it.** `business-settings-form.component.spec.ts`,
`nayax-settings.component.spec.ts` and `nayax-connection-wizard.component.spec.ts` each cover their
write control being disabled while a session is active, the write method refusing to call its
service while one is - including, for Business Settings, a time zone confirmation requested before
a session started but confirmed after one did - and every control rendering and working normally
while none is. `business-settings.component.spec.ts` was given the same `SupportSessionService`
stub `BusinessSettingsFormComponent` now requires, because that page composes the form.

### Extending write-control hiding to Purchases and Suppliers (issue #657)

Issue #554 hid or disabled write controls on two representative pages and left the rest of the
application as follow-up under #513; this slice rolls the same `SupportSessionService.active$`
flag out to Purchases, purchase details/forms and Suppliers - the bounded area #657 named. The
reasoning is unchanged: every endpoint these pages call is `[RequireCapability(Capability
.PurchasingOperate)]`, one of the capabilities `SupportSessionAccessPolicy.Capabilities` grants a
session, so a page that hides a control on the same capability a member's own role uses would
still render it inside a session; `active$` is the one flag that does not make that mistake, and
the backend's read-only method rule is still what would refuse the write if a page failed to hide
or disable it.

**What changed, page by page.** `PurchaseListComponent` hides Add Purchase and Delete (`remove`
checks the flag itself before confirming). Issue #976's "Add document" joined that list on the same
terms and for the same reason: adding a purchase's document is a write on `Purchasing.Operate`,
which a session grants, so the page hides the control while still reporting that the purchase has no
document (see [A purchase's document is optional](#a-purchases-document-is-optional-issue-976)). `PurchaseUploadComponent` (`/purchases/new`, reached
both directly and from a supplier order's Receive action) disables Add Purchase and `upload()`
returns before calling the API. `PurchaseEditFormComponent` - a presentational child with no
service of its own - takes `sessionActive` as an `@Input` exactly as it already takes `saving` and
`error`; `PurchaseEditPageComponent` is what actually subscribes to `active$` (alongside its
existing `Subscription` bag) and passes the flag down, and guards its own `onSave` the same way as
a second line of defence beneath the form's own `submit()` guard. `SupplierOrdersComponent` hides
Receive / Create Purchase and Cancel, and `cancelOrder` checks the flag before calling the API;
Receive is navigation to the already-guarded upload page, so only the control needed hiding, not a
new guard. `SupplierListComponent` disables the Create/Update submit button and hides Delete,
guarding `save()` and `remove()` the same way; Edit is left alone because it only sets local form
state and issues no request of its own - the control that matters is the Save/Create button it
leads to. Issue #934's "Not used" switch joined that list on the same terms, for the same reason:
it is on `Purchasing.Operate`, which a session grants, so the page hides the control and
`setNotUsed()` returns before calling the API
([The link, the lock and the "Not used" switch](#the-link-the-lock-and-the-not-used-switch-issue-934)).

**What this slice deliberately left alone.** `SupplierGstDefaultsComponent` needed no change: its
editor already hides itself on `AccessService.allows('Suppliers.ManageGstDefaults')`, and that
capability is one of the two `SupportSessionAccessPolicy.Excluded` withholds entirely, so a
session's `canManage` is already `false` without reading `active$` at all. Local-only controls
that issue no request of their own - a draft purchase line's Add Product/Remove, every plain form
field - are untouched for the same reason the representative pages in #554 left them alone: the
single Save/Submit control downstream of them is what is actually guarded.

**What proves it.** `purchase-list.component.spec.ts` covers Add Purchase and Delete being hidden,
and `remove` refusing to call the API, while a session is active - and both rendering normally
while none is. `purchase-upload.component.spec.ts` covers Add Purchase being disabled and
`upload()` refusing to call the API. `purchase-edit-form.component.spec.ts` covers Save being
disabled and `submit()` emitting nothing while `sessionActive` is set directly on the form, and
`purchase-edit-page.component.spec.ts` covers the page passing its own `active$` subscription down
as that input and `onSave` refusing to call the API. `supplier-orders.component.spec.ts` covers
Receive and Cancel being hidden and `cancelOrder` refusing to call the API.
`supplier-list.component.spec.ts` (new) covers Create/Update being disabled, Delete being hidden,
`save()` and `remove()` refusing to call the API while a session is active, and normal behaviour
resuming once a session ends.

### Auditing the remaining write actions across the support view UI (issue #661)

Issues #554, #659, #658, #660 and #657 each guarded one named family of pages. This slice is the
audit that closes #513's frontend follow-up: every remaining user-triggered write action in the
Angular application was inventoried, and the ones a support session can still reach now read the
same `SupportSessionService.active$` flag. Nothing about the signal changed - a session grants the
capability these pages gate on, so the capability is still the wrong thing to ask
