  inputs, and write the use case's decisions back to exactly those tracked rows; they never save,
  open a transaction or decide a cost.
- Neither use case owns a transaction. The callers - `EfStockAdjustmentStore`,
  `EfInventoryCountAdjustmentStore` (Take Inventory), `EfMachineStockEventStore`, `EfPurchaseStore`,
  `EfProductStore`, `EfLatestNayaxSalesStore`, the sale-costing use cases (issue #297), the
  inventory-cost transition apply use cases (issue #298), and the uploaded sales import (issue #301) -
  keep their existing transaction around a movement and the rebuild it triggers, so both still
  commit or roll back together.

Sale costing and its backfills are Application use cases since issue #297; see
[Sale import and costing](#sale-import-and-costing).

The inventory-cost transition - the one-time cutover that records each product's opening costing
baseline - is Domain/Application-owned since issue #298 (child 4 of #149, which completes the #149
costing migration). It replaced the removed `InventoryApi.Services.InventoryCostTransitionService`/
`IInventoryCostTransitionService`, unchanged in behaviour:

- `Inventory.Domain.Costing.InventoryCostTransitionPolicy` holds the deterministic rules: a machine's
  stock for a product is the sum over its slots of `PAR - MissingStockByMDB` (a slot missing either
  value, or outside `0..PAR`, is rejected); the opening costing quantity is verified home stock plus
  every machine's stock, valued at the opening average unit cost; the legacy physical replay's
  discrepancy against home stock is recorded as a data-quality note, never corrected; a stored
  preview may be applied once and only within 30 minutes; and a preview is stale when home stock, the
  legacy replay or any machine's stock changed, when its values no longer follow from its inputs,
  or (all products) when the eligible products or an average unit cost changed. Every check throws
  `DomainValidationException` with the message the API has always returned.
  `Inventory.Domain.Costing.InventoryCostBaselineSource` mirrors the persisted
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Models.InventoryCostBaselineSource` value-for-value (a parity test enforces this).
- `Inventory.Application.Costing.PreviewInventoryCostTransition`, `ApplyInventoryCostTransition`,
  `PreviewAllInventoryCostTransitions` and `ApplyAllInventoryCostTransitions` orchestrate them, and own
  the request/response contracts moved unchanged in name and shape from the removed
  `InventoryApi/DTOs/InventoryCostTransitionDtos.cs`. A preview reads Nayax machine stock through the
  existing `INayaxLynxClient` port (a Nayax failure propagates unchanged and stores nothing), fixes the
  cutoff after that read through the `IClock` port, and stores its snapshot. An apply runs in one
  transaction: it re-reads the stored preview, rebuilds it from current data and rejects a stale one,
  saves each baseline exactly as previewed, marks the preview applied and runs the `IRebuildProductCost`
  rebuild from the cutoff, so a failure anywhere rolls all of it back. Baselines keep their cutoff
  semantics for `CostSale` and for `PurchaseCostTransitionPolicy`'s pre-cutover purchase guards, which
  read the same persisted baselines.
- The narrow `IInventoryCostTransitionStore` port (transaction, baseline lookup, products, legacy
  replay sums, preview drafts, baselines, save) is implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfInventoryCostTransitionStore`, which keeps the former EF
  queries and baseline mapping behind `AppDbContext`'s business query filter and ownership stamp; it
  moved to `Inventory.Infrastructure`, beside `AppDbContext`, in Persistence 8/8 of #153 (issue #309). `InventoryCostTransitionsController`
  calls the four use cases directly with unchanged routes (`POST api/admin/inventory-cost-transition/
  preview`, `apply`, `preview-all`, `apply-all`), request/response JSON, status codes and messages.

#### Costing repairs (issue #359)

A costing repair is the one supported way to restore costing history that was never recorded. It
exists for a single situation: physical stock the business genuinely held was never valued in the
ledger - an incomplete opening or acquisition history - so `WeightedAverageCostReplay` reports
`UnknownCost`/`MissingOpening` for the completed sales that depend on it, and every later write to
that product (purchase, count, refill apply, sales sync) fails on the same fatal issue. Restock,
Correction, Damaged, Expired and MachineRefill are physical movements and keep their meanings, so
none of them can express "the costing history was incomplete" without misstating physical stock; a
repair is the explicit, auditable, costing-only alternative. It is never inferred - not from
machine-refill gaps, not from Nayax events, never from the product's current cost or selling price -
and it never substitutes for a real purchase, correction or write-off.

- **It is costing-only, and append-only.** `Inventory.Infrastructure.Models.InventoryCostRepair` is tenant-owned
  (`IBusinessOwned`, so filtered, indexed and stamped centrally) and stores the product, the UTC
  effective instant, a positive quantity, a non-negative unit cost, the total value, the reason, the
  creation time and the creating identity as the validated Entra `(tid, oid)` pair - the same
  identity convention as `BusinessMembership`, and deliberately no email or display name of its own
  (the display-only pair issue #524 added to the membership row is not repeated onto a repair: a
  historical record must not carry a value that is refreshed later). Applying
  one changes `CostingQuantity`/`InventoryValue` and historical sale costs only: never
  `Product.QuantityInStock`, machine quantities, `StockAdjustment` rows, MachineRefill history or a
  transition baseline. There is no update or delete path anywhere - no use case, port method or
  endpoint - because an applied repair is a historical fact that was recorded; the migration that
  adds the table backfills nothing.
- **Costing-only is enforced by what the apply stages, not by convention.** A full rebuild restates
  the product's physical quantity and every movement's running position from the replay, so routing
  a repair through it would overwrite `Product.QuantityInStock` with the replayed quantity whenever
  the two differ - which is exactly the state a product needing a repair tends to be in. The apply
  therefore calls `RebuildCostingOnlyAsync` (same ledger, same `WeightedAverageCostReplay`, same
  decide-before-staging rule - not a second costing algorithm), which stages the costing position
  and the recosted sale costs and nothing else. Two consequences are deliberate and visible in
  `EfInventoryCostRepairStoreTests.A_repair_changes_neither_physical_stock_nor_a_stored_movement`:
  a stored physical quantity that disagrees with the movement history stays as it is, still reported
  as a data-quality issue rather than silently corrected by a repair; and a stock movement after the
  repair keeps its stored `UnitCost`/`TotalCost` and running-position snapshot even when the repaired
  ledger could now cost it, because #359 recosts completed sales only and excludes changing stock
  adjustments. The product's own position does account for those movements - the replay consumes
  them - so the gap is in the movement's audit snapshot, not in the valuation. The next ordinary
  rebuild (a purchase, count, refill apply, product edit or sales sync for that product) refreshes
  those snapshots; recosting a movement from a repair would need its own issue.
- **`Inventory.Domain.Costing.CostingRepairPolicy`** holds the rules, each throwing
  `DomainValidationException`: quantity > 0, unit cost >= 0 (zero allowed - free stock is a real
  acquisition), a reason that is neither empty nor a placeholder, an effective instant strictly after
  the product's transition cutoff (the replay ignores everything at or before it, so a repair there
  would silently do nothing), and a placement that actually reaches the sale it must cover.
- **Placement is judged by the replay's own ordering**, through
  `WeightedAverageCostReplay.ReplaysBefore`, not by comparing timestamps in the use case. Sale
  authorization times are machine-local (Sydney) while movement and repair times are UTC, and the
  replay compares them without converting (existing behaviour, unchanged here), so the only
  trustworthy question is where the replay itself puts the two events. A repair replays first at its
  own instant, because it is the opening it restores: anything else at that instant - a restock, a
  refill, the very sale being covered - must already see the repaired value.
- **`Inventory.Application.Costing.PreviewInventoryCostRepair`** persists nothing, not even a draft.
  It replays the ledger twice through the shared `InventoryCostRepairProjection` - as it stands, and
  with the proposed repair - and reports the costing quantity/value immediately before the repair,
  the quantity/value it adds, the resulting average unit cost, the first completed sale the ledger
  cannot cost today, whether the repair replays before it, the projected costing quantity/value, and
  the fatal issues a partial repair would leave behind.
- **`ApplyInventoryCostRepair`** runs in one transaction, and in one order deliberately: the
  authoritative ledger read, the expected-state comparison and the write are a single operation.
  Because the preview stores nothing, the stale-preview model of
  `PreviewInventoryCostTransition`/`ApplyInventoryCostTransition` is carried by
  `Inventory.Domain.Costing.CostLedgerFingerprint` rather than a stored draft: a deterministic
  SHA-256 over everything the replay consumes (product position, movements, completed sales, existing
  repairs, baseline), with timestamps as ticks and decimals normalised, which the preview reports and
  the apply recomputes and requires to match. It then enforces the placement rule, appends the
  repair, and rebuilds costing-only through the existing `IRebuildProductCost` path from the repair's
  effective instant. The rebuild decides before it stages (issue #362), so a repair that leaves any
  fatal data-quality issue fails and persists nothing at all - a partial repair cannot half-cost a
  product.
- **The narrow `IInventoryCostRepairStore` port** (transaction, product lookup, append, history,
  save) is implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfInventoryCostRepairStore`; it moved to
  `Inventory.Infrastructure`, beside `AppDbContext`, in Persistence 8/8 of #153 (issue #309). The replay inputs themselves come from
  `IInventoryCostLedgerStore`, whose `InventoryCostLedger` now carries the product's repairs, so a
  preview, an apply and a rebuild all read one ledger. `GetInventoryCostRepairHistory` returns a
  product's repairs newest effective first (ties by most recently recorded), and reports a product
  belonging to another business exactly as it reports one that does not exist.
- **The HTTP surface (issue #360)** is `InventoryApi.Controllers.InventoryCostRepairsController`,
  three thin adapters over the use cases above, following `InventoryCostTransitionsController`:

  | Endpoint | Request | Success response |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `POST api/admin/inventory-cost-repair/preview` | `InventoryCostRepairRequest` (`productId`, `effectiveAt`, `quantity`, `unitCost`, `reason`) | `200` `InventoryCostRepairPreview`, complete: the before/after and projected costing positions, the resulting average unit costs, `firstUncostableSale`, `replaysBeforeFirstUncostableSale`, `remainingFatalIssues` and the `ledgerFingerprint` the apply requires back. Persists nothing. |
  | `POST api/admin/inventory-cost-repair/apply` | `ApplyInventoryCostRepairRequest` - the same proposal plus the `ledgerFingerprint` the preview reported | `200` `InventoryCostRepairApplied`: the stored `repair` record (including `createdAt` and the creating `(tid, oid)` pair) and the product's rebuilt `costingQuantity`, `inventoryValue`, `averageUnitCost` and `recostedSaleCount`. |
  | `GET api/admin/inventory-cost-repair/{productId}` | - | `200` the product's `InventoryCostRepairRecord` list, newest effective first. |

  The controller binds a request, invokes one use case with the request's cancellation token and
  returns its result unchanged. It holds no costing logic, no EF query, no transaction, no
  recomputation of an Application result and no business filter of its own - ownership is the
  central query filter and `SaveChanges` stamp, so another business's product is invisible and is
  reported exactly like a product that does not exist (`400`, `Product {id} does not exist.`).
  There is no update, delete or reversal endpoint, because a repair has no such path.
- **Error contract.** Nothing is caught at the boundary. Every deliberate refusal - quantity, unit
  cost, reason, the transition cutoff, placement before the sale being covered, a repair that would
  leave the history fatally incomplete, and a **stale preview** whose fingerprint no longer matches
  the ledger - is a `DomainValidationException`, so `DomainExceptionHandler` answers `400`
  ProblemDetails with the Application's caller-safe message in `detail` and in the `message`
  extension the Angular client reads, plus a `traceId`. A stale preview is deliberately part of
  that `400` contract and not a `409`: the HTTP boundary does not reclassify what the use case
  decided. An authenticated caller with no usable business membership is `BusinessScopeMiddleware`'s
  `403`, and an unexpected failure stays unmapped - `GlobalExceptionHandler`'s logged, generic `500`
  with no exception message - with the apply's transaction leaving no repair behind.
- **Timestamps.** `effectiveAt` is a UTC instant in both directions. `CostingRepairPolicy`
  normalises what the request named - an offset-bearing value is converted, and a timezone-less one
  is read as UTC (issue #359's policy, unchanged) - so the preview, the apply and the history all
  report the UTC spelling of the instant the caller meant. The machine-local sale time versus UTC
  movement time mismatch the replay already carries is untouched by #360; placement is still judged
  by the replay's own ordering, not by comparing those timestamps.
- **Authorization** is the same as the inventory-cost transition - authenticated, `access_as_user`,
  and any member of the business - because the application has no admin role; adding one is out of
  scope. Applying a repair changes historical COGS for later sales, so production use needs human
  scrutiny. `InventoryCostRepairApiTests` exercises all of this through the real request pipeline on
  relational SQLite: the JSON contracts, the fingerprint round trip, the `400` mappings, the UTC
  timestamps, the unauthenticated and missing-scope refusals, and two businesses proving a
  cross-business product is indistinguishable from a missing one.
- **The UI (issue #361)** is `frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/admin/costing-repair/
  costing-repair.component.ts`'s standalone `CostingRepairComponent`, composed through `[products]`
  rather than grown inside the page component, per [Page composition
  boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) - by `AdminComponent` until issue #390 moved it to
  the dedicated `/admin/costing-repair` page (`CostingRepairPageComponent`): it owns the whole preview/apply/history
  workflow's own form, loading and error state, and its own calls to the three endpoints above.
  The effective date/time is entered and displayed in the current business's time zone (issue #499) and converted to/from the UTC
  instant the contract carries through `zonedDateTimeToUtc`/`currentDateTimeInTimeZone`/
  `toDateTimeLocalValue`/`fromDateTimeLocalValue` (added to `business-time-zone.ts` alongside the
  existing `startOfDayUtc`, which issue #361 re-expressed as `zonedDateTimeToUtc` called with a
  midnight time-of-day so the two stay one conversion, not two). Apply always resubmits exactly the
  previewed proposal object - never the form's current field values - matching the inventory-cost
  transition UI's own apply call; a stale-preview `400` (or any other apply failure) clears the
  shown preview so Apply is disabled until a fresh preview is taken, consistent with the use case's
  own "preview again" message. Preview and history responses are guarded by a per-kind request
  sequence number and their subscriptions are cancelled on a product change, so a late response for
  a previously selected product (including after A -> B -> A switching) is discarded and cannot
  touch the current loading or error state; history is cleared on every selection change; Apply
  refuses a preview whose product is not the one currently selected; and the product selector is
  disabled while an apply is in flight. The operator's effective time goes through
  `resolveZonedDateTime`, not `zonedDateTimeToUtc`: a wall-clock time in the October daylight-saving
  gap (`nonexistent`) or the April repeated hour (`ambiguous`) is rejected with a form message
  before any preview call, so the effective time is never silently moved or guessed;
  `zonedDateTimeToUtc`/`startOfDayUtc` keep their normalising behaviour for start-of-day callers. The product dropdown reuses the `ProductService.getAll()` product list its
  host page loads (`AdminComponent` before issue #390, `CostingRepairPageComponent` after it); #361 does not add a per-product
  fatal-issue list of its own - the Dashboard's existing aggregate unknown-cost
  count/completeness indicator (see [Dashboard "Inventory Value" tile](#dashboard-inventory-value-tile-issue-42))
  remains the signal that a product may need one, and the preview itself reports whether the
  selected product still has a fatal issue once the proposed repair is applied.

#### Dashboard "Inventory Value" tile (issue #42)

The business-owned perpetual inventory value - the sum of every product's persisted
`InventoryValue` (the AVCO valuation the `RebuildProductCost` use case maintains), never a
quantity × retail-price value and never home/storage stock quantity on its own - is
the figure behind the home Dashboard's "Inventory" card (see
[Home dashboard: four headline cards](#home-dashboard-four-headline-cards-issue-460) below).

The backend is authoritative: `Inventory.Domain.Reporting.Dashboard.InventoryValuationPolicy`
aggregates the per-product values. `Inventory.Application.Reporting.Dashboard.GetInventoryValuationSummary`
is the dedicated use case for this figure alone (retrieving it through the narrow
`IInventoryValuationFactsProvider` port, whose EF adapter is
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Reporting.Persistence.EfInventoryValuationFactsProvider` since issue
#308), exposed by `ProductsController` as `GET /api/products/inventory-value-summary`. A product's
`InventoryValue` is `null` only when it has never had a cost rebuild run for it - a genuinely
unknown cost, not a zero one - so the policy makes the whole total unavailable
(`InventoryValuationSummaryDto.IsComplete = false`, `TotalInventoryValue = null`) whenever any
product that **holds inventory** has an unknown cost, rather than silently summing only the known
ones. What "holds inventory" means is the evidence rule below.

The same valuation, with the same completeness rule, is also part of the combined Dashboard summary
contract described in [Home Dashboard summary API](#home-dashboard-summary-api-issue-459) below. That
endpoint reuses the Domain `InventoryValuationPolicy` directly rather than calling this use case, so
its valuation, product count and storage units all describe one catalogue read. Issue #460 moved
`DashboardComponent`'s own display from this dedicated endpoint to that combined summary's
`inventory` card, so the home Dashboard no longer calls `GET /api/products/inventory-value-summary`
directly; the endpoint itself is unchanged and stays available for any other caller that needs the
valuation alone.

##### A product that has never held inventory (issue #861)

A `null InventoryValue` on its own cannot tell *costed at nothing* from *never costed*, and before
issue #861 it was the only evidence the valuation had. So a product created yesterday and never
bought, stocked, refilled or sold - value `null`, no costing quantity, no storage units, no history
anywhere - made the whole Dashboard total read **Unavailable** with "1 of 3 products missing cost
data", as though the business were holding stock of unknown worth. It is holding nothing, and owning
none of something is a measured `$0`, not a gap.

`Inventory.Domain.Reporting.Dashboard.ProductInventoryValuationFact` is therefore what the policy now
aggregates, and it carries the product's whole position rather than its value alone:

| Part of the evidence | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `InventoryValue` | The persisted AVCO valuation, `null` when no rebuild has ever run |
| `CostingQuantity` | Business-owned costing units **wherever they sit, including inside a machine** |
| `QuantityInStock` | Storage/home stock only, which **excludes** units in a machine |
| `HasInventoryHistory` | Whether anything records inventory ever having been in this product |

`ProductInventoryValuationFact.HasNeverHeldInventory` is true only when **all four** say so: no
established value, no costing units, no storage stock, and no recorded history. Such a product
contributes `0` to the total and `0` to `ProductsWithUnknownCost`, and is still counted in
`TotalProducts`, because it is in the catalogue - how many products a business has and how many block
its valuation are deliberately different figures. A catalogue of nothing but never-stocked products is
a known `$0.00`.

**Zero storage quantity is deliberately not the test.** Units already loaded into a vending machine
are business-owned costing inventory that `QuantityInStock` does not count, so an empty shelf says
nothing about what the business owns. The seven kinds of row that count as history are, exactly:

- a `StockAdjustment` - a restock, correction, write-off or **refill into a machine**, which also
  covers every purchase that was received;
- a `PurchaseItem` line;
- a stored `NayaxSales` row through the sale's own `ProductId` (issue #758), never a provider id or a
  name - a sale whose product was never resolved belongs to no product and is evidence about none;
- an operator's `MachineStockCount` (issue #56);
- an `InventoryCostTransitionBaseline`, whose opening position includes machine-held stock (issue #57);
- an `InventoryCostRepair` (issue #359);
- a `NayaxMachineStockEvent` matched to the product - **including one still unprocessed**, because an
  unresolved machine movement is an unresolved position rather than an absent one.

A `SupplierOrderLine` is deliberately **not** evidence: ordering is an intention, nothing has been
received, and the purchase that receives it is recorded as both a purchase line and a stock movement.
That is the one place this question differs from the deletion rule's reference counts (issue #736),
which exist to stop a row being erased rather than to describe a position.

**Active status decides nothing here.** The same evidence rule applies to an active and an inactive
product alike: deactivating a product is not what makes its inventory empty, and a retired product
that still holds stock of unknown value still makes the total unavailable. Blanket active-only
valuation was explicitly rejected - it would silently drop a discontinued product's real stock out of
the business's inventory value.

**Nothing is fabricated.** A never-stocked product is *excluded* from the aggregation; its `null`
inventory value is never turned into a zero, no opening quantity, purchase or costing history is
invented for it, and **its unit cost stays unknown** - `DisplayUnitCost` still answers `null` for it
(see [One product's average cost](#one-products-average-cost-and-whether-it-has-been-established-issue-788)
below). That is not a disagreement between the two rules: the catalogue total asks what the business
owns, and this asks what a unit costs, which nothing has ever established.

**Where the evidence is resolved.** `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfProductInventoryHistoryQueries`
is the one query behind `HasInventoryHistory`, shared by the two adapters that need it -
`EfInventoryValuationFactsProvider` for the endpoint above and `EfProductCatalogStore.ListUnorderedAsync`
for the combined summary below - so the two surfaces cannot come to disagree about whether a product is
empty. Tenant scoping is the central `AppDbContext` query filters as always: another business's
movements, sales and counts are invisible and can never become evidence about this business's product.
Both adapters ask about history **only** for the products whose own stored columns could still be empty
(`ProductInventoryValuationFact.CouldNeverHaveHeldInventory`, the Domain rule, read rather than
restated), one grouped read per kind for the whole set and none at all when there are no such products -
so a fully costed catalogue costs exactly what it did before. No schema change, no migration and no
backfill: this is a projection of rows that are already stored.

On `ProductRecord`, `HasInventoryHistory` is a `bool?` and `null` means **not resolved on this read
path**, never "no history" - the same convention `DeletionEligibility` uses. `GetDashboardSummary`
reads an unresolved value as *has history*, which is the safe direction: a read that did not look for
the evidence has not proved its absence, so the product keeps blocking the total exactly as it did
before this rule existed.

**No presentation changed.** The card's own wording is untouched: `isInventoryValueComplete` is simply
true in the reported case, so the card shows the real total and "Business-owned inventory at cost"
instead of "Unavailable" and "1 of 3 products missing cost data", and its storage-only footer
("`productCount` products · `unitsInStorage` units in storage (excludes machines)") is unchanged - the
never-stocked product is still one of those products. No API property was added, removed or renamed.

##### One product's average cost, and whether it has been established (issue #788)

The same `null InventoryValue` evidence answers a second question, about one product rather than the
catalogue: **may this product's average unit cost be displayed at all?** `Product.AverageUnitCost` is a
non-nullable column, so a product no cost rebuild has ever run for still carries a number in it — a
create can seed one — and a screen that rendered that number would present an unestablished figure as
a costed one. Before issue #788 a client had no authoritative way to tell the two apart: the only
available signal was `inventoryValue`, which the product responses **withhold** from a caller without
`Dashboard.ViewFinancials` (issue #698), so reading it would have reported every product's cost as
unknown to an Operator.

`InventoryValuationPolicy.DisplayUnitCost(inventoryValue, averageUnitCost)` is that answer, and it is
deliberately the one-row form of the rule the tile above already applies rather than a new AVCO
calculation: a `null` inventory value means no rebuild has run, so the display cost is `null`;
otherwise it is the **persisted** `AverageUnitCost` exactly as the rebuild left it, **including a
genuine zero**. The Dashboard's `ProductsWithUnknownCost` count is the same evidence counted, so a
product cannot be counted as unknown there and shown a cost here.

Issue #861 deliberately does not reach this rule. A product that has never held inventory is excluded
from the catalogue total and is not counted as missing cost data there, and its displayed unit cost is
still `null` here. Those are two different questions - what the business owns, and what one unit costs -
and answering `0` here would invent a cost rather than report an absence, exactly what this rule exists
to prevent.

On the wire it is `ProductResponse.averageUnitCostForDisplay`, and these properties are the contract:

- **Additive and non-breaking.** It is appended after issue #736's `providerManagedFields` and issue
  #737's `canDelete`/`deletionRefusal`, so every key a client already read keeps its name, type, value
  and position (`ProductJsonContractTests`). The legacy `averageUnitCost` and every persisted costing
  value — `AverageUnitCost`, `CostingQuantity`, `InventoryValue` — are unchanged, and there is no
  migration and no historical recalculation: this is a projection of what is already stored.
- **Absent, never `0`, when the cost is unknown.** It is omitted from the JSON rather than sent as
  `null`, so in TypeScript it is `averageUnitCostForDisplay?: number | null` and a client renders an
  absent value as unknown (`—`). A rebuilt cost of `0` is present as `0`, which is a measured answer
  and must render as `$0.00`.
- **Available to exactly the roles that already read `averageUnitCost`** — every role that may
  operate inventory. It is decided from the product record's own inventory value, not from the
  withheld response field, which is why an Operator gets a real answer. It carries no revenue, profit,
  margin or valuation figure, so it is outside the restricted vocabulary
  `OperatorReadableFinancialFigureTests` guards, and it exposes **none** of the gated last/cheapest
  supplier facts: those stay on `GET api/products/purchase-cost-summary` behind
  `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` (see
  [Supplier product price history and comparison](#supplier-product-price-history-and-comparison-issue-63)).
- **Published only by the `/api/products` reads.** It is deliberately absent from the product snapshot
  nested in a purchase line or a supplier-order line and from a machine slot's product: those are
  pinned contracts of their own and are not surfaces a product's cost is presented from, so they keep
  every key they had and say nothing rather than answering a question their reader cannot act on — the
  same treatment issues #736 and #737 gave their keys there. `PurchaseResponseJsonContractTests`,
  `SupplierOrderJsonContractTests`, `MachineJsonContractTests` and `ProductJsonContractTests` each pin
  the absence. An absent key on one of those payloads says nothing about the cost, exactly as an
  absent `canDelete` is not permission.

#### Home Dashboard summary API (issue #459)

`GET /api/dashboard/summary` (`InventoryApi.Controllers.DashboardController`, thin: it binds no
input and only invokes the use case) is the authoritative contract behind the home Dashboard's
sales, refill, ordering and inventory cards. It is **additive and read-only**: no existing endpoint,
response or figure changed with it, and it creates no inventory movement, refill or persisted state.
It carries no business, machine or site identifier - the business is resolved from the authenticated
actor's membership, and every read it makes is scoped by the central `AppDbContext` query filters.
Issue #460 renders it; before it existed, `DashboardComponent` aggregated machine rows and totalled
product quantities in TypeScript, which is exactly the duplication this endpoint removes.

The contract described below is the one a caller whose role grants `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` - a
Manager or an Owner - receives, and it is unchanged. Since issue #527 a caller without that
capability is answered the same response **without** the `salesThisWeek` object and without
`inventory.inventoryValueAtCost`, and those figures are not calculated for them at all; both
properties are absent from the JSON rather than `null` or `0`. See
[Dashboard financial redaction](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527) for the exact two shapes
and why absence is the chosen representation.

Since issue #552 there is a third shape, for a request inside a platform administrator's support
session: the same contract with `needsRefill` and `needsOrdering` replaced by
`{ "available": false, "reason": "SupportView" }`, because a support session resolves no Nayax
credentials and those two cards are the only part of this summary the live fleet feeds. The fleet
read is not attempted at all in that state, and every other section is the real local figure. See
[Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551).

**The machine restock-sync reminder is deliberately not part of this contract** (issue #891). The
Dashboard's reminder banner reads `GET /api/machine-restock-sync/reminder`, its own endpoint with
its own capability, because it answers a different question from a different source: it is a purely
local aggregate over the business's machines and their imported restock events, it needs
`Inventory.Operate` rather than `Dashboard.View`, and its failure must leave every card below it
usable. Adding it to this summary would have coupled a local read to the live fleet read, and
widened who sees restock work to every role that may open the Dashboard. See
[Dashboard reminder for overdue machine restock sync](#dashboard-reminder-for-overdue-machine-restock-sync-issue-891).

Since issue #726, `needsRefill` is additionally withheld - and `needsOrdering` is counted over
storage alone and says so - for a business whose Nayax connection is unusable or whose Nayax account
has not granted the fleet reads. The summary is answered rather than refused in that state. See
[Provider-optional reorder and dashboard summary](#provider-optional-reorder-and-dashboard-summary-issue-726)
below, and [Provider-optional dashboard and Needs Ordering screens](#provider-optional-dashboard-and-needs-ordering-screens-issue-727)
for the screens that present it, which is also where the page reads that state from.

`Inventory.Application.Dashboard.GetDashboardSummary` is the use case. It owns no formula of its
own: every figure comes from an authority that already existed.

- **Sales this week.** Week-to-date gross vending revenue - the sum of `SettlementValue` over
  approved (status `12`) sales, the same definition the bookkeeping, daily and reporting-dashboard
  reports use - over the current business's business week (`Australia/Sydney` for the existing business). The period boundaries are
  `MachineDashboardWindow.CurrentWeek`/`PreviousComparableWeek`, the very same window the Sites and
  Machines dashboards resolve (see [Time](#time)), so the week starts at business-day midnight rather than
  UTC midnight and the comparison is the **same elapsed trading time into the previous business
  week**, never the whole of it. Across a daylight-saving transition the two weeks start 167 or 169
  hours apart, and each period is measured from its own week's business-day Monday midnight; the
  comparable period is held at the previous week's own end so it can never reach into the current
  week and count one sale on both sides. `IDashboardSummarySalesFactsProvider` is the narrow port
  and `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfDashboardSummarySalesFactsProvider` its EF adapter,
  which totals both periods in one grouped read filtered by
  `EfNayaxSalesQueries.CompletedSalePredicate`.
- **The comparison's availability and its zero-prior rule** belong to
  `Inventory.Domain.Reporting.Dashboard.PeriodRevenueComparisonPolicy`. The percentage is
  `(current − prior) / prior × 100`, and it is `null` when the prior period's revenue is zero: there
  is no honest percentage change from nothing, and an infinite or 100% rise would misstate a
  financial figure. The comparison is available only when the business's earliest recorded completed
  sale is at or before the comparable period's start; a prior period the recorded data never reached
  back to returns `isComparisonAvailable: false` with every comparison field `null`, because its
  zero or part-week total would read as a collapse in trade rather than as missing data. Each case
  carries the note the UI shows instead.
- **Needs refill** counts the **distinct machines** with at least one low or empty selection, using
  `Inventory.Domain.Machines.MachineRefillAlertPolicy`. Its per-selection
  `Classify(quantity, vendOutAlertThreshold)` - empty at or below zero, otherwise low up to and
  including the threshold - is now the one authoritative low/empty test, and
  `Inventory.Domain.Sites.SiteStockPolicy.CalculateAlertCounts` calls it too, so the site rows and
  this card cannot come to mean different things. The quantity is `PAR − MissingStockByMDB`, the
  arithmetic the Pick List and the machine product list already use, summed first across however
  many MDB slots carry one product on one machine. **Overlap semantics:** the low and empty
  *selection* counts are disjoint; the low and empty *machine* counts overlap (a machine with both
  appears in both); and `machinesNeedingRefill` is the distinct union, never the sum. Aggregating
  the site counts instead would double count, because one product low on two machines at a site is
  one site alert and two machine alerts. `machinesEvaluated`/`selectionsEvaluated` are what make a
  zero honest: zero of zero is "nothing to look at", zero of many is "everything is stocked".
- **Needs ordering** counts the distinct products the authoritative reorder policy says must be
  purchased - exactly the set `GET /api/products/alerts/low-stock` lists for the unnarrowed
  catalogue, including its treatment of outstanding supplier-order quantity. Both come from
  `ListLowStockProducts.SelectReorderAlerts`, which issue #459 extracted from that use case's
  `Handle` so the count and the list are one implementation; `ProductReorderPolicy` still owns the
  formulas and no threshold changed.
- **Inventory** reports three figures with deliberately different scopes, and they are not
  interchangeable. `inventoryValueAtCost` is the business-owned perpetual AVCO valuation from
  `InventoryValuationPolicy` over the same catalogue snapshot - never a selling-price valuation -
  and is `null` with `isInventoryValueComplete: false` and an unknown-cost count whenever any
  product **that holds inventory** has an unknown cost, the same rule as the
  [Inventory Value tile](#dashboard-inventory-value-tile-issue-42) above, including its
  [never-held-inventory evidence](#a-product-that-has-never-held-inventory-issue-861). `unitsInStorage`
  is the sum of `Product.QuantityInStock`: physical storage/home stock, which **excludes** units
  already loaded into a machine, and is never a valuation input. `productCount` is every product in the
  caller's catalogue, active and inactive, including the never-stocked ones that block nothing - which
  is why the count a card shows and `productsWithUnknownCost` are separate figures and must stay so.

**Aggregation strategy.** The summary makes exactly three reads: one grouped sales read, one
unnarrowed `IProductCatalogStore.ListUnorderedAsync` catalogue read, and one
`CalculateReorderNeeds` fleet read. The two persistence reads are awaited one at a time, because the
scoped EF adapters share a single `AppDbContext`, which supports one operation at a time - the same
constraint `GetSiteSummaries` documents. The ordering count, product count, storage units and
valuation all come from that one catalogue snapshot, so they cannot disagree with one another.
Since issue #861 the catalogue read resolves one more thing for the valuation - whether each product
has any recorded inventory history - and it does so **inside** that one read rather than as a second
read the cards could disagree across; it asks nothing at all unless some product's stored columns
leave open that it has never held inventory (see
[A product that has never held inventory](#a-product-that-has-never-held-inventory-issue-861)), which
for a stocked catalogue is never.

**No new Nayax fan-out.** The refill and ordering cards are both answered from one
`CalculateReorderNeeds` call: one `GetMachinesAsync` plus one `GetMachineProductsAsync` per machine,
bounded by the existing `CalculateReorderNeeds.MaxConcurrentMachineRequests`. Issue #459 made that
use case additionally keep the individual selections it already read
(`ReorderNeedsResult.MachineSelections`) and the machines it covered (`MachineIds`), rather than
adding a second fan-out for the cards; its reorder aggregation is unchanged, and existing callers
ignore the new members. A failing machine request or a cancelled request propagates out unchanged,
surfacing as the usual `502` from `NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandler`, so a partial aggregate is never
presented as a complete summary - the behaviour the reorder-alert list and the Pick List already
have. The `PAR`, `MissingStockByMDB` and `VendOutAlertThreshold` fields the refill rules read are
confirmed against the published Nayax `GET /machines/{id}/machineProducts` contract; a selection is
attributed to the machine the request was made for, not to the payload's own nullable `MachineID`.

**Placement.** The slice is `Inventory.Application.Dashboard`, not
`Inventory.Application.Reporting.Dashboard`: it is the home Dashboard's own summary across
reporting, stock and ordering, not a report with a date filter and an export, and the reporting
namespace is reserved for the `/reports/*` slices (`GetDashboardReport` is the reporting dashboard at
`/reports/dashboard`, a different feature). `GetInventoryValuationSummary` stays where it is; this
use case reuses the Domain `InventoryValuationPolicy` it is built on rather than calling it, so the
valuation and the product count describe one catalogue read instead of two.

#### Provider-optional reorder and dashboard summary (issue #726)

Nayax is an optional add-on; stock-storage management is what the application is for. Issue #726 is
the backend half of that for reorder and the home Dashboard (the #328 release gate, child D1 of
issue #329), and the frontend half is #727, below. Before it, `GET /api/dashboard/summary`,
`GET /api/products/alerts/low-stock` and the Needs Ordering page all answered `409
nayax_not_connected` for a business with no usable connection, because `CalculateReorderNeeds`
starts with a live `GetMachinesAsync` and every caller of it propagated that refusal - so three
screens made of local stock data went down with the fleet read.

**Reorder has two explicit modes, and every result carries the one it was produced in.**
`Inventory.Application.Reorder.ReorderMode` is the vocabulary and `ReorderNeedsResult.Mode` is
`required`, so a result without a stated mode cannot exist:

| Mode | What it accounted for | How it is reached |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MachineAware` | Storage stock, low-stock threshold, restock target, outstanding supplier orders **and** the machines' current replenishment need | The fleet read and every machine-products read succeeded |
| `StorageOnly` | The same local facts, with the machines' replenishment need taken as **0** | The business has no usable connection, or Nayax has not granted one of the two fleet reads |

`StorageOnly` is the enum's default value deliberately: a result nobody labelled claims less rather
than claiming the machines were read. A storage-only result is built only through
`ReorderNeedsResult.StorageOnly(onOrderQuantities, reason)`, which is why it can never carry a
machine need, a machine id or a machine selection, and never carries no reason. Nothing about the
formulas changed - `ProductReorderPolicy.NeedToOrder` is still the one authoritative calculation,
and storage-only is simply that formula with a machine need of zero, not a second formula.

**Availability is per feature, and exactly two answers are availability answers** (decision P9 of
issue #329). `CalculateReorderNeeds` degrades on `NayaxNotConnectedException` (nothing stored,
`NotConfigured`, or the `NeedsAttention` the `NayaxConnectionStatusGate` refuses → reason
`NayaxNotConnected`) and on `NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException` (the credentials are usable and
Nayax answered a fleet read with `403` while the connection is `PendingPermissions` → reason
`PermissionNotGranted`). That is the same line `GetMachineStockReconciliation` already draws, and the
403 case stays a per-feature answer that writes no connection status: the Nayax contract documents
403 as the token's scopes not covering the requested resource or action, and each Lynx endpoint
carries its own permission, so the fleet reads being refused says nothing about the rest of the
integration.

**Everything else is still an error, including mid-fleet.** A transport failure (`502` through
`NayaxUpstreamExceptionHandler`), a cancellation, a `401` that closes the status gate part-way
through the fan-out, and the support-session refusal all propagate unchanged. A fleet that was half
read is an outage, not a smaller fleet, and must never be published as a business whose machines
need nothing - the storage-only mode is not a place to absorb failures into. A permission refusal
inside the fan-out is recorded rather than thrown (so the availability answer does not arrive
wrapped beside the sibling cancellations a faulted parallel loop raises), the remaining machines are
skipped, and everything already read is **discarded**: a fleet this business may not read produces a
storage-only answer, never a partial one.

**In the mixed case the failure wins, not the availability answer.** If one machine request is
refused for lack of permission while a sibling request that is already in flight fails upstream, the
upstream failure propagates out of the fan-out and the caller gets the error - a fleet that was half
read is an outage whatever else the fleet answered, and a `403` somewhere in it is no reason to
publish a business as needing nothing. The permission refusal only decides the answer when it is
recorded before a sibling request starts, in which case the remaining machines are skipped and no
other request is made at all. `CalculateReorderNeedsTests`'s
`Handle_PropagatesAnUpstreamFailure_EvenWhenASiblingReportsPermissionNotGranted` pins that
precedence deterministically, with both requests genuinely in flight together.

**What each consumer publishes.**

- `GET /api/dashboard/summary` keeps its three role/session shapes. In storage-only mode
  `needsRefill` is `UnavailableDashboardSectionDto` - `{ "available": false, "reason":
  "NayaxNotConnected" | "PermissionNotGranted" }` - because every figure on that card is a figure
  about machines and `0 of 0 machines` would read as a fact about the fleet. `needsOrdering` is a
  real count and carries `mode`, the published code of `ReorderMode`. `salesThisWeek` and
  `inventory` are untouched. The refill section is therefore a union
  (`IDashboardRefillSectionDto`, two `[JsonDerivedType]` declarations with no type discriminator, so
  the JSON is the member's own object), which is the shape `models.ts` already declares for the
  frontend and which `isDashboardSectionUnavailable` already branches on.
- A **support session** is unchanged (#512/#552): both sections are
  `{ "available": false, "reason": "SupportView" }` and no fleet read starts, because that branch is
  taken from `IBusinessScope.State` before `CalculateReorderNeeds` is called at all.
- `GET /api/products/alerts/low-stock` (and `GET /api/products?lowStockOnly=true`, the same use
  case) returns the storage-only alerts instead of `409`. The product rows are unchanged, with
  `machineReplenishmentNeed: 0` - which is exactly why the listing publishes its mode as well: that
  `0` means "the machines need nothing" in machine-aware mode and "the machines were never read" in
  storage-only mode, and a caller must not have to fetch the dashboard summary to tell the two apart.
  The body stays the JSON **array** it has always been, and the mode is additive response metadata
  beside it:

  | Header | Value |
  | --- | --- |
  | `X-Reorder-Mode` | `MachineAware` or `StorageOnly`, the published `ReorderMode` code |
  | `X-Reorder-Machine-Need-Unavailable-Reason` | `NayaxNotConnected` or `PermissionNotGranted`, in storage-only mode only |

  Headers rather than an envelope or a per-row field, because the array contract is established and
  the mode belongs to the whole answer: an **empty** list still has one, and that is the case a
  per-row field could not express at all. An existing caller ignores both headers and reads the same
  body it read before. The plain catalogue listing (`GET /api/products` without `lowStockOnly=true`)
  calculates no reorder needs and so publishes neither header - an absent mode means "no reorder facts
  were involved", never a guess at which mode would have applied. The two header names live in
  `InventoryApi.Adapters.Mapping.ReorderListingMetadataHeaders`, and that one list is what the CORS
  policy exposes (`WithExposedHeaders`): a browser client cannot read a response header a policy does
  not expose, and no origin, method or request header was widened to add them. A reverse proxy or
  gateway in front of the API that enumerates the response headers it forwards must forward these two,
  which is deployed configuration outside this repository; a caller that never sees them reads the
  same array it read before. `ListLowStockProducts`
  and `ListProducts` answer `ProductListing` (the products plus the mode and reason) rather than a
  bare list, which is what carries the two out of the use case; the selection, the ranking and every
  figure on a row are unchanged.

**No deployment or schema change, and no behaviour change for a connected business.** There is no
migration, no new configuration and no new port. A business whose status is `Ready` or
`PendingPermissions` with the fleet reads granted gets exactly what it got before, which
`DashboardControllerTests`, `DashboardSummaryRedactionApiTests` and
`GetDashboardSummaryTenancyTests` pin. `NayaxConfigurationFreeStartupTests` proves the API starts
and serves requests with no `NayaxLynx` section at all (the base URL then comes from
`NayaxLynxOptions`' own default), and `ProviderOptionalReorderApiTests` exercises both endpoints
through the real pipeline against a business with no `BusinessNayaxConnection` row and the real
`NayaxLynxClient` registered. `LowStockReorderMetadataApiTests` covers the listing's response
metadata through the same pipeline for both low-stock endpoints, in all three modes/reasons and for an
empty result.

#### Provider-optional dashboard and Needs Ordering screens (issue #727)

The frontend half of the above (child D2 of issue #329, decisions P9 and P10). Without a usable
provider the home Dashboard is a storage-management dashboard: it states what the business has
rather than what it is missing, and it asks for nothing it cannot be given.

**The page reads the provider's availability out of its own summary, and there is no second probe.**
`GET /api/dashboard/summary` already answers the question - the refill card is the one section of
that response whose every figure comes from the live fleet, so a real card means the fleet was read
and a withheld one carries the reason it was not. `DashboardComponent.providerAvailability`
(`DashboardProviderAvailability`) is that answer: `usable`, `notConnected`, `permissionNotGranted`,
`supportView`, or `unknown` before the summary has been read and after one that failed. The
business's Nayax **connection status** is deliberately not consulted: a second probe would be a
second answer that could disagree with the cards beside it, and the summary is what those cards are
actually built from. Issue #728 added the application-wide signal every **other** screen shares
([Shared provider availability and error-versus-empty
states](#shared-provider-availability-and-error-versus-empty-states-issue-728)); this page and Needs
Ordering keep their own for that reason, and did not change.

**Only `notConnected` hides anything**, and what it hides is everything on the page whose every
figure is about machines: the "Sales this week" and "Needs refill" cards and the Site and machine
performance card (`isLiveFleetShown`; two separate sections until issue #987 combined them). They
are hidden rather than rendered empty or "Unavailable" - "No
sites available yet" is a claim about the business, not about Nayax. "Needs ordering" and
"Inventory" are shown as usual, so the reorder alerts become the page's main section without the
page having to reorder anything. `PendingPermissions` with a read ungranted is **not** this state:
the connection is usable, every card and section stays, and only the affected one says so.

**The summary is what starts the live-fleet half of the page**, which is the one load-order change
this issue makes. `ngOnInit` runs the reorder-alert load and the summary; the summary's handler -
success or failure - then calls `refreshSalesDashboard`, which is where `POST /api/nayax-sales-sync`
and the Sites and Machines loads live. Without that order the synchronization would already have
been sent by the time the answer arrived, and "sales sync is not called when the provider is not
usable" cannot be satisfied after the fact. A business with a usable provider gets the same three
calls in the same order as before, one summary later; both reads start in their loading state
so a pending decision is never rendered as an empty one. A **failed** summary says nothing about the
provider, so it leaves `unknown` and keeps the connected behaviour - a transient failure must not
hide a connected business's live sections.

**A storage-only figure is labelled, and the machine column goes with it.** The "Needs ordering"
card's label comes from `needsOrdering.mode` with the reason from the same response's refill
section; the Reorder Alerts list's comes from its own response headers, so the table and its label
always describe one read. In storage-only mode the list drops the "Machine need" column, because
`machineReplenishmentNeed` is `0` there for the one reason that is not "the machines need nothing",
and a column of zeroes would assert the opposite. The label is rendered for an **empty** list too.

**The Reorder Alerts columns, and what the row now reports (issues #787, #792 and #789).** The table
is Product, Stock, Low Stock Threshold, Machine need (machine-aware mode only), Restock To, On order,
Need to Order, and then "Last purchase" and "Cheapest purchase". Three columns left it: Supplier
(issue #787 — a product carries no supplier), Unit Price (issue #792 — a product carries no selling
price), and "Stock after machine need" (issue #789), which was a frontend subtraction of two figures
already on the row and is replaced by what the business actually paid. So the row answers "how much
do I have, how much do I need, and what does it cost me to buy" without a selling price anywhere
near it.

**The two cost columns are one read, gated on the capability behind them.** `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`
decides it, through `AccessService` as everywhere else on this page: without it neither column is
rendered **and no request is sent** — these are supplier purchasing figures, and a role that may not
see them must not cause them to be fetched. The capability is read asynchronously, so the request
waits for the answer: `canViewFinancials` still starts `true` (hiding a figure from the role it
belongs to over an unread capability is the wrong default), but `DashboardComponent` only *asks*
once the answer has arrived and granted it, and asks then if the alert list was already read.
`ProductPurchaseCostService.getSummaries` is called **once** with the alert products' ids, never once
per row; an **empty** alert list is asked nothing at all, because no ids deliberately means "every
product of the business" (issue #788) and this table is about the products in front of the reader.
Each cell is `supplier · cost` (`Acme · $1.25`), with `None` for a purchase that recorded no supplier
— a fact about that purchase, never another purchase's supplier, and independent of the cost beside
it — and the cost formatted by the shared `money`. Angular computes no last or cheapest cost, no tie
break and no saving: `SupplierPriceComparisonPolicy` decides all of them on the server.

**Loading, no purchase history and unavailable are three different answers.**
`DashboardComponent.purchaseCostState` (`PurchaseCostLoadState`) is `idle`/`loading`/`loaded`/
`failed`, and only `loaded` may say `—`: "this product has never been bought" is a fact about the
purchase history, which a pending or failed request is not evidence of. A pending or not-yet-issued
read therefore shows `Loading`, a failed one shows `Unavailable` in both columns with an actionable
**Retry** beside the table — and the rest of the page, whose figures are local data that was never
part of that request, renders exactly as it would have. A recorded `$0.00` is a **real cost** (a free
sample, a replacement delivery) and is shown as `$0.00` with its supplier, never as `—`: the response
carries no entry at all for a product with no history, which is the only thing `—` means. The
Reorder Alerts table is not sortable, so there is no missing-cost sort order to define here; #790 and
#791 are the sortable screens.

**One request's answer belongs to one product set.** Every read supersedes the previous one and
clears what it had already read, so a changed alert list never renders the previous list's costs
while the new ones are outstanding, and a response for a superseded request — a slower first read, or
the failure a Retry has already replaced — is discarded instead of published over the current answer
(`purchaseCostRequest` is the generation it is checked against). Retry re-issues the same read for
the product set currently displayed.

**One vocabulary, one sentence each.** `provider/nayax-availability.ts` is the frontend's copy of
the published availability vocabulary and the only place it is worded:
`nayaxUnavailabilityOfReason` for a withheld summary section or an `X-Reorder-*` header,
`nayaxUnavailabilityOfError` for the two stable `409` codes
(`nayax_not_connected`/`nayax_permission_not_granted`), and `nayaxUnavailableMessage`/
`storageOnlyReorderLabel` for the wording. It mirrors
`support-session/support-session-messages.ts`, which does the same for a session's two refusals, and
the support-view sentence stays there - a session says nothing about the business's connection.
Every message **names its feature**, because availability is per feature: one page can carry a
permission message for one card and real figures beside it. A reason or code this build does not
recognise is never guessed into one of the two: the feature is reported as unavailable with no cause
claimed, and an unrecognised summary reason leaves the page's behaviour unchanged.

**A failed request is an error, not an empty result.** `sitesError`, `machinesError` and
`reorderAlertsError` are rendered in place of the list, so a request nobody answered is never shown
as "No sites available yet", "No machines available yet" or "No reorder alerts. Everything looks
good! ✅". A `409` carrying one of the two availability codes gets that feature's own message; every
other failure - a transport failure, a `502` from a real Nayax outage, a `403` about the caller's own
access - is reported as an error, because presenting one of those as "Nayax is not connected" would
describe a connection nobody tested. Each loader also settles its own loading flag in both its
`next` and its `error` handler rather than in `complete`, which RxJS does not call after an error and
which used to leave a failed section loading forever.

**Products → Needs Ordering** is the same change in one page: it reads the mode from the listing it
already fetches, labels a storage-only list, and hides the "Machine need" column there. Its
filters, sorting and "Mark as ordered" are untouched and work without a provider - the supplier
order it creates is local data. Its error-versus-empty distinction already existed (`ListLoadState`)
and is unchanged.

**What that page shows now (issue #790, D of #786).** Its columns are the checkbox, Name, Category,
Stock, "Machine need" (in machine-aware mode only), the thresholds, "On order", "Need to order",
"Last purchase", "Cheapest purchase" and the Stock link - and nothing else:

- **The name looks the product up on Google**, as `https://www.google.com/search?q=<URL-encoded
  name>` in a new tab (`target="_blank"`, `rel="noopener noreferrer"`), labelled "Search Google for
  &lt;name&gt;". Clicking it does nothing else in the app; the checkbox and the Stock button are
  unchanged.
- **No route to the product editor.** #790 had restored an `Edit` link beside Stock, because the
  Name anchor stopped being the editor's link and a row click is not a keyboard action. The owner
  later removed both the row click and that Edit link (see [Needs Ordering: row navigation, sortable
  columns, and Delete removal](#needs-ordering-row-navigation-sortable-columns-and-delete-removal-issue-498)),
  so the page deliberately offers no way into the editor, by pointer or keyboard; products are
  edited from All products.
- **No Price and no Status column.** The price left with issue #792 (a product carries no selling
  price); the Status column, its sort and this page's product-status write left with #790, because
  the list holds **only active products**. `GET /api/products/alerts/low-stock` already excludes
  retired products, and the component drops any product with `isActive === false` as well - the same
  defence the dashboard's reorder-alert card applies. Product activation stays on
  Products → All Products, which is the page that lists both states.
- **"Last purchase" and "Cheapest purchase"** come from issue #788's bulk
  `GET /api/products/purchase-cost-summary`, requested **once** for the ids the page actually lists
  and never recomputed here: what was last paid and what was cheapest, with the supplier each was
  paid to, are decided by `SupplierPriceComparisonPolicy` on the server. Both columns sort by cost,
  and a row with no cost - still loading, unavailable, or never bought - sorts last in **both**
  directions rather than as a zero.

**Those two columns keep four answers apart**, for the same reason the availability model exists: a
figure nobody established must never be rendered as a measured one.

- Both columns and the request appear **only** with `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`. Without it there are
  no columns and no request at all - the endpoint answers `403`, so asking before the capability is
  known would be asking for a refusal, which is why this gate starts closed rather than at the
  fail-open `true` other hidden figures use. `AccessService` still fails open where it matters: a
  capability set that could not be read answers `true`.
- While the request is outstanding both columns say **"Loading…"**. A **`—`** is published only once
  a successful response establishes that the product has no recorded purchase history (a product
  with none is absent from the response). A **genuinely recorded `$0.00`** - a free sample, a
  replacement delivery - is a measured cost and is shown as `$0.00` with its supplier, never as
  `—`. An unknown supplier is **"None"** independently of the cost beside it.
- A **failed** request shows **"Unavailable"** in both columns with one actionable **Retry** above
  the table, and the rest of the page keeps working: the reorder figures and "Mark as ordered" are
  the business's own data and are unaffected. Retry re-asks for the same listed ids.
- **A stale answer cannot land on a newer list.** The previous list's costs are dropped
  synchronously with the product set they belonged to, and the cost request runs under a `switchMap`
  on the product ids, so a superseded response - or a superseded failure - is unsubscribed, its HTTP
  request cancelled, and neither its rows nor its "Unavailable" can appear under the products that
  replaced it. An empty list makes no request, because the endpoint reads "no ids" as "every product
  of the business".

**What proves it.** `dashboard.component.provider-optional.spec.ts` covers the five states the issue
names - not usable, permission not granted, support session, usable, and a failed request - over the
rendered page: the hidden cards and sections, the sync that is not called and the warning that is
not shown, the sites and machines that are not even asked for, the storage-only label, the dropped
machine-need column, the per-feature permission message (both from the summary and from a refused
section request), the three error states and the empty states they must not be confused with, and
the unchanged connected and support-session pages including the `sync → machines → sites` order.
`product-needs-ordering.component.provider-optional.spec.ts` covers that page in both modes, and
that its purchase-cost columns are present and filled without a provider.
`dashboard.component.purchase-costs.spec.ts` covers the two cost columns over the rendered page: the
column list with "Stock after machine need" gone, the supplier/cost cells, `None`, a genuine `$0.00`,
`—` only after a successful answer, the single request for the alert ids only and the empty list that
asks nothing, the hidden columns and absent request without the capability and the request that
follows a later capability answer, `Unavailable` with a working Retry while the rest of the dashboard
renders, and the cleared and discarded answers when the displayed product set changes.
`product.service.spec.ts` covers the response-header contract, including an empty listing, an
unrecognised code and a reason published beside a machine-aware mode, and
`provider/nayax-availability.spec.ts` covers what is **not** an availability answer.
`product-needs-ordering.component.purchase-costs.spec.ts` covers issue #790: the Google URL and its
encoding (`&`, spaces, accents, `+`, `?`), the name click and the row click that do not open the
editor, the absent Edit link, the Name link that only searches Google, the absent Price
and Status columns, the retired product the page refuses to list, the one request for the listed
ids, loading versus `—` versus "Unavailable", a recorded `$0.00`, an unknown supplier, Retry, the
superseded response and the superseded failure, the cost sorting in both directions with no-history
last, and the capability gate that renders no column and sends no request.

#### Home dashboard: four headline cards (issue #460)

`DashboardComponent` renders the [Home Dashboard summary API](#home-dashboard-summary-api-issue-459)
contract as four headline stat cards, in this order, replacing the former separate Total
Products/Units In Stock/Inventory Value tiles and the permanent Admin tools banner (Admin remains
reachable from the existing sidebar `Admin` group; issue #460 added no replacement alert system).
`DashboardService.getSummary()` is the one HTTP call behind all four; a request failure clears the
summary, so every card shows "Unavailable" rather than a fabricated zero, and the page shows a
warning banner alongside the existing sales-sync-failure one. These four cards still assume the full
API contract: a caller without `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` is no longer sent the sales figures or the
valuation (issue #527, [Dashboard financial redaction](#dashboard-financial-redaction-issue-527)),
and teaching the page not to ask for or render them is issue #503. Angular performs no revenue,
percentage, refill, reorder or valuation calculation anywhere in this card section - every value
and completeness flag is the backend's, read and displayed as returned (`DashboardComponent.money`
is the one exception, formatting an already-known amount via `components/reports/report-formatting`'s
shared `money`).

1. **Sales this week** (`summary.salesThisWeek`) shows the week-to-date gross revenue and, in the
   card footer, the week-on-week comparison exactly as the backend decided: the arrow/percentage
   when `changePercent` is not `null`, and `comparisonNote` verbatim - never a frontend-computed
   percentage - when `isComparisonAvailable` is `false` or the prior period's revenue was zero, so a
   missing-data or zero-baseline period is never misread as a collapse or a 100% rise. Links to
   `/reports/bookkeeping` (`BookkeepingReportComponent`), the financial summary report - issue #806
   retired the separate Reporting Dashboard page (`DashboardReportComponent`, the former "Dashboard"
   entry under the Reports navigation group) once Bookkeeping covered its distinct figures (issues
   #804 and #805), and repointed this card and the old `/reports` address, now a compatibility
   redirect to `/reports/bookkeeping` with its query string intact (see
   [Retired Reporting Dashboard redirect](#retired-reporting-dashboard-redirect-issue-806) below), at
   it instead; no query parameter is added because that report has no week-to-date filter to target,
   and inventing one would duplicate a filter the page does not have.
2. **Needs refill** (`summary.needsRefill`) shows the distinct machine count
   (`machinesNeedingRefill`) as the primary value, with the low/empty selection counts and
   `machinesEvaluated` as supporting footer detail - distinguishing "no machines to evaluate yet"
   (`machinesEvaluated === 0`) from "every evaluated machine is adequately stocked"
   (`machinesNeedingRefill === 0` with machines evaluated). Links to `/pick-list`
   (`PickListComponent`), the existing Pick List workflow.
3. **Needs ordering** (`summary.needsOrdering`) shows `productsNeedingOrdering` as the primary
   value, with `productsEvaluated` (the whole catalogue) as supporting footer detail, distinguishing
   an empty catalogue from every product being adequately stocked. Links to
   `/products/needs-ordering` (`ProductNeedsOrderingComponent`), the existing Needs ordering
   workflow.
4. **Inventory** (`summary.inventory`) shows `inventoryValueAtCost` as the primary value -
   "Unavailable", never a real `$0.00`, whenever `isInventoryValueComplete` is `false` - with
   `productCount` and `unitsInStorage` as explicitly scoped footer detail ("excludes machines"; since
   issue #972 a separate note, "Storage units exclude stock in machines."), so
   storage/home stock is never read as a whole-business count. This card replaces the former
   dedicated "Inventory Value" tile described above. Links to `/products`
   (`ProductListComponent`), the existing Products/inventory list.

Every card is a single `<a class="stat-card">` using the existing #453 icon-top-right stat-card
layout and an explicit `aria-label` naming the card and its destination (e.g. "Sales this week. View
Bookkeeping."), so its accessible name stays stable and descriptive regardless of the
currently displayed figures; the icon inside is decorative (`app-icon` without a `label`, so it
renders `aria-hidden`) because the label text already carries the meaning. The cards lay out
`sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4` - four columns where width permits, stacking without horizontal
scroll below that - and rely on the existing global `a:focus-visible` outline for keyboard focus;
no new interaction styling was added.

The existing Sites/Machines detail sections, their report meanings, the Reorder Alerts product
table and the available profit detail are unchanged by this issue; no profit headline was added, and
no unknown profit/cost figure was turned into a zero.

#### Restockroo dashboard and authenticated navigation (issue #972)

Issue #972 restyles the home Dashboard and the authenticated shell in the approved Restockroo
design. It is a presentation change: no endpoint, DTO, calculation, capability, guard, route or
provider lock was added or changed, and the page still never turns `null` into `0`.

**Dashboard composition.** `DashboardComponent` keeps one data flow — the summary, the coordinated
sales sync (#187), the Sites, Machines and reorder-alert reads, and the purchase-cost read — and
renders it as five parts:

1. **Four summary cards**, the #460 cards relabelled (Sales this week, Machines needing refill,
   Products needing ordering, Business-owned inventory at cost) with the same `stat-card` hooks,
   links and `aria-label`s. The inventory card's storage-unit scope is the separate
   `storageUnitsNote`.
2. **Needs attention**, `attentionAlerts`: empty selections and machines needing refill (only while
   the live fleet is shown, #727), products needing ordering, and the existing
   `MachineRestockSyncReminderComponent` (#891), rendered inside the same grid (`host` class
   `contents`). `attentionCount` counts the alerts actually rendered plus the reminder when it shows
   pending work or a failed read, so the badge can never disagree with the tiles. The reminder's
   14-day window and its `restockFrom` link to the oldest pending date (#948/#949) are unchanged;
   since #1011 that link also carries `syncRestock=open`, so it lands on the machine with its Sync
   Restock dialog already open. The only actions are the existing Pick List and Needs Ordering
   routes.
3. **Site and machine performance**, one card composed from `SiteMachinePerformanceComponent` and
   described in [its own section](#site-and-machine-performance-issue-987) below. It replaced the
   separate **Site performance** and **Machine performance** cards this issue shipped, and the
   machines-under-their-sites grouping of issue #980 that followed them, on the owner's decision of
   29 October 2026. Its data is the two existing reads: `GET api/sites` for the site rows, which
   since issue #1012 publishes all four sales periods and since issue #1013 also publishes each site
   machine's own stock percentage (see
   [Per-machine stock levels on the site read](#per-machine-stock-levels-on-the-site-read-issue-1013)),
   and `GET api/machines` for the machine rows and the fleet totals.
4. **Reorder priorities**: `reorderPriorities` is the first `REORDER_PRIORITY_LIMIT` (5) rows of the
   authoritative low-stock list in its own order, and `reorderViewAllLabel` names the list's real
   length. The purchase-cost read (#788/#789) is requested only for those rows and still only with
   `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`. Last and Cheapest purchase remain labelled as historical costs from
   this business's own purchases. The **Cheapest supplier** column (issue #981, the same column #939
   asks for) reuses #930's `CheapestSuppliersComponent` and `CheapestSupplierCellComponent`
   unchanged, beside - never in place of - the historical columns: `reorderPriorityIds` is set once
   per reorder read, so the component makes one summary request for the five ids and re-reads only
   when the list changes. It follows the endpoint's `Dashboard.View`, so it shows without
   `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`; its failure (with Retry) and support-session "unavailable" states are
   the component's own and leave the rest of the dashboard alone. A note above the table says these
   are observed supplier prices, not costs paid.

Financial gating (`canViewFinancials`), provider-optional rendering (`isLiveFleetShown`,
`isProviderUsable`), the support-session behaviour and the business-timezone date rules (#499) are
the existing ones, untouched.

**Navigation rendering and visibility.** `primaryNavigation` now carries four `NavSectionHeading`s —
Operations (Dashboard, Pick List, Sites, Machines), Inventory & purchasing (Inventory, Purchases),
Finance & reports (Expenses, Reports) and Settings (Admin) — over the unchanged order of #868.
`navigationFor` appends `superAdminNavSection` ("Super admin") with `superAdminNavGroup` only when
the platform-diagnostics probe grants access (#335/#605). Capability filtering (#528), the business
navigation withholding (#676) and provider locks (#729) apply before headings are considered, and
`withOccupiedSections` drops a heading unless an entry follows it, so a role never sees a heading
over nothing. The sidebar renders an expanded heading as a visible `h2`, and a collapsed rail as an
`sr-only` `h2` plus a divider.

**Narrow layout.** Below the wide breakpoint `AppComponent` renders `BottomNavComponent`, whose
shortcuts are `shortcutsOf(navigationFor(...))` — Dashboard, Pick List, Sites and the Inventory
group's first page — so the bar can only offer an entry the member's own menu offers, with the same
lock summary. Its More control, like the top bar's menu button, opens the existing sidebar drawer
as a bottom sheet: a native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, so the browser makes the rest of
the page inert — no pointer, programmatic focus or assistive-technology navigation reaches it while
the sheet is open. The sheet has a sticky Close header, a scrolling body and safe-area padding;
`containFocus` keeps Tab and Shift+Tab cycling inside it; the dialog's own close request (Escape) is
cancelled and reported, and a click on its `::backdrop` dismisses it, so the shell always closes it.
`closeSidebar` removes the dialog before returning focus to the control that opened it
(`openSidebarFrom`, or the top-bar button), because nothing behind a modal dialog can take focus.
Groups start open in the sheet so its whole menu can be scrolled. The browser run in
`e2e/visual/dashboard-redesign.visual.ts` proves the modality from both openers: focus starts inside,
repeated Tab and Shift+Tab stay inside, background controls refuse focus and a press over one only
dismisses the sheet, and Escape and Close return focus to the opener.

**Styles.** The shell and the Dashboard use the `rr` tokens and `font-rr` of issue #954 through
Tailwind utilities in their own templates. No global class changed meaning and no other
authenticated page changed; `design-tokens.contrast.spec.ts` covers the new text/background pairs.
Visual evidence at 360, 390, 768 and 1440px, with a no-horizontal-overflow assertion, is
`e2e/visual/dashboard-redesign.visual.ts`, written to `docs/screenshots/issue-972/`. Issue #987's
collapsed-group, period-control and keyboard-focus captures are written beside them by the same run.

#### Site and machine performance (issue #987)

The owner reviewed #972/#980 on 29 October 2026 and asked for the original Stitch arrangement: one
**Site and machine performance** card whose site summary rows expand to the machines standing at
that site, rather than a Site performance card and a Machine performance card beside it. Issue #987
is that correction. It is composition and presentation only - no endpoint, DTO, calculation,
capability, guard, route or provider lock changed, both reads are the existing `GET /api/sites` and
`GET /api/machines`, and the page still never turns `null` into `0`.

**Where it lives.** `SiteMachinePerformanceComponent`
(`components/dashboard/site-machine-performance/`) is a dedicated feature component under the
[page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191): it has substantial UI plus its
own state - the shared period selection and one expansion state per site - while `DashboardComponent`
keeps owning the two reads, their loading/failed states, the `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` answer and
the provider-optional decision, and hands all of them over as `@Input`s. It calculates nothing: the
figures are the responses', `trendLabel`/`trendClass` and `siteStockClass` are the existing shared
helpers, and the only arithmetic is the direct margin and the per-period fleet sums the former
Machine performance card already displayed, moved across unchanged.

**The hierarchy.** `groupSitesAndMachines(sites, machines)` pairs the sites read with the `siteId`
issue #980 added to the machine read (the provider's `NayaxMachine.CustomerID`, the same key
`ListSites`/`GetSiteSummaries` group by): one group per site, in the sites order, holding the
machines whose `siteId` is that site's in the machine read's order; then every remaining machine -
at no site, or at a site the read did not return - under "Other machines". Each machine lands in
exactly one group. Two cases differ from #980's grouping, both deliberately: a site with **no**
returned machine keeps its own group and shows an empty state, because it is a site the business has
