`ProductPurchaseCostSummaryApiTests` compares the bulk answer field by field against what
`price-history` answers for the same product over a fixture built to make a divergence show — four
lines for one product, two of them on the same latest date and one of them a genuine $0.

Three properties of that endpoint are deliberate and tested:

- **The tie-breaks are the policy's, and they are pinned rather than assumed.** The last cost is the
  latest `PurchaseDate`, then the **higher** `PurchaseItemId`; the cheapest is the lowest `UnitCost`,
  then the **earliest** `PurchaseDate`, then the **lower** `PurchaseItemId`. The use-case tests supply
  equal-cost and same-date records in an order that would give a different answer if anything sorted
  by arrival.
- **A genuine $0 purchase line is a real recorded cost** — a free sample, a replacement delivery, a
  promotional case — and stays one. It can be the cheapest cost paid and it can be the last cost
  paid; it is never filtered out, and never reported as a missing figure. A `null` supplier name means
  the purchase had no supplier recorded and is published as such, never replaced with another
  purchase's supplier and never used as a reason to drop the line (dropping it would quietly move the
  last cost to an older purchase).
- **A product with no purchase history is absent, not zero.** The response is an array of
  `{ productId, lastUnitCost, lastSupplierName, lastPurchaseDate, lowestUnitCost, lowestSupplierName,
  lowestPurchaseDate }` holding one entry per product with at least one recorded purchase line, in
  product id order, so it is normally shorter than the catalogue; a client matches rows up by
  `productId` and shows "no purchases recorded" for a product it does not find. The optional repeated
  `productIds` query value narrows the read in the query itself; with no ids the answer covers every
  product of the business, **retired products included**, because a retired product's purchase history
  is exactly what a tool reaching into the past needs. The whole-business read is a second method on
  the port (`GetForAllProductsAsync`) rather than an empty id list, so "no products were asked about"
  keeps answering nothing for the report that passes a filter. Scoping is the ordinary tenant query
  filters on the EF adapter; nothing in the request names or carries a business.

The Angular client is `ProductPurchaseCostService`
(`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/services/product-purchase-cost.service.ts`) with its
`ProductPurchaseCostSummary` model (`src/app/models/product-purchase-cost-summary.ts`). It fetches and
presents; it sorts nothing, picks no cheapest and derives no saving. The home Dashboard's Reorder
Alerts table is its first caller (issue #789), Needs Ordering the second (issue #790), and All
Products (`ProductListComponent`, issue #791, E of #786) the third — see
[Average cost and purchase cost columns, and the retired-product filter, on All Products](#average-cost-and-purchase-cost-columns-and-the-retired-product-filter-on-all-products-issue-791)
below.

Product Profitability's **Last Cost**/**Lowest Cost**/**Saving per unit** columns (issue #207) are the
same purchasing insight surfaced on the report used to compare sales performance against purchasing
opportunity, not a second lowest/latest-cost algorithm. `Inventory.Application.Reporting.ProductProfitability.GetProductProfitabilityReport`
fetches every matched row's actual Purchase history in one bulk call through the narrow
`IProductPurchaseCostFactsProvider` port (implemented by
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfProductPurchaseCostFactsProvider`, avoiding a per-product query),
then applies the same authoritative `SupplierPriceComparisonPolicy.Evaluate` this section describes to
each product's entries, so the report and the product's own price-history view always agree on latest
cost, lowest cost, supplier, and tie-break behaviour. The result populates
`ProductProfitabilityRowDto.LastCost`/`LastCostSupplierName`/`LowestCost`/`LowestCostSupplierName`/`SavingPerUnit`,
which stay purchasing intelligence only: they never feed `CostOfGoods`, `GrossProfit`, `MarginPercent`,
or any other historical costing/valuation figure the report already computes from completed-sale
costing data, and an unmapped sale group's raw Nayax product identifier is never used to look up
Purchase history. A product with no recorded Purchase history reports these fields as null, which
`ProductReportComponent` (`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/reports/product-report.component.ts`)
renders as `—` rather than a fabricated zero; the Last/Lowest Cost cells show the supplier underneath
the cost, and the export (`GetReportExportRows`) deliberately does not add these fields to the CSV/XLSX
column contract - they stay a UI-only presentation, matching the issue's frontend presentation intent
of pairing currency and supplier text in one report cell.

##### OpenAPI documentation

`PurchasesController` no longer pins an explicit legacy route; its `[Route("api/purchases")]`
publishes the canonical route, and the tag still comes from Swashbuckle's default controller-name
derivation — there is no `LegacyOpenApiCompatibility`/`UseLegacyReceiptNames` step in
`SwaggerServiceCollectionExtensions.AddInventoryApiSwagger` any more. The published document carries
the `Purchase`/`PurchaseItem`/`PurchaseResponseDto`/`PurchaseValidationDto` schema ids and the
`Purchases` tag, with no remaining `Receipt*` schema id or `Receipts` tag.

Issue #429 added the per-line and per-charge GST classification keys to both published schemas
(`deliveryGstClassification`/`deliveryGstClassificationSource`,
`packageGstClassification`/`packageGstClassificationSource` on `Purchase`, and
`gstClassification`/`gstClassificationSource` on `PurchaseItem`), each referencing a new
`GstClassification`/`GstClassificationSource` integer-enum component. That is the one deliberate,
additive move of the pinned baselines in
`InventoryApi.Tests.Swagger.PublishedResponseSchemaContractTests`: no existing key was renamed,
retyped, reordered relative to the others or dropped.

The `Purchase`/`PurchaseItem` ids are **public contract, not a reflection of the current CLR
names**. Issue #304 replaced the serialised EF `Purchase`/`PurchaseItem` entities with the API-owned
`InventoryApi.DTOs.PurchaseResponse`/`PurchaseItemResponse`, and Swashbuckle derives the published
description from the CLR types: it would otherwise have renamed both schemas, added a `required`
list from the DTOs' C# `required` members, and repointed the nested `product`/`supplier` objects at
the DTOs' own `ProductResponse`/`SupplierResponse`. All three are API-contract changes, which issue
#304 excludes, and byte-identical runtime JSON does not excuse them, because a generated client
reads the document rather than the payload.

`InventoryApi.Swagger.PublishedResponseSchemaContract` is the **Swagger compatibility boundary**
that holds the published description still. It does four narrowly scoped things:

- maps `PurchaseResponse`/`PurchaseItemResponse` and the equivalent
  `SupplierOrderResponse`/`SupplierOrderLineResponse` pair on the supplier-order endpoints back onto
  the `Purchase`/`PurchaseItem`/`SupplierOrder`/`SupplierOrderLine` ids, by wrapping Swashbuckle's
  own schema-id selector so every other type keeps the default CLR-name derivation;
- clears the `required` list on exactly those four schemas, leaving the C# members `required`, where
  they stop a response mapper forgetting a field at compile time;
- inside exactly those four schemas, replaces a property that references `ProductResponse` or
  `SupplierResponse` with the schema Swashbuckle generates for the legacy
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Models.Product`/`Supplier` entity, so `product` keeps pointing at
  `#/components/schemas/Product` and `supplier` at
  `#/components/schemas/Supplier`. Because the replacement runs through the generator rather than
  rewriting a reference string, the referenced component is registered with its complete shape —
  including its own nested `category`/`stockAdjustments` references — instead of dangling. The
  legacy `Product` component had a nested `supplier` reference of its own until issue #787 dropped
  the product's supplier; the purchase's and the supplier order's **own** `supplier` reference, which
  is what this bullet is about, is unchanged (see
  [A product carries no supplier](#a-product-carries-no-supplier-issue-787));
- describes the stock history/adjust operations' response with the schema of the legacy
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Models.StockAdjustment` entity (issue #305), through an operation filter rather than
  a schema-id redirect. Those two actions return the API-owned
  `InventoryApi.DTOs.ProductStockAdjustmentResponse`, whose own schema id the product endpoints
  already publish as the item type of `ProductResponse.stockAdjustments` (issue #303), and one CLR
  type cannot carry two schema ids — so the *response* is substituted instead of the id, and both
  operations keep describing `#/components/schemas/StockAdjustment`. The substitution regenerates the
  schema from the legacy type with the same generator call Swashbuckle makes for a declared response
  type (substituting the element type inside the declared `IEnumerable<T>` for the history
  endpoint), so the published media types, status codes, content types and request body come out
  exactly as the base branch generated them; nothing else about the operation is touched. A pinned
  response description is only honest while the type that actually serialises is schema-identical to
  it and its payload byte-identical, which `StockAndExpenseSchemaContractTests` and
  `InventoryApi.Tests.DTOs.StockAdjustmentResponseJsonContractTests` assert respectively.

This boundary is where the API project names the EF entity namespace
(`Inventory.Infrastructure.Models` since issue #307) for presentation purposes deliberately. The controllers and the use cases are free of it - since issue #305 no file under
`InventoryApi/Controllers` references it at all, enforced by
`ProjectDependencyDirectionTests.No_controller_references_the_persistence_models` - and the DTOs and
response mappers name it for exactly one thing: the `StockAdjustmentReason`/`StockAdjustmentSource`
wire enums that the stock request DTO (`InventoryApi.DTOs.StockAdjustmentDto.Reason`) and the stock
response DTO (`ProductStockAdjustmentResponse.Reason`/`Source`) carry, and that this boundary itself
keeps published - from the pinned `StockAdjustment` response component and from the legacy `Product`
component's `stockAdjustments` reference. An API-owned enum of the same simple name cannot coexist
with those references - Swashbuckle fails document generation with
`Can't use schemaId "$StockAdjustmentReason" ...` - so those two enums are pinned here until the
persistence models relocate under #153/#154, and
`InventoryApi.Tests.Swagger.StockAndExpenseSchemaContractTests` reproduces that exact collision and
records the reachability that forces it. Nothing global changes: `ProductResponse` and
`SupplierResponse` keep the contracts the product and supplier endpoints already published - since
issue #302 `ProductResponse` is what the machine-product endpoint publishes too, and the legacy
`Product` component is registered only by this boundary now, for the pinned schemas that reference
it - and if an endpoint ever publishes the EF entity one of the four pinned ids belonged to,
Swashbuckle fails document generation with a duplicate-schema-id error rather than renaming one of
them silently.

`InventoryApi.Tests.Swagger.PurchaseOpenApiContractTests` (schema ids, tag, and the schemas the

### Machine refill

1. A refill moves units out of storage.
2. The movement is linked to the machine when known.
3. It does not create an expense or COGS and does not reduce costing inventory/value.
4. Two sources exist: an operator-entered manual restock (`StockAdjustmentSource.Manual`) and an
   imported Nayax Sync Restock event (`StockAdjustmentSource.Nayax`, issue #183, described below).
   Both use `StockAdjustmentReason.MachineRefill` and the same movement logic;
   `StockAdjustment.Source` is what keeps them distinguishable in the audit trail. Manual restocking
   remains the supported fallback for when Nayax is unavailable or a machine/MDB is not yet mapped;
   Sync Restock is the preferred path when a Nayax stock-adjustment alert already reports the
   physical event.
4a. The manual source has **two entry points and one movement**: the per-product manual adjustment
   form shared by the Stock History page and the `/products/:id/stock` entry point
   (`POST api/products/{id}/stock`), and since issue #743 the pick list's batch refill
   (`POST api/pick-list/refills`), which records a whole pick in one transaction under an
   idempotency key. They produce the same row - same reason, same `Manual` source - so everything
   downstream reads one kind of fact; see [Batch refill from the pick
   list](#batch-refill-from-the-pick-list-issue-743). The machine-detail page's own former
   per-product Restock action was one more caller of the first entry point; issue #744's
   machine-page consolidation replaced it with a **Record refill** link into the second instead (see
   [Machine-page consolidation: the "Record refill" link](#machine-page-consolidation-the-record-refill-link-issue-744)),
   so the machine-detail page itself now calls only the batch endpoint, never the per-product one.
5. The reverse transfer - units taken back **out of** a machine and returned to storage - is the
   same `MachineRefill` movement with a **positive** quantity change and the machine recorded on it.
   `StockAdjustment.QuantityChange` is signed from storage's point of view throughout the
   application, so a refill is negative and a return is positive, and both are equally
   costing-neutral: the business owns the units in either location. A cost-bearing disposal is not
   this movement - discarding units from a machine follows the existing Damaged/Expired write-off
   semantics, which do consume costing inventory.
6. What a machine is then expected to be holding, and how that compares with what the machine
   reports, is the [machine stock ledger](#machine-stock-ledger-and-shrinkage-reconciliation-issue-56)
   below.

### Machine stock ledger and shrinkage reconciliation (issue #56)

The machine-stock ledger answers one question storage inventory and costing inventory cannot:
**how many units should be in this machine right now, how many are, and what is the difference?**
It is a *physical* ledger for one location. It changes no costing value, creates no COGS, and
proposes no correction - identifying shrinkage is the point, so writing it away would defeat it.

**It is derived, not duplicated.** Every movement it needs is already a persisted fact:

| Movement | Where the fact lives | Machine stock | Business costing inventory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Refill | `StockAdjustment`, reason `MachineRefill`, negative quantity, machine recorded | `+n` | unchanged |
| Return to storage | the same movement with a positive quantity | `-n` | unchanged |
| Completed sale | `NayaxSales` with status `12` for that machine | `-1` per transaction | reduced once, by the sale-costing path |
| Counted reconciliation | `MachineStockCount` (the one table this feature adds) | sets the level | unchanged |

`Inventory.Domain.MachineStock.MachineStockMovementPolicy` is the single place a fact becomes a
movement and the single statement of which kinds consume costing inventory (only a completed sale -
and the ledger never performs that consumption itself). Because the ledger *reads* the refill
movements and the completed sales rather than writing its own copies, a refill cannot be counted
twice and a sale cannot create COGS twice: there is only one record of each event to begin with, and
nothing to keep in step. One completed transaction dispenses one unit, which is exactly the quantity
`WeightedAverageCostReplay` consumes from costing inventory for that sale, so the physical and
costing ledgers cannot disagree about quantity.

**Nothing is inferred from incomplete inputs.** `Inventory.Domain.MachineStock.MachineStockLedger`
replays a machine's movements in effective-instant order (ties: refills, returns, sales, then the
count, which is the authority on its own instant, then source id) on top of a baseline:

1. the most recent **counted reconciliation** for that machine and product; otherwise
2. the **opening machine stock the inventory-cost transition recorded** for it
   (`InventoryCostTransitionMachineStock`, issue #298) at that transition's cutoff, with only
   movements strictly after the cutoff replayed on top - the same boundary the costing replay
   applies to its own baseline; otherwise
3. **nothing**, in which case expected stock is `null` and the product is reported as
   `AwaitingOpeningCount`. The refilled, returned and sold quantities are still reported, because
   they are facts; what cannot be derived from them is a physical level.

A count supersedes rather than corrects: it sets the level from its own instant onward, resets the
movement totals to "since the baseline", and reports the difference it absorbed as
`unexplainedChangeAtLastCount` (positive means units were missing). That figure is **derived on
every read**, never stored, so there is one authoritative number rather than a stored copy that
could drift. An expected stock that replays below zero is reported as the negative value it is, with
`ExpectedStockNegative`, instead of being clamped - a clamp would hide a missing refill or a sale
attributed to the wrong machine.

**The observed side keeps its own uncertainty.** `MachineStockObservationPolicy` resolves the
quantity the machine reports as the sum over the product's slots of `PAR - MissingStockByMDB` - the
same arithmetic the Pick List, the site dashboard and the inventory-cost transition use, with both
fields confirmed as nullable `int32` in the published Nayax `machineProducts` contract. It returns
`null` - unknown, never zero - when the product occupies no slot, when any slot is missing either
value, or when any slot's quantity falls outside `0..PAR`. Deliberately *not* the
`(PAR - MissingStockByMDB) ?? 0` coercion the machine product list applies: a zero that means "Nayax
did not say" would read as an empty machine and invent a shrinkage. It is also deliberately separate
from `InventoryCostTransitionPolicy.MachineQuantity`, which performs the same arithmetic and
*refuses* incomplete data - a one-time costing cutover must be exact or not happen, while this report
must stay readable and say what it could not confirm.

`MachineStockReconciliationPolicy` then compares the two: `discrepancy = observed - expected`, with
`shrinkageQuantity`/`overageQuantity` as its one-sided views and a
`Balanced`/`Shortage`/`Overage`/`Unknown` status. All four are `null` whenever either side is
unknown.

**The data-quality states are the feature, not an afterthought** (`MachineStockDataQualityIssueCodes`):
`AwaitingOpeningCount` and `ExpectedStockNegative` per product on the ledger side,
`ObservedStockUnavailable` per product on the observed side, and three machine-level states -
`ObservationSourceUnavailable` when the machine's own report could not be read at all,
`PendingNayaxStockEvents` when Sync Restock still holds unprocessed events for that machine (so a
shortage may be an unapplied refill rather than shrinkage), and `UnattributedCompletedSales` when
completed sales on the machine are unresolved (so their units are missing from every
product's expected stock). A sale is attributed by the local product persisted on its own row
(`NayaxSales.ProductId`, issue #758) - the same association the costing ledger reads - so the two
always agree about which product a transaction dispensed, and a product renamed after the sale does
not move it. See [The sale's own product](#the-sales-own-product-issue-758).

**The layers.** `Inventory.Application.MachineStock.GetMachineStockReconciliation` orchestrates and
decides nothing: it reads the machine's report through the narrow `IMachineStockObservationSource`
port (implemented by `Inventory.Infrastructure.Nayax.NayaxMachineStockObservationSource` over the
existing `INayaxLynxClient.GetMachineProductsAsync`), reads the persisted facts through
`IMachineStockLedgerStore` (`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfMachineStockLedgerStore`), and
hands both to the Domain. `RecordMachineStockCount` appends a count at the server's instant from the
`IClock` port - the request carries no instant, no expected quantity and no discrepancy, because the
server derives all of them. `MachinesController`'s `GET /api/machines/{id}/stock-ledger` and
`POST /api/machines/{id}/stock-ledger/counts` are thin and inherit the controller's
`Inventory.Operate` capability: reconciling a machine is the refill work an Operator does.

Two Nayax conditions are reported as data quality rather than as a failed request, because both mean
"this business has no usable connection" while the expected stock is local and still available:
`NayaxNotConnectedException` and `NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException`. Everything else propagates
unchanged - a transport failure must not be presented as an unreadable machine, and a support
session's Nayax refusal (issue #551) applies here exactly as it does to every other Nayax read.

Tenant isolation is the central query filter's: the adapter adds no `BusinessId` predicate, which is
also what makes the observed product ids safe to pass into it - a machine id is a remote Nayax
identity, so two businesses can be told about the same machine number, and an observed slot resolves
to a product only if the caller's own catalogue holds it. Since issue #733 the slot's product id is
the local one its `NayaxProductID` is linked to, resolved in the observation adapter (see
[Resolving a Nayax product id](#resolving-a-nayax-product-id-to-a-local-product-issue-733)).
Unresolvable slots are dropped, the same exclusion the Pick List applies.

**Not in this slice.** There is no Angular page yet (the API is the exposure), no back-dated count,
no machine-level write-off, and no automatic correction of a discrepancy - by design, since
"automatically writing corrections to hide shrinkage" is explicitly out of scope.

### Global Stock History (issue #384)

Stock History is one page over every product's movements, not one page per product. `/stock-history`
(`StockHistoryPageComponent`) lists the persisted `StockAdjustment` history across the whole
catalogue, newest first, and narrows it by product, date range, reason, machine and source. It is a
**read** over the movements the flows above persisted: nothing here recalculates, rewrites or
synthesises a movement, and no second stock-adjustment implementation exists.

**The API boundary is one bounded, tenant-scoped query.**
`GET /api/stock-history` (`StockHistoryController`, thin) binds the filter and invokes
`Inventory.Application.Stock.ListStockHistory`, which answers a `StockHistoryPage` through the
`IStockAdjustmentStore.QueryHistoryAsync` port (implemented by
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfStockAdjustmentStore`, as the rest of that port already is).
The response is the API-owned `InventoryApi.DTOs.StockHistoryPageResponse`/`StockHistoryEntryResponse`
pair - never an EF entity - following the pattern issue #305 established for the product-specific
stock endpoints, and `InventoryApi.Tests.Swagger.StockHistoryOpenApiContractTests` pins the published
operation, its parameters and both components. The entry carries the owning product's `productName`,
read in the same query, because a cross-product listing has to label every row and the alternative is
the per-product fan-out this endpoint exists to replace. It does not carry `effectiveAt` (see below).
`reason`/`source` stay the one published `StockAdjustmentReason`/`StockAdjustmentSource` vocabulary,
for the compatibility reason recorded in [the stock API-owned-response
entry](#backend-migration-track).

**The result is bounded by the server, not by the client.** A movement history grows without limit,
so `Inventory.Application.Stock.StockHistoryPaging` resolves the requested page: a missing, zero or
negative page size becomes the default (50) and anything above the maximum (200) is clamped to it,
rather than refused. The response echoes the `page`/`pageSize` actually served plus the filtered
`totalCount` and `hasMore`, so the page can offer paging without a second count request, and
`EfStockAdjustmentStore` orders by `CreatedAt` descending with the movement id as a tie-break, which
makes successive pages a stable partition even for movements recorded in the same instant.

**One instant drives ordering, the date filter and the displayed time: `StockAdjustment.CreatedAt`.**
It is the instant the product-specific history has always ordered by, it is persisted as UTC and
keeps its UTC identity at the persistence boundary (see [Serialised instant identity at the
persistence boundary](#time)), and the frontend renders it with `BusinessDateTimePipe`. The date
filter is a pair of **business calendar days** in the current business's own timezone, not instants:
the client sends calendar
dates and `ListStockHistory` converts them through `IBusinessCalendar.StartOfBusinessDayUtc` into the
UTC instant the first day begins (inclusive) and the instant the day after the last one begins
(exclusive), so a 23-hour or 25-hour day across a daylight-saving transition is still covered
whole - `ListStockHistoryTests` pins both transitions. `EffectiveAt` drives neither the ordering nor
the filter and is not published by this query.

**Mutation stays where it was.** The selected-product workflow on the page is
`StockAdjustmentFormComponent`, a dedicated feature component (see [Page composition
boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191)) that posts to the existing
`POST /api/products/{productId}/stock`. That endpoint remains the single authority on costing, the
required restock unit cost, correction sign handling, insufficient-stock validation and
reason/source semantics; the global page adds no stock mutation of its own and the product-specific
`GET`/`POST api/products/{productId}/stock` contracts are unchanged.

**The product entry point maps onto the global page.** Every existing product "Stock" link points at
`/products/:id/stock`. That route now loads `StockHistoryPageComponent` with the product preselected
from the `:id` route parameter - the same state as `/stock-history?productId=123`, which is the
canonical URL - so existing links, bookmarks and deep links keep working and arrive at the global
experience filtered to that product, with its adjustment form. The former
`stock-history.component.ts` page it replaced is gone; its adjustment form moved into
`StockAdjustmentFormComponent` unchanged. A preselected product that is not in the current product
list still has its movements listed, but no adjustment form, because an adjustment needs a product
the catalogue can resolve.

Tenant isolation is the central query filter's, as everywhere else: the query adds no `BusinessId`
predicate of its own, and `EfStockHistoryQueryTests` proves with two synthetic businesses (plus an
unresolved caller) that neither the rows, the total count, nor an explicit request for another
business's product id can cross the boundary.

### Take Inventory (issue #245)

Take Inventory (`/take-inventory`, `TakeInventoryComponent`) is a compact per-product table for
counting physical storage stock (`QuantityInStock`) across the whole catalogue, distinct from a
machine refill: a refill is an internal transfer *out of* storage to a vending machine, while a
count difference here is a correction *to* storage itself, so it must never use
`StockAdjustmentReason.MachineRefill`. `Adjustment = CountedStock - CurrentStock`, resolved by the
deterministic `Inventory.Domain.InventoryCounting.InventoryCountAdjustmentPolicy`:

1. **Counted = Current.** No stock movement. This is the same outcome whether the operator clicks
   the clickable Current Stock value to confirm an unchanged count (a pure frontend/session
   interaction - it never calls the backend) or types the same value into Counted Stock and clicks
   Apply (which does call the backend and returns a `Confirmed` outcome with no persisted
   `StockAdjustment`). Either way the green/confirmed row state is frontend/session state only: it
   is not written to any backend session/history model, and this repository deliberately has none
   for inventory counting - a durable count-session record would be its own schema change and issue.
2. **Counted > Current.** The positive difference reuses the existing positive physical-stock
   Restock movement (`StockAdjustmentReason.Restock`, the same operation `StockController`'s manual
   Restock action already applies), at the same restock-cost suggestion that action already offers
   (last purchase cost, else average unit cost). When neither is available, Apply is refused with a
   validation error rather than assuming a zero or fabricated cost.
3. **Counted < Current.** The negative difference reuses the existing Correction movement
   (`StockAdjustmentReason.Correction`).

Both non-zero cases persist an ordinary `StockAdjustment` through the same
`IRecordInventoryMovement.RecordAsync`/`IRebuildProductCost.RebuildAsync` transaction every
other stock movement in this document uses, so a successful count difference is auditable in the
existing Stock History view exactly like a manual Restock or Correction - there is no separate
audit trail for Take Inventory.

`InventoryCountController`'s `POST /api/products/{id}/inventory-count/apply` is thin;
`Inventory.Application.InventoryCounting.ApplyInventoryCount` is the use case, reading and applying
through the narrow `IInventoryCountAdjustmentStore` port (implemented by
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfInventoryCountAdjustmentStore`, the same pattern as
`EfMachineStockEventStore`). The request carries both the counted quantity and the current quantity
the operator counted against (`ExpectedCurrentStock`); the use case re-reads the authoritative
current quantity at the mutation boundary and throws `DomainConflictException` (409) when it no
longer matches, instead of silently applying a delta against a quantity that has since changed
underneath a stale UI row. An invalid count or a missing restock-cost suggestion throws
`DomainValidationException` (400). Both map to a `ProblemDetails` response through the existing
central `DomainExceptionHandler`, described under [Domain and application error
mapping](#domain-and-application-error-mapping).

### Sale import and costing

1. Imported transaction facts are persisted using the Nayax transaction identity.
2. Status and payment type are classified centrally.
3. Only completed sales enter sales/profit calculations.
4. Historical cost is persisted on each sale with its status and source.
5. Unknown products, statuses, payment methods, or missing costs remain visible.

Sales reach the application two ways, and both follow those five rules: the operator uploads a Nayax
transaction export (`POST api/imports/nayax-sales`, below), and the home dashboard synchronises each
machine's latest transactions (see [Home dashboard coordinated Sites/Machines sales
sync](#home-dashboard-coordinated-sitesmachines-sales-sync-issue-187)).

A completed sale reduces business-owned costing inventory exactly once, here, and nowhere else. The
[machine stock ledger](#machine-stock-ledger-and-shrinkage-reconciliation-issue-56) (issue #56) also
deducts that sale from the machine's *physical* expected stock - one unit per completed transaction,
the same quantity this path consumes from costing inventory - by reading the same completed-sale row.
It records no movement and no cost of its own, so a machine's physical ledger can never become a
second deduction of COGS.

#### Uploaded transaction export import (issue #301)

`POST api/imports/nayax-sales` is `Inventory.Application.Imports.ImportNayaxSales` (issue #301,
child 3 of 3 of #151), moved unchanged in behaviour out of
`InventoryApi.Services.ImportService.ImportNayaxSalesFromExcelAsync`:

- **The use case** reads the upload's rows, decides per row whether it is importable, persists it as
  a new or updated sale, costs it, and finally replays the inventory cost of every product a
  completed sale affected. It owns the reported counts (`NayaxSalesImportResult`, moved here from
  `InventoryApi.Services.Interfaces` with no JSON change): a row without a positive transaction
  identifier, a positive machine identifier *and* an authorization time is counted as skipped and
  stays visible, never imported with a guessed identity. The instant it imports at follows the
  precedence in [Nayax sale timestamps](#nayax-sale-timestamps-issue-380): a valid
  `AuthorizationDateTimeGMT` value is authoritative and may correct a stored instant; without one a
  stored sale keeps its instant, a new sale with a malformed GMT value is skipped, and only a new sale
  from an export without a usable GMT value is imported at the export's own unverified, unconverted
  `MachineAuthorizationTime` column. A transaction this business already holds
  is updated in place rather than counted again, and an update never erases a transaction cost price
  the business already has - a row that simply does not carry the column leaves the stored one in
  place, while every other imported fact is overwritten, exactly as the legacy loop did. Statuses
  are classified by the Domain `NayaxTransactionStatusClassifier` and products matched by the Domain
  `Inventory.Domain.Reporting.ProductMatching.ProductMatcher` on the store's candidate projection;
  neither status identifiers nor matching rules are reimplemented. Since issue #745 a row's remote
  `NayaxProductID` is resolved to a local product through the id recorded on this business's product
  (`Product.ExternalProductId` since issue #759, read once per import through
  `INayaxProductLinkStore`) before that matcher's name fallback, rather than compared with
  `Product.Id`; an id recorded on no product is an unknown product, handled exactly as an unmatched
  id already was. Since issue #758 that answer is *persisted* as the sale's `NayaxSales.ProductId`
  and is what every later reader uses, the export's own raw product id stays in `NayaxProductId`,
  and the product a stored sale is moved *off* by a re-import is read from the same column - so one
  pass replays both the product it left and the product it joined. A sale the migration marked
  conflicting keeps its (absent) product until a human decides it; see
  [The sale's own product](#the-sales-own-product-issue-758). An export carrying no data row at
  all reads nothing and writes nothing, not even the catalogue.
- **Workbook/CSV parsing** sits behind the `INayaxSalesWorkbookReader` port, implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Imports.ClosedXmlNayaxSalesWorkbookReader` - a real Infrastructure
  adapter from the start - unlike the EF adapters of the time, which were still API-owned - for the
  same reason as
  `FileSystemPendingReimbursementXmlSource`: it needs no `AppDbContext`, only the uploaded bytes.
  ClosedXML therefore moved to `Inventory.Infrastructure`, and the former
  `InventoryApi.Services.NayaxSalesWorkbook` CSV-to-worksheet conversion moved into the adapter with
  it. The adapter keeps the parsing decisions imported financial data depends on: headers matched on
  letters and digits only (so `Product Cost Price`, `ProductCostPrice` and `product_cost_price` are
  one column, with `ProductCost`/`CostPrice` additionally accepted for the transaction cost),
  invariant-culture numbers, an unparsable number left `null` rather than zero (the one exception
  being an absent settlement value, which the legacy import read as `0`), and an instant taken from
  a date cell, an Excel serial number, or the export's own `d/M/yyyy h:mm:ss tt` text and otherwise
  left `null` so the row is skipped. Unlike the pending-XML source, a read failure is deliberately
  *not* translated into a plain answer: a corrupt upload stays a failure (ClosedXML's
  `FileFormatException`, which the controller's `InvalidOperationException` handling does not claim,
  so it reaches `GlobalExceptionHandler` as a generic `500` exactly as before) rather than being
  reported to the operator as an import of zero rows. A CSV, by contrast, is always readable, so
  unusable CSV content surfaces as skipped rows.
- **Persistence** sits behind the narrow `INayaxSalesImportStore` port (the product candidates, the
  conflicting transactions issue #758's migration recorded, the
  existing-transaction lookup, staging an added or updated sale, staging a decided cost, the
  affected products' transition cutoffs, and save), implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfNayaxSalesImportStore`, which moved there with the rest of
  the adapter family in issue #309. It decides nothing. The
  existing-transaction lookup is the same tenant-filtered `NayaxSales` query as before, with no
  business predicate of its own, so a remote `TransactionID` two businesses both hold is an insert
  for the importing business rather than an update of somebody else's sale; ownership of a new row is
  stamped centrally on save.
- **Costing and the replay** use the Application contracts: `ICostSale` (issue #297) decides each
  sale's historical cost and provenance, and `IRebuildProductCost.RebuildAsync` (issue #296) replays
  an affected product's cost from the earliest completed sale that touched it, but only for a product
  whose transition-baseline cutoff that instant actually follows. Which sales are a product's is the
  persisted `NayaxSales.ProductId` association (issue #758), part of the replay's own SQL rather
  than a catalogue match made afterwards.
- **The save order and its failure behaviour are unchanged, and deliberately differ from the
  latest-sales sync's.** The imported and updated sales are saved first, the affected products are
  replayed next, and the replayed costs are saved last, so a fatal `InventoryCostDataQualityException`
  in the replay aborts the replay loop and prevents the second save: the sales stay saved and no
  rebuilt cost is. Issue #362's per-product catch-and-continue is **not** applied here, because that
  sync can never reconsider a sale it has already stored whereas re-uploading the export runs this
  import again; whole-import atomicity would be its own change. Both behaviours are pinned by
  regression tests.
- `ImportsController.ImportNayaxSales` calls the use case directly; the route, the
  `NayaxSalesImportResult` response shape, the status codes and both `400 Bad Request` validation
  messages ("An Excel file is required." for a missing or empty upload, "Only .xlsx, .xls, or .csv
  files are supported." for an unsupported format) are unchanged. The `IFormFile` stays at the HTTP
  boundary: the use case receives only `NayaxSalesFileInput` (the uploaded name and a way to open the
  bytes, the same shape `PurchaseFileInput`/`ExpenseAttachmentInput` use) and opens and disposes the
  stream itself. The format rule still throws `InvalidOperationException`, which this action still
  catches, rather than the `DomainValidationException` the centralized mapping would want: that would
  change the response body from a bare JSON string to `ProblemDetails`, which is the separate later
  change [Domain and application error mapping](#domain-and-application-error-mapping) already
  records for this action.

Historical sale costing and its backfills are `Inventory.Application.Costing` use cases (issue #297,
child 3 of #149), moved unchanged in behaviour from the removed
`InventoryApi.Services.SaleCostingService`/`ISaleCostingService`:

- `CostSale` (`ICostSale`) decides one sale's cost and provenance. A sale that is not completed is
  left uncosted and pending. A completed sale already costed or legacy-estimated with both costs
  present is kept unless forced. Otherwise the precedence is the inventory-ledger (AVCO) cost from
  `IRebuildProductCost.GetAverageUnitCostAtAsync` (skipped for an unresolved sale or a sale at or
  before the product's transition-baseline cutoff), then the persisted transaction-level Nayax
  `Product Cost Price`, then uncosted: `Error` for an unresolved sale or a negative Nayax cost,
  `Pending` otherwise. The product is the one persisted on the sale (`NayaxSales.ProductId`, issue
  #758), read rather than matched: nothing here falls back to the provider's product id or the
  reported name, which is what stops a rename or a duplicate name moving historical COGS. Its
  Application-owned
  `SaleCostStatus`/`SaleCostOrigin` mirror the persisted `SaleCostingStatus`/`SaleCostSource`
  ordinal-for-ordinal (a parity test enforces this).
- `CostPendingSales` costs every pending completed sale, optionally for one product it is
  persisted against, and saves once.
- `BackfillSaleCosts` (`POST api/sale-costing/backfill`) re-costs completed sales through
  `CostSale`. Without `force` it counts already costed or legacy-estimated sales as finalized and
  leaves them untouched. `BackfillNayaxHistoricalSaleCosts` (`POST
  api/sale-costing/nayax-cost-backfill/dry-run` and `/apply`) costs pending or error sales (any status
  with `force`) that have a non-negative persisted Nayax export cost, optionally within an
  authorization-time range or for one product. It reads only the cost the Nayax transaction import
  already persisted and makes no Nayax API call, so a Nayax outage cannot fail or partially apply
  it. For both backfills a dry run loads untracked rows and stages and saves nothing, and repeating
  an applied run yields the same costs.
- The narrow `ISaleCostingStore` port (product candidates, transition cutoff, completed-sale
  selection, stage and save) is implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfSaleCostingStore`, which keeps the former EF queries behind
  `AppDbContext`'s business query filter and writes each decision back onto exactly the loaded row.
  The `NayaxSaleCosting` mapping lets `EfNayaxSalesImportStore` (the uploaded transaction
  export, issue #301) and
  `EfLatestNayaxSalesStore` cost the `NayaxSales` entity they are importing through `ICostSale`
  without changing their own transactions or the #187 synchronization boundary.
  `SaleCostingController` calls the backfill use cases directly with unchanged routes,
  request/response shapes and status codes. The pass-through `GetAverageUnitCostAtAsync` is
  `IRebuildProductCost.GetAverageUnitCostAtAsync`.

### Reimbursement import and reconciliation

1. Preserve imported period, gross, device, fee, GST, adjustment, and net facts.
2. Match completed card sales within the reimbursement coverage period.
3. Compare both gross/count and expected/actual settlement.
4. Mark reconciled only within the `$0.01` tolerance.
5. Surface pending, unmatched, partial, unknown, or unsupported data.

The import side of that flow (`POST api/imports/pending-xml`) is the
`Inventory.Application.Imports.ImportPendingReimbursementXmlFiles` use case (issue #299, child 1 of
3 of #151), moved unchanged in behaviour from the removed
`InventoryApi.Services.ImportService.ImportPendingXmlFilesAsync`:

- **The use case** walks the pending queue and, per file, reads it, skips it when this business has
  already imported the same bytes, otherwise persists it, and removes it from the queue either way.
  It owns the reported counts (`ImportedFileImportResult`, moved here from
  `InventoryApi.Services.Interfaces` with no JSON change): a file that could not be read, parsed or
  removed is counted as failed and stays in the queue rather than being silently dropped, a file
  whose hash is already present is counted as skipped, and the reimbursement rows of a file that was
  persisted but then could not be removed are still counted as imported - the same counter order the
  legacy loop had. A persistence failure is deliberately not caught and still propagates.
- **Discovery and parsing** sit behind the `IPendingReimbursementXmlSource` port, implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Imports.FileSystemPendingReimbursementXmlSource` - a real Infrastructure
  adapter from the start - unlike the EF adapters of the time, which were still API-owned - because
  it needs no `AppDbContext`. It resolves
  `{WebRootPath}/ImportedFiles` from the `PendingReimbursementXmlOptions` host paths the composition
  root supplies through `AddPendingReimbursementXmlSource()` (the same arrangement
  [Document storage](#document-storage) uses, so no filesystem path reaches the Application layer),
  and keeps the parsing decisions imported financial data depends on: invariant-culture numbers and
  dates, a date without an offset assumed to be UTC, a numeric attribute read as a boolean when it
  parses to a non-zero integer, an unparsable number or date left `null` rather than zero, every
  attribute preserved as raw JSON, a root `row` element treated as the single row, and a bare
  `row` fragment retried wrapped in a root element. Filesystem and XML failures are translated here
  and never cross the port: an unreadable, malformed or row-less file is logged (by file name, never
  by server path) and answered as `null`, and a file that cannot be deleted as `false`, matching the
  "translated to a plain answer at that layer's own boundary" rule in the
  [exception ownership table](#exception-ownership-table). Caller cancellation is excluded from that
  translation and stays cancellation.
- **Persistence** sits behind the narrow `IImportedReimbursementStore` port (the hash question plus
  one atomic write of the file with its reimbursement/device/device-payment/fee/payment-method
  graph), implemented by
  `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfImportedReimbursementStore`, which moved there with the
  rest of the adapter family in issue #309. The duplicate lookup is the same
  tenant-filtered `ImportedFiles` query as before, with no business predicate of its own, so
  file-hash idempotency stays per business: two businesses may legitimately import the same file and
  neither is told its own first import is a duplicate. Ownership is stamped centrally on save.
- `ImportsController.ImportPendingXmlFiles` calls the use case directly; the route, the
  `ImportedFileImportResult` response shape and the status codes are unchanged. The action now also
  binds the request's `CancellationToken` and passes it through both ports, which the legacy
  signature did not. This was the first of the three import endpoints to leave `IImportService`; the
  product catalogue import followed under issue #300 (see [Nayax product catalogue
  import](#nayax-product-catalogue-import-issue-300)) and the uploaded sales import under issue #301
  (see [Uploaded transaction export import](#uploaded-transaction-export-import-issue-301)), which
  deleted `ImportService`/`IImportService` entirely.

### Report availability model (issue #730)

Reports used to answer "no sales this month" and "nobody has read this month's sales" with the same
figure: `0`. Nothing in the application could tell the two apart, because nothing recorded which
period a run or a file actually covered — the sales synchronization reads a rolling `lastSales`
window per machine, and settlement imports were recorded per file with no period at all. Issue #730
(parent #329, decision P9) adds the missing evidence and the one rule that reads it.

**The evidence: `ProviderDataCoverages`.** One additive, tenant-owned, append-only table
(`Inventory.Infrastructure.Models.ProviderDataCoverage`). A row says: for this business, this
`ExternalProvider` and this `ProviderDataSource`, every provider record whose instant falls in the
half-open range `[FromUtc, ToUtc)` is now stored — and `RecordedAtUtc` says when the run that
claimed it finished. `Source` is part of the row rather than implied, because the three routes
account for different things: `SalesSync` and `SalesFileImport` account for sale instants, and
`SettlementImport` for the reimbursement periods the provider itself reported, so a settlement file
arriving never makes the sales figures complete. There is no unique constraint and no update path:
successive successful runs legitimately claim overlapping ranges, and the merge below joins them.

**A claim needs range *and* scope evidence.** A coverage row is a business-wide statement, so the
run that writes it has to be able to say both how far its range reaches and that it covered the
whole business inside that range. That is why `SalesFileImport` is part of the vocabulary but
nothing writes it (below): a transaction export declares neither.

**A row is written only for work that fully succeeded**, through the narrow Application port
`IProviderDataCoverageStore`:

- `SyncLatestNayaxSales` claims `[the latest machine window start, the instant it began reading)`.
  The *latest* of the per-machine window starts is the only defensible lower bound, because the
  business-wide claim needs every machine's window to reach back that far; a machine whose window
  returned nothing constrains it not at all, since "the last N sales" being empty is the provider
  saying that machine has nothing to miss. The write is last, after every machine was read and the
  whole batch was persisted and replayed, so a run that failed, was cancelled or failed for one
  machine records nothing. A batch holding a sale with no authoritative `AuthorizationDateTimeGMT`
  also records nothing, because the store does not import such a row and the run therefore did not
  account for its own range; so does a run in which no machine returned a single dated sale, which
  is evidence of nothing at all.
- `ImportNayaxSales` claims **nothing at all**, however completely it imported. Importing every row
  of a workbook says what was stored; it does not say the workbook held every transaction of the
  span those rows cover. The upload is a file a person exported from Nayax Core and it declares
  neither its range nor its scope — it may have been filtered to one machine, one payment type or
  one site — and the authoritative contract carries no requested-period metadata either
  (`GET /v1/machines/{MachineID}/lastSales` takes only a machine id and returns no window boundary;
  verified against the Nayax developer portal). Recording the interval between the earliest and
  latest imported instants, as the first implementation of this issue did, would therefore claim
  business-wide completeness for time nothing accounted for. The imported sales are reported in
  full and their period stays `Unverified` until a fully successful synchronization covers it.
  **Do not reintroduce a range derived from the instants a workbook happens to contain.**
- `ImportPendingReimbursementXmlFiles` claims the periods the file **proves**, one coverage row per
  proven interval, immediately after that file's graph is committed. Each reimbursement row declares
  its own `[ReimbursementStartDate, the midnight after ReimbursementEndDate)` — the provider's own
  statement of what that row settles, never the payout date and never the import instant
  (§ Reimbursements and reconciliation in `AGENTS.md`) — and only a row carrying **both** dates
  declares an interval. Overlapping and exactly touching rows merge into one range through
  `ReportCoverageRange.Merge`; a **gap between two rows is never bridged**, because a file settling
  July and September proves nothing about August. Pooling the earliest start with the latest end, as
  the first implementation did, claimed exactly those unsettled days. The claim is business-wide
  because the row is: a reimbursement row is the operator account's own statement for its period,
  carrying the account's company name, customer id and device counts with every device it settles
  nested beneath it, and `EfReportingSharedQueries.ImportedSummaryAsync` sums the reports' fee
  figures from exactly those rows and devices — so coverage claims the same scope as the figures it
  governs. A file that declares no period, a duplicate, and an unreadable file all claim nothing.

**One merge, used in both places: `ReportCoverageRange.Merge`.** Overlapping and exactly touching
ranges become one range, because two successful runs that meet at an instant leave nothing uncovered
between them; a gap is never bridged. It is the Domain's single implementation, called where coverage
is recorded as well as where a report decides a state, so the two cannot disagree about what a set of
intervals proves.

**The rule: `Inventory.Domain.Reporting.Availability.ReportAvailabilityPolicy`.** Given a period,
the coverage overlapping it and whether the period holds any provider data, it clips and merges the
ranges and returns exactly one of four states:

| State | When | What it means for a zero |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Complete` | merged coverage spans the whole period | a zero is a real zero — this is the only such state |
| `Stale` | covered without a gap from the period start to a point before its end, reported "as of" that instant | the figures are complete up to that instant and say nothing after it |
| `Unverified` | data exists that coverage does not account for: it predates coverage recording, or a failed or partial run left a gap | real partial data, not known to be all of it |
| `Missing` | no coverage and no data | the figures are absent, not zero |

The states are answers, never labels on each other, and `ReportAvailabilityState` is numbered in
severity order (`Missing = 0` … `Complete = 3`) so a figure derived from several sources takes the
least complete of them through `LeastComplete` — and so a state nothing decided can never read as
complete. "Does the period hold data" is counted from stored rows before the completed-sale filter,
not from an amount: a period holding only cancelled rows has sales data and a gross total of zero.

**What the reports do with it.** `GetBookkeepingReport` decides two states per period — sales, from
`SalesSync` + `SalesFileImport` coverage; fees, from `SettlementImport` coverage — derives a third,
`Combined`, as the least complete of the two, adds a conditional data-quality note for each family
that is not complete, and returns all three in `BookkeepingReportDto.ProviderAvailability`.
`GetGstAccountingAid` reports the same block and repeats the combined state as `NetGstAvailability`,
under the name of the figure a reader is looking at, because net GST subtracts both. The combination
is made once, on the server, by the Domain `LeastComplete` rule — no presentation combines two
states itself. The state travels as the enum's **name**, so a renumbered enum cannot silently change
what a stored response meant. Which figures each state governs is written out on the two DTOs; the
short version is that every provider-sourced figure carries one, a figure depending on both families
(net and direct profit and their margins, the net card settlement, total operating costs, net GST,
and since issue #805 bookkeeping's expected reimbursement and its difference from the actual)
carries the combined one, and every figure the business records itself — delivery and package costs,
operating expenses and their GST, purchase input GST — carries none and stays visible and exact.

**Every surface follows the same rule, including the exports.** The Angular reports render
`moneyOrState`/`percentOrState`, which print the state instead of a figure wherever an incomplete
period's amount would otherwise read as a bare `$0.00` or `0.0%`, and a badge beside a real partial
amount; that applies to every provider-dependent figure in every section of both pages, not only the
headline cards. Both pages show one banner saying the provider side is incomplete and the business's
own records are not. The bookkeeping and GST CSV/XLSX exports apply the identical rule through
`Inventory.Application.Reporting.Export.AvailabilityExportCells` and add explicit
`SalesDataAvailability`/`SalesDataAsOfUtc`/`FeeDataAvailability`/`FeeDataAsOfUtc` columns, plus
`CombinedDataAvailability` on bookkeeping and `NetGstAvailability` and `DataQualityNotes` on GST — an
exported file is read away from the application and pasted into a working paper, so it is the surface
where an unlabelled `0` does the most damage. A status count stays a plain count there, as it is a
statement about the stored rows themselves and the report's own UI shows it that way.

**One behaviour change beyond labelling:** the GST accounting aid no longer raises the
"GST classification missing" warning when no settlement file has been imported at all. That flag is
about imported reimbursement rows, and a period with none has no rows to be missing a
classification; the fee availability state is what reports that the fee figures are unavailable.

The table starts empty and is deliberately not backfilled: a coverage row is evidence that one run
retrieved one range, and no such evidence exists for anything that happened before the table did.
Periods before this ships therefore report `Unverified` — which is exactly what they are. Issue #731
(F2, below) extends the same model to every other sales-based report and export; the report provider
filter arrives with the second provider (parent #329, P5).

### Report availability across the remaining sales reports (issue #731)

Issue #731 (F2 of parent #329, decision P9) applies the model above to the reports #730 deliberately
left alone: daily, transactions, reconciliation, product profitability, machine profitability and
`/api/reports/dashboard`, their CSV/XLSX exports, and Site Commissions. **No financial formula
changes and no figure moves**; what changes is that an unaccounted-for period is no longer presented
as a measured zero, and that an unusable provider no longer fails the whole report.

**One shared facts carrier and one shared query.** The six reports do not each carry four loose
coverage fields. `Inventory.Application.Reporting.Shared.ReportCoverageFacts` holds the coverage the
period rests on — the two source families' ranges, whether the period holds sales rows and whether
it holds settlement rows — **and the period instants themselves**, because the adapter that queried
the rows is the only thing that knows which window it filtered them by, and a coverage range may
only be compared with the window the figures were measured over. The daily report selects sales
between business-day midnights; the others between plain calendar-date bounds. Its `Availability()`
and `SalesAvailability()` call the Domain policy and nothing else, and a record carrying no period
reports `ReportProviderAvailabilityDto.Undecided` — deliberately `Unverified`, never `Complete`.
`EfReportingSharedQueries.CoverageFactsAsync` is the one coverage query every reporting adapter
calls, including the bookkeeping one #730 introduced, so the reports cannot read coverage
differently. It takes no machine predicate (coverage is about whether provider data was retrieved
for the business at all) and no provider predicate (P5).

**Two families or one, decided by what each report actually shows.** A figure is never labelled by
evidence that does not feed it, so the contract differs by report on purpose:

| Report | Reports | Which state governs what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily | `ProviderAvailability` | sales: gross sales, card/cash, counts, COGS, gross profit, margin · fees: the imported and net reimbursement · combined: the reconciliation status |
| Reconciliation | `ProviderAvailability` | sales: recorded vending/card/cash sales and counts · fees: Nayax-reported gross and count, the processing and other fees, the actual net reimbursement · combined: every difference, the expected net and the statuses |
| Machine profitability | `ProviderAvailability` | sales: each machine's sales, quantity, COGS, gross profit, margin, commission, and the machine list itself · fees: the actual Nayax fees · combined: direct profit and its margin |
| Dashboard | `ProviderAvailability` | the bookkeeping report's own three states, republished — see below |
| Product profitability | `SalesAvailability` | one state: every figure, and the product list itself. Nothing here comes from a settlement import, and the Last/Lowest purchase costs are the business's own records |
| Transaction sales | `SalesAvailability` | one state: every total. The per-transaction fee is an effective-dated estimate over stored card transactions, not an imported settlement amount |

The dashboard **republishes** `bookkeeping.ProviderAvailability` rather than deciding its own: it
already composes that report for every provider figure it shows, so a second decision could only
disagree with the first. Its machine, product and unmapped-product counts are distinct counts over
the same completed sales — not a catalogue size — so they carry the sales state too.

**One wording, in one place.** `Inventory.Application.Reporting.Shared.ReportAvailabilityNotes`
holds the sentence for each non-complete state, and every report (bookkeeping included, which is
where the wording came from) adds its notes through it, naming only the two things that genuinely
differ: which of its figures the state governs, and what "nothing at all" means for that family. A
complete period adds nothing, exactly as issue #476 established. A list which is empty because the
period has no rows is named in those notes on purpose — an absent machine, an absent product and an
empty transaction list are the figures a reader is most likely to misread as "nothing happened".

**An empty list is not a measured zero either.** Machine profitability, product profitability and
transaction sales produce a row only where sales exist, so these pages say why the table is empty
rather than leaving an empty table to speak for itself.

**The exports carry the same flags as their source report.** Every one of the six goes through
`AvailabilityExportCells` — only `Complete` coverage prints a zero as a zero, a real non-zero amount
stays exact beside the state columns, and a figure the business records itself never passes through
it. The state columns are repeated on every row, header excepted, because a downloaded row is read
on its own: `SalesDataAvailability`/`SalesDataAsOfUtc` on all six, plus
`FeeDataAvailability`/`FeeDataAsOfUtc`/`CombinedDataAvailability` on daily, machine profitability and
the dashboard, and `SettlementDataAvailability`/`SettlementDataAsOfUtc`/`CombinedDataAvailability` on
reconciliation. The transactions export is the one that substitutes no amount: each row there is one
stored transaction, so the row's existence is the measurement; what the file could not otherwise say
is whether those rows are all of the period's, which is what its two state columns report.

**And an empty download says it too.** Repeating the state on every data row leaves one gap: the
three per-record reports — transaction sales, product profitability and machine profitability —
produce a row only where sales exist, so a result with no rows had nowhere to put its state and
downloaded as column headings alone, where `Missing` or `Unverified` is indistinguishable from a
`Complete` period that genuinely sold nothing. Those three therefore append **one** trailing
metadata row when, and only when, they have no data row at all: `ReportExportTable.NoRowsLabel`
(`NO ROWS`) in the first column, the report's own availability cells in its trailing availability
columns — two for the single-state reports, five for machine profitability — and every other cell
empty, built once by `AvailabilityExportCells.NoRowsRow`. It is the marked-row convention the daily
and reconciliation exports already use for their `TOTAL` row; those two always carry a totals row,
so they were never stateless, and bookkeeping, GST and the dashboard are single-row reports. CSV and
XLSX need no separate rule, because both encode this one table: the row is the second line of the
file and the second row of the sheet, identically. The alternative — inventing a transaction,
product or machine row to hang the metadata on — was rejected outright: a fabricated record in a
financial download is worse than the missing label it would fix. An export that *has* rows is
completely unchanged.

**Site Commissions answers "unavailable" instead of erroring.** A site is known only from the live
Nayax fleet read's `CustomerID`, so `GetSiteCommissionReport` previously threw whenever the provider
was unusable — and because `EfReportingSharedQueries.GetMachineCommissionsAsync` composes it, that
exception took the bookkeeping, GST, dashboard and machine profitability reports down with it. It now
catches the per-feature availability answers issue #726 established for reorder —
`NayaxNotConnectedException` (no credentials an ordinary operation may use, or, since issue #967, a
plan that does not include the sales provider, which it reports as its own `PlanRequired` reason) and
`NayaxPermissionNotGrantedException` (usable credentials, and Nayax refused this read) — and returns
`SiteCommissionReport.Unavailable(from, to, reason)`: no rows, and the reason. Everything else still
propagates: a transport failure, a cancellation, a `401` and the support-session refusal
(`SupportSessionNayaxUnavailableException`, issue #551) are outages, not businesses without sites,
and nothing here writes a connection status. A fleet read that succeeds and finds no site-mapped
machine stays an **available** report with no rows — a different answer, and the two must not
collapse into each other.

`SiteCommissionUnavailableReason`/`SiteCommissionUnavailableReasons` publish the two codes
(`NayaxNotConnected`, `PermissionNotGranted`), written out rather than taken from the enum member and
spelled exactly as `MachineNeedUnavailableReasons` spells the same two answers, so a client meets one
vocabulary. `GET /api/site-commissions` answers `200` with `isAvailable: false`, the code and one
explanatory sentence; the Angular page shows that sentence instead of a table, because an empty table
there reads as "no site is owed anything". Inside the reporting adapter, an unavailable commission
report makes commission **incomplete** rather than zero, so the direct and net profit figures it
gates come out unavailable — the established rule, not a new one (`AGENTS.md` § Site commissions: no
agreement is a valid zero-commission case).

**The frontend helpers are shared too.** `ReportPageBase.salesState()`/`feeState()`/`combinedState()`
read either contract shape, `providerIncomplete()` decides whether a page shows its banner, and
`countOrState` joins `moneyOrState`/`percentOrState` for a transaction count, a quantity or a machine
count — a count of `0` with no coverage behind it reads as "nothing happened here" just as `$0.00`
does, and must not be formatted as currency. Every page keeps one banner saying the provider side is
incomplete and the business's own records are not.

### Provider identity on the local row (issues #732, #759 and #735)

`Product.Id` and `Category.Id` *were* the Nayax `NayaxProductID` and `ProductGroupID`: the catalogue
import wrote the remote identifier as the local primary key. A local key that another system
issues is global rather than per business, cannot be chosen at all by a business with no provider
connected, and has room for exactly one provider's answer. Issue #732 (child A1 of #329, decision
P1) added the place a provider id belongs instead — two link tables, `ProductExternalIds` and
`CategoryExternalIds`, each carrying `BusinessId`, `Provider`, the opaque text `ExternalId` and the
local row's id — and issue #759 (A1b) **moved that id onto the local row**, because decision P1 was
revised on 18 October 2026: a business has zero or one sales provider, so a column of every mapping
saying which provider issued it was answering a question that has one answer per business.

Neither of those changed the keys: that is issue #735 (A4), below, which is where a row the import
creates stopped being keyed by the provider's number. Which product a *sale* belongs to stopped
being derived from either id in issue #758, also below.

**One provider per business, and it is fixed once set.** `Business.SalesProvider` is a nullable
`Inventory.Domain.Providers.ExternalProvider`: null means no provider at all, and inventory —
purchases, stock, costing, the business's own expenses — works fully without one. Storing a
provider's credentials is the one thing that sets it: `INayaxConnectionStore.SaveCredentialAsync`
claims `Nayax` inside the credential save's own transaction, with a conditional
`UPDATE … WHERE SalesProvider IS NULL` so two simultaneous first saves end as one claim, then reads
the row back and refuses the save through `Inventory.Domain.Providers.SalesProviderPolicy` when the
business already sells through a different provider. The claim lives in that one port rather than in
each caller, so no path can store credentials without recording the provider they belong to, and
neither can land without the other. Nothing changes it afterwards: no endpoint writes it, and
`BusinessSalesProviderEnforcer` refuses every change — including clearing it — on `SaveChanges`,
beside the other business enforcers. Switching provider is a separate design (#761), because it would
have to decide what happens to every external id, sale and coverage row the previous provider issued.
Because nothing can switch it, every external id a business holds belongs to its one provider, which
is what makes a single column enough.

**The external id is opaque text, and a column.** `Product.ExternalProductId` and
`Category.ExternalCategoryId` are nullable text of at most `ExternalId.MaxLength` characters, stored
as written and compared exactly; shared code never parses one and never assumes it is numeric, which
is what lets a later provider that issues a GUID or a code need no schema change.
`Inventory.Domain.Providers.NayaxExternalId` is the one place a Nayax numeric id becomes that text
(`From`) and is read back from it (`TryParse`), in the invariant decimal form — the Lynx contract
declares `NayaxProductID` as `integer<int64>` and `ProductGroupID` as `integer<int32>`, so both fit a
`long`. `ExternalProvider` names the issuer and has one member, `Nayax = 1`; it is numbered from 1 so
an unwritten column is not a provider by default.

**Unique per business, among the rows that have one.** The index on `(BusinessId, ExternalProductId)`
/ `(BusinessId, ExternalCategoryId)` is unique and **filtered** on `IS NOT NULL`. Both halves are
deliberate. Per business, for the reason every constraint over an externally supplied value is (see
[Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)) — two operators' catalogues may legitimately both
contain product 100, and a global index would let whichever imported first deny the other its own id.
Filtered, because "this row has no provider id" is a real state that every row of a business with no
provider is in, and a plain unique index would allow exactly one such row per business. There is
deliberately no uniqueness the other way round: a local row holds at most one provider id because the
column is single-valued, which is the simplification this model exists for.

**Nothing can cross a business any more, by construction.** The id is on the row it belongs to, so it
cannot name another business's row and cannot outlive a deleted one — the composite foreign key and
cascade the link tables needed have nothing left to guard. The `(BusinessId, Id)` alternate keys that
#732 added to `Products` and `Categories` stay, and two consequences of them are worth knowing: the
migration that added them rebuilt both tables (SQLite cannot add a constraint in place), and
`BusinessId` being part of a key means EF refuses outright to modify it on a tracked entity, before
`BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`'s immutability rule is reached. The one on `Products` is **not** only the
link tables' principal and does not go away with them: since #758 it is what
`NayaxSales.ProductId`'s `(BusinessId, ProductId)` foreign key points at (see
[The sale's own product](#the-sales-own-product-issue-758)), so #760 drops the link tables alone and
that constraint stays — it is the database-level guarantee that a sale names a product of its own
business. The one on `Categories` has only the link table behind it today.

**The migration copies, verifies, and refuses rather than guessing.** `AddProviderIdentityColumns`
adds the three columns and two indexes, sets `SalesProvider = Nayax` for every business with a
`BusinessNayaxConnection` row, any provider link or any stored Nayax sale (and leaves every other
business with none), then copies each `Provider = Nayax` link row into its local row's column. Before
copying it checks the three things the column model needs — a link names a row in its own business, a
business holds an external id once, a row carries at most one — and **aborts with the rule it broke**
rather than copying something ambiguous; each is guaranteed by the link tables' own constraints, and
checked anyway because SQLite enforces foreign keys only while `PRAGMA foreign_keys` is on, so a
restored backup or an out-of-band write could leave a state they would have refused. After copying it
verifies that every Nayax link equals its row's column, aborts on any difference, and records the
counts and the instant in `ProviderIdentityColumnVerifications`, which exists so #760 can confirm the
verification happened before it drops the tables. That table is deliberately not part of the EF
model: it is evidence about a migration, read by a migration, and no application code touches it.
`AddProviderIdentityColumnsMigrationTests` covers the copy, the three refusals and the recorded
verification.

**The link tables are not dropped in this release, and are not read either.** Production applies
migrations at startup, through `DatabaseSchemaStartup` (AGENTS.md § Database and migrations), so when
this migration lands the code already running there is still reading `ProductExternalIds` and
`CategoryExternalIds`; dropping them in the same release would break it. Nothing reads or writes them
after this change — `ProviderLinkTableDisuseTests` scans the production projects and fails if anything
does — and #760 drops both once this release is in production.

**Rollback policy.** Once this release has written external ids only to the columns, rolling back to
code that reads the link tables is **not supported**: the tables stop being kept up to date, so that
code would see a catalogue frozen at the moment of the release. A recovery goes forward with a fix.
The migration's `Down` exists to undo the schema, not to make that rollback safe.

**The import keeps the column true.** The catalogue import writes
`ExternalProductId`/`ExternalCategoryId` on the product or category each decided entry links or
creates, and leaves an existing one exactly as it is — it is the same id, and rewriting it would be
the one way the import could move an identifier between rows. It refuses to run at all for a business
whose `SalesProvider` is not Nayax, rather than recording Nayax ids in a column another system's ids
would be read from. It also *reads* those ids as the identity of a provider entry (below, issue
#745), and writes no `Id` at all (issue #735). Since issue #739 the one adapter doing all of that is
`EfCatalogueReviewStore`, and a link it records is always an explicit operator decision;
`EfNayaxProductCatalogImportStore` did it before, and wrote every entry it recognised without
asking.

#### The local key is the database's own (issue #735)

Issue #735 (A4) is where a provider's number stopped being a local primary key. The catalogue import
sets no `Id` on the product or category it creates: SQLite assigns it, and the remote id it came from
goes in the external id column beside it. `Product.Id` and `Category.Id` are this application's own
keys everywhere now, and a local key equal to a Nayax id is a coincidence — the thing every lookup
migrated in #733, #745 and #758 was made to stop depending on.

**What it unlocks, and what it protects.** Three things, each of which was impossible or unsafe while
the key was the operator's number:

- **Two businesses can hold the same provider id.** The key is per row and the external id is unique
  only per business, so two operators who stock the same Nayax product each get their own product.
  Before, the second import collided on the shared primary key — the known single-operator limit
  recorded in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64), which this removes.
- **A local row that merely holds that number is another row.** An entry whose Nayax id this business
  has recorded nowhere creates its own product or category and leaves the local row untouched, with
  its name, price, stock and costing exactly as they were. Issue #745 had to *refuse* that import by
  name, because the key the new row needed was taken; stopping an operator's whole catalogue over a
  number collision they did not cause is gone with the collision.
- **Nothing can quietly overwrite the wrong row.** Merging a remote product into whichever local row
  happened to hold its number is a silent error in financial data. It is now structurally impossible
  in the import, and `ProviderIdIsNeverALocalKeyTests` fails the build if any production code
  assigns a `Product`/`Category` `Id`, compares a `NayaxProductID` or `ProductGroupID` with one, or
  reads the stored `NayaxSales.NayaxProductId` as a local product key. The same test asserts the EF
  model still generates both keys, because a model that stopped would make the import write `0`
  rather than fail.

**A category the same snapshot creates, without predicting a key.** A product's `ProductGroupID` is
resolved through `Category.ExternalCategoryId` as before, but a category this import is creating has
no key yet, so the product is pointed at the category **row** (the `Product.Category` navigation) and
EF writes the key the insert assigns into `Product.CategoryId`. A recorded category is still named by
its foreign key, and an unresolvable group still leaves the product uncategorised rather than
pointing it at a local category that merely shares the number.

The import writes **both** the navigation and the foreign key on every entry, including to
clear them. Writing one of the pair alone would leave the other holding what an earlier write put
there — a navigation to a category this import is creating beside a foreign key since cleared or
pointed elsewhere — and `SaveChanges` would then write whichever of the two disagreeing values EF's
change detection happens to prefer. So a recorded category is assigned to both, no resolvable group
clears both, and a created one is assigned to the navigation with the foreign key left empty, which
is the ordinary way to name a principal whose key does not exist yet. `EfCatalogueReviewStore`'s
`ApplyProviderOwnedProductFields` is where that happens since issue #739, and `CatalogueReviewTests`
reads the category back from a reopened context for a created group, a linked one and a group no
local category carries; the removed import's `AssignCategory` did the same for a snapshot that named
one product twice, which a decided review cannot do.

**No migration, and no re-keying.** Every id already stored stays exactly as it is — including the
Nayax ids the #732 backfill and the #759 copy recorded on the rows that existed — and every foreign
key pointing at them stays valid. Nothing had to change on the target database: both tables have
declared their key `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` since the schema was created and the EF model
has always had it `ValueGeneratedOnAdd` (manual product creation relied on that all along), so SQLite
