simply assigns above the highest key the table has held. `ProductAndCategoryGeneratedKeyTests` reads
that generation back out of the *migrated* schema rather than trusting it, because issue #732's and
#759's table rebuilds are exactly the kind of change that could have altered the declaration.

**Rolling forward is safe; the sale is what carries attribution.** A sale stores the local product it
belongs to (#758), so a generated product id travels through synchronize → cost → inventory cost
replay → report with no reader ever comparing two numbers;
`ImportedProductGeneratedIdAttributionTests` proves that end to end over a fixture where an unrelated
local product carries both the provider's number and the name the sale reports, at a different unit
cost.

### Local machines and external machine ids (issue #740)

Child G1 of issue #329, after [the local key is the database's
own](#the-local-key-is-the-databases-own-issue-735) and reusing [#759's external-id column
pattern](#provider-identity-on-the-local-row-issues-732-759-and-735). Until it, **a machine was never
persisted at all**: every machine list was a read of the live Nayax fleet, and every stored machine
reference — a sale's `MachineID`, a refill's `MachineId`, a machine count's, an expense's, a stock
event's, a timestamp repair's, an inventory-cost transition's — was Nayax's own number. A business
with no sales provider therefore had no machines, in an application whose whole purpose is the
machines it refills.

**The table.** `Machines`, mapped by `Inventory.Infrastructure.Models.LocalMachine`:

| Column | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Id` | this application's own key, **assigned by the database** (#735's rule, decision A4). Nothing assigns it, and a local id equal to a Nayax machine id is a coincidence |
| `BusinessId` | the owning business. Ordinary tenant-owned data: the central query filters and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` scope every read and stamp every write, and no adapter writes a `BusinessId` predicate of its own |
| `Name` | required, and otherwise unconstrained. Deliberately **not** unique per business: two machines in one corridor may legitimately be called "Level 3", and nothing resolves a machine by its name |
| `IsActive` | whether the machine is in service. A machine with history is deactivated rather than deleted; a machine nothing refers to can be deleted (issue #896, below) |
| `ExternalMachineId` | the business's sales provider's own id for the machine, as **opaque text** bounded by `ExternalId.MaxLength`, or `null` when the provider names none. For Nayax it is written only through `Inventory.Domain.Providers.NayaxExternalId` |
| `LastSuccessfulRestockSyncStartedAtUtc` | when the last fully successful **Sync Restock** for this machine that left nothing to sync (issue #1018) *started*, or `null` for "no recorded sync" (issue #891). Integration state like `ExternalMachineId`: off the machine wire contract, never a value a request chooses, and written only by the monotonic conditional update described in [Dashboard reminder for overdue machine restock sync](#dashboard-reminder-for-overdue-machine-restock-sync-issue-891) |
| `LastSuccessfulRestockSyncCredentialRevision` | the `BusinessNayaxConnection.CredentialRevision` that fetch authenticated under, or `null` (issue #891). Coverage stamped with a superseded revision is read as no recorded sync at all |

`(BusinessId, ExternalMachineId)` carries a **filtered** unique index, `WHERE "ExternalMachineId" IS
NOT NULL`, for the two reasons the product and category columns do: "this machine has no provider id"
is the normal state of every machine of a business with no provider, so a plain unique index would
allow exactly one of them, and two operators' fleets may legitimately both contain machine 7. There
is **no machine link table** — the id is a column on the row it belongs to.

**The entity is called `LocalMachine` and the table is called `Machines`.** The type name `Machine`
is still occupied by the retired live-fleet response shape the machine wire-contract test compares
against, and removing that belongs to issue #153's legacy-structure removal. The table name is
declared explicitly in `AppDbContext.ConfigureMachines`, so it does not depend on which type owns it.

**The backfill.** `AddMachines` is additive — one table, its indexes, and an insert into it — and
**nothing was repointed by it**: every stored machine reference still held the provider's number.
That is what made the migration releasable on its own, which matters because Production applies
migrations at startup and the code already running there read no machine row at all. [Expense
machine references](#expense-machine-references-issue-780) (#780, G2a) has since moved
`OperatingExpense.MachineId` onto `Machines.Id`; every other stored reference still holds the
provider's number, and issue #741 (the stock half of G2) is what moves those.

It creates one machine per distinct machine number each business refers to, across all seven columns
that hold one, de-duplicated. A number of `0` is excluded: it is the absent value a non-nullable
column records, not a machine. The name comes from the most recent stored data that carried one — a
sale's `MachineName` at its authorization instant, or an inventory-cost transition's recorded machine
name at its baseline's creation instant — and otherwise from
`Inventory.Domain.Machines.MachineCataloguePolicy.DefaultName`, "Machine" and the provider's number.
That shape is mirrored in SQL because a migration cannot call into the Domain, and
`AddMachinesMigrationTests` compares the two so they cannot drift.

**It asserts the provider rather than assuming it.** A business has one sales provider and it cannot
change (#759, `BusinessSalesProviderEnforcer`), so a machine number stored against a business was
issued by that business's provider. The migration therefore **refuses before it writes anything** if
any business holds machine data while its `SalesProvider` is anything other than Nayax, including not
set at all: copying such a number into a column every later lookup reads as "the provider's id for
this machine" would record a claim nothing supports. It then verifies the result — exactly one
machine per referenced number, and no other row — and aborts the whole upgrade rather than leaving it
half applied. Both refusals are raised the way #759's copy raises its own, through a scratch table
and a SQLite trigger, and the scratch table is dropped again.

**The API.** `/api/local-machines` — `GET` (the list, active and inactive, ordered by name), `GET
{id}`, `POST` (create), `PUT {id}` (rename), `POST {id}/deactivate`, `POST {id}/reactivate`, `DELETE
{id}` (issue #896, below) — behind `Inventory.Operate`, the capability the fleet reads and the rest of
day-to-day stock keeping already declare. It is a **separate resource from `/api/machines`**, which is
the live Nayax fleet and needs working credentials for every one of its reads; nothing on this one
touches the provider, so it works identically for a business that has never connected one.

Two things it deliberately does not do. It **never writes `ExternalMachineId`**: no request field
corresponds to it, a created machine has none, a rename leaves it alone, and the [provider machine
review](#provider-machine-linking-automatic-or-reviewed-issue-742) (issue #742) is the one thing that
attaches one. And it **publishes no provider identifier** either — the response carries
`isProviderNamed`, the fact and not the id, and the deletion refusal below names the *provider*, never
its id for the machine. Because the capability is `Inventory.Operate`, which a support session grants,
every write here is refused in a read-only support session by the one central rule that allows it only
`GET` and `HEAD` (issue #551) — there is no per-action check for it.

**A provider-named machine is not renamed or deactivated here.** #740 originally allowed both;
the owner reversed that, because a machine the provider names is managed at the provider.
`EfLocalMachineStore` refuses a rename, and a deactivation, of a row carrying `ExternalMachineId`
with `MachineCataloguePolicy.ProviderMachineRenameRefusal` / `ProviderMachineDeactivationRefusal`
(a `400` naming the provider, worded from `Business.SalesProvider` as the catalogue refusals of
[issue #736](#manual-catalogue-who-owns-a-products-fields-issue-736) are). The refusal is decided
against the stored row inside the write's own transaction, so a machine linked between a caller's
read and the write is still refused. **Reactivation is never refused**, so a provider machine
deactivated before the rule existed can be put back in service. `LocalMachineListComponent` hides
Rename and Deactivate on a row whose `isProviderNamed` is true, and refuses both in code as well.
Nothing synchronises a machine's name, so a provider machine keeps the name it was recorded or
linked with even after a rename at the provider.

#### Deleting a machine added by mistake (issue #896)

`DELETE /api/local-machines/{id}` removes a machine **only while nothing refers to it and no provider
names it**. A machine added by mistake is a mistake an operator has to be able to undo; a machine with
history is not, and gets deactivation instead. `204` on success, `404` for a machine that is not this
business's (the central tenant query filters, so another business's id is simply not a machine the
caller named), `400` with the reason otherwise — the same shape every other refusal on this resource
uses.

**The five protected references.** Exactly five columns hold `Machines.Id`, each as a composite
`(BusinessId, MachineId)` foreign key on the `(BusinessId, Id)` key of `Machines`, restricted on
delete: `MachineStockCount.MachineId` and `StockAdjustment.MachineId` (issue #741),
`PickListRefill.MachineId` (issue #743), `OperatingExpense.MachineId` (issue #780) and
`PickListRefillLine.MachineId`, a multi-machine refill's per-allocation machine (issue #897). Any row in any
of them refuses the delete, with the kinds and counts named — "2 machine stock counts, 1 operating
expense" — so an operator knows where to look. **Nothing is cascaded, nulled, reassigned or
compensated for**: every stored count, movement, refill and expense stays exactly where it is, which
is what refusing is for. The provider's own stored data (`NayaxSales.MachineID`,
`NayaxMachineStockEvent`, `NayaxSaleTimestampRepair`, `InventoryCostTransitionMachineStock`, the
report filters and the calculated pick list) names the *provider's* machine number and is not a
reference to this row at all — which is why a machine carrying `ExternalMachineId` is refused outright
rather than counted: it is managed at the provider, exactly as its rename and deactivation are, and
its provider id is what every later lookup resolves that machine's sales through. No inventory,
costing or report total changes either way, and the delete makes no provider request at all.

**One rule, published and enforced from the same place.**
`Inventory.Domain.Machines.MachineDeletionPolicy` decides the refusal, and
`LocalMachineDeletionEligibility` is a projection of that same call — the shape a product's deletion
established in [Manual catalogue: who owns a product's
fields](#manual-catalogue-who-owns-a-products-fields-issue-736) (issues #737 and #825). Both machine
reads publish it as `canDelete`/`deletionRefusal`, so the page offers **Delete** only where the API
allows it and explains every other machine in the server's own words; `LocalMachineListComponent`
offers it only on a plain `true` (an absent answer is not permission), hides it during a support
session, opens the shared confirmation dialog naming the machine, sends one request, and reloads only
on success so a refusal leaves the row it is about on screen. The eligibility is **advisory**: it
describes rows as they were read.

**The check and the delete are one operation, under the link's own write lock.** `EfLocalMachineStore.DeleteAsync`
reads the machine, counts the five references and removes the row inside one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`
transaction (`SqliteWriteLockTransaction`, the shape issues #522, #537 and #743 each use), and
`EfProviderMachineLinkStore` takes **that same** lock. That is the race the foreign keys cannot stop:
linking is a write to the machine row itself, not a reference to it, so a deferred transaction would
let a delete and an apply both read a machine with no provider id and SQLite could then only answer
one of them with a lock error. With the write lock taken when the transaction opens, the loser waits
and reads the winner's committed state, so the two coherent outcomes are the only ones — the machine
is gone and nothing was linked, or the machine carries the provider id and the delete is refused as a
provider machine. The restricted foreign keys remain the **database's own backstop** under the count:
a reference that lands inside the delete's transaction makes SQLite refuse the statement, and that
violation is translated into `MachineDeletionPolicy.ReferencedWhileDeletingRefusal` — the same kind of
`400` an operator can act on, never an unhandled `500`.

**The page, and why it stopped being provider-locked.** The Machines menu entry came off the
provider signal - out of the "Needs Nayax" section issue #868 has since removed altogether - and
`/machines` carries no `requireProvider` guard any more
(see [Provider-locked navigation](#provider-locked-navigation-issue-729)): the page always has
something to show, so it is never locked. It is two lists. `LocalMachineListComponent` — the
dedicated feature component the [page composition
boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) requires, holding the list, its load state, the add
and rename drafts, the delete confirmation, the refusal message and every write — is always shown. The live Nayax fleet below
it (revenue, profit, and the links into each machine's stock and Sync Restock workflow) is shown only
while the shared availability signal says the fleet read can be served, through the one shared path
`loadProviderList` (issue #728): an unavailable provider withholds that section entirely rather than
rendering a screen of refusals, while an outage is reported as an error **in place of** it, because
presenting a `502` as "this business has no machines" is a claim nobody made. The machine **details**
page is still a live provider destination and keeps its guard — every panel on it is a Nayax read —
so a direct request for `/machines/{id}` with no provider reaches the "needs a provider" page with
its generic explanation rather than one naming a read the navigation no longer claims. Giving that
page a local half is still outstanding: issue #742 linked provider machines to local ones and left
the details page exactly as it is.

Write controls are hidden while a support session is active, on the established rule of issues #554
and #658: the session grants `Inventory.Operate`, which is what the page would otherwise gate them
on, and the backend refuses the write by its read-only method rule rather than by withholding the
capability.

**What was deliberately out of scope of #740**: repointing the stored machine references (#780 did
the expenses, #741 does the stock half), the provider machine review ([#742 does
it](#provider-machine-linking-automatic-or-reviewed-issue-742)), provider switching
(#761), slots, planograms, par levels, and manual sites — a site is known only from the live fleet
read's `CustomerID`, so the Sites destination stays in the provider section with nothing local to
fall back on.

### Expense machine references (issue #780)

Child G2a of issue #329, the first half of G2, after [local
machines](#local-machines-and-external-machine-ids-issue-740) created the rows to point at. **An
operating expense that names a machine now names the business's own machine row**, so an expense
keeps working for a business with no provider — which is the whole point of the G group.

**What changed, and what deliberately did not.**

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OperatingExpense.MachineId` | the raw Nayax machine number, no foreign key | `Machines.Id`, with `(BusinessId, MachineId)` a foreign key on the `(BusinessId, Id)` key of `Machines`, restricted on delete |
| Expense create/update/read/filter | the provider's number | the local machine id, and a machine that is not one of this business's is refused |
| `GET api/machines` | the provider's number only | adds `localMachineId` beside `machineID`; every existing field is unchanged |
| `GET api/machines/{id}` | the provider's number only | **unchanged** — out of scope (issue #741); it resolves no local machine id and answers `null` in the field the shared wire shape carries. [#741](#stock-machine-references-issue-741) has since moved the route onto the local id |
| Report machine filters and machine keys | the provider's number | **unchanged** — still the provider's number |
| `StockAdjustment.MachineId`, `MachineStockCount.MachineId`, `NayaxSales.MachineID`, the provider event tables, `InventoryCostTransitionMachineStock` | the provider's number | **unchanged** — issue #741, which [has since repointed](#stock-machine-references-issue-741) the first two |

**The migration is two, and the second one refuses rather than guesses.**
`AddMachineBusinessKey` declares the `(BusinessId, Id)` alternate key on `Machines` and changes no
data; it is separate only because SQLite builds a dependent table's replacement before renaming the
principal's, so a foreign key added in the same migration would reference a `Machines` that does not
carry the key yet. `RepointOperatingExpenseMachines` then joins every non-null machine number to its
business's machine on `ExternalMachineId = CAST(MachineId AS TEXT)` — the exact text
`NayaxExternalId.From` writes and the `AddMachines` backfill wrote — updates only rows it has
already matched, and verifies afterwards that every attributed expense names a machine of its own
business. **A non-null number with no local machine aborts the whole upgrade**, before anything is
written: an expense silently detached from its machine would move money out of that machine's direct
profit, and a stored `0` (the absent value a non-nullable machine column records, which `AddMachines`
created no machine for) is exactly such a value and has to be corrected by a person. A null stays
null — that is a whole-business expense. `Down` puts the provider's numbers back, and refuses if an
attributed machine carries none, because the release it returns to reads the column as a provider
number.

**Reports are unchanged, and that is the point.** The machine profitability report's rows are keyed
by the provider's machine number and the bookkeeping report's machine filter is one, because that is
what the fleet, the sales rows and the UI all speak and #780 does not touch them. Their expense
facts therefore translate: `EfMachineProfitabilityReportFactsProvider` resolves the sale machines'
numbers to local machine ids and groups the expenses by those, and
`EfBookkeepingReportFactsProvider` resolves the filtered number before narrowing. A number this
business has recorded no machine for contributes **no** expenses and narrows the bookkeeping report
to none — never silently to the whole business's, which would report another machine's costs against
the one that was asked about.

**The expense form reads the machine records themselves since issue #746** (see [Machine fields from
the business's own machines](#machine-fields-from-the-businesss-own-machines-issue-746)), rather than
the fleet list this section describes. What it submits is unchanged: the same local machine id, under
the same server-side check. The same issue gave the expense **list** the Machine filter that this
section's `machineId` list parameter was waiting for; the parameter, its `AND` and its refusal of a
machine the business does not have are the ones described above, unchanged.

**One lookup, gated on the provider.** `Inventory.Application.Nayax.INayaxMachineLinkStore` is the
machine half of [`INayaxProductLinkStore`](#resolving-a-nayax-product-id-to-a-local-product-issue-733),
with the same rules and for the same reason: `ExternalMachineId` holds whatever provider the business
sells through and does not say who issued the value, so the read asks for machines whose owning
business's `SalesProvider` is Nayax, in the same statement. A number recorded on no machine resolves
to nothing, never to the machine whose local id happens to be that number.
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfNayaxMachineLinkStore` is the adapter the use cases hold and
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Data.EfMachineLinkQueries` is the read itself, which the two reporting
fact providers call directly — one translation, not one per caller.

**The API and the form.** `GET api/machines` adds `localMachineId` as an appended, nullable field;
it carries no financial figure, so it survives the `Dashboard.ViewFinancials` redaction with the rest
of the machine's identity. **`GET api/machines/{id}` resolves nothing and publishes nothing**: that
route is out of scope for #780 (issue #741 owns it), so `GetMachineDashboard` makes no machine-link
lookup at all and leaves the field the shared wire shape carries `null`. A `null` from the
single-machine read therefore means only "this route does not resolve it" — a consumer that needs a
machine's local id reads the fleet list, which is the read the expense form makes. Giving the detail
route its own answer, or its own wire shape, is #741's decision to take. The expense form
(`components/expenses/operating-expense.component.ts`) submits `machine.localMachineId`, and a listed
machine with no local record is not offered at all — there is no id to store for it. The server does
not trust the form: `CreateOperatingExpense`/`UpdateOperatingExpense` check the submitted machine
against the business's machines through `ILocalMachineStore` (which reads through the ordinary tenant
filters, so another business's machine is simply invisible) and refuse anything else with
`OperatingExpenseDetails.UnknownMachineMessage`, before the expense is read or an attachment is
written. A **deactivated** machine is accepted: it is a machine the business operated when the cost
was incurred, and retiring a machine must not make its historical expenses uneditable.

**What is deliberately out of scope**: the stock half (#741) — `StockAdjustment.MachineId`,
`MachineStockCount.MachineId`, the ledger, sync restock and the `api/machines/{id}` route's own
changes; the provider event tables and `InventoryCostTransitionMachineStock`; changing any report
filter to a local id; and the provider machine review (#742), machine dropdowns without a provider
(#746) and provider switching (#761).

### Stock machine references (issue #741)

The second half of G2 (parent #329), after [the expense half](#expense-machine-references-issue-780).
**A stock movement and a machine count now name the business's own machine row, and every
`api/machines/{id}` route takes that row's id**, so the machine-stock ledger and its counts work for
a machine the provider does not know.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `StockAdjustment.MachineId`, `MachineStockCount.MachineId` | the raw Nayax machine number, no foreign key | `Machines.Id`, each with `(BusinessId, MachineId)` a foreign key on the `(BusinessId, Id)` key of `Machines`, restricted on delete |
| `api/machines/{id}` (detail, products, latest-sales, sync-restock and its apply/resolve routes, stock-ledger, counts) | the provider's number | the local machine id; an id that is not a machine of this business — including a provider number an older client sends — is a `404` |
| `GET api/machines/{id}` | `localMachineId` always `null` | answers the route's local id beside `machineID` |
| Stock adjustment body, stock history filter | the provider's number | the local machine id; a machine that is not one of this business's is refused with `ManualStockAdjustmentPolicy.UnknownMachineMessage` |
| `NayaxSales.MachineID`, `NayaxMachineStockEvent.MachineId`, `NayaxSaleTimestampRepair.MachineId`, `InventoryCostTransitionMachineStock.MachineId` | the provider's number | **unchanged** |
| Pick list, report machine filters, admin cost-transition and timestamp-repair screens | the provider's number | **unchanged** |

**The route id is resolved once, into both names.** `Inventory.Application.Machines.ResolveMachineIdentity`
turns the route's local id into a `MachineIdentity(LocalMachineId, NayaxMachineId)`: the machine must
be visible through `ILocalMachineStore` (the ordinary tenant filters), and its Nayax number comes
from `INayaxMachineLinkStore.GetNayaxMachineIdAsync`, the reverse of the #780 lookup with the same
rules — only while the business sells through Nayax, and only a value `NayaxExternalId` could have
written. A provider number is never tried as a fallback: a local id equal to a Nayax number names a
different machine. Features that touch both kinds of data carry the pair rather than one number, so
a local id is never sent to the provider and a provider number is never stored as a local reference.

**What each route does with a machine that has no Nayax number** — one the business created
itself, or any machine of a business with no provider. The detail and products reads and Sync Restock
answer `404`, because they read only the provider. Latest sales answers `200` with the
`NoSalesProvider` state #768 already defined, without calling Nayax. The stock ledger and counts work
normally: they are this application's own data, and the reconciliation reports the observation as
unavailable rather than asking the provider about a machine it does not know.

**The ledger reads by both ids.** `EfMachineStockLedgerStore` reads refills and counts by the local
id and sales, opening baselines and pending stock events by the same machine's Nayax number (none,
when it has none), and writes counts with the local id. Sync Restock finds the provider's stock events
by the Nayax number and records the movement it writes, and the manual refills it compares against,
by the local id, so a Nayax refill and a manual refill of the same machine still meet.

**The migration is two, for SQLite's sake.** `RepointStockMachineReferences` refuses before it writes
— both tables are checked before either is updated, and a non-null number with no local machine in
its business, a stored `0` included, aborts the upgrade with nothing changed — then repoints both
columns on `(BusinessId, ExternalMachineId = CAST(MachineId AS TEXT))` and verifies the result, the
pattern #780 used. `AddStockMachineForeignKeys` then adds the index and the two foreign keys. They are
separate because SQLite rebuilds a table to add or drop a foreign key, and EF Core runs that rebuild
at the **end** of the migration that asks for it: in one migration, `Down` would write the provider's
numbers back while the foreign key still stood and fail on every database with a machine reference.
Split, the foreign keys' `Down` drops them first and the repoint's `Down` then restores the numbers,
refusing if a referenced machine has none. Downgrade is therefore not unconditional: that refusal
leaves the database at `RepointStockMachineReferences` (local ids, no foreign keys), because the
foreign keys' `Down` has already committed. The code of the release that introduced both reads that
state correctly, but no earlier release does, so a verified backup is the real rollback. `RepointOperatingExpenseMachines` (#780) keeps the
combined shape and so has the same `Down` ordering; that is not changed here.

**The frontend.** The machine list and the dashboard link to `/machines/{localMachineId}` and link
nothing for a listed machine with no local record; the machine page passes the route id to its tabs;
the restock, the stock adjustment form and the stock history filter submit and match the local
machine id. The restock still takes it from the fleet row it is already showing and so offers only
machines that have one; the stock adjustment form and the stock history filter stopped reading the
fleet at all in issue #746 (next section) and read the machine records themselves.

### Machine fields from the business's own machines (issue #746)

Child G2b of issue #329, and frontend only: no endpoint, contract, stored value or migration is
involved. [#780](#expense-machine-references-issue-780) and [#741](#stock-machine-references-issue-741)
had already moved what these screens *store* onto the business's own machine row, but each still
**discovered** its machines by reading the live Nayax fleet (`MachineService.getAll()` through
[`loadProviderList`](#shared-provider-availability-and-error-versus-empty-states-issue-728)) and
keeping the rows that carried a `localMachineId`. A business with no provider therefore had no
machine list, and so no machine field at all, even with machines of its own recorded - the one thing
the G group exists to fix.

**Three screens, one source.** `StockAdjustmentFormComponent` (fed by its page),
`StockHistoryPageComponent` and `OperatingExpenseComponent` read `LocalMachineService.getAll()`
(`GET /api/local-machines`, issue #740) and key every option by `LocalMachine.id`. That is the same
id they submitted before, so nothing about a stored movement or expense changes; what changed is that
the id now comes from the resource that owns it instead of from a provider read that could not be
made. The fleet read is **not** made by these screens at all - not as a fallback, and not for a
label. The label is `LocalMachine.name` and nothing else: that resource publishes no provider name or
number (it publishes `isProviderNamed`, the fact), so there is none to show and none is invented.

**Active for a new record, every machine for history.**

| Surface | What it lists |
| --- | --- |
| Stock adjustment form (a new movement) | the **active** machines |
| New expense | the **active** machines |
| Expense being edited | the active machines **plus the machine that expense already names**, deactivated or not |
| Stock History machine filter | **every** recorded machine, deactivated included |
| Stock History machine column | named from that same list, deactivated included |
| Expense list machine filter | **every** recorded machine, deactivated included |

A retired machine is not somewhere stock is being put or a cost is being incurred now, so it is not
offered for a new record. It is still part of what happened, so it stays in both filters and in the
column - and it stays as the selected value of an expense being edited, which is why
`machineOptions` reads the machine from the **stored expense** rather than from the form: choosing
"None" and changing one's mind must not make the machine unreachable, and saving the form again must
not silently detach the cost from the machine that incurred it. The server already accepts a
deactivated machine for exactly that reason ([#780](#expense-machine-references-issue-780)), and
still refuses one that is not this business's.

**The expense list's filter rides a parameter that already exists.** `GET /api/operating-expenses`
has accepted an optional local `machineId` since [#780](#expense-machine-references-issue-780) -
`OperatingExpenseFilter.MachineId`, applied by `EfOperatingExpenseStore` as one more `AND` beside the
date, category, supplier and site filters - so `OperatingExpenseComponent`'s Machine filter is the
frontend finally using it, and no endpoint, DTO or query was added or changed for it. It is the same
id the field submits, so the filter and the field cannot disagree about which machine a row is, and
the server still answers nothing for a machine the business does not have. The totals row sums the
rows the server returned, which is what makes a machine-narrowed list state that machine's cost
rather than the whole business's.

**The field is offered once there is an active machine, and the three other states stay distinct.**
A read still outstanding says it is loading, a read that **failed** renders an explicit error in
place of the field or filter, and a business with no active machine simply has no field - with no
error, because that is a true statement about the business. This is issue #728's error-versus-empty
rule kept on a read that is no longer the provider's: `loadProviderList`'s `unavailable` outcome has
no counterpart here, because `/api/local-machines` has no availability answer to give. The page owns
the read and the adjustment form takes `machines`, `machinesFailed` and `machinesLoading` as inputs,
so the two agree about which of those states they are in; a machine staged on the form that the list
stops offering - the list went away, or that machine was deactivated - is dropped rather than
submitted.

**What stayed where it was.** `MachineService` and the provider fleet screens are untouched; the pick
list's manual entry is issue #794; the report machine filters stay on the provider's machine number
by the G2 decision ([#780](#expense-machine-references-issue-780)); and the Nayax source filter, the
"Nayax monthly fee" category and the Expenses subtitle stay on the shared provider signal, because
they are about whether Nayax is part of this business rather than about a machine list. No
support-session guard changed. Every role that can reach these screens already holds
`Inventory.Operate`, which is what `/api/local-machines` requires, so no role loses a field it had.

**What proves it.** `stock-history-page.component.local-machines.spec.ts` and
`operating-expense.component.local-machines.spec.ts` each cover the four cases the issue names -
without a provider, with one, with a deactivated machine, and with a failed read - plus the
outstanding read and the id that is actually submitted; the Stock History spec also asserts the
adjustment field through its page, which is where the form's list comes from. The expense spec covers
the list's Machine filter over the same four cases, including the deactivated machine it lists and the
local id it narrows by, and `operating-expense.service.spec.ts` pins the request itself: the chosen id
is sent as `machineId`, and no machine parameter is sent while none is chosen.
`stock-adjustment-form.component.spec.ts` covers the active-only offer, the error and loading states,
and the staged machine dropped when the list stops offering it.

### Provider machine linking: automatic or reviewed (issue #742)

Child G3 of issue #329, after [local machines](#local-machines-and-external-machine-ids-issue-740)
created the rows and [#780](#expense-machine-references-issue-780)/[#741](#stock-machine-references-issue-741)
pointed the stored references at them. Until it, `LocalMachine.ExternalMachineId` had exactly one
writer, the `AddMachines` backfill, so **a Nayax machine that appeared after that migration had no
local machine at all** — and neither did any machine of a business that connected Nayax later. This
is what records one, and the whole of the behaviour is about not recording the *wrong* one.

**One endpoint reads the fleet, one applies decisions, and both are `POST`.**
`InventoryApi.Controllers.MachineLinkReviewController`:

| Endpoint | Capability | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST api/machine-link-review` | `Inventory.Operate` | Reads the provider fleet and reports it against this business's machines. Links the new ones itself **only** when nothing of the business's own is unlinked. |
| `POST api/machine-link-review/apply` | `Inventory.Operate` | Records the submitted link-or-create decisions, as one transaction. |

It is a **third** machine resource on purpose. `/api/local-machines` (#740) is the machines an
operator maintains by hand and touches no provider; `/api/machines` is the live fleet with this
business's sales and costs resolved onto it. This one is the join, and it is the only surface in the
application that writes `ExternalMachineId` at all. The capability is the one both of those already
declare — deciding which machine a provider number means is the same day-to-day inventory work as
recording the machine or refilling it — so no role gains or loses a surface. The review is a `POST`
even though an operator reads it: it may link machines by itself, and a cached `GET` would hand back
a fleet nobody read.

**The rule that decides whether a link is automatic.**
`Inventory.Domain.Machines.ProviderMachineLinkPolicy.MayLinkAutomatically` is the whole of it: a
provider machine no local machine carries the id of is created as a new local machine, with the
provider's name and that `ExternalMachineId`, **only while the business has no machine of its own
without a provider id**. The failure it exists to prevent is the duplicate fleet: a business that
recorded its machines by hand before connecting Nayax has exactly the machines Nayax is about to
describe, and creating a second row for each of them is the one outcome that cannot be undone by
renaming anything. With nothing unlinked there is no local machine a new provider machine could
already be, so creating one invents nothing and asks nobody a question with a single possible answer.
A **deactivated** machine without a provider id counts as unlinked: a retired machine is still a
machine of this business that the provider's may be, and linking a retired row beats duplicating it.
The rule is read about *this* business only, inside the same transaction as the write it permits, so
a machine somebody recorded while the fleet was being read stops the auto-link rather than being
duplicated by it.

**Nothing is matched by name**, exactly as in the [catalogue
review](#provider-catalogue-review-link-or-create-and-change-review-issue-738). A local machine
called precisely what the provider calls its machine stays unlinked and is reported for review, and a
local key that happens to equal a provider machine number is a coincidence (issue #735). The only
ways a link comes about are the operator naming one of their machines and a machine this feature
creates — which is why the automatic case only ever *creates*.

**What the review reports.** `Inventory.Application.Machines.ReviewProviderMachines` reads the fleet
through the existing `INayaxLynxClient` port and resolves each machine through `ExternalMachineId`
alone: `autoLinked` is what this read linked by itself, `awaitingReview` is what it deliberately did
not, and `linked` is every provider machine that resolves to a local machine afterwards. A fleet
entry with **no identifier** is not a machine and is left out: the authoritative Lynx contract for
`GET /v1/machines` declares `MachineID` as `integer<int64> | null` (Nayax developer portal, Get All
Machine Basic Info), so `0` is the absent value this application's non-nullable field records — the
same exclusion `AddMachines` makes. `MachineName` is `string | null` there too, so a machine the
provider names nothing takes `MachineCataloguePolicy.DefaultName` ("Machine 7"), the shape the
backfill already wrote for a machine nothing had named.

**The apply writes the operator's decisions and nothing else.** The request carries one of three
actions per provider machine (`Defer`, `LinkExisting` with a machine of theirs, `CreateNew`) and
**no provider value at all**: the provider's name for a created machine comes from the fleet read
`ApplyProviderMachineLinks` makes itself, and a decision naming a provider machine that fleet does
not contain is refused. A machine nobody decided about is deferred, which is the honest default — a
half-decided review must not link the other half by omission.

**The authoritative read, the comparison and the write are one operation**, and for the same reason
the catalogue apply's are: two of the refusals are statements about *stored* rows.
`Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfProviderMachineLinkStore.LinkAsync` re-reads the business's
machines inside the caller's transaction and applies
`ProviderMachineLinkPolicy.LinkRefusal` to each link there —

- the chosen machine already carries a **different** provider id, or
- **another** machine of this business already carries this one.

The second is the acceptance criterion "one business cannot link two machines to the same provider
machine id", stated as a sentence an operator can act on; the filtered unique index on
`(BusinessId, ExternalMachineId)` refuses it as well, and two decisions in one apply cannot both
claim one id because the staged list grows with the rows the apply creates. Recording the id a
machine already carries is deliberately **not** a refusal: it is the state the apply was asked to
reach, which is what makes applying the same decision twice a no-op. One refused decision refuses the
whole apply — nothing linked, nothing created — because the links a half-applied review did write are
the ones the next review treats as settled.

**Linking is the only thing that happens.** No sale, stock movement, machine count, expense, cost or
report is read or written, and a linked machine keeps **its own name**: nothing synchronises a
machine's name (#740). Once linked, the machine can no longer be renamed or deactivated locally
(see [Local machines and external machine ids](#local-machines-and-external-machine-ids-issue-740)).
Until a provider machine is linked, its provider data stays under its raw provider number exactly as
before — `NayaxSales.MachineID`, the stock events, the timestamp repairs and the report machine
filters are unchanged — and it keeps appearing on every provider-only page, because those pages are
the fleet read itself. `INayaxMachineLinkStore` resolves it to nothing until the link exists, which is
the same answer it gave before.

**Tenancy is the central one.** No `BusinessId` predicate is written anywhere in the adapter: another
business's machine is invisible to the read and so unreachable to the write, a created machine is
stamped by `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`, and two businesses may link the same provider machine id
without either seeing the other's. Every method refuses outright unless `Business.SalesProvider` is
Nayax, for the reason the catalogue review's do (issue #759): the column holds *that* provider's ids
and nothing in it says who issued them.

**No migration, and no new table.** The review is derived from the fleet read and the machines each
time, so there is no pending-review storage to add: a provider machine is "awaiting review" exactly
while no machine carries its id, which is a fact about the rows rather than a draft. That is also
what makes the change releasable on its own — a business that never opens Machines with a working
provider sees no change at all, and nothing about the schema moved.

**The page.** `ProviderMachineReviewComponent`
(`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/machines/provider-machines/`) is the dedicated feature
component the [page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) requires, composed by
`MachineListComponent` between the business's own machine list and the live fleet. The page renders it
**only once the shared availability signal (issue #728) says the fleet read can be served**, because
the panel reads that fleet the moment it appears: that is what makes the automatic half automatic — an
operator who connects Nayax and opens Machines finds the new machines already recorded — and it is
also what leaves a business with no usable provider, or one whose fleet read failed, alone instead of
showing it a refusal. The panel states what was linked automatically, offers Skip / "It is one of my
machines" / "Add it as a new machine" per waiting machine with every row starting on **Skip**, offers
only machines the provider does not already name (a machine that carries an id would be refused by the
server's own rule, and a retired one is offered and marked), refuses a link that names no machine
locally rather than sending it, and asks the page to reload the machine list afterwards — the list is
what the server stored. It is withheld entirely while a support session is active (issues #554, #658,
#661): both of its calls are writes the read-only rule refuses, and the Nayax credentials they need
are refused in that state anyway (issue #551).

**The machine list shows both kinds together**, and always did: a linked provider machine *is* a local
machine, so it appears in `LocalMachineListComponent` beside the ones the operator created, marked
"From Nayax" from the `isProviderNamed` fact the response already carried (#740). No provider
identifier is published there, and none is accepted.

**What proves it.** `ProviderMachineLinkTests`
(`backend/Inventory.IntegrationTests/Application/Machines/`) is relational over two businesses and
covers each case the issue names: the automatic link with nothing unlinked (and beside machines
already linked), the review when something is unlinked (including a deactivated machine), the link,
the create, no name matching (and no key matching), the two second-link refusals, the atomic refusal,
a decision about a machine outside the fleet, the repeat apply that changes nothing, the provider
machine that resolves to no local machine until it is linked, and the two-business cases — another
business's machine unreachable, the same provider id linked by both, and one business's unlinked
machines not making the other's review wait. Two of them are specifically about the gap the
transaction exists to close, and change the stored machines **between** the review's read and the
apply's write, through a second database scope: another machine takes provider machine 7 after the
review reported it as waiting, so the stale decision linking 7 to a different machine is refused and
the acceptable decision in the same batch is not kept either; and the machine the operator chose
takes a *different* provider id after the review, so its own identity is not overwritten.
`ProviderMachineLinkPolicyTests` covers the rules themselves, and `provider-machine-review.component.spec.ts` and
`provider-machine-review.service.spec.ts` cover the panel and the two routes it calls.

### Resolving a Nayax product id to a local product (issue #733)

Every feature that reads a machine's live selections gets `NayaxProductID` values back — the Lynx
contract's "unique identifier of the product in the Nayax system" (`GET
/v1/machines/{MachineID}/machineProducts`, `integer<int64>`, nullable). They used to be compared
with `Product.Id` directly, which worked only because the local key *was* the Nayax id. Issue #733
(child A2 of #329) makes those features read the recorded provider id instead —
`Product.ExternalProductId` since #759 moved it onto the row. It is a lookup change and nothing else:
no endpoint, response shape, calculation or stored value changes, and because the #732 backfill
recorded each product's Nayax id as the one it was keyed by and #759's migration copied that onto the
row, a business whose data predates either sees identical results.

**One narrow port, read at the edge.** `Inventory.Application.Nayax.INayaxProductLinkStore` answers
one question — the local product id for each of these Nayax product ids, keyed by the Nayax id —
and `Inventory.Infrastructure.Persistence.EfNayaxProductLinkStore` implements it over
`Product.ExternalProductId` alone, matching the exact text that `NayaxExternalId.From` produces. One
statement does it: `EfSalesProviderQueries.ProductsIdentifiedBy` adds the condition that the row's
owning business sells through Nayax, because the column holds the id of whichever provider the
business has and does not say which that was. A business with no provider, or with another one,
resolves nothing — the answer every caller already handles as an unknown product. The read is scoped
by the ordinary tenant query filters, so one business's product is never an answer to another's
question, and a stored id that the one Nayax conversion could not have written matches nothing rather
than being read as the number inside it.

The translation happens where Nayax data enters the application, so every persistence port
downstream of it speaks local product ids only — `IMachineStockEventStore.GetStorageProductsAsync`
changed from taking Nayax ids to taking local ones for exactly that reason. The six paths:

| Path | Where the id is resolved | What an unresolved Nayax id means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reorder (`CalculateReorderNeeds`) | after the fleet fan-out, before the outstanding-order read | the selection carries no product id, the same state a selection with no `NayaxProductID` already carried; it is summed into no product's replenishment need and the Domain refill rules skip it as unmapped |
| Pick List (`GetPickList`) | after the fan-out, before the storage read | the selection is excluded from the result, as one with no local catalogue row already was |
| Machine products (`ListMachineProducts`) | after the catalogue read, before the slots are matched | the slot is dropped, as an unmatched slot already was |
| Site products (`GetSiteProducts`) | after the fan-out, before the facts reads | no row is produced, as a selection with no catalogue cost basis already produced none |
| Site summaries (`GetSiteSummaries`) | after the fan-out, before the completed-sales read | the stock fact carries no product id: it still counts toward the site's physical stock percentage, exactly as an unmapped selection always has, and raises no low/empty product alert |
| Sync Restock (`SyncMachineStockFromNayax`) | after the machine-products read, before the storage read | the MDB position resolves to no local product, which is `NayaxMachineStockMatchPolicy`'s existing "no local product is mapped to Nayax product …" Needs Review branch, so no inventory ever moves for it |
| Machine stock (`NayaxMachineStockObservationSource`) | in the adapter that translates the slots | the slot is dropped, as one whose product was not in the caller's catalogue already was |

In every case an unresolved id is treated as an unknown product, never matched to the local product
whose id happens to be the same number. That is the point of the change: since #735 a local key and
a Nayax id that coincide are a coincidence.

**Each lookup is awaited on its own.** All of these use cases run a concurrent Nayax fan-out and
then one or more reads on the request's scoped `AppDbContext`, which supports a single operation at
a time, and since issue #520 each remote call resolves the business's credentials through that same
context (issue #667). The lookup is therefore awaited after the fan-out has completed and in
sequence with the other database reads, never beside them;
`NayaxParallelCredentialAccessTests` pins that for the reorder and site-dashboard fan-outs over the
real adapters, with the id resolved from the real product row.

**No Nayax group id is resolved here.** None of these paths reads a `ProductGroupID`: a category is
reached through the local `Product.CategoryId`. `Category.ExternalCategoryId` has one reader, added
in #745 (A2b): the catalogue import, below.

### Resolving Nayax ids in the sale paths, the catalogue import and reconciliation (issue #745)

Issue #745 (child A2b of #329) is the same lookup change for the paths that read *stored or uploaded*
Nayax data rather than a machine's live selections: the two sale paths, the catalogue import and the
catalogue source-state reconciliation. Like #733 it changes identity resolution and nothing else — no
endpoint, response shape, calculation, stored amount or import rule moves — and a business whose data
predates it sees identical results, because the #732 backfill recorded each product's and category's
Nayax id as the one it was keyed by and #759's migration copied that onto the row.

| Path | What is resolved | What an unresolved Nayax id means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latest-sales sync (`EfLatestNayaxSalesStore`) | each payload item's `NayaxProductID`, once per batch through `INayaxProductLinkStore`, before the per-sale work | an unknown product: the name fallback still runs, and a sale that matches nothing is still imported, stays visible, is left uncosted and replays no product's inventory cost — exactly as an unmatched id already was |
| Uploaded sales export (`ImportNayaxSales`) | each row's `NayaxProductID`, once per import through the same port | the same: the row is imported and counted, stays visibly uncosted, and no inventory cost is replayed for it |
| Catalogue import (`EfCatalogueReviewStore` since #739, `EfNayaxProductCatalogImportStore` before it) | each entry's `NayaxProductID` through `Product.ExternalProductId`, each group's and each product's `ProductGroupID` through `Category.ExternalCategoryId`, both read from the rows the import already has in hand | an entry nothing is linked to: since #739 the operator decides it, and the row they create is keyed by the database (#735) and carries that id; for a product's group, no local category at all, so the product is imported uncategorised |
| Catalogue reconciliation (`EfLocalCatalogSnapshotProvider`) | the local product snapshot is built *from* the recorded ids, so each product is reported under the Nayax id it carries | a local product with no recorded id has no provider identity and takes no part in the comparison: it is a product Nayax never named, not one Nayax stopped returning |

Three things are worth stating explicitly.

**The group id and the product id come from one identifier space each.** The Lynx contract declares
the product endpoint's `ProductGroupID` as `integer<int32>`, nullable, "the unique identifier of the
product group to which the product belongs" (`GET /v1/operators/{OperatorID}/products`), and the
group endpoint issues ids from that same space (`GET /v1/operators/{ActorID}/productGroups`), which
is what makes one column — `Category.ExternalCategoryId` — the answer for both. A category the same
snapshot creates joins the lookup immediately, so a first import still categorises its products.

**A local row with no recorded id is not claimed by a Nayax id that merely equals its key.** Merging
the two would write a remote product's catalogue fields onto whichever local row happened to hold its
number — a silent error in financial data, which is the thing this slice exists to end. While a
created row was still keyed by the Nayax id this was a conflict with nowhere to go, so the import
refused the entry by name and wrote nothing (it is one `SaveChanges`), and a human recorded the id on
the local row or re-keyed it and imported again. Since #735 (A4) the entry simply creates its own row
under a key the database assigns and the local row is left untouched — see
[The local key is the database's own](#the-local-key-is-the-databases-own-issue-735).

**The stored `NayaxSales.NayaxProductId` column had mixed provenance, and #758 ended that.** Until
then the latest-sales sync wrote the *local* product id it matched into it while the uploaded export
wrote the row's raw remote id, so the column could not be read as either kind of identifier without
being wrong about half the rows. Issue #758 (A2c), below, gave the sale its own `ProductId` column
and left `NayaxProductId` holding only the provider's own id.

The settlement (pending reimbursement XML) import carries no product or group identifier at all, so
there is nothing in it to resolve.

### The sale's own product (issue #758)

Issue #758 (child A2c of #329) is where a stored sale stopped being matched to a product and started
**recording** one. `NayaxSales.ProductId` is the local product the sale belongs to, decided once by
the writer that stored it, and it is what costing, the inventory cost replay, the timestamp repair,
the reports and the machine-stock ledger all read. A sale is therefore attributed to the same product
everywhere, and a product rename, a duplicate name or a database-generated product id cannot move it.

**Why a column rather than a match.** Every one of those readers used to call
`Inventory.Domain.Reporting.ProductMatching.ProductMatcher` over the stored `NayaxProductId` and the
reported `ProductName`: id first, then the unambiguous name. That re-derived an answer on every read,
from data that changes. Renaming a product moved historical sales between report rows; two products
sharing a name made sales ambiguous retroactively; and since #735 (A4) a local key and a Nayax id
that coincide are a coincidence, so the id half would quietly have started matching the wrong row. An
earlier attempt (#747, PR #755) read the column as a *raw* provider id everywhere instead, which was
wrong for the rows the sync had written with a local id in it — reproduced on that pull request as
sales left `Error`/uncosted with their product's inventory never consumed.

**The three columns.**

| Column | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `ProductId` | The **local** product, nullable. Foreign key on `(BusinessId, ProductId)` to the products' `(BusinessId, Id)` business key, so a sale can never name another business's product — and `DeleteBehavior.Restrict`, never cascade and never set-null, because deleting the product a sale sold must fail loudly rather than delete the sale or detach its COGS from any product. |
| `Provider` | The originating `ExternalProvider`, `Nayax` on every row. The table's name only implies it; a provider switch (#761) needs it stated. |
| `ProviderProductIdIsRaw` | Whether `NayaxProductId` is known to be the raw provider id. `true` on every row written since this change, `false` — provenance-unknown — on every row that predates it. |

`NayaxProductId` keeps the provider's own product id and nothing else: a remote identity, never a
local key, `null` when the payload or the export carried none.

**The writers decide once.** The latest-sales sync, its enrichment branch and the uploaded-export
import resolve the provider id through `INayaxProductLinkStore` (`Product.ExternalProductId` since
#759) and then the unambiguous-name rule — exactly as #745 made them match — and persist that answer
in `ProductId` instead of leaving it to be redone. The import's `TrackStoredProduct` is keyed on the
stored `ProductId`, so re-importing a transaction whose product changed replays both the product it
left and the product it joined, in the same pass. Neither writer touches the product of a sale the
migration marked **conflicting**: only an audited decision settles one.

**A null `ProductId` is unresolved, and unresolved is a reported state.** No reader matches such a
sale by name or by number. It takes no inventory-ledger cost, is consumed by no replay, the
machine-stock ledger counts it as unattributed, and the transaction and product-profitability reports
show it under the name the provider reported, with the existing "could not be mapped to a Product"
data-quality note — visible, never silently dropped from a total.

**Approved decision: product attribution and transaction cost are separate.** On 18 October 2026,
Cristhyan approved preserving the transaction-level Nayax fallback for unresolved sales (issue #758,
PR #766). An unresolved sale never takes a local product's inventory-ledger cost and is consumed by
no inventory replay. When its own persisted Nayax `Product Cost Price` is non-negative, `CostSale`
may return `Costed`/`NayaxTransactionExport`, retaining explicit provenance without resolving
`ProductId` or changing any product's quantities or inventory value. Without a valid recorded cost it
remains uncosted; never substitute zero or today's product cost. Reports keep product attribution
visibly unresolved even when transaction COGS is known. This preserves AGENTS.md's historical-cost
precedence and `An_unresolved_sale_with_a_Nayax_cost_is_costed_from_the_Nayax_export`.
The historical migration failure gates below are unchanged: this decision does not permit losing an
existing product attribution during migration.

#### Migrating the sales that already exist

Two migrations, in one release, neither of which guesses.

**Step 1, `AddNayaxSaleProductAssociation`.** Adds the three columns, the index, the foreign key and
the two append-only tables below; records `Provider = Nayax` on every existing row and leaves them
all provenance-unknown; then fills `ProductId` from what the recorded ids already say. A sale is
resolved when its stored number names a product of the same business **directly** — which is what
`ProductMatcher` does today — *and*, when some product of that business carries that same number as
its `ExternalProductId`, it is that same product. Those two agree for every row in the current data,
because #732's backfill recorded each product's Nayax id as the one it was keyed by and #759 copied
it onto the row. `NayaxProductId` is left exactly as it was.

**Conflicting sales.** When the direct candidate and the external candidate are *different*
products there is no honest answer — the stored number is of mixed provenance — so the sale stays
unresolved and a `NayaxSaleProductConflicts` row records both candidates as the reason. **A
conflicting sale is never resolved automatically, by name or otherwise**, including by step 2, whose
name rule would otherwise silently pick one of two products a recorded identifier already disagrees
about.

**Step 2, `ResolveNayaxSaleProductsByName`.** In the same release, a sale that is still unresolved
because its stored id matched *no* product — never a conflicting one — and whose `ProductName`
matches exactly one product under the current `ProductMatcher` rule gets that product, through the
audited `NayaxSaleProductResolutions` operation: one row per sale carrying the old value, the new
value and the rule. Ambiguous and absent names stay null. The step only ever fills a null, which is
what makes it idempotent. Together, steps 1 and 2 reproduce the readers' existing precedence exactly
— id, then unambiguous name — which is why a sale costed before the migration comes out with the
same product, the same cost and the same COGS after it.

**Where SQL cannot promise the Domain's answer, it does not answer.** SQLite's `NOCASE` folds ASCII
only and its `TRIM` removes the characters it is given, while .NET's `OrdinalIgnoreCase` and `Trim()`
cover the whole of Unicode. Over an all-ASCII catalogue the two rules are identical character for
character; over a catalogue holding any non-ASCII product name they are not provably identical, and
a backfill must never assign a product the current code would not. The name step is therefore skipped
entirely for a business whose catalogue holds a non-ASCII product name, and for a sale whose own
product name is not ASCII. Those sales are not guessed at either: the second gate below refuses the
release over every one of them a product's name attributes, so a human records the audited decision
instead of the attribution being lost.

**Two failure gates, for the two ways an attribution could be lost.** Step 2 ends by counting, and
aborting the migration over, each of:

1. **Costed.** A sale that carries a historical cost today (`CostingStatus`
   `Costed`/`LegacyEstimated`, or a stored `UnitCostAtSale`/`CostOfGoodsSold`) and would come out
   with no product. It would otherwise be dropped from every future cost replay while still carrying
   COGS.
2. **Attributed by a product name today.** A sale that is still unresolved, whose stored number names
   no product of its business, and whose reported name matches exactly one product — costed or not.
   Those are precisely the sales `ProductMatcher`'s name fallback attributed for every reader until
   this release and step 2 could not preserve, which is the "costed *or attributed to a product
   today*" half of #758's gate; leaving one unresolved would move its product-level revenue and its
   machine-stock attribution.

An unresolved sale that no product's name attributes and that carries no cost stops nothing — it is
reported as unresolved, exactly as an unmatched sale already was. That is also what keeps the gate
clearable: it only ever refuses a sale a human can name a product for. A conflicting sale is outside
gate 2 by its own definition (its stored number *does* name a product directly) and is caught by
gate 1 when it is costed.

**One shape SQLite cannot decide.** Two names differing only in the case of a non-ASCII character
match under .NET's fold and not under `NOCASE`, so gate 2 cannot see that such a sale was attributed.
`resolve-nayax-sale-products --dry-run` evaluates the real `ProductMatcher` rule in .NET and marks
every unresolved sale a product's name attributes today, which is what the pre-deploy count #758
requires is read from — so the one case the SQL fold is blind to is still in front of a human before
the release.

**Why two migrations.** The gate can stop the release, and a migration that aborts rolls its own work
back. Step 1 always succeeds, so the conflicts and the audit table survive a refused step 2; the
operator then records the decision through the command below — a human-invoked command that applies
no migration and therefore runs while the API is refusing to start — and the next start gets past the
gate. `AddNayaxSaleProductAssociationMigrationTests` covers both steps, both writers' row shapes, the
conflicting-and-uncosted case, the conflicting-and-costed refusal and its recovery, the name step's
audit row, the ambiguous and absent names, the cross-business refusal and the restricted delete —
and, for gate 2, an uncosted Unicode-named sale a product matches, an all-ASCII sale the catalogue
guard skipped (refused, then activating once the decision is recorded), and an unresolved sale no
product's name attributes, which activates the release rather than deadlocking it.

**Both migrations work with the code already in production**, which applies migrations at startup
(AGENTS.md § Database and migrations): every column and table they add is new, and the running code
neither reads nor writes any of them.

#### Deciding a conflicting sale: `resolve-nayax-sale-products`

How a conflicting sale gets a product after the migration, and a human-invoked command rather than a
screen, which parent #329 left out of scope here. It was the only such path until issue #738, which
added the one other: the catalogue review's sale resolution settles an unresolved sale whose stored
provider id is the one a product was just linked to, which is a different question from a conflict
between two recorded candidates and is deliberately never answered automatically either (see
[Provider catalogue review](#provider-catalogue-review-link-or-create-and-change-review-issue-738)).
Both only ever fill a null, through the same guarded statement, so neither can move a decided sale and
running one after the other changes nothing twice.

```bash
dotnet InventoryApi.dll resolve-nayax-sale-products --dry-run
dotnet InventoryApi.dll resolve-nayax-sale-products --decide 4821=5001 --decided-by "A. Operator" --apply
```

A dry run writes nothing and lists, per business, every unresolved sale with its own key, its
transaction and machine, its reported name, its provider id (only when the provenance is known), both
recorded candidates where there are any, whether it is costed today, and whether exactly one
product's name attributes it today — those last two counts being exactly what the failure gates
refuse to start over. The name answer is `ProductMatcher`'s own rule applied in
`ResolveNayaxSaleProducts` over the business's catalogue, never a rule of the store's, and it is
deliberately the Domain rule rather than the migration's SQL approximation. A conflicting sale is
never counted there: its stored number names a product directly, so the name fallback never ran for
it. `--apply` must be typed; `--decided-by` is
required with it, because who decided is part of the audit row. A decision names the **sale**, by the
local key the dry run prints: there is no `--business-id` flag, and the business is the one the
stored sale belongs to. Every write goes through `Inventory.Application.SaleProductResolution
.ResolveNayaxSaleProducts` over a context scoped to that business, fills only a null `ProductId`, and
appends a `NayaxSaleProductResolutions` row with the candidates, the chosen product, who decided and
when — so re-running an applied decision writes nothing and cannot move a sale off the product it
already carries. A product the business does not hold is refused before anything is staged.

**Filling the product is one guarded statement, not a comparison and then a write.**
`EfNayaxSaleProductResolutionStore.ApplyDecisionsAsync` claims each sale with an `ExecuteUpdate`
whose own predicate carries the expected null (`Id = @sale AND ProductId IS NULL`), inside a
transaction that commits the claim and its audit row together or neither. The "still unresolved"
test therefore happens in the database at the moment of the write: two runs that both read the sale
while it was unresolved cannot both succeed, the one that arrives second settles nothing and appends
no audit row claiming the previous value was null, and the audit trail never records a change that
did not happen. Because the `ExecuteUpdate` bypasses `SaveChanges`, the store calls
`SetBasedWriteEnforcer.RequireWritableScope` first, exactly as `EfNayaxConnectionStore` does for its
own conditional writes. `ResolveNayaxSaleProductsTests` pins both halves relationally: two contexts
that each read the unresolved sale first, and a batch whose second sale another writer settled in
between.

### Manual catalogue: who owns a product's fields (issue #736)

A business with no sales provider has to be able to keep its own catalogue, and a business with one
must not have the provider's values quietly overwritten locally. Issue #736 (parent #329 decision
P2) settles both with one idea: **a local row's fields are this business's, except the ones the
provider's import rewrites on every run.**

**The write surface.** `POST api/products`, `PUT api/products/{id}` and `DELETE api/products/{id}`
on `ProductsController`, and `POST api/categories`, `PUT api/categories/{id}` and
`DELETE api/categories/{id}` on `CategoriesController`. They declare the same `Inventory.Operate`
capability the catalogue reads declare — maintaining the catalogue is the same day-to-day inventory
work as refilling from it — so no capability is added, a read-only support session is refused them
by the central `GET`/`HEAD` rule (issue #551), and the business is resolved from the caller's
membership as everywhere else. `PUT api/products/{id}` now also binds `name` and
`categoryId`, which the request body always carried and the action used to ignore. It bound
`unitPrice` too until issue #792 removed the field (see [A product carries no selling
price](#a-product-carries-no-selling-price-issue-792)).

**Create and update validation, and the unit label's deliberate asymmetry** (issue #895).
`Inventory.Domain.Products.ProductCataloguePolicy` is the one statement of the invariants on the
fields an operator maintains by hand, and it holds two: a product has a **name**, and a product has
a **unit label**. The name rule is symmetric and unchanged — `CreateProduct` and `UpdateProduct`
both call `Validate`, so a product cannot be edited into a state it could not have been created in.
The unit label is required **asymmetrically**, and that is the rule rather than a concession to it:

- `POST api/products` refuses a null, empty or whitespace `unit` with `400` and
  `ProductCataloguePolicy.UnitRequiredMessage`, and saves nothing — not the product, and not the
  opening stock movement a quantity would have recorded. The check is `ValidateUnit`, applied by
  `CreateProduct`, because a create's answer depends on nothing but the request: a new product has no
  stored label to preserve. `EfProductStore.CreateAsync` applies it again at the write, exactly as it
  does for the name, so the column cannot be written blank by a future caller that forgets.
- `PUT api/products/{id}` refuses a null, empty or whitespace `unit` **only while the stored label is
  nonblank**, with the same `400` and the same message. So **no request can erase a label**, and a
  product whose stored label is already blank — a row from before this rule, which nothing ever gave
  one — is still accepted with none and keeps the blank it has. That exception exists because
  activation is written through the *whole* product: `ProductListComponent.writeActive` sends every
  field back with `isActive` flipped (issue #825's Deactivate, and issue #900's Reactivate), so a
  blanket required rule on `PUT` would have made every such legacy product impossible to deactivate
  or reactivate from the list. The rule is `ProductCataloguePolicy.UnitChangeRefusal`, and it is
  decided by `EfProductStore.UpdateAsync` — inside the write's own transaction, on the row that
  transaction read — for the same reason the provider-managed and category refusals are: it compares
  a *stored* value, so the read, the comparison and the write have to be one operation. `UpdateProduct`
  deliberately does not check it; checking the request alone could only either blank a label or
  strand a legacy row out of use.
- An accepted label is stored **trimmed** on both routes (`NormalizeUnit`) — trailing space is not a
  different unit — and the column's length and type limits are unchanged. The wire contract is
  unchanged too: `unit` stays nullable on `ProductCreateDto`/`ProductUpdateDto`, because what changed
  is which values are *accepted*, not which are bound.
- **Nothing is backfilled, and the provider paths are untouched.** A legacy product with no label
  stays readable with its history exactly as it is, and gets a label only when a person edits it.
  The catalogue import and the catalogue review still create a product without setting `Unit`, so the
  `Product.Unit` entity default `"unit"` applies, and a linked product keeps its own local label; no
  provider field is read for the unit, because the authoritative Lynx product contract publishes no
  unit or volume label at all (see [Provider catalogue
  review](#provider-catalogue-review-link-or-create-and-change-review-issue-738)). Proposing one
  from the provider is issue #902.

`ProductFormComponent` matches the server rather than wording a second rule: **New Product** and
**Edit Product** label the field `Unit Label *`, mark the input `required`, show
"Unit label is required." beside it and disable Save while it is blank, and submit the trimmed value.
**New Product opens the field empty** (no `"unit"` prefill, removed after #895 at the owner's
request), so an untouched field is refused rather than saving a label nobody chose. Editing a product whose stored label is null or blank opens
the field **empty** — the `p.unit ?? 'unit'` prefill is gone — so the operator chooses the label
instead of having one substituted and silently saved.

**Provider-managed fields.** `Inventory.Domain.Providers.ProviderManagedCatalogueFields` is the one
statement of which fields a provider owns: a product carrying an `ExternalProductId` has its `name`
and `categoryId` managed, a category carrying an `ExternalCategoryId` has its `name` managed, and a
row with no external id has nothing managed. The product and category responses publish that list as
`providerManagedFields`, so a client locks exactly the inputs the server refuses — the same function
produces both, which is what stops the lock and the enforcement from drifting apart. A *change* to a
managed field is refused with `400` and a message naming the provider; submitting the stored value is
not a change, so a client may send the whole row back, and the price, SKU, unit, restock
settings and active flag stay editable for every product. (A supplier was in that list until issue
#787 removed the field entirely — see
[A product carries no supplier](#a-product-carries-no-supplier-issue-787).) Nothing here clears an external id; if a
future provider switch (#761) does, the fields become editable again with no further change.

`providerManagedFields` is the key issue #736 appended to the catalogue response (issue #737 appended
`canDelete`/`deletionRefusal` after it; see below), and it is absent (`null`, omitted from the JSON)
wherever a product or category is carried inside another resource — a purchase line's or a supplier order line's product snapshot, a machine slot's product,
and a product's nested `category`. Those payloads are pinned contracts and none of them is an
editing surface, so they say nothing about locks rather than saying "none".

**Deletion.** `Inventory.Domain.Products.ProductDeletionPolicy` refuses a product that anything
refers to: stock movements, purchase lines, supplier order lines, sales (through the sale's own
persisted `ProductId`, issue #758), machine stock counts, and costing records (an inventory-cost
transition baseline or a costing repair). Two of those foreign keys cascade and four are restricted,
so without the refusal a delete would either erase inventory history or fail inside the database;
the refusal names what is in the way and points at `IsActive`, which is how a product is retired —
it keeps all of its history, stays out of the catalogue listing, the reorder alerts and the Pick
List, and can be reactivated. A
provider-managed product is refused for its own reason: the next import would create it again. The
`NayaxSales.ProductId` foreign key stays `Restrict`, never cascade and never set-null.
`Inventory.Domain.Categories.CategoryCataloguePolicy` refuses a category products still use, with
the count in the message, because `Product.CategoryId` is set to null when its category disappears.
A refused delete answers `409` with that message; a validation refusal answers `400`. Since issue
#737 the same product refusal is also readable *before* the attempt, on the catalogue reads - see
"Whether a product may be deleted is published" below; the delete's own transactional decision is
unchanged and remains the authority. **Since issue #1026, a category the business's sales provider
names is never deleted here either** - the same reason its rename is refused above:
`CategoryCataloguePolicy.ProviderCategoryDeletionRefusal` names the provider, and
`EfCategoryStore.DeleteAsync` checks `ExternalCategoryId` first, inside the same transaction, before
the product-count check, so the provider refusal wins when both apply. `CategoryListComponent`
hides **Delete** for such a row from the same `providerManagedFields` signal that locks its name.

**Whether a product may be deleted is published, by the rule that refuses the delete** (issue #737,
B2). The criterion is that **Delete** is offered only where the API allows it, which a client cannot
decide for itself: five of the six refusals are statements about stored rows. So the two reads a
person maintains the catalogue from answer the question instead.
`Inventory.Domain.Products.ProductDeletionEligibility.Decide` is a *projection* of
`ProductDeletionPolicy.Refusal`, not a second rule - it calls it - and
`EfProductCatalogStore.WithDeletionEligibilityAsync` hands it the same six counts over the same
tables the delete counts, for `ListOrderedByNameAsync` and `FindAsync`. `GET api/products` and
`GET api/products/{id}` publish the answer as two appended keys: `canDelete`, and `deletionRefusal`
carrying the exact message the delete would answer `409` with. `ProductListComponent` renders
**Delete** only on `canDelete: true` and offers nothing in its place on every other row;
`confirmDelete` refuses to open the confirmation for the same rows, so the write is unavailable
rather than merely invisible.

**Where the refusal is read, and what the row offers instead** (issue #825). The refusal is a
per-product explanation, so it is shown once, on that product's own page, rather than as a paragraph
on every ineligible row of the list: `ProductFormComponent` reads the same `canDelete`/
`deletionRefusal` from `GET api/products/{id}` and renders `deletionRefusal` **verbatim** in an
