amber `alert alert-warning` notice (a warning, not the red error style: it explains the product,
it does not report a failure) directly under the "Edit Product" header whenever `canDelete` is not a
plain `true`, falling back to "This product cannot be deleted." when the response carries no
wording. That notice is informational only - it gates no field, no Save and no other control, and is
rendered for an active product, a deactivated one and a support-session reader alike - and New
Product has none, because there is no product to answer for. The list row offers the action instead
of describing it: every **active** product gets a **Deactivate** button (beside Delete where
`canDelete` is `true`, alone where it is not), which opens the shared `ConfirmationDialogComponent`
naming the product and what deactivation keeps, and on confirmation writes the one existing
activation update - `ProductService.update` with `isActive: false` and every other field as it was
fetched. The Status badge routes a *deactivation* through that same confirmation, so the two
controls cannot come to mean different things, while a *reactivation* stays the single immediate
write it always was. Since issue #900 an **inactive** product gets **Reactivate** in that same
fixed-width slot instead of leaving it empty, calling the same `toggleActive` method the Status
badge uses for its own one-click reactivation - no second endpoint or payload. `confirmDeactivate`
refuses a support session and an already-inactive product in code as well as in the template, the
same belt-and-suspenders shape `confirmDelete` uses; `toggleActive` itself refuses a support session
the same way, hiding Reactivate alongside Deactivate and Delete. A refused deactivation or
reactivation surfaces the API's own message through `apiErrorMessage` with the row left as it was
fetched - both controls share that reporting because they share `toggleActive`. The deletion rule
itself is untouched: this is presentation, and `ProductDeletionPolicy` stays the one authority.

Three things keep that honest:

- **The advisory read never replaces the transactional one.** These counts are taken outside the
  delete's transaction, so a product can gain a stock movement, a sale or a provider link
  immediately afterwards. `EfProductStore.DeleteAsync` therefore counts again inside its own
  transaction and refuses there - unchanged by this issue - and the screen still shows a `409` it
  did not expect, with the row left in place. Concurrency is the reason the recheck exists, not a
  reason to withhold the answer from the screen.
- **An unanswered read is not permission.** `ProductRecord.DeletionEligibility` is `null`, and both
  keys are absent from the JSON, on every path that did not resolve it: `ListUnorderedAsync` (the
  reorder alerts, the home Dashboard summary and `ListMachineProducts` - none of them deletes a
  product, and the answer costs six grouped reads), a machine slot's product, and the product
  snapshots nested in a purchase or a supplier order. The screen offers **Delete** only on an
  explicit `true`.
- **It costs a fixed number of round trips.** Six grouped counts for the whole page rather than six
  per product, each reading one table once for every listed product id; the seventh kind, the stock
  movements, is counted from the rows the record's own include graph already loaded.

A category has no such answer: `CategoryCataloguePolicy.DeletionRefusal` depends only on a product
count, `Category` has no `IsActive` to retire one with, and nothing in #737's scope published a
category count on the response - so the categories screen attempts every delete and explains the
server's refusal, which names how many products use the category.

**Where each rule is decided.** The deterministic ones — a name is required, a price is not
negative, a category name is required — are Domain policies the use cases apply before anything is
read. The ones that are statements about *stored* rows are decided inside the EF adapter, in the
same relational transaction as the write: which provider-managed fields the row carries, whether the
category named belongs to this business, whether the name is already used, and what refers to the
product. That is deliberate rather than convenient: a use-case read followed by a separate write is
a window in which a product can gain a stock movement that the delete then cascades away, or a name
can be taken between the check and the insert. Category-name uniqueness is **not** a database
constraint — this issue adds no migration — so the window is the only thing holding it; the names
are compared without case or surrounding space, in memory over this business's own categories,
because SQLite's `=` on text is case-sensitive and its `LIKE` is case-insensitive only for ASCII.

**A product's category may not cross a business.** The category id is the one thing a request
supplies that could point a tenant-owned row at another business's, so create and update both check
it through the tenant-filtered read and refuse an unknown one with the same message either way — a
category of another business is invisible, exactly like one that does not exist.

**Creating a product with opening stock is one transaction.** `POST api/products` is the first
public path that writes stock through `IProductStore.CreateAsync`, and that create performs three
writes: the product, the opening `StockAdjustment` that explains its `QuantityInStock`, and the cost
rebuild that movement implies. `EfProductStore.CreateAsync` commits them as a single relational
transaction, so a cancellation or a failure part-way through leaves nothing at all rather than a
persisted quantity whose ledger and costing position were never written — under a request the caller
saw fail and would retry, which would otherwise create a second product beside the first.

**Retirement, and the two catalogues it creates.** `IsActive` is the retirement path the deletion
refusal points at, and a retired product is one the business has taken out of use: it must not be
offered to purchase from, count, pick or refill, and none of its history may move. So there are two
reads of the catalogue, and every caller says which one it wants —
`Inventory.Application.Products.ProductCatalogFilter.IncludeRetired` has no unset value:

- **The working catalogue** leaves retired products out, in the SQL
  (`EfProductCatalogStore.Filtered`, beside the search/category/supplier narrowing). It is what
  `GET api/products` answers, and therefore every product dropdown an Angular screen builds from it.
  The reorder alerts and the Pick List reach the same answer through their own Domain rules, which
  stay the authority there: `Inventory.Domain.Products.ProductReorderPolicy.IsReorderAlert` requires
  an active product, and `Inventory.Application.PickList.GetPickList` drops a retired product from
  the picking matrix with a stated rule rather than by absence (so does `SiteStockPolicy` for the
  site stock lists and `MachineRefillAlertPolicy` for the machine refill alerts).
- **The whole catalogue** is every product the business owns, asked for explicitly:
  `GET api/products?includeRetired=true`, and `ProductCatalogFilter.None` for the two internal
  consumers that resolve activity themselves — the home Dashboard summary and
  `ListMachineProducts`, where a machine slot or a refill alert naming a retired product must still
  be able to describe it. Narrowing `None` would silently stop both describing those rows.

**The name/SKU search ignores ASCII letter case** (issue #827), on both `GET api/products` and
`GET api/products/alerts/low-stock` — the two callers of `ProductCatalogFilter.Search` through the
same `EfProductCatalogStore.Filtered`. It is matched with `EF.Functions.Like` rather than
`string.Contains`: EF Core's SQLite provider translates `Contains` to `instr(...)`, which SQLite
compares byte-for-byte, where SQLite's `LIKE` folds ASCII letter case by default — the only
case-insensitivity SQLite offers without the collation change this issue left out of scope. `Filtered`
escapes `%`, `_` and the escape character itself in the typed search before wrapping it in the
leading and trailing `%` that make it a substring match, so a person searching for a literal `%` or
`_` matches that character rather than a wildcard. Non-ASCII letters are not folded (for example "É"
does not match "é"), because SQLite's default `LIKE` only folds ASCII.

Reading one product is unchanged by retirement: `GET api/products/{id}` answers a retired product
like any other, because retirement decides what a listing offers to work with, never what the
business may look at. That read, the explicit listing, and `PUT api/products/{id}` with
`isActive: true` are the reactivation path; all of the product's history, its machine slots and its
stock are untouched throughout.

**`GET api/products` hiding retired products is a deliberate read-contract change** (issue #736's
criterion that a deactivated product is hidden from lists, pick lists and reorder while keeping its
history and staying reactivatable). **The catalogue page passes `includeRetired=true` through its
Status filter since issue #737 (B2), now "Only active" (default)/"All" rather than a "Show retired"
checkbox (issue #791, E of #786 — see below)**, which is how a retired product is found again to
reactivate; the Admin costing-repair and AVCO-transition tools and the stock-history product filter
still call the endpoint without it and show active products only - picking those three up is
unrelated follow-up work, not part of #737. Nothing on the server depends on any of them.

#### Searchable category with inline category creation on New Product (issue #830)

Creating a product whose category does not exist yet meant leaving the form for **Categories**,
creating it there and starting the product again. Issue #830 removes that detour, and **no API, DTO,
schema, Domain rule, capability or duplicate-name policy changed with it**: this is one Angular
control sequencing the two endpoints #736 already shipped, `GET api/categories` and
`POST api/categories`.

**It is a dedicated feature component, not markup on the page.** Searching the options, filtering
them, offering the create, making that write and owning its pending, refusal and retry states is a
workflow with its own state and lifecycle, so `ProductCategoryPickerComponent`
(`components/products/product-category-picker`) owns all of it and the routed `ProductFormComponent`
keeps only the answer — the category id to submit, reported through `(categoryIdChange)`, with the
current selection passed down through `[categoryId]`. That is the
[page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) applied the same way issue #829's
`ProductCreateGstRuleComponent` applies it, and it is what makes a pending or refused *category*
write unable to touch a *product* field: the picker holds no product state and the page holds no
category state.

**What is submitted is an id, never text.** The box is a combobox (`role="combobox"`,
`aria-autocomplete="list"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-activedescendant`) over a labelled
`role="listbox"` of `role="option"` rows: "No category" first — the optional-category semantics the
replaced `<select>` carried as its `None` option — then the matching categories, then the create
action. Matching is a case-insensitive substring of the typed text, and whenever the list closes the
box's text is set back to the selected category's name (or empty). So text that matched nothing can
never be read as a selection, and leaving the field creates and selects nothing. Keyboard focus never
leaves the box: the rows carry `tabindex="-1"` and the active one is published through
`aria-activedescendant`, with Arrow keys moving (wrapping at both ends), Enter acting on the active
row, Escape dismissing, and Enter *while the list is open* kept off the product form's submit.

**Creating is explicit, and it is the existing create.** The create row appears only while the
options are known — read, and read successfully — the typed name is non-blank and no existing
category's name equals it ignoring case and surrounding whitespace — the same comparison
`CategoryCataloguePolicy` makes — and is labelled with the proposed name
("Create category “Choc Bars”"). Typing offers it; only activating it writes. `CategoryService.create`
posts the trimmed name to `POST api/categories`, so that endpoint's validation, its per-business
duplicate-name refusal and its `Inventory.Operate` capability decide the outcome, and the picker
words none of them: a refusal is shown verbatim through `apiErrorMessage`. On success the returned
category is added to the options in the server's own by-name order and selected, with every other
field on the product form untouched and no navigation.

**A pending create is the only thing that prevents a second one**, and it is checked in the component
as well as disabling the row, so the write is unavailable rather than merely inert. A refusal keeps
the typed name and the open list and **re-reads the options**, because the usual reason for one is
that the category now exists — created in another tab or by somebody else — and the answer to that is
that the existing category becomes selectable while the create row withdraws. The picker invents no
duplicate policy of its own. A failed option read says so and offers **Retry**, and still lets the
product be saved without a category, because a product's category is optional.

**While the options are unknown the list says nothing about them.** The create row is the answer to
"no category of yours is called this", and a read that is still in flight or has failed is not a
business with no such category — so neither it nor the "No category matches …" line is shown until
a read has succeeded, and the load error's own wording ("none can be searched or created here")
is what the panel then offers. A successful **Retry** keeps the typed name and the open list, so the
create it now knows is missing appears without the name being typed again. The alternative — offering
the create over options nobody read — would contradict both that message and the server's
duplicate-name refusal, which is the only authority on the name either way.

**A read-only support session is offered no create** (issue #551): a session grants
`Inventory.Operate`, so the row would otherwise render, and the backend refuses the write only by its
central `GET`/`HEAD` rule — the same reason the Categories page hides its own create. Searching and
selecting stay available, as every other field on the form does; Save is already disabled in a
session.

**The edit page is deliberately untouched.** `ProductFormComponent` renders the picker only on New
Product and keeps its `<select>` whenever there is a product id, because a provider-managed category
is locked there (`providerManagedFields`, above) and preserving that restriction exactly is worth
more than one shared control. The page also no longer reads the category list itself on New Product —
the picker reads it — so the options are fetched once either way.

#### Average cost and purchase cost columns, and the retired-product filter, on All Products (issue #791)

Issue #791 — E of parent #786 — is one of the three product screens (issues #789-#791) to
use `ProductPurchaseCostService`; it changes `ProductListComponent`'s filters and columns and adds
the `ProductPurchaseCostsComponent` feature component the page composes for that read, with no
backend change: `includeRetired` already existed, and #788 already owns the average-cost
availability projection this issue only displays.

- **The "Show retired" checkbox is now a Status filter.** `statusFilter: 'active' | 'all'`
  replaces the boolean `includeRetired` field; "Only active" (the default, and what Reset returns
  to) sends no `includeRetired`, and "All" sends `includeRetired=true` — the same two
  `GET api/products` reads issue #737 already defined, under clearer labels. The reactivation path
  and the "a deactivated product drops out of the 'Only active' list after the next refresh"
  behaviour are unchanged, because both were already properties of `includeRetired` and this issue
  only renames the control that sets it.
- **The Price column stays gone** (issue #792, A2 of #786): this issue adds no selling-price
  column or sort back.
- **The Status column is hidden while "Only active" is selected** (issue #828): since every row is
  active under that filter, its header and cells render nothing (`@if (statusFilter === 'all')` in
  the template, so the header and row cell counts stay equal in both states), including on first
  load and after Reset. Switching to "All" shows the column and its toggle again, unchanged from
  #825. Switching back to "Only active" while sorted by Status clears the sort back to the default
  order (`ProductListComponent.clearStatusSortWhenHidden`), rather than leaving it pointed at a
  column no longer on screen.
- **Three cost columns are added**, none of them computed in Angular: "Average cost" is
  `ProductResponse.averageUnitCostForDisplay` (issue #788) formatted to two decimals, `—` when it
  is absent and `$0.00` for a genuine recorded zero — the legacy `averageUnitCost` default is never
  read as evidence of a known cost. "Last purchase" and "Cheapest purchase" are
  `ProductPurchaseCostSummary.lastUnitCost`/`lowestUnitCost` with their suppliers
  (`lastSupplierName`/`lowestSupplierName`, `None` when null), from one
  `ProductPurchaseCostService.getSummaries(ids)` call per loaded product page, keyed by
  `productId`; a product absent from that answer has no recorded purchase, shown as `—`. All three
  columns are sortable through the same missing-values-sort-last mechanism
  (`compareSortValuesDirectionalNulls`) every other column here uses; Average cost sorts on
  `averageUnitCostForDisplay`, and Last/Cheapest purchase sort on their cost figure, never their
  supplier.
- **The purchase-cost read is its own feature component, not a second workflow inside the page.**
  `ProductPurchaseCostsComponent`
  (`components/products/product-purchase-costs/product-purchase-costs.component.ts`) owns the whole
  lifecycle of that read — when it starts, the capability that permits it, its
  loading/loaded/failed state, its failure message and the Retry control that re-enters it — and
  `ProductListComponent` composes it through `@Input`/`@Output` only: it passes `productIds` (the
  ids it is displaying) and records what `costsChange` publishes, which is one
  `{ state, summaries }` answer. That is [Page composition boundary (issue
  #191)](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191) applied to this screen: the routed page keeps its
  own filters, fetch, load state, sorting and layout, and nothing of the second read beyond laying
  its answer out. The two cost columns stay as cells in the page's own `<table>` — this codebase
  has no pattern for a child component contributing cells to a parent's table, and inventing one
  was not in this issue's scope — but the *rules* those cells follow are stated once, in that
  component's exported `purchaseCostDisplay`/`purchaseCostSupplierDisplay`/`purchaseCostSortValue`
  helpers, which the page calls rather than restates. Issues #789 and #790 (the other two product
  screens) can compose the same component instead of repeating the workflow.
- **Average cost is shown to every role**, matching `averageUnitCostForDisplay`'s own availability
  (issue #788). **Last purchase and Cheapest purchase, and the request behind them, require
  `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`** — `ProductListComponent.canViewFinancials` (the same fail-open-until-read
  field every other capability-gated control here starts from) hides both columns and their header
  cells for a role without it, and the bulk request is gated a second time, independently, inside
  `ProductPurchaseCostsComponent`, by a fresh one-shot read of
  `AccessService.allows('Dashboard.ViewFinancials')` taken before the request is ever issued — so no
  request reaches the endpoint for a role that may not see its answer, even during the fail-open
  window before the page's own capability read settles. The two reads are deliberately separate:
  one decides what is rendered and lives with the page's columns, the other decides whether a
  request may leave at all and lives with the request.
- **Three distinct states, decided in this order: loading, then failed, then the data.** A
  product set change (a new search, a new category, the Status filter, Reset) clears the previous
  purchase-cost results immediately and starts a fresh read; "Loading" shows while that read is in
  flight, "Unavailable" shows once it has failed (with a Retry control next to the table), and only
  a *successful* response may answer "—" for a product it did not find — never the other way
  round, so an in-flight or failed read is never misread as "no purchase history". A genuine `$0`
  last or cheapest cost displays as `$0.00` with its supplier, never `—`; an unknown supplier shows
  `None` independently of the cost.
- **Retry re-enters the same read for the same product ids**, and a stale or failed response can
  never overwrite a newer product/filter selection's results: the read for one product set is one
  switchable RxJS stream per set inside `ProductPurchaseCostsComponent` (the `productIds` input
  outer, `retry$`/the initial request inner), so a new product set arriving — from a filter change,
  not from Retry — unsubscribes whatever the previous set's stream was still waiting on, Retry
  included.

**The provider import was refused for a manual catalogue, and issue #739 removed that refusal by
removing the import it protected against.** `Inventory.Domain.Providers.ManualCatalogueImportPolicy`
answered `POST api/imports/products` with `409` and a count while the business held products with no
external id, because that import identified a product only by the provider's own id and would have
created a duplicate of each of them. Both the policy and the endpoint are gone: since #739 (decision
C2) the catalogue import *is* the review, for every business, so the state the refusal existed for is
the state the import now handles deliberately — the operator links each provider entry to a row they
name, or creates one. See
[Provider catalogue review](#provider-catalogue-review-link-or-create-and-change-review-issue-738)
and [The catalogue review screen](#the-catalogue-review-screen-issue-739) below. Nothing else about
this section changed: the provider still owns a linked row's name and category, the price is still
local and still editable, and a row with no external id is still the business's own in full.

### A supplier's optional website (issue #847)

A supplier record carries an optional website, `Supplier.Url`, so a buyer can open the supplier's
own ordering page from the Suppliers list. It is child A of #835 and independent of that issue's
other children.

**The schema.** `AddSupplierUrl` adds one nullable `Url` column of at most 2048 characters to
`Suppliers`. It is purely additive: no backfill, no table rebuild, no index and no other table.
Every supplier recorded before it keeps every value and gets `NULL`, which is the real state "no
website recorded" and is never an empty string. `Down` drops only that column.
`AddSupplierUrlMigrationTests` proves both directions, including that the upgrade adds exactly one
column and leaves the index list and the table list alone. The length is configured in
`AppDbContext` rather than with a `[MaxLength]` attribute on the entity, deliberately: an attribute
would have published a `maxLength` keyword on the legacy `Supplier` component below.

**One rule, written in the Application layer.** `Inventory.Application.Suppliers.SupplierUrlPolicy`
is the only place the rule lives on the server, and `CreateSupplier`/`UpdateSupplier` run it before
anything is stored, so a refused value creates nothing and leaves an existing supplier exactly as it
was. It is not a DTO attribute, because an attribute guards only the one contract it is written on,
and a stored URL is rendered as a link — which makes the accepted scheme a security boundary rather
than a formatting preference. The rule: the value is optional; blank or whitespace-only becomes
`null`; otherwise it is trimmed, must be at most 2048 characters, and must be an absolute URI with
scheme `http` or `https` (compared case-insensitively) and a non-empty host. `javascript:`, `data:`,
`file:`, `ftp:`, `mailto:`, a relative path and a scheme-less host name such as `coles.com.au` are
all refused with `400` and a field-level message on `url`
(`ValidationProblemDetails`, the same error contract model binding already produces). An accepted
value is stored as the operator typed it, trimmed and nothing else: re-serialising through `Uri`
would re-encode a path or append a trailing slash, storing a value nobody typed. An over-long value
is reported against the length rather than the scheme, so the message names the limit the caller
can act on.

**The server never fetches the URL.** Nothing resolves, follows, previews, scrapes or checks the
reachability of a supplier's website, and nothing infers GST status, an ABN or anything else from
it. The server stores text.

**It is in the nested `Supplier` component.** The `Supplier` entity's serialisable surface *is* the
published legacy `Supplier` component that a purchase's, a supplier order's and an operating
expense's nested `supplier` object references (see
[Purchase rename plan](#purchase-rename-plan)), so under the
owner's decision of 23 October 2026 `url` appears in all of them as an additive nullable string,
not hidden with `[JsonIgnore]` the way the GST defaults are. `SupplierResponse` gains it too and
stays schema-identical to that component. Nothing else about either schema moved: no rename, no
requiredness, no `maxLength` keyword and no repointed reference, which
`PublishedResponseSchemaContractTests` compares literally. `SupplierDto` accepts `url` on create and
update; `GET /api/suppliers`, `GET /api/suppliers/{id}` and every nested `supplier` return it, and
`null` when the supplier has none. Since issue #934 the two suppliers endpoints publish
`SupplierDetailResponse`, which carries `url` under the same name and in the same position and adds
the link state beside it; `SupplierResponse` is untouched and is still the nested component's shape
(see [The link, the lock and the "Not used" switch](#the-link-the-lock-and-the-not-used-switch-issue-934)).

**The frontend mirrors the rule and links carefully.**
`components/suppliers/supplier-url.ts` is the browser-side copy — same limit, same schemes, same two
messages — used both by the create/edit form, which refuses before the request, and by the list,
which renders a website as
`<a href=… target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">` only when that same check still accepts the
stored value. Anything else renders as plain text, so a value that somehow reached the database
without passing the server rule is never clickable. Angular's own URL sanitisation stays in place
behind that; no `bypassSecurityTrust*` call belongs anywhere near a supplier's website. The server
remains the authority: the form check is for the operator's benefit and for defence in depth, never
instead of the server's.

Everything else about a supplier is unchanged: its contacts, its
[GST defaults](#product-and-supplier-gst-rules-issue-430) on their own resource, the purchases,
supplier orders and operating expenses that name it, the `Purchasing.Operate` capability the
controller requires, the tenant query filters and the `BusinessId` stamp — which is still never read
from input.

**One supplier may not change its website: a copy of the platform's supplier master** (issue #934).
The rule above is unchanged — the submitted value is still normalised by this same policy before
anything else happens — but on a linked copy the normalised value is then compared with the stored
one, and a change is refused with `400` and that link rule's own sentence on the `url` field. A
supplier the business created itself is unaffected. See
[The link, the lock and the "Not used" switch](#the-link-the-lock-and-the-not-used-switch-issue-934).

### A product carries no supplier (issue #787)

A product held one supplier — `Product.SupplierId`, a nullable foreign key to `Suppliers` with
`OnDelete(SetNull)` — described as a default for ordering. **Nothing ever read it as one.** No
reorder, pick-list, purchasing, costing or reporting decision consulted it; the supplier-order
create has always taken its supplier from the request and validated it against the business's own
suppliers; and the per-product
[supplier price comparison](#supplier-product-price-history-and-comparison-issue-63) was always
derived from the purchase history instead. Issue #787 (A1 of #786) removed the field, its stored
values, and the whole surface built on it.

**Why removal rather than reinterpretation.** A supplier is a party to a transaction, so the place
to record one is the transaction: the purchase that was bought, and the supplier order that was
placed. Both of those already do, and both are untouched. A product bought from whoever is cheapest
this month has no single supplier, so a stored default on the catalogue row was a field that could
only be stale or wrong, and the one screen that pre-filled from it — the Needs Ordering order dialog
— was guessing at a decision about *this order*.

**The schema.** `RemoveProductSupplier` drops the column with its foreign key and its
`IX_Products_SupplierId` index. It is **destructive, by the repository owner's approval on
21 October 2026**, and it is the whole of what it touches: every other product column keeps its
value — the selling price `UnitPrice` explicitly, which the very next migration then removed under
its own approval (issue #792, see [A product carries no selling
price](#a-product-carries-no-selling-price-issue-792)) — and the table
keeps its own key, its category foreign key, and its `Sku`, `BusinessId` and filtered
`(BusinessId, ExternalProductId)` indexes. `Down` recreates the column, index and foreign key so the
schema matches the previous release's code, and every row comes back `NULL`: a dropped value is not
recoverable and nothing is inferred in its place. `RemoveProductSupplierMigrationTests` proves both
directions, including `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` finding nothing after the rebuild.

**The code.** `Product.SupplierId`/`Product.Supplier` and `Supplier.Products` are gone with their
`AppDbContext` relationship. `ProductRecord.SupplierId`/`Supplier` and `ProductSupplierRecord`,
`ProductCreateFields.SupplierId`, `ProductUpdateFields.SupplierId` and
`ProductCatalogFilter.SupplierId` are gone from `Inventory.Application`, and with them the
`Include(product => product.Supplier)` and the supplier `Where` in `EfProductCatalogStore` and the
two assignments in `EfProductStore`. `Products.SupplierId` left
[the platform diagnostics allowlist](#platform-diagnostics-issue-336) with the column, because that
allowlist names physical columns.

**The API contract breaks, deliberately and once.** `ProductResponse` no longer carries
`supplierId`/`supplier`, so neither does `GET /api/products`, `GET /api/products/{id}`, the reorder
listing, `GET /api/machines/{id}/products`, nor the product snapshot nested in a purchase line or a
supplier-order line (`PurchaseProductSummaryRecord`/`SupplierOrderProductSummaryRecord` lost the
field too). The keys are **removed, not nulled**: a product has no supplier to report, and an
explicit `null` would state "no supplier recorded", which is a different and now meaningless claim.
`GET /api/products` and `GET /api/products/alerts/low-stock` no longer bind a `supplierId` query
parameter, and `ProductCreateDto`/`ProductUpdateDto` no longer bind one either — a client that still
sends it is simply not bound, so the write succeeds and stores nothing for it, rather than being
refused. **The purchase's and the supplier order's own `supplier` is untouched** in the payload and
in the published `Supplier` component, which is what their contract tests and
`PublishedResponseSchemaContractTests` still assert.

**The UI.** The product form has no Supplier dropdown and loads no supplier list. All Products and
Needs Ordering lose their "All Suppliers" filter, their Supplier column and its sort; All Products
loads no supplier list either, while **Needs Ordering still does**, because its order dialog needs
one. The home Dashboard's Reorder Alerts table loses its Supplier column. `ProductNeedsOrderingComponent.openOrderForm`
opens with `orderForm.supplierId` **null** instead of inferring it from the selected products, and
the selector stays `required`, so an order still cannot be sent without a supplier a person chose.
The product edit page's supplier price comparison and its GST-rule note still speak of suppliers, and
should: both are about the purchases a product was actually bought in.

**What is explicitly not in this change.** `Product.UnitPrice`, the selling-price table columns and
catalogue price negotiation were issue #792, which has since removed all three (see [A product
carries no selling price](#a-product-carries-no-selling-price-issue-792)). The purchase summaries
and the other screen changes are issues #788–#791. No cost, average cost, inventory value, COGS,
reorder figure or stored purchase is recalculated or backfilled.

**Release sequence, because Production migrates at startup.** `DatabaseSchemaStartup` applies pending
migrations when the API starts (issue #201), so for a short period the deployed API is the previous
build running against a schema with no `Products.SupplierId`. That build's EF model still declares
the column, so **a product read or write by the old code fails until the new build is serving**;
purchases, supplier orders and everything else are unaffected. The deployment is therefore
human-sequenced in the ordinary way — one **Deploy Production** run for an exact `main` commit,
API first and then the frontend from the same commit — and the window is the API's own restart, not
a period either build can be left in. **Rolling back to a release that reads the column is not
supported**: `Down` restores an empty column, so the old build would read every product as having no
supplier, and the deleted associations do not come back.

### Supplier price catalogue (issue #923)

The section above is about who owns a *product's* fields. This one, the second task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817) after the [supplier-master fields](#the-supplier-master-fields-issue-931), is about what a product *costs at a supplier* — and specifically about not asking that question once per business. The owner's decision of 27 October 2026 is the whole design: *"we can't search Coca-Cola 375 five times because we have five businesses"*. So the catalogue of products and supplier listings is **shared**, and what each business keeps is a short statement that it wants one of *its* products priced and which shared product that is.

**That task was the schema, the ownership rules and the persistence adapters only.** The switch that creates and removes a mapping is [#938](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/938), described in [Tracking supplier prices on a product](#tracking-supplier-prices-on-a-product-issue-938) below; the collector work list and its authentication are [#924](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/924), automatic matching is [#941](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/941) and has since arrived ([Collector product matching](#collector-product-matching-issue-941)), and the Super Admin matching and review are [#928](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/928), which has arrived too ([Super Admin review of the supplier price catalogue](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928)) and is the only writer of `MasterProducts` there is. The price observations and the cheapest-unit comparison are [#925](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/925), which has since added them beside these tables ([Supplier price observations and comparison](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925)). **Nothing about an existing product, purchase, cost, inventory or report changed**: the migration is purely additive, it writes no data at all, and it adds no column to any existing table.

```text
MasterProducts (platform)              ProductPriceTrackings (tenant-owned)
  brand, name, size + unit               BusinessId  ← stamped, never from a request
  NormalisedKey (unique)                 ProductId   → Products (BusinessId, Id), cascade
        ▲            ▲                   MasterProductId ─────────────┐  restrict
        │ restrict   └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │                                Status, MatchSource
SupplierListings (platform)              WaitingKey, SearchName, UnitLabel
  SupplierPresetId → SupplierPresets, restrict
  exactly one of: MasterProductId | WaitingKey     ← database CHECK
  OriginWaitingKey        ← provenance, outside that CHECK
  SupplierProductId (unique per supplier preset)
  Url, Title, UnitsPerPack?, Barcode? + BarcodeScope?, MatchStatus

ProductMatchSuggestions (platform)
  WaitingKey, and exactly one of: MasterProductId | (brand, name, size, unit)   ← database CHECK
  Confidence, Reason, CollectorRun, Status (Tentative/AutoApplied/Accepted/Rejected/Undone)
```

**Three platform tables and one tenant-owned one, and the split is the design rather than a detail.** A brand, a name, a size, a supplier's shelf and a matcher's opinion about them are facts about *products*, so `MasterProduct`, `SupplierListing` and `ProductMatchSuggestion` are **platform** tables on exactly the terms `SupplierPreset` is — no `BusinessId`, no query filter, no ownership stamp — and they are declared in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests.PlatformEntities`, never in `DeliberatelyGlobalEntities` (see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)). `ProductPriceTracking` is the opposite: a business saying it wants one of its own products priced is that business's data, so it implements `IBusinessOwned` and gets the ordinary central treatment with **nothing added** — a required business key, an index leading with it, a global query filter, the stamp on insert and `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer`'s refusal of every cross-business write. One mapping per `(BusinessId, ProductId)`, scoped by business because two businesses may legitimately track the same product and a global constraint would let whichever tracked it first deny the other.

**The waiting key is the deduplication, and it carries no business identity.** `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.PriceCatalogueWaitingKey.For(searchName, unitLabel)` folds the two values with `PriceCatalogueKey` — every character upper-cased invariantly, every whitespace character dropped, each part written **length-prefixed** so no two different pairs can produce one key — so five businesses' five spellings of one product are **one** key and one search. Case and spacing, and nothing else: a hyphen stays, because merging `Coca-Cola` with `Coca Cola` would be the rule guessing at a difference it was not asked to erase. The fold is invariant rather than current-culture for the reason `SupplierPreset.NormalisedName` is. A master product's own `NormalisedKey` is the same builder over brand, name, size and unit code, stored under a unique index so "one description is one master product" is the database's rule rather than a `WHERE` clause two concurrent inserts can both pass — two master products for one product is what the parent issue exists to prevent.

**The encoding is length-prefixed rather than escaped, because escaping was not injective at a part boundary.** A part is written as its normalised character count, a `:`, then those characters, and the parts are joined by `|`: `PriceCatalogueKey.Of("Coca-Cola Classic", "375mL")` is `16:COCA-COLACLASSIC|5:375ML`, and a master product's key is `9:COCA-COLA|7:CLASSIC|3:375|2:ML`. Nothing is escaped, because the count says exactly where a part ends, so a part may contain `|` freely. The rule this replaced (PR #945, the owner's own reproduction) doubled a part's own `|` and then joined parts with a single one, which collapsed at the boundary: `Of("AB|", "CD")` and `Of("AB", "|CD")` both produced `AB|||CD`, so a brand ending in `|` could be refused as a duplicate of an unrelated description, and two businesses' unrelated products could deduplicate into one search and be priced as each other. Brand, name and a product's name and unit label are all free text with no character restriction, so that was reachable input rather than a theoretical case. A key is only ever compared and never decoded, but the framing is unambiguous in the strict sense — count, separator, characters, part for part — because master-product uniqueness and cross-business waiting-key deduplication both rest on exactly that. The stored key columns are bounded by `PriceCatalogueKey.MaxLengthOfParts` over the part limits, length prefixes included, so a widened part limit cannot leave a key column too narrow: 356 characters for a master product's `NormalisedKey`, 509 for every waiting-key column.

**The search text is captured when tracking is turned on, not derived on demand** (the owner, 27 October 2026). `SearchName` and `UnitLabel` are taken from the product's own `Name` and `Unit` and stored as plain text, so a product renamed afterwards keeps being searched for under the text the business was shown rather than silently changing what a collector looks for. A product with no unit label stores the **empty string**, not `null`: `Product.Unit` is nullable and the key is built from both parts, so "no unit label" must have exactly one spelling or one product becomes two searches. A name longer than `ProductPriceTrackingPolicy.MaxSearchNameLength` is refused rather than truncated, because a truncated search is a search for something else.

**The five mapping statuses are answers, never labels on each other.** `Requested` is waiting and is what the collector work list is a list of; `AutoMatched` is #941's answer and `Matched` is a settled one; `NotFound` is **looked for and not found**, which is a recorded outcome rather than a gap and is precisely what stops the same search running every run; and `AwaitingProductDetails` (added by #938's repair, below) is a mapping waiting on *its own product's* name and unit label rather than on the catalogue — it names no master product and the work list does not send it. `ProductPriceTrackingPolicy` holds the two consistency rules: a mapping names a master product in exactly the two matched states, and records `MatchSource` (`CollectorAutomaticMatch` or `SuperAdmin`) exactly when it names one. That rule is deliberately the Domain's rather than a check constraint, because expressing it in SQL would hard-code the status enum's numbers into migration history.

**A supplier listing belongs to exactly one of two owners, and the database says so.** Either `MasterProductId` — the normal state — or `WaitingKey`, the search the listing was discovered under before anything matched it. `CK_SupplierListings_OneOwner` refuses both and refuses neither, beside `SupplierListingPolicy.HasExactlyOneOwner`, because a row in either condition is not something an application-level check can be trusted to have prevented. **`OriginWaitingKey` is a second column precisely so that constraint can stay strict**: when a match moves a listing to a master product (#941) the active key has to be cleared, and which search found the listing is exactly what a reviewer of a wrong match needs afterwards — one column would have forced a choice between losing that provenance and breaking the exclusive rule.

**Unknown stays unknown, and a barcode is text.** `UnitsPerPack` is `null` when the supplier does not publish a pack size — never 1, which would make a carton's price read as a single's, and never 0, which divides — and a positive integer otherwise, checked by `CK_SupplierListings_UnitsPerPackPositive` as well as by the policy. The same restraint the [report availability model](#report-availability-model-issue-730) shows about a missing provider figure. `Barcode` is `TEXT` and is trimmed at the ends and otherwise never touched: `0012345678905` and `12345678905` are different barcodes and the leading zeros are not recoverable once a column has parsed them away. It travels with `BarcodeScope` (`Unit` or `Carton`) — `CK_SupplierListings_BarcodeAndScopeTogether` refuses either alone — because a carton code read as a unit code prices one can at the price of thirty. A master product's size is a positive decimal of at most three decimal places in the closed unit list `ml`, `l`, `g`, `kg`, `each`; a finer value is **refused rather than rounded**, because a per-unit price divides by it.

**The match suggestions are kept forever, and that is the point of the table.** One row per suggestion with its `Confidence`, `Reason` and `CollectorRun`, proposing *either* an existing master product *or* a complete description of a new one (`CK_ProductMatchSuggestions_OneProposal`) — two different things to do about one waiting key, and a row holding both would leave #928's reviewer unable to tell which was meant. A `Rejected` or `Undone` `(waiting key, master product)` pair is never deleted and is what `ProductMatchSuggestionPolicy.BlocksAutomaticMatching` reads, so #941 cannot re-apply a pair a person refused: a matcher that forgot a rejection would repeat it every run. A later suggestion for the same pair is a third row rather than something that replaces the refusals, and the master product a kept refusal names cannot be deleted from under it — every reference in this catalogue **restricts**, with one exception.

**The one cascade is the mapping's own product**, on the products' `(BusinessId, Id)` business key, which is also what makes a mapping unable to name another business's product even in principle. A mapping is a statement *about* a product and has no meaning without it; restricting there would mean a product could no longer be deleted once somebody had asked for its price, which would be exactly the change to existing product behaviour this issue forbids.

**Two Application ports, and neither takes or publishes a business.** `IProductPriceTrackingStore` is one business's own mappings — since #938 track, untrack, find by product, list and find by id — read and written through the central filters and the stamp, with no `IgnoreQueryFilters`, no raw SQL, no unscoped context and no hand-written `WHERE BusinessId = …` in `EfProductPriceTrackingStore`; another business's mapping is unreachable by listing and by id alike. `IPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` is the two deduplicated reads [#924](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/924) will be built from: the products awaiting a match, as distinct `(search name, unit label)` pairs by waiting key with one deterministically chosen spelling each, and the distinct master products any mapping points at with their listings, one per `(supplier preset, supplier product id)`. Two businesses tracking one master product produce **one** entry, because that read names the master products the mappings point at instead of joining the mappings to the listings. Neither answer has anywhere to carry a business id, a product id or a count of who is waiting — asserted on the record shapes themselves, since that is the only place such a value could travel.

**Who may read the work list across businesses was left to #924, and #924 decided it.** Issue #923 shipped `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` reading the mappings through the ordinary tenant query filters and recorded that the caller was a tenancy decision in its own right rather than an implementation detail. That decision is made: the collector is not an actor, it carries a denied scope, and the adapter makes one reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` read over the mappings' business-free text columns — see [Collector work list](#collector-work-list-issue-924) and [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The two reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` paths.

**What proves it.** `MasterProductPolicyTests`, `SupplierListingPolicyTests`, `PriceCatalogueWaitingKeyTests`, `ProductPriceTrackingPolicyTests` and `ProductMatchSuggestionPolicyTests` cover the Domain rules: the size scale and its refusal to round, the closed unit list, the pack rule including zero, the barcode's leading zeros and its scope in both directions, the fold's two halves (case and spacing folded, punctuation not), the part-boundary cases the length prefix exists for — `("AB|", "CD")` against `("AB", "|CD")`, separator-only and empty parts, a brand ending in the separator against a name beginning with it, and equivalent spellings of a part containing one still folding to one key — and the status/master/source combinations. `SupplierPriceCatalogueConstraintTests` is the relational half over the real migration history: a listing with both or neither owner refused, the origin key surviving the move to a master product, the pack, size, barcode and one-proposal checks, the two uniqueness rules in both directions (one description refused twice, and two descriptions differing only at a part boundary kept as two master products), the restricted references, and the rejected and undone pair kept beside a later suggestion for the same pair. `EfProductPriceTrackingStoreTests` and `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStoreTests` run over **two** businesses: the stamp, the captured search text, a denied scope writing nothing, another business's mapping unreachable by listing and by id, a business unable to track another's product, one mapping per product, the master-product restrict, a product delete still cascading its mapping and leaving every other alone, the awaiting-match deduplication ignoring case and spacing, two search texts differing only at a part boundary staying two searches, `NotFound` and matched mappings not being re-sent, a suspended mapping sent to **neither** collector read, two businesses tracking one master product producing one entry with its listings once, and the same adapter answering for one business alone under that business's scope. `AddSupplierPriceCatalogueMigrationTests` is the upgrade from the previous schema: the four tables created empty, the check constraints declared, the business key and indexes on the mapping table and **no** business column on the three platform ones, a seeded business, product, supplier, purchase and purchase line unchanged column for column, and the `Down` removing the four tables and nothing else. `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests` holds the two classifications, including that the platform list is now five and that it does not overlap the structurally global one.

### Tracking supplier prices on a product (issue #938)

The section above is the shared catalogue's schema. This one, the fourth task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), is what finally puts something into it from a business's side: the product form's **"Track supplier prices"** switch. A business chooses which of its products should have supplier prices checked and can see whether each one has been matched yet; nothing was ever sent to the collector before, because [#923](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/923) deliberately shipped the `ProductPriceTracking` mapping with no writer.

**The product's own name and unit label are the search text** (the owner's decision of 27 October 2026): "Coca-Cola Classic" and "375mL", captured when the switch goes on and stored as plain text beside the mapping. Nothing a caller submits decides either — `PUT /api/products/{id}/price-tracking` carries one boolean.

```text
GET  api/products/price-tracking          → [{ productId, status }]            ← currently no frontend caller (issue #1022)
GET  api/products/{id}/price-tracking     → { productId, tracked, status, searchName, unitLabel,
                                              masterProduct?: { name, sizeValue, sizeUnit },
                                              canTrack, trackRefusal }
PUT  api/products/{id}/price-tracking     ← { tracked }        204 · 400 refusal · 404 unknown product
```

**No new capability, and the two read-only states refuse the write without being mentioned.** All three actions sit on `ProductsController`'s existing `Inventory.Operate` — the "existing product-edit capability" the issue names — because deciding which of its products a business wants priced is the same day-to-day catalogue work as the rest of that controller. The write is refused in a read-only support session and in a Super Admin's role preview by those features' own method rules (`SupportSessionAccessPolicy`, `RolePreviewPolicy`), not by anything written on the controller, exactly as #934's "Not used" switch and #935's supplier add are; the two reads are `GET`s a support session may make.

**A real unit label is required, and the generic one is not a real label.** `ProductPriceTrackingPolicy.IsTrackableUnitLabel` refuses a blank label and the generic default `"unit"` — which every product the provider catalogue import creates carries, because `Product.Unit` defaults to it. Searching a supplier's shelf for "Coca-Cola Classic unit" matches nothing, and a mapping created from it would wait forever on a search that could never succeed, which is worse than a refusal because waiting looks like progress. The comparison is ordinal-ignore-case on the trimmed value, so `"Unit"` and `"  unit  "` are the same placeholder; everything else is accepted as typed, including `"can"` and `"units"`, because this rule is not in the business of judging which real labels are good ones. **The rule is stated once and read twice**: the write refuses with `ProductPriceTrackingPolicy.UnitLabelNotSpecificMessage`, and the status read publishes that same sentence as `trackRefusal` beside `canTrack` — the shape the product's own `canDelete`/`deletionRefusal` already has (issue #737) — so the switch explains itself without the Angular component wording the rule a second time. **Changing the unit-label rules themselves is out of scope** (#895): this issue adds a gate on turning tracking *on* and changes nothing about what a product may be saved with.

**The turn-on is one atomic operation, and that is what makes it authoritative.** `EfProductPriceTrackingStore.TrackAsync` opens the `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction of `SqliteWriteLockTransaction` — the same write lock #935's supplier add and #896's machine delete take — and *then*, with the lock held, reads the product's name and unit label, decides the unit-label rule, checks for an existing mapping, and inserts. A deferred transaction would not do: it takes the write lock at the first *write*, which is after the reads the capture was made from, and a captured name that is no longer the product's name is a search for something else. So a rename, a unit-label edit or another tab's switch either lands before the lock and is seen, or waits behind it. The per-business unique index on `(BusinessId, ProductId)` is the backstop under that for a writer this process did not serialise with, and its violation is translated into the *same* answer the in-lock read gives — `AlreadyTracked`, a `204` — by `IsDuplicateMapping`, which recognises that one constraint and nothing else. Both directions are idempotent for the same reason: the switch states an intention, so a double click, a second tab or a retried request needs no different answer.

**A new mapping is a request and nothing more.** Its status is always `Requested`, its master product and match source are `null`, and no endpoint here can set any of them: deciding *which* master product a product is belongs to the automatic matcher (#941) and the Super Admin review (#928). A business asking for a price is not a business asserting what its product is.

**Turning tracking off removes one row of one tenant-owned table.** No master product, supplier listing, match suggestion or price observation is touched — the mapping's reference to a master product *restricts*, so removing a mapping cannot reach it even in principle — and no other business's mapping is reachable to touch. A business that names another business's product id gets `404` for the read and for both directions of the write, because the product is resolved through the central tenant query filters: knowing a real product id of another business yields nothing and writes nothing.

**The matched status publishes the master product's name and size, and that is the third member-facing read of a platform table.** `MasterProduct` is shared across every business, so what a business endpoint may say about one was fixed by this issue's own review before the code existed — the name and the size of a *matched* mapping's master product, and nothing else. The brand is stored on that row and is deliberately **not** published, and nor is the row key, the normalised key, an instant, a supplier listing or a price. The limits, and why a wider projection needs its own reviewed issue, are in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64). **"The business never sees which other businesses track the same product" is true by construction rather than by filtering**: a master product carries no business identity at all, so there is nothing on it to leak, and the mapping half of every answer is the caller's own row.

**Editing the product's name or unit label follows the mapping, inside the product update's own transaction.** `ProductPriceTrackingPolicy.RefreshFor` is the one rule and `TrackedProductSearchTextRefresh` applies it from `EfProductStore.UpdateAsync` — beside the four refusals that method already decides (issues #736 and #895), for the same reason: the comparison is against *stored* text, so the read, the comparison and the write are one operation.

| The mapping is | and the edit changes | then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Requested` | the name, the unit label, or both | the search text and the waiting key both move; the status stays `Requested` |
| `AutoMatched` or `Matched` | the **unit label**, to another real size | it returns to `Requested` with the new text, and the master product and match source are cleared — the size the match rests on may no longer agree |
| `AutoMatched` or `Matched` | the **name only** | the match is kept, and so is the text it was decided from, which is what a reviewer of a wrong match needs |
| `Requested`, `AutoMatched` or `Matched` | the name or unit label **to something unsearchable** — the generic `unit`, a blank label, or a name longer than `MaxSearchNameLength` | it is **suspended**: the status becomes `AwaitingProductDetails`, the master product and match source are cleared, and the stored text is left as it is because nothing reads it in that state |
| `AwaitingProductDetails` | the name or unit label, to anything still unsearchable | nothing: it is already waiting on the product |
| `AwaitingProductDetails` | the name or unit label, to something searchable | the product's **current** name and unit label are captured afresh and it returns to `Requested` — unconditionally, even when the corrected text is the text it was suspended with, because the status itself is the change |
| `NotFound` | anything | nothing: "looked for and not found" is a recorded answer, and re-running a search that came back empty is what recording it prevents |

**The suspension is the review repair of this issue, and it is what keeps a changed size from being priced as the old one.** Reviewed head `2b94fe9` left a matched mapping exactly as it was when the unit label became the generic `unit`: the master product, the match source and the previous size's search text all stood, so that master product's prices could still be read as this product's and the collector could still be sent "Coca-Cola Classic 375mL" for a product that no longer says it is 375 mL. `AwaitingProductDetails` is the state that says the truth instead — nothing is matched, nothing is searched, and `trackRefusal` is the sentence that says how to resume it. It is a fifth status rather than a flag beside the four because the four are *answers about the catalogue* and this one is an answer about the product: a boolean beside `Requested` would have been a second thing the work-list query had to remember to check, and the query already checks the status.

Three things that rule deliberately does **not** do. It never creates or removes a mapping, so an edit of an untracked product is byte for byte the write it always was, and a suspended mapping is kept rather than deleted because the business never withdrew its request. **It refuses nothing**: an otherwise valid product edit succeeds for a tracked product exactly as it does for an untracked one, because what a product may be saved with is the unit-label rule of #895 and this issue changes none of it — the mapping reports a state instead of vetoing a catalogue edit. And it reads through the central query filters, so one business's product edit cannot reach another business's mapping, including for the product whose text folds to the same waiting key: the other business's match of the same master product stays matched and stays eligible. One limitation remains, and it is the criteria's own: #941's matcher is the natural place to revisit a `NotFound` mapping whose product was renamed, which this issue was not asked to decide.

**The Angular side is a composed panel.** `ProductPriceTrackingComponent` owns the switch — its own read, its own write, its loading, refusal and error states — and the product-edit page only hands it the product id (issue #191's [page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191)), exactly as the GST rule panel above it works. It saves separately from the product form because tracking is its own API resource. What the checkbox shows is what is **stored**, never what was clicked: the control is put straight back to the model on change and moves only when a re-read says the server stored it, so a refused or failed write cannot leave a switch saying the opposite of what the business has. Turning *off* stays available for a product whose label has since become generic, or a business tracked before #938 existed could not withdraw a search it can no longer start. A **suspended** mapping reads as `Paused - this product cannot be searched for` with the server's own `trackRefusal` sentence under it and **no** "Searched for as" line, because nothing is being searched for and the text the row still holds is the product's previous size; the sentence is shown whenever the server reports one, tracking on or off, since on it is the only thing that says how to resume. New Product offers no switch at all — there is no product yet, and the search text is read from the stored row rather than from the form — and says where to find it instead; bulk turning tracking on for many products is explicitly out of scope. The catalogue listing carried a plain-projection **Tracked** column of `GET api/products/price-tracking` until issue #1022 removed it, because it only repeated what the Cheapest supplier column (issue #940) already states for the same product; that endpoint now has no frontend caller, and the Products list relies on the Cheapest supplier column instead, with all five statuses still visible on the Edit page's Track supplier prices panel described in this section.

**What proves it.** `ProductPriceTrackingSwitchPolicyTests` (unit) is the rules: every blank and generic spelling of the unit label refused and five real ones accepted, each refusal's own sentence, the capture's trimming and its key, and the refresh table above state by state — including saving the same text refreshing nothing, every unsearchable edit (the generic label in three spellings, and a name past the limit) suspending the mapping from each of the three live states, a further unsearchable edit of a suspended mapping changing nothing, a correction resuming it with the current text, a correction *back to the stored text* still resuming it, and `NotFound` still left alone. Two of those tests replaced the earlier assertions that an edit to the generic label refreshed nothing: that rule intentionally changed on review and was not weakened. `ProductPriceTrackingUseCaseTests` covers what the use cases add: the eligibility answer published from the stored product (including a tracked product whose label became generic, which reads as tracked *and* not trackable), the index violation translated to "already tracked" while any other failure is not, and the tracked list carrying a product id and a status each. `EfProductPriceTrackingStoreTests` is the relational half over **two** businesses and the real migration history: the stamp, the captured search text, the blank and generic refusals writing nothing, a denied scope writing nothing, another business's product untrackable and its tracking state unreadable, one mapping per product with the real index's refusal recognised, the turn-off leaving the master product, the listing and the other business's mapping untouched, both idempotent directions, the matched read in both matched states and the absence of a master product in the other two, and the refresh table through the real `EfProductStore` — including that editing an untracked product creates no mapping, that one business's edit leaves the other's mapping exactly as it was, that relabelling a matched product to the generic label leaves the edit **accepted** with the mapping suspended, its master product and match source cleared, that master product still present with its listing and no longer eligible for *either* collector read, that correcting the label to another real size resumes the mapping with the new text and key while the old master product stays unmatched, and that suspending one business's mapping leaves the other business's match of the **same** master product matched and still eligible. `ProductPriceTrackingApiTests` is the whole pipeline over the two synthetic E2E businesses: the switch on and off, the status read, the generic-label refusal and its published reason, every status including auto-matched with the master product's name and size, the published keys of both responses, the refresh cases through the ordinary `PUT api/products/{id}` — including the suspension of a matched and an auto-matched product with the published state, the published refusal sentence, the cleared row, the `Paused` entry in the tracked list, the untouched master product, listing and other business's match, and the correction that resumes it with the new search text and waiting key — the tracked list holding only the caller's own products, and `404` in both directions for another business's product — plus the decisive assertion that the matched description carries **only** `name`, `sizeValue` and `sizeUnit` and that the master product's brand, a supplier listing's id and the other business's name appear nowhere in the body. `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests`, `SupportSessionRequestApiTests` and `RolePreviewApiTests` pin the capability and the two read-only refusals. On the frontend, `product-price-tracking.component.spec.ts` covers the switch, the unit-label message and the five statuses (including the switch that must not lie after a failed write, turning off a product that could no longer be turned on with its reason now shown, the paused mapping's line with no "Searched for as" text, and the corrected one reading as awaiting a match again), `product-form.component.spec.ts` the panel's placement and its absence on New Product, and `product.service.spec.ts` the three requests. `product-list.component.spec.ts` instead asserts the Products list has no Tracked column and makes no `GET api/products/price-tracking` request at all (issue #1022).

### Supplier price observations and comparison (issue #925)

The section above stores what a supplier *lists*. This one, the third task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), stores what that listing **cost on a day**, and answers the question the whole parent issue exists for: which of a business's own suppliers is cheapest per vending unit for one product, on the GST basis that business actually pays.

**This task is the storage and one pure policy.** Nothing read the comparison when it shipped, and nothing wrote the tables: [#937](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/937) is their writer and did arrive — see [Collector results](#collector-results-issue-937). What reads the comparison is the summary endpoint and shared column of [#930](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/930), in [the section below](#the-cheapest-supplier-summary-and-the-cheapest-supplier-column-issue-930). **No existing product, purchase, cost, inventory, GST or report behaviour changed**, and that is pinned by a test rather than asserted in prose — see *The boundary* below.

```text
PriceCollectorRuns (platform)            SupplierPriceObservations (platform, append-only)
  StartedAtUtc, CompletedAtUtc?            SupplierListingId → SupplierListings, restrict
  Status (Running/Succeeded/               PriceCollectorRunId → PriceCollectorRuns, restrict
          PartiallySucceeded/Failed)       PackPrice, RegularPackPrice?, Currency = 'AUD'
  ListingsCheckedCount                     PriceBasis (ex/inc GST, as observed)
  ObservationsRecordedCount                SupplierGstRate?            ← the supplier's own rate
  FailureCount                             IsPromotion + PromotionEndsAtUtc?
                                           StockStatus (InStock/OutOfStock/Unknown)
SupplierPresets (platform, #931)           ObservedAtUtc               ← freshness is measured here
  + PriceCheckFreshnessHours               SourceReference?, SourceUrl?
      30 daily · 102 for BIG W             CreatedAtUtc                ← no updated instant
SupplierListings (platform, #923)
  + LatestObservationId? → SupplierPriceObservations, restrict
  + LastCheckedAtUtc?        ← last successful check
  + LastPriceChangeAtUtc?    ← when the price last moved
```

**Two more platform tables, for the reason the three beside them are.** What a supplier charged for a pack, and the run that read it, are facts about that supplier's shelf: `PriceCollectorRun` and `SupplierPriceObservation` carry no `BusinessId`, no query filter and no ownership stamp, and they are declared in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests.PlatformEntities`, never in `DeliberatelyGlobalEntities` (see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)). An observation names the listing it is a price *of* and never anybody who wanted that price, which is what keeps one business from learning that another is tracking anything. The migration is additive — two tables, four columns, two check constraints — and it writes exactly one value, which the next paragraph is about.

**The observations table is append-only and raw.** There is no `UpdatedAtUtc`: a correction is a later observation, never an edit of a stored one, and the amounts, the basis and the stock answer are kept exactly as published. That is the separation AGENTS.md § Nayax integration requires of imported facts — the raw fact and the derived comparison stay apart so the comparison can be rerun and audited — and it is why the per-unit figure is nowhere in the schema: it is `pack price ÷ units per pack`, derived at full precision and rounded only where something is displayed.

**The freshness limit is stored per supplier master record, and that is a deliberate schema decision rather than a convenience.** `SupplierPreset.PriceCheckFreshnessHours` is the owner's decision of 27 October 2026: 30 hours for a supplier checked daily, 102 for BIG W, which is checked on Thursday and Sunday. Both numbers are the longest expected gap between two checks (24 and 96) **plus a six-hour margin**, and the margin is the whole reason the limit is not the gap: a run that starts a little later than yesterday's would otherwise mark every price it has not re-read yet as stale, and a price nobody can compare is worse guidance than a price that is a few hours old. `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.SupplierPriceFreshnessPolicy` owns that arithmetic (`LimitForCheckInterval` is how a third cadence would be derived rather than invented), the accepted range and the staleness boundary; the column holds one supplier's answer. **Nothing in the application names a supplier**: the column default is the daily limit, and `AddSupplierPriceObservations` set 102 on the one shipped record whose cadence the owner stated, as an `UPDATE` over one normalised name that matches at most one row — the shape `AddSupplierPresetMasterFields` used to record that same record's collection route. A limit of zero is refused by the policy and by a check constraint, because it would read as "never stale" or "always stale" depending on who resolved it.

**A listing keeps three facts about its own price checks, and a failed check changes none of them.** `LatestObservationId` is the latest accepted observation, `LastCheckedAtUtc` the last *successful* check and `LastPriceChangeAtUtc` when the price last moved — three columns rather than one "last updated", because a daily re-read that finds the same price answers "how old is this price?" and not "when did this supplier last move it?", and the comparison needs the first while a person deciding whether a supplier has shifted needs the second. **None of them is ever cleared.** A run that fails, or that never reaches a listing, leaves all three exactly as they were and `SupplierPriceFreshnessPolicy` is what eventually stops that price being compared — the owner's own constraint, because every run searches by name (#926) and a listing missing from a day's results is a missed check rather than a supplier with no price. Emptying them on a failure would be the mistake the [report availability model](#report-availability-model-issue-730) exists to prevent: a missing figure read as a zero. `SupplierListingPriceStatePolicy` and `CK_SupplierListings_PriceStateConsistent` hold the one consistency rule — the observation and the check instant are recorded together, and a price that was never observed cannot have changed — and the pointer at the observation **restricts**, so the last good price cannot be removed by tidying the price history.

**The GST basis comes from two stored facts, in a fixed precedence** (the owner, 27 October 2026). What an observed price *means* is the supplier master record's basis (`SupplierPreset.PricesIncludeGst`, [the supplier-master fields](#the-supplier-master-fields-issue-931)), **copied onto each observation as it was observed** rather than read back through the supplier — a supplier that changes how it publishes prices must not silently restate every price already observed on the other basis. What rate applies comes from the product: the supplier's own per-product rate when it publishes one (the JB Metro `gst` field, stored on the observation), otherwise the product's own GST rule ([Product and supplier GST rules](#product-and-supplier-gst-rules-issue-430)) — `Taxable` is 10%, `GstFree` is nothing at all, and `GstRules.None` is **no rate**, not zero. If neither is known the offer is **shown and not compared**, on the basis it was observed on, because assuming a rate would put a price on the wrong side of the tax and name the wrong supplier cheapest.

**The comparison is `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.CheapestUnitOfferPolicy`, and it is deliberately not the purchase one.** `Inventory.Domain.Purchases.SupplierPriceComparisonPolicy` (issue #63) compares the unit costs a business has actually **paid**, from its own immutable purchase history, and feeds the product page's lowest-versus-latest view; this one compares prices this application has **observed** on suppliers' shelves, for packs nobody has bought, and feeds purchasing guidance only. The names say which — a purchase price history against a cheapest unit offer — and neither reads the other. The new policy is pure: given the candidate offers, the product's rate, the comparison basis and an instant, it returns each offer's unit price **ex-GST and inc-GST at full precision**, the reason an offer could not be compared, and the cheapest comparable offers with **every tie** in them. Both figures are always published so the UI never derives the other one; the **comparison basis follows `Business.GstRegistered`** (ex-GST for a registered business, inc-GST otherwise), which is also the displayed basis, because "cheapest" and "the smallest number on the page" have to be the same offer. There is no cheapest when nothing is comparable: the cheapest price is `null` and the list is empty, never `0`, which is a price and the cheapest one there is.

**Six reasons an offer is ineligible, and an ineligible offer is still shown with its reason**: the pack size is unknown (so there is no per-unit price at all — never 1, which reads a carton as a single, and never 0, which divides); the listing's match is not confirmed (a proposed match may be another product, and pricing from it would present the matcher's guess as the cheapest supplier); the GST rate is unknown; the supplier said it is out of stock (an **unknown** stock answer is still compared — a supplier that says nothing about availability has not said the product is gone); its promotion has ended, which is true at the stated end instant and never true of a promotion with no stated end; or it is stale under that supplier's own freshness limit. Exactly one reason is reported, in the order the issue states them, so a page shows the first thing that has to change rather than arguing with itself about which of two true statements to display. Candidacy itself is the caller's: only the business's own linked, not-hidden suppliers take part ([Supplier records by business state, and "Available to add"](#supplier-records-by-business-state-and-available-to-add-issue-935)), and the policy compares whatever it is handed.

**The boundary: observed supplier prices never become money the business has recorded.** They never reach a purchase, a unit cost, an `AverageUnitCost`, an `InventoryValue`, a COGS figure, a GST accounting figure or a line of any report, and `SupplierPriceObservationBoundaryTests` pins that in two directions: no file in the named purchase, cost, inventory, GST and reporting areas may so much as name these tables or policies, and the only production files that name them at all are a declared list — the Domain policies, the entities, the supplier listing and master record that carry the new columns, `AppDbContext`, and the collector's own use cases, adapters and contracts. The next reader is a reviewed decision: #937 arrived at that list on purpose and writes them, and #930's summary port, use case, adapter, DTOs and controller arrived at that declared list on purpose. The rule is also an invariant in AGENTS.md § Observed supplier prices.

**What proves it.** `CheapestUnitOfferPolicyTests` covers the comparison: the pack arithmetic and its full precision, an inc-GST and an ex-GST supplier for one product compared on each basis, GST-free and taxable products, a supplier's own rate beating the product's rule, an unknown rate shown and not compared on both bases, ties including across differently scaled decimals, each of the six ineligibility reasons, the order they are reported in when several hold, staleness at 30 hours and at 102, the promotion-end boundary in both directions, no eligible offer, no candidates at all, and
