the refusals of a rate that is not a proportion and a basis that is not declared. `SupplierPriceFreshnessPolicyTests` covers the limits themselves, including that one price can be fresh for a twice-weekly supplier and stale for a daily one. `SupplierPriceObservationPolicyTests`, `PriceCollectorRunPolicyTests` and `SupplierListingPriceStatePolicyTests` cover what may be stored. `SupplierPriceObservationStorageTests` is the relational half over the real migration history: an observation stored and read back fact for fact, its unknowns still unknown, the latest observation per listing with its tie-break, **a failed run that records nothing leaving the last good price, its check instant and its change instant exactly as they were**, a re-read at the same price moving only the check instant, every check constraint's refusal, the restricted references in all three directions, and the stored rows joined into the comparison policy's own candidate shape — which is also where the shipped BIG W record is shown to carry 102 hours and every other record 30. `AddSupplierPriceObservationsMigrationTests` is the upgrade from the previous schema: the two tables created empty, the constraints declared, no business column on either, the one decided value written, every shipped supplier record otherwise identical column for column **across the SQLite table rebuild** that adding a constraint to an existing table requires, a pre-existing listing carried across with its three new columns empty, the seeded business, product, purchase and purchase line unchanged, and the `Down` removing the two tables and the four columns and nothing else.

### The cheapest-supplier summary and the Cheapest supplier column (issue #930)

The section above compares offers; this one, the fifth task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), is what a person finally sees. On Needs Ordering each tracked product shows its cheapest supplier per unit — "JB Metro $0.95/unit (special)" — and clicking it opens a popup listing every one of the business's own suppliers with their prices. The Dashboard's Reorder Alerts ([#939](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/939), delivered as the Dashboard's Reorder priorities column by [#981](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/981)) and Products ([#940](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/940)) are the same column on two more pages and are outside this task; this one ships the endpoint, the shared component and Needs Ordering.

**One endpoint, called with a page's product ids.**

```text
POST api/cheapest-suppliers/summary   ← { productIds: [ … ] }        Dashboard.View
                                      → { displayBasis,
                                          products: [ { productId, trackingStatus?, cheapestUnitPrice?,
                                                        suppliers: [ { supplierId, supplierName,
                                                                       hasListing, hasPrice,
                                                                       packQuantity?, packPrice?, packPriceBasis?,
                                                                       unitPrice?, unitPriceExGst?, unitPriceIncGst?,
                                                                       isSpecial, promotionEndsAtUtc?,
                                                                       stockStatus?, lastCheckedAtUtc?,
                                                                       productUrl?, ineligibility?,
                                                                       isCheapest } ] } ] }
                                        400 · no ids, or more than 200 distinct ones
```

**A `POST` that changes nothing, and only because of the id list** (the review finding of 27 October 2026, which fixed both the method and the maximum): a page of up to 200 ids does not belong in a query string. It takes 1 to 200 distinct ids — duplicates collapse first, so a page that listed a product twice asks once and never spends part of its allowance on a repeat — and an empty list or more than 200 is `400` before anything is read. One consequence is deliberate rather than overlooked: a read-only support session refuses every non-`GET` request ([Support sessions in the request pipeline](#support-sessions-in-the-request-pipeline-issue-551)), so the column reports itself unavailable in a support view instead of being specially permitted.

**And the Starter plan, since issue #977.** The controller declares `[RequirePlan(PlanFeature.ObservedSupplierPrices)]`, so a business whose effective plan is Free is refused `403` with the `plan_required` code and the plan it would need, after the capability check and before anything is read — while a Free business still switches tracking on and off, and the collector is no longer sent out for products only Free businesses track. See [Plan enforcement on supplier price data](#plan-enforcement-on-supplier-price-data-issue-977).

**`Dashboard.View`, which Operator, Manager and Owner all hold.** An observed shelf price is purchasing guidance about a pack nobody has bought, so it is deliberately *not* behind `Dashboard.ViewFinancials`, which guards what the business actually **paid** (issue #788's purchase-cost summary, two columns away on the same table). It is its own controller for the reason that one is: a controller declares one capability, and putting this action on `ProductsController` would have given it the catalogue's.

**The business is resolved from the caller's membership and the read is bounded by their own mappings.** `GetCheapestSupplierSummary` resolves the business, `ICheapestSupplierSummaryStore` makes five statements — the business's own `GstRegistered`, its linked not-hidden suppliers, its products among the ids asked for, their mappings, and finally the listings of the master products *those mappings name* from the supplier records *this business holds a copy of* — and the Domain policy does the rest. An id of another business matches nothing and is **absent** from the answer rather than refused, which is the same answer an id that exists nowhere gives, so nothing confirms that an id exists somewhere. This is the fourth member-facing read of a platform table and is bounded by issue #930's own review; see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64).

**Every figure is `CheapestUnitOfferPolicy`'s** ([the section above](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925)). The use case hands it stored facts and arranges its answer; the controller maps it; the Angular component formats it. None of the three divides a pack price, converts between GST bases, decides a basis, ranks offers or picks a cheapest — a second copy of that arithmetic is exactly what one shared endpoint and one shared component exist to prevent. `displayBasis` is published so a page labels its figures rather than guessing: ex-GST for a GST-registered business, inc-GST otherwise, and a business that has recorded no answer is treated as not registered, which shows it the price it actually hands over. Unit prices travel unrounded on both bases; the only rounding is `toFixed(2)` where a figure is displayed.

**What is not a price stays not a price.** A supplier that does not list the product is published as itself with `hasListing: false` ("Woolworths: no match") rather than left out; a listing nobody has checked yet carries `hasPrice: false` ("Not checked yet"), which is not a missing supplier and never `0`; an offer that could not be compared carries its one `ineligibility` reason and is still listed; and a product that is matched but has no comparable offer has `cheapestUnitPrice: null`. A product the business does not track, or whose mapping is waiting, suspended or recorded as not found, carries its status and **no supplier rows at all** — there is no master product whose listings they would be, and a popup of suppliers all saying "no match" would read as an answer about a product nobody has looked for yet.

**One shared standalone component, in two halves.** `CheapestSuppliersComponent` owns the read for a page's rows — when it starts, the batching into requests of at most 200 ids, its loading/loaded/failed state, its own failure message and the Retry that re-enters it, and the support-session case where it asks for nothing at all — and publishes the answers keyed by product id. `CheapestSupplierCellComponent` is the cell and its popup: the cell shows the cheapest supplier and unit price on the business's basis, or `Loading`, `Unavailable`, `Not tracked`, `Awaiting match`, `No match found` or `No eligible price`, and only a successful read may say anything about a product. Clicking opens a modal dialog — labelled by the product's name, focused on open, closed by Escape, the backdrop or Close, returning focus to the cell — listing every supplier in the server's own order (comparable offers cheapest first, then the ones it could not compare, then the unchecked listings, then the suppliers with no match) with pack size, pack price, unit price on **both** bases, special, stock, last check and a link to the supplier's page, a note that these are observed prices and not recorded costs, and "Matched automatically" when the match was the collector's and nobody has checked it ([#941](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/941)). Both live in `components/shared/cheapest-supplier/`, so #939 and #940 add a column rather than a second answer, and the page keeps its own dialog markup out of a routed template ([Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191)).

**The popup is a native modal `<dialog>`, because that is the only way "modal" is true** (the source-review finding of 28 October 2026). It is opened with `showModal()`, so the browser puts the panel in its top layer, makes the rest of the page inert and paints the overlay as the panel's own `::backdrop`: the page behind it cannot be clicked, tabbed into or reached by assistive technology while it is open. The first shape of this popup was the repository's older pattern — a fixed backdrop `div` around a `div` carrying `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` — which focused itself and returned focus on closing but trapped nothing, so a keyboard user could Tab straight out of a panel that told a screen reader it was modal. The element therefore carries **no** `role` or `aria-modal` of its own (the platform maps a modal `<dialog>` to both), and its dismissal, Tab cycle and focus return are bound in the component rather than in the markup: `::backdrop` is the panel's own pseudo-element, so an outside click arrives on the panel and is told apart from a click on its content by the event's target, and the panel's `keydown` answers Escape and every Tab itself so the cycle — panel → first control → … → last control → first — is one definition in one place instead of an assumption about the browser's. Closing closes the dialog *before* moving focus, because the cell underneath cannot take focus while the page is still inert. This popup is deliberately the only one changed: the older pattern beside it (`ConfirmationDialogComponent`, `product-price-history`, `MachineRestockSyncComponent`) has the same gap and its own follow-up, and reproducing a gap for consistency is not a reason.

**Last checked is a true instant, so it is the business's own clock.** Each supplier row renders `lastCheckedAtUtc` through `BusinessDateTimePipe` in the current business's configured IANA zone, never through Angular's `date` pipe in the operator's accidental browser zone — a check made at 04:00 UTC is mid-afternoon in Sydney and the small hours of the same date in New York, and the shown day has to be the business's. `SupplierListing.LastCheckedAtUtc` carries the `AppDbContext` UTC conversion that keeps the `Z` on it (serialised instant identity at the persistence boundary, [Time](#time)), so the instant the pipe parses is unambiguous. A zone that is not known yet renders nothing rather than a confidently wrong time, and blank is not `Never`: that answer belongs to a listing nobody has checked.

**Needs Ordering shows the column and changes nothing else.** It is the last column before the row's action, it is deliberately **not sortable** (sorting by price is outside this issue, and a sort over values still arriving would reorder the page under the reader), and the existing purchase-cost columns, the row behaviour, the capability gating and the support-session controls are untouched.

**What proves it.** `CheapestSupplierSummaryTests` covers the use case over a fake store: the request bound in both directions and exactly at it, a repeated id read once, the basis for a registered and an unregistered business with both figures published, ties, each of the six ineligibility reasons passed through with the offer still listed, a supplier with no listing, a listing with no observation, an unmatched and an untracked product, an automatic match, and an id the store does not answer for. `EfCheapestSupplierSummaryStoreTests` is the relational half over two businesses and the real migration history: only the caller's own products answered, a caller with no resolved business reading nothing at all, only linked not-hidden suppliers, the listings reached through the caller's own matched mapping with the supplier's freshness limit, a listing with no observation, the price being the one the listing *points at* rather than the newest row, an unmatched mapping reading no listings, and the business's own GST registration. `CheapestSupplierSummaryApiTests` is the whole pipeline over both E2E businesses: the cheapest named per unit, hidden and unlinked suppliers excluded, a supplier with no listing published, the basis following `GstRegistered`, ties, an ineligibility reason, an automatic match, an untracked product, the other business's product ignored while it is tracked and matched to the same master product, the published keys in order, and a body that contains no other business's name, no master product brand and no catalogue key. `CapabilityAuthorizationApiTests` holds the capability row. On the frontend, `cheapest-supplier.service.spec.ts` covers the batching and the collapse of duplicates, `cheapest-suppliers.component.spec.ts` the one-request-per-page lifecycle, the failure message and Retry and the support session, `cheapest-supplier-cell.component.spec.ts` every cell state, the popup's content and order and its keyboard and screen-reader behaviour, and `product-needs-ordering.component.cheapest-supplier.spec.ts` the page: one request for the rows on screen, a cell per row, the popup, and a failed read leaving the rest of the page usable. The popup's modality is covered by the half of it this component owns: that it opens with `showModal()` and never `show()`, that Tab and Shift+Tab from the panel and from either end of its cycle stay on the popup's own controls — asserted over real `keydown` events and `document.activeElement`, with a live control on the page behind it that the cycle never reaches — and that Escape, the browser's own close request, a click beside the panel and Close each close it and return focus to the cell, while a click on the content does not. The other half is the platform's: `jsdom` implements no top layer, no inert and no `::backdrop`, so `setup-jest.ts` supplies only `<dialog>`'s open/close state machine and the specs assert the call that makes the page inert rather than the inertness of a stub. Last checked has its own cases in both zones, one instant either side of each zone's daylight-saving transitions, plus the unresolved-zone case that must render nothing and the unchecked listing that must still say `Never`.

### Collector work list (issue #924)

`GET /api/price-collector/work` is the one thing the scheduled price collector reads. How it authenticates is [The price collector's app-only path](#the-price-collectors-app-only-path-issue-924); this section is what it is answered with, what that costs in tenancy terms, and what is stored so a result can be believed. Parent design: issue #817, the owner's design and decisions of 27 October 2026.

**Reading the work list is a write, and that is the point.** Issuing a run stores a `PriceCollectorRun` and one `PriceCollectorWorkItem` per product-and-supplier pair **before** the list is answered, in one transaction, and expires any run still open. Every result row of #937 — including a newly found pack — references the work item it answers, which is what makes "did the collector search this, and what happened?" a recorded fact rather than something inferred from whether a price turned up. It is therefore a `GET` that is deliberately not idempotent in the "changes nothing" sense; what it *is* is safe to repeat, because a second call cannot leave two open runs.

**One run open at a time, and expiring is not failing.** `PriceCollectorRunPolicy` gained a fifth status, `Expired`, and a run carries its own `ExpiresAtUtc` — `PriceCollector__RunExpiryHours` after it was issued, defaulting to the owner's six hours. A run is expired either by its own expiry passing or by a later run being issued, and it is expired **in the same transaction** as that later run, so there is never an instant with two open runs and never one with none because the expiry committed and the issue did not. `Expired` is its own outcome rather than a `Failed` one: a failed run reported failing, an expired run reported nothing at all, and the difference is what answers "did the collector run last night?". The lifetime is stored on the run rather than recomputed from today's setting, so editing the setting cannot retroactively expire or revive work already issued; the runs #925 shipped the table for carry no expiry and are expired by nothing automatically.

**What the response carries, and what it cannot.** The run id and its instants; the suppliers due on this run with their collection route (`priceConnector`, `priceConnectorKey`, and the record's own `siteUrl`, which is what the JB Metro route talks to); every distinct **matched** product as its master-product description with the listings the catalogue already holds for it — listing id, the supplier's own product id, the confirmed units per pack and the last successful check instant, so a known listing is recognisable in search results; every distinct product **awaiting a match** as its stored search name and unit label with its waiting key, the proposals a previous run already found under that key, and the master products a Super Admin rejected or undid for it; and, **only while something is actually waiting**, the master products to match against (the owner's decision of 27 October 2026, for the automatic and tentative matching of #941). Under each product, one work item per due supplier, each with its own id. The listings, proposals and refusals under a product are bounded per product, and a product whose context was omitted says so — see the bound paragraphs below. There is **no business id, business name, business product id or price anywhere in it** — asserted both over the whole serialized response and structurally, on the published record shapes, because that is the only place such a value could travel.

**One entry per product, however many businesses track it.** That is the parent issue's whole business outcome — "we can't search Coca-Cola 375 five times because we have five businesses" — and it is the #923 port's job rather than a second grouping rule here: matched products are read as the distinct master products the mappings *name*, and waiting products as distinct waiting keys with one deterministically chosen spelling each.

**And since issue #977, only the mappings of businesses whose plan includes the observed supplier prices.** The adapter decides that itself, from those businesses' plan records and the Domain's own entitlement rule, and the deduplication above is what turns it into "at least one entitled business": a matched product is issued while one entitled business tracks it, a waiting key while one entitled business's product folds to it, a product a Free and an entitled business both track is still issued once, and a product only Free businesses track is absent with nothing about it removed. While plan enforcement is not being enforced — the shipped state — no plan record is read and both statements are unchanged. See [Plan enforcement on supplier price data](#plan-enforcement-on-supplier-price-data-issue-977).

**Which suppliers are due comes from each supplier's own record.** `PriceCollectorWorkListPolicy.IsSupplierDue` is the one rule: a supplier is due when the platform still suggests it, something collects its prices at all, and either it has never been checked successfully or its own check interval has elapsed since the most recent successful check of any of its listings. The interval is `SupplierPreset.PriceCheckFreshnessHours` **less** `SupplierPriceFreshnessPolicy.MarginHours` — the exact inverse of how that limit was derived — so a deployment records one cadence per supplier and nothing in the code names a supplier. A supplier with no connector is never due, however stale it is: Costco is in that state, and a route that cannot be taken is not work. A last check in the future leaves a supplier not due, for the same reason an observation from the future is treated as fresh.

**The response is bounded, and it says when it was.** `PriceCollectorWorkListPolicy.MaxWorkItemsPerRun` (2000) bounds the work, and `MaxMasterProductsForMatching` (5000) bounds the matching vocabulary separately, because that list grows with the whole catalogue rather than with the run. A product is added to the run only when there is budget for a work item against **every** due supplier, so no published product is half-issued and every result row can cite its work item; when the budget runs out the response sets `workItemLimitReached` rather than returning a silent prefix, because a truncated work list nobody is told about reads as "this is everything there is to search". The stretch is deterministic — matched products by master product id, then waiting products by waiting key — so two reads of an oversized catalogue in the same state agree.

**And the bound is a schedule rather than a cut-off.** The products form one rotation in that order, and a run starts at the product **after** the one the most recently issued run stopped at, wrapping around to the beginning. The cursor is read from the work that was actually issued — the last work item of the newest run, which is written in publish order (`IPriceCollectorRunStore.LastIssuedWorkAsync`) — so there is no counter to keep in step with it and nothing to migrate. That is what makes "every run searches every distinct tracked product" true for a catalogue larger than one run's budget: the products one run omits are the next run's first, and the whole catalogue is searched over successive runs. Without the rotation a bounded run would re-issue the same prefix for ever and everything past it would never be priced at all. The comparison is on the stored master product id and the ordinal waiting key (`MatchedProductComesAfter`, `WaitingProductComesAfter`), not on a position, so a product added or removed between two runs cannot send the rotation back to the start.

**What travels under each product is bounded too, and an omission is never silent.** The work-item limit bounds how many *products* a run carries and says nothing about how much travels under each, so one product whose catalogue entry holds ten thousand listings would otherwise be an unbounded response that honoured every other limit. `MaxListingsPerProduct` (50) bounds a matched product's known listings and a waiting key's proposals, and `MaxRefusedMasterProductsPerWaitingProduct` (100) bounds that key's refusals. A product beyond a bound is still issued its work and is published with **none** of that context and the omission stated — `knownListingsOmitted`, `proposedListingsOmitted` — rather than with an unflagged prefix that would read as the product's whole catalogue entry; what is lost is a recognition aid, and a listing the collector re-reports is reconciled by the unique `(supplier master record, supplier product id)` pair. The refusals are the one case with a **rule** attached, because they are a safeguard rather than context: a key beyond their bound is published with no refusals and `matchingSuppressed`, which means no master product may be proposed or applied for that key on that run (#941). Half a refusal list would let a pair a Super Admin rejected be proposed a second time, so it is never sent. The reads themselves are bounded, not only the response: `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` reads the listings, proposals and refusals **for the products the run was issued for** and counts them per product in one grouped statement before reading any, so a product beyond a bound is never materialised in full.

**The tenancy cost, stated plainly.** Two platform tables are written and one tenant-owned table is read across businesses. `PriceCollectorRuns` and `PriceCollectorWorkItems` are about no business — a product description and a supplier's shelf — so they carry no `BusinessId`, no query filter and no ownership stamp, and `PriceCollectorWorkItem` is the **eighth** entry in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests.PlatformEntities` (see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)). The read is the one issue #923 left for this issue to review: `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStore` makes two `IgnoreQueryFilters` statements over `ProductPriceTracking`, projecting the waiting key, the search name, the unit label and the master product id, because under the denied scope a collector carries the central filter matches no mapping at all and the work list would be silently empty. What makes it safe is the **projection** — none of those four says whose product a mapping is — and what bounds it is **authorization**: the only endpoint that reaches the adapter is class 5, and no member, Super Admin or support session can call it. Issue #977 added the plan read that narrows those two statements to the entitled businesses — the ownership key, the plan and the period of the businesses that hold a plan record, read only while enforcement is on and never published — which is the fifth reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` path and is described in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) and [Plan enforcement on supplier price data](#plan-enforcement-on-supplier-price-data-issue-977). A wider projection, a further such path, an unscoped context or raw SQL here is a boundary change needing its own reviewed issue.

**The schema.** `AddPriceCollectorWorkItems` is additive: one table, `PriceCollectorRuns.ExpiresAtUtc`, and an index on the run status. Every reference restricts — a run, a supplier master record and a master product cannot be deleted from under the work issued against them. Two check constraints are the database's as well as `PriceCollectorWorkItemPolicy`'s: exactly one of `MasterProductId` and `WaitingKey`, and an outcome with its instant or neither. "One work item per product and supplier in a run" is **two filtered unique indexes** rather than one over four columns, because SQLite treats `NULL`s as distinct in a unique index and one of those two key columns is always `NULL` — a single index would have enforced nothing while appearing to state the rule. The outcome vocabulary (`Complete`, `Truncated`, `NoMatches`, `Failed`, `NotSearched`, and **empty** for issued-and-not-reported) stays the Domain's, because expressing it in SQL would hard-code the enum's numbers into migration history; #937 is what writes one.

**What proves it.** `PriceCollectorWorkListPolicyTests` and `PriceCollectorWorkItemPolicyTests` cover the Domain rules: the cadence boundary for a daily and a twice-weekly supplier derived from the stored limit, a supplier with no connector and a disabled one never due, a future check instant, a limit inside the margin, the budget clamp and its refusal of a non-positive one, the two context bounds being their own positive limits, where a bounded run continues from (no cursor, a matched cursor's higher ids, a waiting cursor's ordinally greater keys, and no matched product coming after a waiting cursor), the exactly-one-product rule including a blank waiting key, and the outcome vocabulary including the empty state. `PriceCollectorRunPolicyTests` adds the lifetime and the expired status. `PriceCollectorWorkListTests` runs the whole use case over **two** businesses on the denied scope a collector request carries: one product two businesses track appearing once with its known listings, a waiting product appearing once with its proposals and only the rejected and undone pairs, the matching list sent only while something is waiting, no supplier due meaning no work and no published product, two due suppliers producing two work items per product with their routes, every published work item stored against the run with an empty outcome and ids unique within it, a second run expiring the first and keeping its work, the configured lifetime stored, the response carrying neither business's name nor any business or price field, an oversized catalogue yielding a flagged deterministic stretch, **five successive runs with a budget of one product issuing the whole rotation and then coming round again** — matched products first, the waiting products behind them next, each with its own stored work item in its own run, which is the regression for the starvation an unrotated bound has — a product with more listings than a run may carry published without them and flagged while the product beside it keeps all of its, a waiting key with more proposals than a run may carry published without them and flagged, and a key with more refusals than a run may carry published with no refusals and matching suppressed while the key beside it keeps its one refusal. `EfPriceCatalogueWorkListStoreTests` adds the adapter half of the bounds: the tracked products ordered by their own key because that is what the rotation continues from, and a product, a waiting key's proposals and a key's refusals each answered as "beyond the bound" with none of their rows while the one beside them keeps all of its — with a pair refused twice counting once, so a key inside the bound is not pushed past it by one person's two decisions. `PriceCollectorWorkItemConstraintTests` is the relational half: both check constraints' refusals by name, one work item per pair per run with the same pair accepted in a later run, and the three restricted references. `AddPriceCollectorWorkItemsMigrationTests` is the upgrade: the table created empty, both constraints and both filtered unique indexes declared, #925's own constraint surviving the rebuild, no business column, a pre-existing run unchanged column for column **with a null expiry**, and the `Down` removing the table, the index and the column and nothing else.

### Collector results (issue #937)

The section above hands the collector its work. This one, the fifth task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), is what happens when it reports back — and it exists because of one sentence in the owner's decision of 27 October 2026: *"the backend must still enforce product matching, quantities and price validation before accepting results"*. **Claude's output is untrusted input.** A search run by a model can match the wrong product, read the wrong pack size or lose a decimal point, and each of those is a wrong "cheapest supplier" rather than a visible error, so nothing a collector sends decides anything on its own.

Three endpoints, all class 5 on the collector's own app-only path ([The price collector's app-only path](#the-price-collectors-app-only-path-issue-924)):

- `POST /api/price-collector/results` — one batch of rows for one run, at most 200 of them.
- `POST /api/price-collector/work-items/{workItemId}/outcome` — finishes one search.
- `POST /api/price-collector/runs/{runId}/complete` — closes the run.

```text
PriceCollectorResultRows (platform)            SupplierListingPendingObservations (platform)
  PriceCollectorRunId      → restrict            SupplierListingId  → cascade, UNIQUE
  PriceCollectorWorkItemId → restrict            PriceCollectorRunId      → restrict
  SupplierProductId                              PriceCollectorWorkItemId → restrict
  UNIQUE(run, work item, supplier product id)    Reason           ← why it was held
      ← the idempotency key                      PackPrice, Currency, PriceBasis, GST rate,
  Outcome (Accepted/SentToReview/                  promotion, stock, ObservedAtUtc, source
           Pending/Rejected)                      Variant, SizeValue/Unit, Barcode/Scope,
  Reason?, SupplierListingId?,                      UnitsPerPack, Title ← the identity read
  SupplierPriceObservationId?                    RecordedAtUtc

SupplierListings  + Variant, SizeValue?, SizeUnit?   ← the identity a row is checked against
                  + LastNotFoundAtUtc?               ← only a *complete* search writes it
PriceCollectorRuns + CompleteSearchCount, TruncatedSearchCount, NoMatchesSearchCount,
                     FailedSearchCount, NotSearchedCount        ← one count per outcome
PriceCollectorWorkItems + FailureReason?, SubmittedRowCount?
```

**A row cannot choose its own product, and the contract is the first reason it cannot.** A submitted row carries no listing id and no product id at all. Which listing it is comes from the unique `(supplier master record, supplier product id)` pair; which product that listing belongs to comes from the **work item** — a master product, or the waiting key of a product nothing has matched yet. A row citing a work item nothing issued, one from another run, or one issued for a different supplier is refused (`unknown work item`, `work item belongs to another run`, `supplier differs from the work item's supplier`).

**Same-run key resolution.** A work item issued for a waiting key is resolved, *when its rows are processed*, to the master product that key has been matched to since the list was issued — by [#941](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/941)'s automatic matching earlier in the same run ([Collector product matching](#collector-product-matching-issue-941), whose own end-to-end test is this property), or by a Super Admin. The match is read from the suggestion that applied it (`ProductMatchSuggestion` in `AutoApplied` or `Accepted`), which is the platform's own record of "this key is that product". Its rows then attach to that master product, and a known listing already under that master is **this** product's listing rather than another product's. A listing still held under the key is this product's listing too: moving it to the master product is #941's and #928's work, never a result's.

**No silent re-linking, and the refusal is itself evidence.** If the supplier product id already belongs to a listing linked to a different product, the row is refused with `listing belongs to another product` and the existing link is not touched — only #928 may change it. When the work item is a waiting key and that listing belongs to a master product, the refusal is also recorded as a **tentative `ProductMatchSuggestion`** for that key, once per pair: the search found evidence that the key and the master product may be the same thing, and the Super Admin is who decides. A pair that already has a suggestion — a rejected one above all — gets no second row, because the refusals are kept precisely so a pair is never proposed twice.

**What a row becomes depends on the listing's match status, and only a confirmed listing can produce a price.** `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.PriceCollectorResultPolicy` is the one rule and it stores nothing:

| Listing | Row becomes |
| --- | --- |
| New (never seen) | **Pending** — created `Proposed`, its first reading held, never a price |
| `Proposed` / `NeedsReview` | **Pending** — reading held, listing untouched |
| `Rejected`, identity unchanged | **Rejected** (`listing was rejected`) |
| `Rejected`, identity changed | **SentToReview** — back to `Proposed`, reading held |
| `Confirmed`, identity changed | **SentToReview** — to `NeedsReview`, reading held |
| `Confirmed`, price outside its band | **SentToReview** — to `NeedsReview`, reading held |
| `Confirmed`, everything agrees | **Accepted** — a `SupplierPriceObservation`, and the listing's new price |

**Identity is the variant, the individual size and its unit, the barcode and its scope, and the pack quantity** — the facts that change what a per-unit price *means*. The title and the URL are evidence and move freely; the supplier's own product id is the key the listing was found by. A barcode is compared **exactly**, because `0012345678905` and `12345678905` are different codes; a variant is compared trimmed and case-insensitively, because a restyled page is not a new product. A confirmed, flagged or refused listing's identity is **never overwritten** by a reading — that would quietly resolve the disagreement that sent it to review — and only a listing still in `Proposed` has its identity updated by a rediscovery.

**The band is the owner's decision of 27 October 2026**: no more than 50% below and no more than 100% above the last accepted price, with **both edges inside** the band, so a supplier running a half-price special is not sent to review every time it does. A listing with no accepted price yet has no band at all. A price past either edge is **held**, not discarded: the listing is flagged and the reading waits where #928 can see it, and the listing keeps the price it already had.

**Delivery order decides nothing — neither a row's outcome nor what a listing currently costs.** The collector decides how it splits its searches into batches and in which order it sends them, and two work items of one run can reach the same supplier listing — one issued for a master product, one issued for a waiting key that has since been matched to that product, both finding the same supplier product id. So arrival order says nothing about reading order, and three rules keep it from mattering:

- **Every row of a run is judged against the listing as the run found it** — the match status it held and the accepted price it held when the run started — and never against what another row of the same run did to it. A reading of this run is never another reading's band, and one row sending the listing to review does not turn a later-delivered row of it into a held reading. Judging rows against each other was delivery-order dependent: with a price of 30 before the run, readings of 20 (07:00) and 50 (08:00) flagged the listing with 20 current when 20 arrived first (50 is past 20's ceiling of 40), and flagged it with 50 current when 50 arrived first (20 is below 50's floor of 25). Against the run's starting band of 15 to 60 both are accepted in every order and the 08:00 reading is current. The status the run started from is recovered by `PriceCollectorResultPolicy.StatusAtRunStart` from the status the listing holds now and whether this run has already recorded a `SentToReview` row for it — the only two transitions a run makes (`Confirmed` → `NeedsReview`, `Rejected` → `Proposed`) are both recorded that way — and the starting price is the latest accepted observation from an earlier run. A listing the run created starts as the proposal it became. The cost is stated plainly: within one run the band is anchored to the last *established* price, so two readings of one run inside that band are both accepted even when they differ from each other by more than the band; the next run's band is anchored to whichever of them was observed last.
- **What a listing currently costs is a replay of the run's accepted readings in observed order** (`SupplierListingPriceStatePolicy.StateAfterRun`), recomputed from every reading the run has accepted for the listing after every batch rather than moved by whichever row came last. The latest observed reading is the current one, and of two bearing the same observed instant the one recorded first stands (`ReplacesCurrentReading`) — the others of that instant are not replayed at all, because a reading that never was the price cannot have changed it; the last check is that reading's instant; the last change is the first reading of the trailing stretch at the current price, so a run that moved a price and then re-read it unchanged records the change at the first of the two instants, and a run that only re-read the price it started with leaves the change where it was. An earlier reading is still accepted, still stored and still answered — `SupplierPriceObservations` is append-only history and an accepted price is an accepted price — but it never moves the current price, the freshness or the last change backwards, which is the same sentence [Supplier price observations and comparison](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925) already states about an absence.
- **The one reading a listing holds pending is the latest one observed** (`ReplacesCurrentReading`), and a proposal's identity follows that reading. A listing's identity is rewritten only when it was still a proposal when the run started; a confirmed, flagged or refused listing's identity is never rewritten by a reading.

**Every other failed check refuses the row with a reason**, and the reasons are what a collector reads to fix itself: a pack price that is not above zero, a currency that is not AUD, a pack quantity of zero, a barcode without its scope, a GST rate that is not a proportion, a price basis that disagrees with the supplier master record's own (`SupplierPreset.PricesIncludeGst` — comparing an inclusive price with an exclusive one is off by the GST rate, the one mistake a price comparison must not make), an observation dated before the run started or in the future, and a source link whose host is not the supplier's own site or a subdomain of it. An **absent** supplier website or source link is not a mismatch: there is no host to compare, and refusing those would reject every supplier nobody has filled a website in for.

**Held readings are a separate table, and that is what keeps `SupplierPriceObservations` what it says it is.** Every row of that table is an accepted price — the listing's `LatestObservationId` points into it and #930's comparison reads it — so a reading that was held back lives in `SupplierListingPendingObservations` instead, where nothing can read it as a price by accident. One row per listing, **replaced** rather than appended (the issue's own "replacing the previous pending one"), which a unique index holds; accepting a price clears one an earlier run left, because a disagreement that has been resolved should not still be shown to a reviewer — a reading held by the same run is left alone, so whether it is still held never depends on which of the run's rows arrived first. The reading is found by the listing's own key — the supplier master record and that supplier's product id — and never by its database id, because a listing a batch has just created has no id until the batch is saved: keyed by the id, two searches of one run reporting one new supplier product id would each have added a reading against the same unsaved listing, and the unique index would have rolled back the whole batch rather than refusing one row. Replacement is chronological, like the accepted price above.

**Idempotency is run + work item + supplier product id, and it is a unique index.** The supplier product id is *in* the key deliberately: one search legitimately returns a 24-pack and a 30-pack, and accepting one must never suppress the other. Re-submitting a key returns the outcome the first attempt got — the stored reason, verbatim, not a re-derived one — and writes nothing. Two rows claiming one key inside a single batch have no first outcome to be answered with, so the later one is refused rather than letting ordering decide which was stored. A batch of more than 200 rows is refused **whole**, with `400` and nothing stored; everything else is reported per row, because a collector that mis-read one of two hundred packs must not lose the other hundred and ninety-nine. The response is four lists — accepted, sent to review, pending, rejected — because those are four different facts and merging the middle two would leave a collector unable to tell "somebody will look at this" from "this is waiting on a decision".

**Finishing a search is its own call, because a search can arrive in pieces.** `POST .../work-items/{id}/outcome` sends one of `complete`, `truncated`, `no_matches` or `failed` (with a reason: actor error, provider limit or timeout) **and the total number of distinct supplier product ids submitted for it**. The backend accepts it only while that total equals the rows it actually received for that work item in this run; otherwise `409` and the search stays unanswered, so a batch lost in transit leaves the search unfinished rather than finishing it short. `no_matches` and `failed` require a total of zero. `NotSearched` is the run completion's own answer and a collector may not claim it. Rows arriving after the answer are refused (`the search has already been answered`), and a second answer is refused unless it is identical — a retry whose response was lost is not a conflict.

**Only an accepted `complete` or `no_matches` answer may record that a known listing was not found.** `PriceCollectorWorkItemPolicy.RecordsListingsNotFound` is that rule: a `truncated`, `failed` or `not_searched` search stopped before it had seen everything, so a listing missing from its results is a listing nobody looked for. This is the same restraint the [report availability model](#report-availability-model-issue-730) shows about a missing provider figure — an absence is evidence only when the thing that produced it was complete — and it is why the not-found instant is written *after* the total matched rather than as rows arrive. Recording it changes nothing else: the listing keeps its latest accepted observation, its last successful check and its match status.

**Closing a run turns silence into a recorded outcome, and expiring one does exactly the same.** `POST .../runs/{id}/complete` marks every unanswered search `NotSearched`, writes one count per outcome, and takes the status those counts imply (`PriceCollectorRunPolicy.StatusFor`: nothing short of complete is `Succeeded`, nothing fully accounted for is `Failed`, anything between is `PartiallySucceeded`; a `truncated` search counts as short of complete, for the reason it never records a listing as missing). A run left open past its `ExpiresAtUtc` is expired the next time it is touched — the expiry is committed and *then* the call is refused — or when a later run is issued, and both paths run the same `PriceCollectorRunClosure`, differing only in the status. Results for a completed or expired run are refused with `409`.

**The tenancy cost, stated plainly.** Six platform tables are written — `SupplierListings`, `SupplierPriceObservations`, `SupplierListingPendingObservations`, `PriceCollectorResultRows`, `PriceCollectorRuns` and `PriceCollectorWorkItems` — plus matching evidence on `ProductMatchSuggestions`, and **nothing tenant-owned at all**. `PriceCollectorResultRow` and `SupplierListingPendingObservation` are the **ninth and tenth** entries in `BusinessOwnershipCoverageTests.PlatformEntities` (see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64)): a reading a collector submitted, the decision made about it, and a reading that was held rather than priced are facts about a supplier's shelf and about no business. This surface adds **no** cross-business read: it makes no `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement, takes no unscoped context and issues no raw SQL, and the request carries a **denied** `BusinessScope` throughout, so `BusinessOwnershipEnforcer` refuses every tenant-owned write exactly as it does elsewhere. No business id, business name or business product id appears in any request or response in either direction.

**Each endpoint is one transaction, read and write together.** Deciding a row means reading the run, its work item, the listing and that listing's last accepted price, and then writing a listing, an observation and the row's own recorded outcome; splitting the read from the write would let two submissions of one idempotency key both decide the key was free. `EfPriceCollectorResultStore` holds all of it in one transaction and the unique index is the backstop underneath. Every *rule* is the Domain's — `PriceCollectorResultPolicy` decides what a row becomes, `SupplierListingPolicy` and `SupplierPriceObservationPolicy` decide what may be stored, `PriceCollectorWorkItemPolicy` decides what a search may be answered with and what its absence proves, `PriceCollectorRunPolicy` decides how a run ended — and the adapter reads, writes and sequences without judging.

**The schema.** `AddPriceCollectorResults` is additive: two tables, eleven columns and three check constraints, writing nothing. Every listing that existed keeps a null variant, size and not-found instant, and every run keeps five zero counts — this migration invents no identity for a listing recorded before one was read, and no history for a run that never reported. `SupplierListings` and `PriceCollectorRuns` are **rebuilt**, because SQLite cannot add a check constraint to an existing table; the rebuild is written out in the migration (the shape `20260907123300_RemoveProductMapped` already uses here) rather than left to `AddCheckConstraint`, because this migration was authored by hand and carries no generated target model for the SQLite provider's own rewriter to read. Its designer file therefore holds the `[Migration]` id and no `BuildTargetModel`, like the four earlier hand-written migrations in this history; the authoritative target model is `AppDbContextModelSnapshot`, which `MigrationRelocationTests` compares the live model against.

**What proves it.** `PriceCollectorResultPolicyTests` covers the rules themselves over a table of cases: the band in both directions and on both edges, a listing with no accepted price having no band, each of the six identity fields, a variant differing only in case or spacing not being a change while a barcode differing only by its leading zeros is, the four listing states and what each does to a row, the run window at both ends, the host check including a subdomain and a near-miss (`alpha.example.evil.test` is not `alpha.example`), an absent site or link not being a mismatch, and the batch bound. `PriceCollectorWorkItemPolicyTests` adds the answers a collector may give and the outcomes that prove an absence; `PriceCollectorRunPolicyTests` adds the status a closed run takes from its counts. `PriceCollectorResultsTests` is the relational half over **two** businesses on the denied scope a collector carries: each work-item refusal, a known listing submitted under another product's work item refused with its link unchanged, that refusal recorded as matching evidence exactly once, a waiting key matched to a master product resolving for its own rows so a known master listing is accepted and a new pack attaches to the master, a new listing under an unmatched key held under that key, a confirmed listing accepted with its GST rate stored and left unknown when unpublished, both band edges accepted and a cent past either one held with the old price intact, all six identity changes sending a confirmed listing to review without overwriting what was confirmed, a rejected listing proposed again, each match status surviving a rediscovery with no second listing, a held reading replaced rather than appended, two work items of one run — one for a master product, one for a waiting key matched to it — reporting the same new supplier product id in a single batch leaving one listing, one held reading and two answered rows, an earlier reading delivered in a later batch kept as the accepted price it is while the listing's price, freshness and last change stay where the later reading left them, the same two rows reversed inside one batch, the review of repair attempt 2's two readings of 20 and 50 against a price of 30 accepted with 50 current in both orders and in one batch or two, an in-band and an out-of-band reading of one run giving the same accepted row, the same review flag and the same held reading in both orders and in one batch or two, a price moved and re-read unchanged recording its change at the first reading whichever arrived first, two readings of one instant leaving the one recorded first current and the last change where it was before the run (in one batch and in two), with a later genuine change still recorded, the reading a listing holds being the latest one observed both across batches and within one, two packs from one search each idempotent on its own key, a key repeated inside one batch refused, the batch bound refusing a batch whole, every other failed check with its own reason, a search split across three batches finished only by the right total with a wrong total refused and left unanswered and no listing marked missing before the answer, rows after the answer refused, only a complete or no-match answer recording a listing as not found, an identical retry accepted and a different second answer refused, a run completed with its counts and then closed to results, an overdue run expired on touch with the same effect, and — the boundary — a submission, an answer and a completion together leaving both businesses' products, purchases, suppliers, stock and price-tracking mappings byte for byte as they were. `AddPriceCollectorResultsMigrationTests` is the upgrade: the two tables created empty, a pre-existing listing, run and work item read back column for column with the new columns empty, both rebuilds keeping every constraint, index and reference they already had, the idempotency key and the one-reading-per-listing rule read from the schema as unique indexes, no business column on either new table, and the `Down` removing what it added and nothing else.

### Collector product matching (issue #941)

The two sections above hand the collector its work and take back what it read off a shelf. This one, the sixth task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), is what happens when it has an opinion about **which product** a waiting search was for — and it exists because of the owner's decision of 27 October 2026: *during each daily run Claude compares the products awaiting a match with the master products; when the match is obvious it is applied automatically and flagged as automatic, and otherwise the Super Admin confirms it (#928)*.

That changes the earlier rule "Claude may propose; only the Super Admin confirms" for **one thing only**: linking a waiting product to an *existing* master product. Supplier listings and pack sizes are still never confirmed by Claude, and **Claude never creates a master product**.

```text
POST api/price-collector/matches   ← { runId, proposals: [{ waitingKey,
                                        masterProductId? | (suggestedBrand, suggestedName,
                                                            suggestedSizeValue, suggestedSizeUnit),
                                        confidence: high|medium|low, reason }] }   ≤ 200 proposals
                                   → { runId, autoMatched: [...], tentative: [...], rejected: [...] }
                                      each { waitingKey, outcome, reason?, masterProductId?, suggestionId? }
                                      400 batch too large · 404 unknown run · 409 finished or expired
```

**"Obvious" is the backend's answer and never the matcher's.** Claude's own confidence is not calibrated (the owner, same decision), so the level it reports is **one condition among several** and decides nothing on its own. `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.AutomaticProductMatchPolicy` is the one rule, it stores nothing and reads nothing, and a match is applied only when every one of these holds:

The order below is the order a refusal reports, and it starts earlier than the table: a proposal naming no master product is refused first, as a suggested new one, and one naming a master product this catalogue does not hold is refused next, as `unknown master product` — neither is a condition the table below can state, because neither has a master product description yet to check anything against.

| Condition | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| The pair was never refused | no `Rejected` or `Undone` suggestion for that `(waiting key, master product)` pair — checked first, immediately after confirming the proposed master product exists, and before every condition below |
| Confidence is `high` | `medium` and `low` are tentative matches, whatever else agrees |
| The unit label **parses** | `"375mL"` → 375 ml, `"1.25L"` → 1250 ml; `"can"`, `"each"`, `"375ml bottle"` parse to nothing |
| The size **agrees** | after conversion to a canonical unit, so 375 ml and 0.375 l agree and 375 ml, 355 ml and 375 g do not |
| The brand appears in the search name | word for word, with case and punctuation folded, so `"Cola Classic"` is not Coca-Cola's |
| **The variant agrees** | every word of the master product's own name appears in the search name |
| **No conflicting descriptor** | no descriptor in the fixed list below appears in one of the two descriptions and not the other |
| **Exactly one suitable candidate** | the backend runs the checks over the **whole** master catalogue, exactly one passes, and it is the one proposed |

**The descriptor list is fixed, tested and symmetric**: `zero`, `no sugar`, `sugar free`, `diet`, `max`, `light`/`lite`, `caffeine free`, `decaf`, `vanilla`, `cherry`, `lime`, `original`, `classic`. A descriptor on one side and not the other refuses the match in **either** direction — a search for a plain cola must not be matched to a diet one, and a search for a diet cola must not be matched to the plain one — which is what makes `Coke Zero 375 mL` unable to auto-match `Coke Classic 375 mL` and `Pepsi Max` unable to auto-match `Pepsi`. Each entry holds every spelling that means the same descriptor (`light`/`lite`, `decaf`/`decaffeinated`, `sugar free`/`sugarfree`), so a difference of spelling is not read as a difference of product; a multi-word descriptor matches only as whole words, in order and next to each other. The list is a **list** rather than a rule precisely because nothing may infer that a word changes a product: that is the one judgement this policy is not allowed to make on its own.

**Two conditions are the safeguards the rest rest on.** The brand, variant and size checks are deliberately loose in one direction — a business's product name may say *more* than the master product does, because `"Coca-Cola Classic 375mL can"` is still a Coca-Cola Classic — and what makes that safe is the descriptor rule, which knows which extra words change the product. And "exactly one suitable candidate" is counted by the backend over the whole catalogue rather than taken from the proposal: a proposal naming a perfectly plausible product is refused while a second plausible one exists, because which of two it is is exactly what nobody has decided. The catalogue is therefore read **in full** for that count and never as a bounded prefix — the work list's own `MaxMasterProductsForMatching` bounds a *response*, not a check, and a bound here would make the answer depend on where it fell.

**A `high` confidence is necessary and never sufficient, and the three levels are a closed vocabulary.** They are stored on the suggestion row as three exact, documented proportions (`1.0`, `0.6`, `0.3`) rather than as a number anybody rounded, which keeps them apart from the `0` the results endpoint writes on the evidence it records itself (#937). An undeclared value is refused with `400`-shaped per-proposal reason rather than read as the first declared level, the rule `GstClassifications` states for a classification.

**Which mappings an automatic match may change, and which it must not.** Only the mappings that carry that waiting key and are **still awaiting a match** (`Requested`) become `AutoMatched`, naming the master product with `MatchSource = CollectorAutomaticMatch`:

| The mapping is | then |
| --- | --- |
| `Requested` with that key | it becomes `AutoMatched`, names the master product and records the collector as the source |
| `Matched` (a person decided it) | **untouched** — a manually confirmed mapping is never changed by a matcher |
| `AutoMatched` already | untouched; a second match for a settled mapping is not this run's business |
| `NotFound` | untouched: looked for and not found is a recorded answer (#923) |
| `AwaitingProductDetails` | untouched: it is waiting on its own product's name and unit label, not on the catalogue (#938) |
| tracking turned off | there is no row, so there is nothing to change — and none is ever created |
| the product renamed or relabelled since the work list was issued | its stored key is no longer the issued key (#938's refresh), so the match does not reach it |

The last two are the issue's own skip conditions and both are true **by construction** rather than by a check: the mappings are selected by their stored `WaitingKey`, so a mapping whose current waiting key is not the issued one is not in the set at all, and a mapping that no longer exists is not either. The suggestion row records the run, the confidence and the reason, which is what a reviewer of a wrong match reads; nothing is written on the mapping that a person would have to undo twice.

**A key nothing is waiting under is refused rather than recorded.** The key is a *folded* search name and unit label, so the only statement of what it was a search for is the text the mappings that carry it hold — the backend checks the ordinally first of them, which is the spelling the work list published (#923's representative rule), so the description the backend checks is the description the matcher was given. With no mapping still awaiting a match there is no description to check and nothing for a decision to change, so the proposal is refused with `nothing is awaiting a match under this waiting key`.

**Everything else is a tentative match, and that is most of the work.** A proposal the backend could not call obvious is stored as a `Tentative` `ProductMatchSuggestion` for #928 — naming the existing master product it proposed, or the complete description of a new one — with the matcher's own reason, its confidence and this run's label, and the mappings stay exactly as they are. **A suggested new master product is stored and never created**: no `MasterProducts` row is written by this surface at all. Two refusals store nothing instead: a proposal naming a master product this catalogue does not hold (there is nothing for a suggestion to point at), and a pair a Super Admin **rejected or undid** — which is already recorded, as the refusal that refused it, and the whole reason those rows are kept for ever is so that pair is never proposed again. A pair (or a suggested description) whose suggestion a reviewer is **already looking at** gets no second *proposal*: a reviewer looking at one decision must not be handed the same evidence once per run. What that run writes instead is its own **record** of having decided the key — a `Repeated` `ProductMatchSuggestion` under this run's label, carrying the matcher's own reason and confidence — and the row the reviewer is looking at is left exactly as it was: its label, its status, its pair, its reason, its confidence and its instants all stay theirs. **The record has to be the run's own row.** Recording it by relabelling the waiting proposal instead — which is what this surface did until the repair of 29 October 2026 — hands the record to whichever run last touched that row and takes it away from the run that decided first: with two runs open, the second one's repeat erases the first one's decision, and the first run's next request decides the key afresh and can apply a match it had already declined to apply. `ProductMatchSuggestionPolicy.AwaitsReview` is the one predicate for "is a reviewer still to decide this?" and it is true of `Tentative` alone, which is also why a decided row is not reused: a row recording that an *earlier* run applied the match, or that a person accepted it, is nobody's pending decision, so a pair whose rows are all decided gets this run's own tentative suggestion — which is also what records its decision. So every decided proposal, kept or applied, leaves exactly **one** suggestion carrying this run's label for its key, and exactly **one** row of that pair awaiting a reviewer.

**The listings a key already collected move with the match, and keep where they came from.** When a match is applied, every `SupplierListing` held under that waiting key is re-pointed at the master product: `MasterProductId` is set, the active `WaitingKey` is cleared — a listing belongs to exactly one of the two owners and the database checks that — and `OriginWaitingKey` keeps the key whose search found it, which is precisely why that second column exists (#923). **A moved listing keeps its match status**: a proposal stays a proposal, so nothing about a pack size or a listing's identity is confirmed by a match, and an undo (#928) has the key it needs to move the listing back. The listing's price, its last successful check and its last price change are untouched.

**Idempotency is the run and the waiting key, and the suggestion row is the record.** There is no table of its own for a proposal: the suggestion a run recorded for a key *is* what that run decided about it, stored under this run's own label (`ProductMatchSuggestionPolicy.CollectorRunFor`). Re-submitting the same run and key therefore writes nothing and is answered with the outcome that was recorded — never with a fresh decision against a catalogue, or against a proposal, that may have moved since. That holds for a proposal answered with somebody else's pending suggestion as well, which is what the `Repeated` record above is for: without a row of its own, a run that answered "already suggested" would have nothing recorded for the key, and its next request would decide it again — applying the match if the retry's confidence were higher, or considering another master product if the retry named one. And the record is **immutable once written**: a run's row is never relabelled, so another run repeating the same proposal — the runs of this surface may overlap — cannot take the first run's decision away. One run and one key have one outcome, whatever the proposal says the second time and whatever another run does in between. Two proposals for one key **inside one batch** have no first outcome to be answered with, so the later one is refused, the rule #937 states for a repeated result key. A malformed proposal is refused for its own reason *before* it claims the key, so one bad proposal and one good one for the same key in one batch still land the good one. A batch of more than 200 proposals is refused **whole**, with `400` and nothing stored; everything else is reported per proposal.

**The order of the per-proposal checks is the design**: is the key one this run issued work for (otherwise `unknown waiting key` — the keys are the work list's, and a key nothing was asked about is not an answer to anything); is the proposal itself storable (exactly one complete proposal, a declared confidence, a reason); has this batch already claimed the key; has this run already decided it; is anything still awaiting it; and only then what the Domain decides.

**One transaction, and it takes SQLite's write lock before its reads.** `EfPriceCollectorMatchStore` opens the `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction of `SqliteWriteLockTransaction` — the same lock #938's switch and #896's machine delete take — because the idempotency key here has **no unique index** to fall back on: the record of what a run decided is the suggestion row it wrote, so "has this run already decided this key?" is authoritative only while nothing can commit between the question and the write. The authoritative read, the comparison and the mutation are one operation. The "is this run still open?" gate is shared with the results endpoint (`PriceCollectorOpenRun`): a finished run is `409`, an overdue one is expired — committed — and *then* refused, and an unknown one is `404`.

**The tenancy cost, stated plainly.** One platform table is written (`ProductMatchSuggestions`), the listings of a matched key are moved (`SupplierListings`), and **three columns and an instant of a tenant-owned table are updated** — `ProductPriceTracking.Status`, `MasterProductId`, `MatchSource` and `UpdatedAtUtc`. That last one is this issue's own reviewed exception to "a denied scope writes nothing tenant-owned", and it is bounded by *what may be written* rather than by whose row it is, because a match is decided for a key and the mappings that carry one key may belong to any number of businesses: one entity type, updates only, four columns that do not include the business key, the product, the waiting key or the captured search text, one save, an `internal` lease with one caller, and `Denied`-only. The enforcer asserts the modified columns as a **set**, so a mapping can neither be created, withdrawn, moved between businesses nor re-pointed at another product through it. The read beside it is the third reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` path in a request, for the same reason the work list's is: under a denied scope the central filters match no mapping, so a match decided for a key would reach none of the rows that carry it. Both are described in full in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The second reviewed write and § The three reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` paths. **Nothing about a business leaves this surface**: no business id, business name or business product id in either direction, and deliberately **no count of the mappings a match moved** — that count is the number of businesses tracking the product, which is exactly what the shared catalogue exists to avoid telling anybody.

**No migration.** Issue #923's `ProductMatchSuggestions` already holds everything a decided or proposed match records — the waiting key, the one proposal, the confidence, the reason and the run label, with `AutoApplied` declared for this issue from the start — so this change adds no table, no column and no index, and writes no data of its own. The one thing it adds to that table is a **sixth value** on the status column it already has, `Repeated`, the record described above: the status is stored as the integer the enum declares and the database holds no check constraint over it, so a value is a value and not a schema change. Nothing reads it as a match (`EfPriceCollectorResultStore` resolves a key through `AutoApplied` or `Accepted` alone), nothing reads it as a refusal (`BlocksAutomaticMatching` is `Rejected` and `Undone`), and nothing reads it as a pending proposal (`AwaitsReview` is `Tentative`).

**One limitation, and it is the criteria's own.** A `NotFound` mapping whose product has since been renamed is still not revisited: #938 recorded that as the natural work of this matcher and this issue's criteria do not ask for it, so a key that came back empty stays empty until a person acts. The Super Admin surfaces for tentative and automatic matches, confirm and undo are #928's and have since arrived ([Super Admin review of the supplier price catalogue](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928)), and the prompt and match file the collector runs are #926's.

**What proves it.** `AutomaticProductMatchPolicyTests` (unit) is the rule, condition by condition and each passing and failing on its own: eight unit-label spellings parsing to a canonical size and ten that state none (including `"375"`, `"each"`, `"can"`, `"375ml bottle"` and `"0ml"`), 375 ml against 0.375 l, 355 ml and 375 g, the brand word-for-word including `"Cola Classic"` refused, every variant word required with the reverse direction allowed, sixteen descriptor cases (both of the issue's named pairs in both directions, every synonym pair not conflicting, and an extra `"can"` not conflicting), the descriptor list asserted by name, an obvious match applied, each condition's own refusal reason, two suitable candidates applying nothing even when one was proposed, a proposal that is not the suitable one refused with its own failing condition and the suitable one **not** applied in its place, a rejected and an undone pair never applied with another master still matchable, an unknown master product and a suggested new one applying nothing, the three levels' stored proportions being values the suggestion row accepts, an undeclared confidence refused, and the batch bound. `CollectorProductMatchUseCaseTests` adds the one thing the use case decides: the bound refuses the batch whole and never reaches the store. `PriceCollectorMatchTests` is the relational half over **two** businesses on the denied scope a collector carries: one proposal matching both businesses' mappings with the run, confidence and reason recorded and the search text, key, product and owner left exactly as they were; the listings under the key moved, staying proposed, keeping their origin key, with another product's listing untouched; each non-`Requested` state untouched (a theory over `Matched`, `AutoMatched` and `NotFound`), a renamed product's mapping skipped through the **real** product edit, a suspended mapping skipped, a key nothing is waiting under refused; a not-obvious proposal stored as tentative with the mappings untouched, a suggested new master stored with **no** `MasterProducts` row created, two suitable candidates applying nothing, a pair that already has a suggestion not suggested twice (that row untouched, down to its label and its instants, with this run's own `Repeated` record beside it), the two retries of a suggestion answered that way — one at a higher confidence, one naming another master product — each answered with the recorded outcome and leaving the mappings and the listings as they were, and the same two retries again **with a second open run repeating the proposal in between**, which is the regression the per-run record exists for: run A's outcome survives run B, each run's record carries its own label, and the row the reviewer is looking at is still untouched; a rejected and an undone pair refused with no second row and another master still matchable; an unknown key, an unknown master product and four malformed proposals each refused with their own message and nothing stored; both outcomes idempotent on a second submission, a duplicate key inside one batch refused, an unknown run answered with nothing, a closed and an overdue run refusing with the expiry committed; and — the boundary — a tentative and a refused proposal together leaving both businesses' products, purchases, suppliers, stock and mappings byte for byte as they were. `PriceCollectorMatchApiTests` is the **same-run** test through the real endpoints, which is the one property neither endpoint has alone: the work list is read, its waiting key is matched, and the results for that same work item are then accepted as the newly assigned master product's — the known confirmed listing priced rather than refused as belonging to another product, and a new pack attached to the master product with its origin key kept — over the production collector scheme, policy, middleware and query filters, with the response asserted to name neither business. `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` holds the route as class 5 and nothing else, `BusinessScopeCompositionTests` that the adapter gets the request's own denied-scope context and nothing else, and `EfProductPriceTrackingStoreTests` still asserts that an ordinary denied scope - one with no matching lease open - writes nothing at all.

### Super Admin review of the supplier price catalogue (issue #928)

The three sections above hand the collector its work, take back what it read off a shelf, and let it say which product a search was for. This one, the seventh task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), is where a **person** decides all of it — and it exists because of the owner's decision of 27 October 2026: *Claude may propose; it has no authority to confirm listings or pack sizes. Only the Super Admin confirms them.* The data is shared by every business, so one wrong pack quantity is one wrong "cheapest supplier" for everybody tracking the product, and a Business Owner may not confirm anything here at all.

Five endpoints, all class 2 on the platform-admin surface — `PlatformAdminPolicy` **and** `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute`, with `[Authorize]` and `[RequiredScope("access_as_user")]` kept, exactly as the supplier presets of [#848](#super-admin-supplier-presets-issue-848):

```text
GET  api/super-admin/price-catalogue-review
       → { waitingProducts: [{ waitingKey, searchName, unitLabel, businessesWaitingCount,
                               firstRequestedAtUtc, lastUpdatedAtUtc, suggestions[], proposedListings[] }],
           automaticMatches: [{ suggestionId, waitingKey, searchName?, unitLabel?, masterProduct,
                                confidence, reason, collectorRun, appliedAtUtc }],
           listings:         [{ id, supplierName, supplierProductId, url?, title?, variant?, size?,
                                unitsPerPack?, barcode? + scope?, matchStatus, masterProduct?,
                                waitingKey?, originWaitingKey?, firstSeenAtUtc, lastSeenAtUtc,
                                lastCheckedAtUtc?, lastNotFoundAtUtc?, lastAcceptedPackPrice?,
                                strongBarcodeMatch?, pendingObservation? }],
           masterProducts:   [{ id, brand, name, sizeValue, sizeUnit }] }   ← the picker's own list

POST api/super-admin/price-catalogue-review/listings/{id}/decision
       ← { outcome: confirmed|rejected, unitsPerPack?, barcode?, barcodeScope?, variant?,
           sizeValue?, sizeUnit?, approvePriceException }
       → { matchStatus, priceAccepted, priceExceptionUsed, priceReason?, acceptedObservationId?,
           acceptedPackPrice?, confirmedUnitsPerPack? }      400 · 404 · 409

POST api/super-admin/price-catalogue-review/matches
       ← { waitingKey, decision: acceptSuggestion|chooseMasterProduct|createMasterProduct|
                                 rejectSuggestion|markNotFound,
           suggestionId? | masterProductId? | (newBrand, newName, newSizeValue, newSizeUnit) }
       → { masterProduct?, masterProductCreated, suggestionId?, listingsMovedCount }  400 · 404 · 409

POST api/super-admin/price-catalogue-review/automatic-matches/{suggestionId}/confirm
POST api/super-admin/price-catalogue-review/automatic-matches/{suggestionId}/undo
       → { suggestionId, waitingKey, masterProduct, listingsMovedCount }            404 · 409
```

**A waiting product is a search name, a unit label and a count.** The queue groups the mappings that are still `Requested` by their stored waiting key, shows the ordinally first spelling — the same representative rule the collector work list uses, so the description a reviewer reads is the description the matcher was given — and publishes the number of **distinct businesses** waiting under it. Which business asked is not in the contract and there is no field for it, which is the issue's own constraint: *"never which business asked"*.
