The count is the one thing about businesses that crosses the boundary here, and it is what tells a reviewer whether a decision matters to one business or to twelve; the collector gets no count at all, which is a different answer for a different caller (see [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The six reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` paths).

**Five decisions about a waiting product, and three of them end with a match.** `Inventory.Domain.PriceCatalogue.ProductMatchReviewPolicy` is the rule:

| Decision | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Accept the suggestion | the existing master product it named, or - when it described a new one - that description, **created** and matched |
| Pick another master product | matches the key to it, and **refuses** every other tentative suggestion of that key: choosing one product is saying the others were wrong |
| Create a master product | from values the reviewer submitted, prefilled from the matcher's suggestion on the page but theirs; then matched |
| Reject a suggestion | the key stays waiting, and the pair is never applied automatically again |
| Not found | every mapping still awaiting the key becomes `NotFound` — a recorded answer, which is what stops the same search running every run |

**A match reaches every mapping that carries the key, and nothing else.** Only the `Requested` ones become `Matched` with `MatchSource = SuperAdmin`; a mapping a person already settled, one a run auto-matched, one already recorded as not found and one suspended on its own product's details are left exactly as they are, and a mapping whose product was renamed or relabelled since carries another key now, so it is not in the set at all. The listings the key had already collected move to the master product the same way #941 moves them — the active `WaitingKey` cleared, `OriginWaitingKey` kept, **match status untouched** — so a proposal stays a proposal and nothing about a pack size is confirmed by a match.

**Every applied match leaves an `Accepted` suggestion row, and that is load-bearing.** The collector results endpoint resolves a waiting key to its master product through the `AutoApplied` and `Accepted` suggestions of that key (#937), so a reviewer's match that left none would be invisible to a run searching while it was made. When the reviewer accepted a suggestion naming that very master product, that row *is* the record and becomes `Accepted`; otherwise this surface writes its own under its own label, `super-admin-review`, with a reason that says a person decided it. A suggestion that *described* a new master product cannot name the created row — one proposal per row is that table's own check constraint — so it is accepted **and** a row naming the created product is written beside it.

**Automatic matches are a section of their own, and an undo is why #941 is allowed to exist.** Confirming one settles the mappings it applied to (`AutoMatched` → `Matched`) and records the suggestion as `Accepted`; the **match source is left as `CollectorAutomaticMatch`**, because how the match was *made* is still the matcher's and what changed is that a person has checked it. Undoing one is narrower than the match it reverses, deliberately:

| An undo | and |
| --- | --- |
| mappings that are `AutoMatched` **and** name that master product | return to `Requested`, with the master product and match source cleared |
| a mapping a person settled, or one a later run matched to something else | untouched: an undo of a guess must not take a person's decision back |
| listings that are still `Proposed` and came from that key (`OriginWaitingKey`) | move back to the key, which is why that provenance column exists |
| a confirmed, flagged or refused listing | untouched — somebody decided that pack, and undoing a guess about which product a *search* was for says nothing about it |
| the suggestion | becomes `Undone`, which `ProductMatchSuggestionPolicy.BlocksAutomaticMatching` reads, so the pair is **never applied automatically again** |

No price, observation, check instant or inventory value is touched by any of it.

**Confirming a listing is the only thing in this application that confirms a pack size.** The submitted identity — the variant, the individual size and its unit, the pack quantity, the barcode and its scope — is held to `SupplierListingPolicy`'s own rules and then stored, which is also how a **correction** is made: "correct and confirm" is one request, because a listing that was corrected and then not confirmed would be a row somebody edited for no decision. A listing that is no longer waiting for a decision — confirmed or refused by another reviewer, or flagged by a run in between — is refused with `409` rather than decided against the state the page was read in.

**What confirming does with the reading the listing was holding** is `SupplierListingReviewPolicy.DecidePendingPrice`, and the order is the rule:

| Condition | Then |
| --- | --- |
| the listing holds no reading | confirmed with **no current price**, and priced on the next run |
| the reading is older than the supplier's own `PriceCheckFreshnessHours` (#925) | no price, with that reason |
| the reading's variant, individual size or barcode is not the one confirmed | no price: a reading of another pack is a price for something else |
| the price is outside #937's band and no exception was approved | no price, with that reason |
| the price is outside the band and the exception **was** approved | accepted, and recorded as an exception |
| everything agrees | accepted as a `SupplierPriceObservation`, and the listing's current price |

**The pack quantity is the reviewer's own answer, and that is the one difference from #937's identity check.** That rule compares a reading against what somebody already confirmed, where a changed pack count means the shelf moved under a settled decision. Here the reviewer *is* deciding the pack count with the reading in front of them — a BIG W row publishes no pack count field, so the count is read out of the name (`"Coca Cola 375Ml Coke 36Pk 36 Pack"`), confirmed, and then stored on the listing — so refusing the price because the reviewer corrected what was read would make the correction useless: the listing would be confirmed with no price and the next run would flag it for the same disagreement. The confirmed quantity wins and is what the per-unit price is derived from; every other identity field still has to agree.

**Whether the reading becomes a price and whether the listing keeps the price it had are two questions, and the second one is `SupplierListingReviewPolicy.ConfirmationWithdrawsCurrentPrice`** (the repair of the owner's review finding of 30 October 2026). The cheapest-supplier summary reads the listing's own `UnitsPerPack` beside the observation `LatestObservationId` points at, so a $40 30-pack confirmed as a 36-pack was being published as $40 for 36 — a per-unit price no supplier ever charged. A confirmation that moves **any** field of the identity, the pack quantity included, therefore withdraws that pointer:

| On a confirmation | the price the listing was publishing |
| --- | --- |
| the identity confirmed is the stored one (a correction of nothing, or a restyled variant) | is kept: that accepted reading is still a reading of this pack, and its own freshness limit is what eventually stops it being compared (#925) |
| any identity field moves — variant, individual size and unit, barcode, barcode scope, **or the pack quantity** | is withdrawn: `LatestObservationId`, `LastCheckedAtUtc` and `LastPriceChangeAtUtc` all become `NULL`, which is the one coherent "never checked" state `SupplierListingPriceStatePolicy` describes and `CK_SupplierListings_PriceStateConsistent` allows |
| either way | the held reading is judged on its own merits by the table above, and a **refused** reading is never accepted merely to fill the gap a withdrawal leaves |

The pack quantity is compared here and excluded there, and the two are not in tension: deciding whether the reading *in front of the reviewer* is a reading of the pack being confirmed is what the quantity correction settles, while a price accepted *earlier* was accepted against a quantity somebody had already settled. **Nothing is withdrawn from history.** `SupplierPriceObservations` stays append-only — what a supplier charged at an instant remains true after a reviewer corrected what pack it was — and what is taken away is only the listing's claim that it is the price *now*. A withdrawn price is recovered by the next accepted reading of the confirmed pack, which is the same "priced on the next run" answer a refused reading gives, and never by promoting an older observation: this catalogue records an identity on the *listing* rather than on each observation, so which historical reading described which pack is not a question the stored rows can answer. The business sees `hasPrice: false` — "not checked yet", never a wrong number and never a zero.

**The price exception is explicit, is audited separately, and overrides the band and nothing else.** It is the repair the owner's review of 27 October 2026 asked for — *"so a real large discount cannot stay stuck in review"* — and it is bounded in three directions: it is read only when the band is what would otherwise refuse the reading (an approval that was not needed is not an exception, and nothing is audited as one), it cannot make a stale reading fresh or make a reading of another pack this pack's price, and the accepted price then **becomes the reference the next run's band is measured against**, because it is the listing's latest accepted observation like any other.

**An accepted reading keeps its own provenance.** The observation records the run that read it and the instant it was read — not the review, which read no shelf — and the listing's three price-check facts are then set by `SupplierListingPriceStatePolicy`, the same rule #937's own replay uses: a reading observed no later than the one the listing already holds moves nothing, because a listing's price, its freshness and its last change may only ever move forwards. The held reading is removed, because a disagreement that has been resolved must not still be shown to a reviewer; a **refusal** removes it too, since a reading nobody will ever price is not a disagreement waiting for a decision.

**Decisions are kept, which is what makes a daily run bearable.** A refused listing stays `Rejected` and is simply not in the queue, so the same shelf found again every run proposes nothing — and #937's own rule is what brings it back: a rediscovery whose **identity changed** makes it a proposal again, because a listing that now describes something else is not the thing somebody refused. A confirmed listing returns to the queue only when #937 flags it. A refused or undone `(waiting key, master product)` pair is kept for ever and blocks the matcher, and the review itself may still match such a pair deliberately — a person's decision stands, and the automatic path stays blocked.

**Barcode matches are shown first.** A listing whose barcode equals a **confirmed** listing's barcode, in the same scope, is flagged as a strong match and the queue orders those listings ahead of the rest. The barcode is compared exactly (`0012345678905` and `12345678905` are different codes) and the scope must agree (a carton code equal to a unit code is off by the pack size), and the match is evidence rather than a decision: the listing still needs confirming. It is computed against every confirmed listing in the catalogue rather than one product's, because that is the point — the issue's own examples are a JB Metro inner barcode that is a Woolworths single's and a JB Metro outer barcode that is a Woolworths 24-pack's.

**Supplier text is plain text.** The title, the variant and the supplier's own product id are published as stored and rendered as text; the listing's own URL is the only link the page offers, and only when the one supplier-website helper (#847) says it is a safe absolute http(s) address — the same rule the Suppliers list and the presets page apply to a stored address.

**Every decision is audited, and a price exception is audited separately.** `IPriceCatalogueReviewAudit` is one more `ILogger` sink at the InventoryApi boundary, on the same terms as the platform-admin audits beside it: one `Information` event per **committed** decision, carrying the acting administrator's Entra `(tid, oid)` pair, which decision it was, the listing, master product and suggestion keys, the waiting key, whether a price was accepted and the pack quantity confirmed. A confirmation that used the exception emits a second event, `PriceExceptionApproved`, because that is a separate decision overriding a financial safeguard and the issue asks for it to be auditable on its own. The entry type has **no field** for a business id, a business name, a count of businesses, a supplier name, a listing title or the accepted price, so a sink that printed the whole entry could not emit one; the waiting key is carried because a key-level decision has no other identifier and it is a folded product description that carries no business identity by construction.

**The tenancy cost, stated plainly.** Five platform tables are written — `MasterProducts` (this surface's only writer in the application), `SupplierListings`, `ProductMatchSuggestions`, `SupplierPriceObservations` and `SupplierListingPendingObservations` — and **four columns of one tenant-owned table**: `ProductPriceTracking.Status`, `MasterProductId`, `MatchSource` and `UpdatedAtUtc`, through this issue's own reviewed lease, which is #941's window for the other decider and is bounded by *what may be written* rather than by whose row it is. The read beside it is the sixth reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` path, in one place on the adapter. Both are described in full in [Tenant ownership](#tenant-ownership-issue-64) § The fourth reviewed write and § The six reviewed `IgnoreQueryFilters` paths. **No business id, business name or product id appears in any request or response in either direction**; the one thing published about businesses at all is the count of those waiting under a key.

**Each decision is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction.** Every one of them is a comparison against the state the reviewer was looking at — is this listing still waiting, is this suggestion still tentative, is anything still awaiting this key, does another master product already describe what a create submitted — and a refusal of a stale one, which is authoritative only while nothing can commit between the question and the write. `EfPriceCatalogueReviewStore` takes the write lock of `SqliteWriteLockTransaction` before its reads, the shape #938's switch, #896's machine delete and #941's matches all use.

**No migration.** Issue #923's schema already holds everything a decision records — the listing's own identity and match status, the suggestion statuses `Accepted`, `Rejected` and `Undone`, the mapping's match columns and `MasterProducts` itself — and #925's and #937's hold the accepted and held readings. This change adds no table, no column and no index, and writes no data of its own.

**One limitation, and it is this surface's own.** The master-product picker is the whole catalogue in one response, ordered by brand and name, rather than a search: the catalogue is a list of products a person keeps and nothing has needed a search surface yet. If it outgrows one response that is its own change, and the criterion it serves — "pick another existing master product" — is why the list is published at all rather than left to whichever products a suggestion happened to name. **Browsing and searching the catalogue itself is a separate surface** since issue #1023 ([Super Admin master products](#super-admin-master-products-issue-1023)), which is read-only and changes nothing here: this queue, its endpoints and its picker are exactly as they were.

**What proves it.** `SupplierListingReviewPolicyTests` and `ProductMatchReviewPolicyTests` (unit) are the rules over a table of cases: which listings may be decided and which refuse with their own sentence, an undeclared outcome refused rather than read as the first declared one, a fresh reading of the confirmed pack accepted, a listing holding none confirmed with no price, the freshness boundary on both sides and the twice-weekly limit deciding differently from the daily one, each of the five identity fields refusing the price while a variant differing only in case or spacing does not, **three pack quantities the reviewer may confirm against one reading all still accepted**, the band in both directions and on both edges with "no accepted price means no band", an approved exception accepting an out-of-band price and saying so, an approval that was not needed not counting as one, an approval refusing to override freshness or identity, the barcode match in both scopes and with leading zeros, and the suggestion statuses each decision may act on with what an undo returns. `PriceCatalogueReviewUseCaseTests` adds what the use cases decide: the clock's instant reaching the store, the audit entry's fields, the **two** events a price exception produces, the one a confirmation that accepted no price produces, the master-product creation audited beside the match, nothing audited for an answer of nothing, and nothing decided at all for a request whose actor could not be named. `PriceCatalogueReviewTests` is the relational half over **two** businesses on the denied scope this surface carries: one waiting product with a count of two and the representative spelling, its suggestions and the listings found under it, an automatic match listed separately with its run and confidence, a listing's full evidence with its held reading and the server's freshness and band answers, a strong barcode match ordered first with a cross-scope match **not** one, a refused listing absent from the queue but still in the catalogue, the catalogue published for the picker; a fresh reading accepted as a first price with the listing's three price facts set and the pending row cleared, a stale one not accepted with the listing confirmed and its price untouched, a corrected pack quantity stored and the price still accepted, a reading of another variant not accepted, an out-of-band price refused without the exception and accepted with it as the new reference, an approved exception still refusing a stale reading, a refusal keeping the identity and clearing the reading, a second decision on one listing refused, and a submitted identity the catalogue would not store refused with nothing written; a suggestion accepted matching **both** businesses' mappings and moving the key's listing with its origin key kept, another master product chosen refusing the other suggestion and recording the reviewer's own accepted row, a suggested new master product created and matched with the describing row accepted beside the naming one, a duplicate description refused, a suggestion refused with the key still waiting, "not found" recorded for both businesses, a settled or auto-matched mapping left alone, a key nothing is waiting under answered with nothing, an unknown master product refused, and a decided suggestion refused; an automatic match confirmed with the source left as the matcher's, undone with the mappings returned, the proposed listing moved back, the confirmed listing untouched and the suggestion `Undone`, that pair then **refused by the real matcher** on the next run, and a non-automatic match refused; and - the boundary - a decision leaving every business key, product, waiting key and captured search text exactly as it was, with a review store on a business-scoped context writing nothing at all. `SuperAdminPriceCatalogueReviewApiTests` is the whole pipeline over real HTTP: every endpoint refused for an Owner, a Manager, an applicant and a stranger, `401` for an anonymous request, `403` without the delegated scope, `403` for a member presenting a support-session id, every write refused in a role preview with `read_only_role_preview` and nothing stored, the administrator still reaching no business endpoint, the queue reporting one waiting product with a count of two and - the decisive assertion - **neither no business, a price exception producing **two** audit events, `404` for an unknown listing and `409` for a decided one, `400` for an identity the catalogue would not store, a suggestion accepted matching both businesses with neither named in the response, `404` for a key nothing is waiting under, and an automatic match confirmed, undone and then refused. `EndpointAuthorizationClassificationTests` holds all five routes as class 2 and nothing else, `EndpointPlanRequirementTests` that none of them declares a plan, and `SupplierPriceObservationBoundaryTests` that the three new files naming an observed price are declared readers rather than discovered ones. On the frontend, `super-admin-price-catalogue-review.service.spec.ts` covers the five requests, the waiting key travelling in the body and the enum numbers that are the contract; `super-admin-price-catalogue-review.component.spec.ts` the three sections, the count of businesses, the auto-matched flag, the empty and failed-read states, the confirm, the undo behind the shared confirmation dialog with its warning text, and a stale refusal re-reading the queue; `waiting-product-match.component.spec.ts` the five decisions, the create form prefilled from the suggestion, the two submissions it withholds, the server's own refusal and the form that starts clean for the next product; and `supplier-listing-review.component.spec.ts` the evidence, the single safe link, the plain-text fallback for an unsafe address, the barcode match, the unpublished pack quantity, a confirmation with corrections, the two confirmation outcomes reported differently, the exception offered only when the server says the band would refuse the reading, and the form that starts from what is stored.

### Super Admin master products (issue #1023)

[The review above](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928) is where a person *decides* the shared catalogue. This one, the eighth task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817), is where they can simply **look at it**: every master product the catalogue holds, searchable and one bounded page at a time, and one product with the supplier listings that hang from it. It exists because the review is a *queue* — products awaiting a match, automatic matches to check, listings awaiting a decision — so a product nothing was waiting on could not be found, searched for or inspected at all, and the only place the catalogue appeared in full was the options of the review's "match to an existing master product" picker.

**It is read only, and that is the whole of this task.** Creating, editing and deleting a master product are separate issues that follow this one, and the review of [#928](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928) remains the **only** writer of a master product in the application. Nothing behind these two endpoints opens a transaction, takes a write lease or calls `SaveChanges`.

Two endpoints, both class 2 on the platform-admin surface — `PlatformAdminPolicy` **and** `PlatformDiagnosticsEndpointAttribute`, with `[Authorize]` and `[RequiredScope("access_as_user")]` kept — exactly as the review beside them:

```text
GET  api/super-admin/master-products?search=&page=&pageSize=
       → { products: [{ id, brand, name, sizeValue, sizeUnit, createdAtUtc, updatedAtUtc,
                         listingCounts: { proposed, confirmed, needsReview, rejected, total } }],
           totalCount, page, pageSize, hasMore }

GET  api/super-admin/master-products/{id}
       → { product: { … as above … },
           listings: [{ id, supplierName, supplierProductId, title?, sizeValue?, sizeUnit?,
                        unitsPerPack?, matchStatus, url?, lastCheckedAtUtc?,
                        latestPrice?: { packPrice, currency, priceBasis, observedAtUtc } }] }
       404 — no master product has that id
```

**The page is the server's answer, not the client's request.** `MasterProductCataloguePaging` is `StockHistoryPaging`'s rule reused deliberately: a missing, zero or negative page size becomes **50**, anything above **200** is clamped to it, and the page and size actually served come back in the response. A bounded answer is more useful to a page than a refusal, and a client cannot ask this surface for the whole catalogue by naming a large enough number. `totalCount` is how many products the *search* matched rather than how many were returned, which is what `hasMore` is derived from.

**The order is fixed and ends in the row's own key** — brand, name, size, id for the catalogue, and the supplier's name, the supplier's own product id and the row's key for one product's listings. A paged read has to come out in the same order on every request, and ending in the key is what makes two products that agree on brand, name and size still page stably. No caller chooses a sort.

**The search is the database's, case-insensitively, over the brand and the name.** It is `EfProductCatalogStore`'s rule for the same reason ([issue #827](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/827)): EF Core's SQLite provider translates `Contains` to `instr(…)`, which compares byte-for-byte, so `LIKE` is what folds ASCII letter case — and a `%` or `_` a person types is escaped so it matches literally instead of acting as a wildcard. A blank search narrows nothing.

**The counts are counts of *supplier* listings, and the refused ones are counted.** A refusal is kept rather than deleted ([#928](#super-admin-review-of-the-supplier-price-catalogue-issue-928) keeps it so a rediscovery does not propose the same listing again), so a product with nothing but refusals must not read as a product nobody has ever looked up. A listing still held under a waiting key belongs to no master product and is counted against none, which is [#923](#supplier-price-catalogue-issue-923)'s exclusive-ownership rule showing through the count.

**A listing's current price is published as it was observed, and nothing here divides it.** `latestPrice` is the pack price of the one accepted observation the listing points at — the `LatestObservationId` cursor, read correlated rather than by scanning the append-only table — with the **currency**, the **tax basis** and the **observed instant** it was stored with, because a pack price including GST and the same number excluding it are different figures and a reading from three months ago is not today's price. A listing that has never been checked successfully carries no price at all, which is a state and not a gap. The per-vending-unit comparison stays `CheapestUnitOfferPolicy`'s on its own endpoint ([The cheapest-supplier summary](#the-cheapest-supplier-summary-and-the-cheapest-supplier-column-issue-930)); an observed price is still purchasing guidance and reaches no cost, valuation, GST figure or report (AGENTS.md § Observed supplier prices, and [Supplier price observations and comparison](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925)).

**No business data, in either direction, and nothing tenant-owned is read.** Both endpoints read four platform tables — `MasterProducts`, `SupplierListings`, the `SupplierPresets` that publish those listings and the `SupplierPriceObservation` a listing points at — and **no tenant-owned table at all**: no product, no price-tracking mapping, no business. So this surface needs none of the reviewed cross-business reads the review and the collector surfaces have, adds no `IgnoreQueryFilters` statement anywhere, and opens no write lease: a platform table carries no business key and no query filter, so the **denied** `BusinessScope` these requests run under reads the whole catalogue and none of anybody's own rows. There is no business id, business name or business product id in either response and nowhere for one to travel, and — the owner's clarification of 31 October 2026, *master-catalogue management only* — **no count of the businesses tracking a product**, which is the one thing the review publishes and this surface deliberately does not.

**The page.** `/super-admin/master-products` ("Master Products"), behind `MsalGuard` and `platformAdminGuard` like the four Super Admin routes beside it, in the Super Admin menu group and the breadcrumbs next to Supplier Price Review. The page owns the search box, the table and the page controls; one product's supplier listings are a dedicated feature component (`MasterProductDetailComponent`) with its own read, loading and error lifecycle, composed through `[productId]` and `(closed)` per [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191). Loading, empty and error states follow the Supplier presets page, and the error state offers a retry. The search and the paging are the server's: the page sends what was typed and displays the page the server says it served, because a client-side filter over one page of a paged catalogue would silently hide the matches on every other page. **There is no Add, Edit or Delete control on it**, and `super-admin/master-products` is in `PLATFORM_ADMIN_PREFIXES` (`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/access/member-endpoint.ts`), so a `403` from either endpoint is not read as a member refusal and neither request carries a role-preview or support-session header.

**Only the newest read may describe either surface.** Both reads go through one `switchMap` over a request subject, which cancels the read still in flight, and the detail panel also discards an answer whose product is no longer the one it was given — the cancellation `ProductPriceTrackingComponent` uses, for the same reason ([Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191)). The search box stays usable while a read is outstanding and the page reuses one detail component for whichever row is open, so two reads are genuinely in flight and the slower one can be the older: searching "cola" then "pepsi" must never leave the "pepsi" search box above the "cola" rows, the "cola" total and the "cola" page number, and viewing product A's listings then product B's must never show A's answer — or A's failure — under B's heading. A failed read travels through the pipeline as a result rather than as an error, so one failure cannot end the stream and leave every later search or selection unanswered, and both components unsubscribe and complete their subject on destruction.

**What proves it.** `MasterProductCatalogueUseCaseTests` (unit) is what the use cases decide: the default page and size, a size above the maximum clamped and *reported*, a page or size that is not positive falling back to the first default page, a later page read as a skip of the pages before it, the total deciding whether more remain, a blank search dropped and a typed one trimmed, and an unknown id answered with nothing. `MasterProductCatalogueStoreTests` is the relational half over the real migration history and **two** businesses on the denied scope this surface carries: the brand/name/size/key ordering, the case-insensitive search over both columns, a typed `%` matched literally, a slice with the whole match's total beside it, the four listing counts with a waiting-key listing counted against no product and a product with no listings reporting zeros, both instants, the detail's listings with the supplier's name, wording, pack, status, page, last check and current ### The JB Metro lookup script (issue #927)

[The collector work list](#collector-work-list-issue-924) is the work a run is issued. This one is the first **route** that work can actually be taken on: `scripts/price-collector/jbmetro-lookup.mjs` reads JB Metro's published prices through the site's open Magento GraphQL endpoint, with its fixture tests beside it in `scripts/price-collector/jbmetro-lookup.test.mjs` and `fixtures/`. It is a collector-side script and nothing in the API, the database or any report reads it: it prints what a supplier publishes, and storing an observation is [#937](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/937)'s ([Collector results](#collector-results-issue-937)). Parent design: issue #817, and the contract the owner verified on 27 October 2026.

**Two forms, one of them the fallback.** `--search <text> <site-url>` is what a run uses for every tracked product, and `<site-url> <sku>...` looks a known listing up by SKU when it is missing from that day's search. Both answer one JSON object on stdout and exit `0`, `1` when something was reported against a page or a batch, or `2` when the invocation itself was refused. **Search is the GraphQL `products(search: ...)` query and never `/catalogsearch/`**, which JB Metro's `robots.txt` disallows; the SKU form is `products(filter: { sku: { in: [...] } })` in bounded batches, and a SKU the site answered for and did not return is reported as `notFound` — while one whose batch was never read to its end is `unresolved` instead, because nothing has answered for it yet.

**The site must be one the work list named.** The three JB Metro supplier master records ([the supplier-master fields](#the-supplier-master-fields-issue-931)) are the default allowlist, and `JBMETRO_SITE_URLS` is how the collector passes the `siteUrl` values the work list gave it — which is what keeps "a new JB Metro site is a new record and not new code" true. A URL is matched on its **origin**, and any other host is refused before a request is made, so a mistyped or substituted site is an exit `2` rather than prices read off somebody else's shelf.

**Pagination is read, not assumed.** `products` is paged, so the script reads `total_count` and `page_info.total_pages` from the first page and requests further pages at the configured `pageSize` until every result has been read, a page fails after its retries, or the configured page cap stops it. The result carries `totalCount`, `pagesRead` and `truncated`, and `truncated` is true in each of the last two cases — what was read is then not everything there is, which is what lets the work item be marked `Truncated` rather than `Complete` ([#926](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/926), [#937](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/937)). A silent prefix is the failure this exists to prevent: a half-read search reads as "this is all JB Metro sells".

**An absence is only reported after a complete read.** The SKU batches are paged by the same reader, so a batch can be cut short by the page cap exactly as a search can — and the cap is not an error, so it leaves no entry in `errors` to notice it by. A SKU the site did not return is therefore `notFound` **only** when its batch ran to the end; when the batch stopped early, whether a page failed after its retries or the cap stopped it, every SKU of that batch the site had not yet returned is `unresolved`. The products that *were* read are kept either way. The distinction is the whole point: `notFound` is a fact about JB Metro's catalogue that a later task ([#937](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/937)) may act on, while `unresolved` is a fact about this run only, and reporting an unread page's SKU as missing would retire a listing that is still on sale.

**What it reports per product**, from `price_range.minimum_price` and from `custom_attributesV2` read **unfiltered** (`attribute_codes` is not a valid filter there): `sku`, `name`, `url`, `stockStatus`, `finalPrice`, `regularPrice`, `currency`, `packQuantity` (`pickamntsoldas`), `gstRate` (`gst`), `innerBarcode`, `outerBarcode` (`innerbarcode`/`outerbarcode`) and `specialFromDate`/`specialToDate`. **JB Metro publishes ex-GST prices**, and the stored fact that says so is the supplier master record's `PricesIncludeGst`, not this script: it converts nothing, and what an observed price means is decided where it is stored ([Supplier price observations and comparison](#supplier-price-observations-and-comparison-issue-925)). A barcode stays a **string** so a leading zero survives, a value the site did not publish is `null` and never `0`, and the pack quantity is reported exactly as published — what a pack contains is confirmed against the business's own product ([#937](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/937), [#928](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/928)), not decided here.

**The special dates are reported and never interpreted.** The script derives no "on special" flag from `special_from_date`/`special_to_date`: the **final price is the current price**, whatever an old date attribute left on a product says. Deciding a promotion is live from stale dates would put a price on the wrong footing in a comparison that is about to name a supplier cheapest.

**Failures are bounded, reported and local.** A GraphQL error returned with **HTTP 200** (Magento's normal failure shape, so a 200 is not a result), a timeout, a 5xx and a 429 are retried with bounded exponential backoff; any other 4xx is not retried, because the site will repeat it. What is left is reported against the page or the SKU batch it happened on — with the attempts made — and the rest of the run continues. The public GraphQL API is not a contractual guarantee, which is exactly why a change on JB Metro's side surfaces as a failed lookup rather than as a wrong price.

**What proves it.** `jbmetro-lookup.test.mjs` runs on recorded fixtures and makes **no live call**, in `scripts/validate.sh` and `scripts/validate.ps1`: a single-page search, a multi-page search read to its end, truncation at the page cap, a normal SKU batch, a missing SKU, a SKU batch read over two pages, the page cap stopping a SKU batch so its unseen SKU is `unresolved` and not `notFound`, a GraphQL error returned with 200, a timeout and a 5xx retried and then answered, a 4xx not retried, a leading-zero barcode kept as a string, a product mapped with no derived special flag, batches that keep going after one fails, and a refused host that makes no request at all.

### Manual collector orchestration (issue #929, stage 1)

The first rollout is a manual, test-API-only workflow, not a production schedule. A trusted
`workflow.mjs prepare` process exchanges GitHub OIDC with the pinned Entra tenant, issues work once,
and stores a small sample privately. Claude reads that snapshot with `read-work.mjs`; it never
receives the Restockroo token or the GitHub/OIDC request credentials. The model process runs in a
separate temporary workspace/home with only the explicitly allowed environment and settings.
`workflow-tool-guard.mjs` denies arbitrary shell, file reads, edits and other tools; approved actor
calls still pass through the existing atomic `apify-guard.mjs`. An actor call returns only its run
status and storage ids, so the hook also allows the free `get-dataset-items` (limit capped to the
sample page size, 3 reads per dataset), `get-actor-run` (6 polls per run) and `abort-actor-run`
reads, only for runs this collector started, without counting them as actor calls. A trusted
`PostToolUse` hook records those runs from the allowed calls' answers (`workflow-run-ledger.mjs`,
fixed RunResponse paths only); every other Apify account tool is denied. A native hook failure blocks the
tool rather than silently bypassing the guard. Literal helper arguments cannot expand shell
commands, and sample writes must name an issued work item or matching key of that same run.

The workflow's `always()` finalizer obtains a fresh short-lived API token, filters regular files
to the issued sample, and calls the existing independent file validator/batch/outcome/run-complete
submission path. Finished results survive an interrupted model step; unselected or unanswered
work is `not_searched`. Job cancellation/hard timeout can still skip finalisation, so backend
expiry remains the backstop. Only allowlisted numeric counts/statuses and reported Claude cost
reach the public logs; transcripts, prices, names, raw errors and output files are not published.
Cleanup removes private temporary data and the per-job CLI installation; reset/ephemeral isolation
is still mandatory for credentialed self-hosted jobs.

Manual limits and the explicit retailer-test checkbox apply only to that run's private limits;
they do not turn on repository actor activation or production scheduling. The later Sydney
schedule and production activation remain under #929 after real end-to-end/cost evidence. See
[Manual collector test](price-collector-testing.md) for setup, bounds and the interruption check,
and [automation](automation.md#manual-supplier-price-collector-929-stage-1) for the workflow boundary.

### The collector prompt, the Apify limits and the helper scripts (issue #926)

[The collector work list](#collector-work-list-issue-924) issues the work, [Collector results](#collector-results-issue-937) takes back what was read off a shelf and [Collector product matching](#collector-product-matching-issue-941) takes back which product a search was for. This section is the **collector side** of all three, the seventh task of [#817](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/817): the prompt a scheduled Claude Code run follows, the Apify configuration and per-actor rules it may call, the hook that enforces them, and the two scripts that talk to this API. Everything here lives in `scripts/price-collector/` and nothing in the API, the database or any report reads any of it. The workflow that runs it, its schedule, its CLI flags, its permission settings and its secrets are [#929](https://github.com/cristhyanc/InventoryApp/issues/929)'s.

The owner's decision of 27 October 2026 is what shapes it: **Claude, not scraper code, calls the suppliers and interprets the results**, because a keyword search for one product returns other brands, other flavours and accessories, and a new pack of the same product (a 30-pack beside a 24-pack) has its own supplier product id that an id-only lookup would never find.

```text
prompt.md            the run's instructions: match, search by name, keep the real matches, write files
get-work.mjs         GET /api/price-collector/work  → the run, the suppliers, one entry per search
   (run by trusted preparation; Claude reads the snapshot through read-work.mjs)
apify-mcp.json       the Apify MCP server, offered exactly the actors apify-limits.json allows
apify-limits.json    per-actor page size, page cap, forced-off inputs; the per-run call cap
apify-guard.mjs      PreToolUse hook: enforces every line of that file, and the write-once folder
pagination.mjs       is there another page? and which outcome does this search get?
output.schema.json   what a result file and a match file must hold
output-schema.mjs    the checker, plus the rules the schema document cannot state
submit-results.mjs   matches → rows in batches → each work item's outcome → the run's completion
   (run by the workflow)
```

**Claude writes files and never submits.** One file per issued work item, `price-collector-out/<work-item-id>.json`, written **once** when that search is finished and never rewritten, holding that search's outcome (`complete`, `truncated`, `no_matches` or `failed` with a reason) and its rows; one file per decided waiting key, `match-<key>.json`, holding one proposal. So a run that stops halfway loses only the search in progress: every finished file is complete on its own, and the workflow submits them after Claude finishes **or stops**. The authoritative waiting key is the one *inside* the match file, because a key is folded search text and a file name cannot carry it safely.

**Every search is a name search, every run.** A matched product is searched by its master-product description and a waiting one by its own stored search name and unit label — the same key the work list published. A known listing is *recognised* in the results by its `supplierProductId`, and any other pack of the same product is reported as a row of its own, which is what makes a new pack size a proposed listing (#928) rather than something nobody ever sees. The id lookup — Varnmill products mode with prefixed ids, or the BIG W SKU actor — is the fallback for a known listing missing from that day's search and never how a search starts; the BIG W SKU actor is billed per start, which is the other reason.

**Pagination is a rule rather than a paragraph.** `pagination.mjs` holds both halves of search completeness and stores nothing: a search asks for at most the actor's configured page size, and asks for the next page while the actor filled the page or reports more results than it returned, up to the actor's page cap. A search the cap stopped is reported `truncated`, never `complete` and never `no_matches` — the same restraint [Collector results](#collector-results-issue-937) applies to an absence, because the backend records a known listing as not found only from a search that saw everything. The module has a command line, so the run can ask it rather than reason about it.

**The caps are enforced outside Claude, which is the whole point.** `apify-guard.mjs` runs as a Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook on every Apify MCP tool call, in its own process, before the call is made. It allows only the actors `apify-limits.json` lists **and marks `actorIdConfirmed: true`** — resolved from the call's own actor field or from a per-actor tool name, and an actor it cannot read, does not list, or whose id and input field names are still to be confirmed is **refused** rather than allowed, consuming none of the run's call allowance; it injects the actor's item limit when the call carries none, keeps a smaller request and blocks a larger one; it forces off what is billed and unread (Kmart reviews and local-stock enrichment, Varnmill paid details, and the Varnmill `onlyChanged` watcher, because every listing must get a positive check, #925); and it counts this run's actor calls in its own state file, blocking the call that would pass the per-run call cap. **It sets and counts no dollar amount** (owner decision, 31 October 2026, #926): spending is capped by the Apify account usage limit, which suspends runs once it is reached (overage must stay disabled on the account), so the guard adds no `maxTotalChargeUsd` to an actor's input — Apify does not read it there, and an actor with a closed input schema such as Dromb's would reject it. Reaching the call cap stops a run that loops: the searches it never reached are recorded `not_searched` when the run is completed, which is a true answer. A run that goes wrong below the call cap can use the rest of the month's Apify budget; that is the accepted cost of this decision. The same hook refuses a `Write` (or an `Edit`, which is always a rewrite) outside `price-collector-out/`, to a file that already exists, or to the guard's own accounting — so write-once is a property of the process rather than of Claude's memory.

**A cap it cannot count is a cap it cannot keep, so the accounting is reserved rather than assumed.** Two Apify calls can be in flight at once, each in its own hook process, so the read of the accounting, the comparison against the per-run call cap and the write of the new count are **one operation inside a cross-process lock** (a lock directory beside the state file, because creating a directory is one atomic step: exactly one invocation gets it and every other one is told it already exists). The allowed call is written and flushed to the disk **before** the allow is returned, which is what makes it a reservation: two invocations cannot read the same remaining allowance, both be allowed and then overwrite each other's increment, and every allowed call is accounted for cumulatively. The one state the guard reads as a run with no calls is a state file that is **not there yet** — a run that has made no call. Everything else fails closed: an accounting it cannot read, one that is not JSON, one that is not the shape and `schemaVersion` the guard writes, one holding a call count that is not a whole number, a lock it cannot take, and a reservation it cannot write durably each **refuse the paid call** rather than starting the count again, and a refused call leaves the stored accounting exactly as it was. A limits file that states no per-run call cap refuses every paid call too. A `Write` needs no accounting, so a broken state file can never make the write-once folder permissive — it can only stop a run from spending.

**The matching step runs before the searches** (#941): for each product awaiting a match, one file naming **either** one existing master product **or** a complete suggested new description — never both and never half of one — with `high`, `medium` or `low` and a short reason. The prompt allows `high` only when brand, variant and size clearly agree and only one master product fits, refuses any pair in that key's `refusedMasterProductIds`, and proposes nothing at all for a key whose `matchingSuppressed` is set, because its refusal list was too long to send. A confidence is one condition among several and decides nothing on its own; the backend runs its own checks. The waiting product is still searched by its own name in the same run.

**The submission order is the design, and it is the workflow's.** `submit-results.mjs` validates **each file independently** against `output.schema.json` — a missing, unreadable, misnamed, invalid or other-run file is skipped and reported and loses only its own search — and then: the match files first, in batches of at most 200 proposals, because a key matched now is a key whose rows can attach to its master product in the **same** run (#937's same-run key resolution); then each work item's rows in batches of at most 200; then **that work item's outcome, only after all of its batches succeeded**, with its total row count, because the API accepts an answer only while the declared total equals the rows it received — so a failed batch deliberately leaves the search unanswered rather than finishing it short and recording a listing as not found; then the run's completion, once, at the end, so every unanswered search becomes `not_searched`. Every row is stamped with the work-item id and supplier of the file it came from, so a new pack is reported under the work item of the product it belongs to.

**The checker is stricter than the API in three places, on purpose**: a barcode with no scope, two rows of one file claiming the same supplier product id, and a search the page cap stopped calling itself `complete`. Each of those would be *accepted* — as a price, as a refused duplicate, or as a listing that has gone — so each is refused before a request is made. It is stricter in no other way: it coerces nothing and fills nothing in, and an unknown pack quantity, price, barcode, size or GST rate is left out of a row rather than sent as a zero.

**No credential is in the repository, and none is printed.** Both scripts read the API base URL and the collector's app-only bearer token from `PRICE_COLLECTOR_API_BASE_URL` and `PRICE_COLLECTOR_API_TOKEN` (#929 sets them), never from an argument or a default; the Apify token is `${APIFY_TOKEN}` in `apify-mcp.json`, expanded from the environment. Every message either script raises names the method and the route with the token and base URL redacted, and the submission prints counts and reasons only — no price, product name, supplier product id, business or URL. `get-work.mjs` fails closed on a non-2xx answer, an unreachable API or an answer that is not a work list, printing nothing on stdout: half a work list read as the day's work is a day of listings silently not checked.

**One limitation, stated rather than hidden.** The Varnmill actor id is the owner's own from testing; the Kmart, BIG W search and BIG W SKU actor ids are recorded as `actorIdConfirmed: false` and are to be confirmed in the owner's bounded dry run, together with each actor's input field names and the real cost per search. The page sizes, page caps and call cap in `apify-limits.json` are the pre-dry-run defaults — the issue's own open decision is that cost is unknown until then — and the guard enforces whatever the owner puts there afterwards. An unconfirmed actor fails closed in the strong sense: the guard refuses to call it at all while its `actorIdConfirmed` is not `true`, so today the Varnmill actor is the only Apify actor a run may call (the JB Metro route is not an Apify actor and is unaffected) and confirming the other three is a reviewed one-line change in `apify-limits.json` after the dry run — never something a run, a prompt or a test may decide for itself.

**What proves it.** Five `node --test` suites in `scripts/validate.sh` and `scripts/validate.ps1`, none of which calls Restockroo, Apify or a supplier — the API calls are answered by a loopback stub (`stub-server.mjs`, test support only), so the real `fetch`, the real route, the real bearer header and the real JSON body are exercised. `get-work.test.mjs`: every search printed with its work-item id, a matched and a waiting product's description, the route each search is taken on, a search given only its own supplier's known listings, the omission and suppression flags kept, `--raw`, the bearer header, the token and base URL never printed, a missing or malformed setting refused without a call, and 401, 403, 503, nothing answering and an answer that is not a work list each failing closed with nothing on stdout. `submit-results.test.mjs`: matches before results before the completion, rows stamped with their file's work item, every enum sent as the API's own number, each search outcome and a failure reason, 250 rows split into 200 and 50 with one outcome carrying the right total, 201 proposals split, a refused batch size, a failed first and a failed second batch each leaving the work item without an outcome while the other file is still submitted, a refused outcome, 401, one malformed file skipped while the others are submitted, a misnamed file, a file of another run, an invalid match file, every file skipped and the run still completed, a run id that cannot be guessed or that two files disagree on, the printed counts and reasons, and no price, product name, supplier product id, base URL or token printed. `apify-guard.test.mjs`: the limits file's own shape and the MCP server offering exactly its actors with no token, an unlisted actor and an unreadable one blocked, an actor read from a per-actor tool name, missing limits injected, a smaller request kept, an excessive or non-positive one blocked, the enrichments forced off however they were asked for, a flat input fixed, the per-run call cap, no charge field added to any actor's input, and the accounting between calls, a write outside the folder, a rewrite, an edit, the guard's own state file and a write with no path all refused, an unrelated tool passed through, and the hook end to end over a real state file. Its accounting is tested as the control it is: each of the three unconfirmed actors and a loose confirmation value (`false`, missing, the string `"true"`) refused without consuming budget while the confirmed one still works; a limits file with no per-run call cap refusing a paid call; a first run starting from zero and the reservation on the disk before the allow; an accounting that cannot be read, is not JSON, carries another `schemaVersion`, or holds a negative, fractional or non-numeric figure refused and **left exactly as it was**; a reservation that cannot be written and a lock that cannot be taken each refused; the lock released so the next call is decided rather than refused; and a write still guarded while the accounting is unusable. The concurrency regressions are real processes rather than simulated ones: four node processes released together by a shared start instant against one accounting file, asserting exactly one allow when one call reservation is left, and all four accounted for — no increment lost — when four are left. `output-schema.test.mjs` and `pagination.test.mjs` cover the two rule modules, including the three strictnesses above and a search stopped by the cap never being `complete` or `no_matches`.

### Provider catalogue review: link-or-create and change review (issue #738)

The direct import of the section below wrote straight through: it created a product for every
provider entry it did not recognise and overwrote four fields on every one it did. That is the
right behaviour for a catalogue the provider has always owned, and the wrong behaviour for a business
that kept its own — which is why issue #736 refused it outright for a manual catalogue. Issue #738
(parent #329 decision C1) built the deliberate alternative: **a catalogue import that is previewed as
a review, decided per entry, and then applied as one transaction.** **Issue #739 (decision C2) then
made it the catalogue import**: it built the screen, pointed Admin → Imports → Import products at
it, and removed the direct import — the endpoint, the use case, its port, its EF adapter and #736's
refusal — for every business. There is one catalogue writer now, and every row it writes is a row
somebody decided about. (Issue #888 moved where the screen is reached from: it is the dedicated
`/products/import` page rather than a panel on Admin → Imports. The writer is unchanged.)

**Three endpoints, two capabilities.** `InventoryApi.Controllers.CatalogueReviewController`:

| Endpoint | Capability | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST api/catalogue-review` | `Imports.Run` | Reads the provider's catalogue and reports it against this business's rows. Writes no product, category, price or sale. |
| `POST api/catalogue-review/apply` | `Imports.Run` | Carries out the submitted decisions against a named review, as one transaction. |
| `POST api/catalogue-review/unresolved-sales/apply` | `Data.Repair` | Attributes the still-unresolved sales carrying a linked product's provider id to that product and replays its costing. |

The split is a security decision rather than a tidying one. A review *is* the catalogue import,
decided row by row, so starting and applying it require what running the import requires. Attributing
a historical sale consumes costed inventory, moves product-level revenue and recosts the sales after
it, so it requires `Data.Repair` — an Owner alone, the same authority the costing repair and the sale
timestamp repair are behind. All three are `POST`, including the one that previews: it reads the
provider's live catalogue and records the review the apply is then authorised by, and a cached `GET`
would hand a caller a review id for a catalogue it never read.

**What the review reports.** `Inventory.Application.CatalogueReview.StartCatalogueReview` reads the
operator's products and groups through the existing `INayaxLynxClient` port, as one concurrent
fan-out of two independent calls — the shape the direct import used — and reconciles them against the
business's rows **through the provider id columns alone**:

- A provider group or product that no local row carries the `ExternalCategoryId`/`ExternalProductId`
  of (issue #759) is reported **unlinked**, with the operator's two honest options: link it to a local
  row they name, or create a new one. The review picks neither.
- A linked row's differences are reported in two separate lists, because they are two different kinds
  of fact. `automaticChanges` is what the apply will write **without asking** — the provider's name,
  and the category its group resolves to. `choices` is what it will **ask about** — the negotiable
  fields.
- Each product entry carries `unresolvedSaleCount`: how many stored sales carry that provider product
  id, are still unresolved and have known raw provenance. The review reports them and resolves none.

**Nothing is linked automatically by name.** A local product called exactly what the provider calls
its product stays unlinked, and a local key that happens to equal a provider id is a coincidence
(issue #735). The only ways a link comes about are an operator naming a row and a row the review
creates, which is what keeps a provider id from ever being inferred.

**Name and category follow the provider; nothing is negotiated any more.** Until issue #792 the
selling price was the one field the operator decided, and that issue (A2 of #786) deleted the
product field behind it: a review proposes no price, records none on its stored entries, writes none
onto a created row, and refuses a submitted price decision — see [A product carries no selling
price](#a-product-carries-no-selling-price-issue-792). What remains below describes the negotiation
mechanism because it is still the contract the one surviving negotiable field (`UnitVolume`, which
carries no provider value) and any future field run on.

`Inventory.Domain.Providers.ProviderManagedCatalogueFields` already says which fields a provider owns
on a row it names (issue #736), and this review is where that becomes a *transition*: linking a
product replaces its name with the provider's and its category with the local category carrying the
provider's group id — which the review links or creates first, in the same apply — and linking a
category replaces its name with the provider's. From then on those fields are read-only locally and a
later provider rename or group move is applied automatically and listed. A group no local category
carries leaves the product uncategorised rather than pointing it at a category that merely shares a
number, exactly as the direct import did.

The negotiable fields are `Inventory.Domain.Providers.NegotiableCatalogueField`, and
`CatalogueReviewPolicy` is the one rule about them:

- **A value is proposed only when three things hold**: the provider has one, it differs from the local
  value, and it differs from the provider value this field was **last decided about**. The third is
  what makes a skip stick — an operator who kept their own value over the provider's is not
  asked again until the provider moves it somewhere new.
- That last-decided value is the whole reason `ProviderCatalogueFieldDecisions` exists: one row per
  product and field, holding the provider value and which way it went, replaced rather than appended
  because "what did we last ask about?" has one current answer. Both answers are recorded — keeping
  the local value is a decision about that provider value just as taking it is. The rows an earlier
  release wrote about the retired selling price stay in the table and are read by nothing.
- Values are compared as the opaque text `ProviderCatalogueFieldValue` renders, in the invariant
  culture, so two spellings of one value are one answer rather than two
  and the operator is not asked the same question on every review.
- A field nobody answered is left exactly as it is and proposed again next time. A **created** row has
  no local value to keep, so it takes the provider's.

**The provider publishes no unit/volume label, so none is proposed.** `NegotiableCatalogueField`
declares `UnitVolume` beside the retired `UnitPrice`, and its provider value is always absent. The authoritative
Lynx contract for `GET /v1/operators/{OperatorID}/products` declares no unit or volume *label*: its
only volume-shaped fields are `ProductVolumeTypeID`, an `int32` whose vocabulary the documentation
does not publish, and `ProductPackageQuantity`, which is units per package. `Product.Unit` is a
free-text label ("can", "bottle"), so neither field is it, and mapping one onto it would be exactly
the invented property AGENTS.md § Nayax contract verification forbids. The field, the column and the
decision row stay in place so that the day a human decides which Lynx field means it, only the
projection changes; `CatalogueReviewPolicy.UnitVolumeUnavailableNote` is the one sentence the review
says about it, and the API returns it as `unitVolumeNote`.

**The review is persisted, and the apply is authorised by it.** `ProviderCatalogueReviews` and
`ProviderCatalogueReviewItems` hold the provider's side exactly as it was read. The apply request
carries item keys, one of three actions (`Defer`, `LinkExisting`, `CreateNew`) and the field
answers — **nothing a caller submits reaches a catalogue field**: every provider name and group
id comes from the stored items, and every local value from the rows read inside the transaction. A
stored review that predates issue #792 is refused whole, before anything is staged, because its
entries still carry provider prices and its plan can no longer be carried out in full
(`ApplyCatalogueReview.StaleSellingPriceReviewMessage`). A
business has at most one *pending* review, enforced by a filtered unique index over `(BusinessId)`
where `AppliedAtUtc IS NULL`: a review is a reading of the provider's catalogue at an instant, and an
older reading is not a second opinion, so starting one replaces the unapplied one. An applied review
is never rewritten — it is the record of what was decided, with the actor's `(tid, oid)` and the
instant.

**The apply is one transaction, and its read, its comparison and its write are one operation.**
`EfCatalogueReviewStore.ApplyAsync` re-reads the review and every local row it is about to write
inside the caller's transaction and decides each link there, because two of the refusals are
statements about *stored* rows:

- the chosen local row already carries a **different** provider id, or
- **another** local row already carries this one.

Recording the id a row already carries is deliberately **not** a refusal: it is the state the apply
was asked to reach. A use-case read followed by a separate write would be a window in which a product
takes the provider id this plan was about to record on a different row — the silent identity error the
provider-id work exists to end — so the sequence stays in the adapter, on the precedent
`EfProductCatalogueWrite` and the historical GST apply set, with `CatalogueReviewPolicy` supplying the
rules.

**Atomic, and idempotent.** One refused link refuses the whole apply: nothing is linked, created or
renamed and no field decision is recorded, because a half-applied review is the one outcome an
operator cannot reason about — the rows it did write are the ones the next review treats as settled.
A second apply of an applied review writes nothing and answers `alreadyApplied: true` with the
original instant, rather than failing or repeating itself.

**Linking never touches a sale, and never recosts history.** No statement in the catalogue apply reads
or writes `NayaxSales` beyond the unresolved *count* the review reports. A sale already attributed to
a product keeps that product, its recorded `UnitCostAtSale` and its `CostOfGoodsSold` exactly (issue
#758), and the product's costing position is untouched. The sales a link makes **resolvable** are left
unresolved on purpose.

**Resolving those sales is a separate, explicit, audited apply.** Linking a provider product id to a
local product says what the id means; it does not say that the business's historical sales carrying
that id belong to that product's inventory.
`Inventory.Application.CatalogueReview.ResolveLinkedProviderSales` is where that second decision is
taken, and the counts the review reports are its preview:

- It requires explicit confirmation. Seeing a count is not consenting to recost history.
- It matches on the **provider id**, never a name, and only while the sale's stored provider id has
  known raw provenance (`NayaxSales.ProviderProductIdIsRaw`) — a provenance-unknown value may be
  either a raw provider id or the local product id the old synchronization wrote, so it is read as an
  identifier of nothing.
- It **only ever fills a null**, through the same guarded `ExecuteUpdate` whose own predicate carries
  the expected null that the `resolve-nayax-sale-products` command uses, with one
  `NayaxSaleProductResolutions` audit row per sale recording the previous value, the new product, the
  new `ProviderCatalogueLink` rule, the actor and the instant. A rerun writes nothing, and nothing
  here can move a sale off the product it already carries.
- It replays each affected product's costing from the **earliest completed** sale it resolved, through
  the same baseline-cutoff gate the uploaded sales import and the latest-sales synchronization apply:
  a sale at or before the product's transition baseline cutoff is covered by that baseline, and a
  product with no baseline is replayed by no write path in the application, so this one does not
  invent one either.
- Failure is all-or-nothing. A product whose cost history cannot be replayed rolls the whole run back
  — no sale keeps its new product, no audit row survives — and the message names the product to fix
  first. Nothing fabricates an opening cost, and a failed replay is never reported as a successful
  resolution.

**Three additive tables, and nothing existing changes.** `AddProviderCatalogueReview` creates
`ProviderCatalogueReviews`, `ProviderCatalogueReviewItems` and `ProviderCatalogueFieldDecisions` and
alters no existing table, so it works with the code already in production (which applies migrations at
startup) and a business that never starts a review sees no behaviour change at all. The review items'
`LinkedProductId`/`LinkedCategoryId` and a field decision's `ProductId` are foreign keys on
`(BusinessId, …)` against the `(BusinessId, Id)` business keys, for the reason `NayaxSales.ProductId`
is — but they **cascade** rather than restrict, which is the one place they differ from a sale: a
review is a draft about the catalogue and a field decision is a note about what was last asked, so
neither is historical financial data and neither may be a reason a product cannot be deleted. Every
table is tenant-owned in the ordinary way, so two businesses may review and link the same provider
ids and neither can read, apply or resolve anything of the other's
(`EfCatalogueReviewStoreTenancyTests`).

### The dedicated Import products page (issue #888)

`/products/import` (`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/products/ProductImportPageComponent`)
is the one place the product catalogue import is reached from. Until issue #888 the review had no
page of its own: it was a panel `AdminImportsComponent` rendered below its import cards when a local
`reviewing` flag was set, either by that page's own button or by the `?review=catalogue` query
parameter issue #875's All Products button sent — so closing the review left the operator on
Admin → Imports rather than where they came from. That parameter never reached `main`, and nothing
reads it now.

- **A top-level route, declared above the `products` shell**, carrying `MsalGuard`,
  `accountStateGuard` and `requireCapability('Imports.Run')` — exactly the three guards
  `/admin/imports` carries, because it is the same import behind the same capability. Inside the
  shell it would have inherited an `Inventory.Operate` requirement on top of that; being a
  two-segment path, exact matching also keeps it clear of the three-segment `products/:id/…` routes
  whatever the declaration order. It takes **no provider route guard**: a connection that cannot
  serve the catalogue is answered by the review's own unavailable/error handling, which is where
  that answer has always been given, and nothing here bypasses a backend check.
- **It renders `<app-catalogue-review>` straight away**, so the review starts reading the Nayax
  catalogue on load exactly as it did when the button opened it, and the review's `closed` output
  navigates to `/products` rather than only taking a panel off screen. The page composes the review
  from where it still lives (`components/admin/imports/catalogue-review/`) and owns nothing of its
  workflow — see [Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191).
- **A support session withholds the review and the page says so.** The page keeps the rule Admin →
  Imports applied (issue #661): a session grants `Imports.Run`, so the review would otherwise render
  fully and be refused only by the backend's read-only method rule. It is withheld rather than
  disabled because the review reads the catalogue the moment it renders.
- **Three entry points, one destination.** The sidebar's `Inventory` group carries `Import products`
  directly under `Products` as `providerToolLink('Import products', '/products/import',
  'Imports.Run')`, so it is left out without a usable provider and for a member without
  `Imports.Run`, like the Admin `Imports` entry (see
  [Provider-locked navigation](#provider-locked-navigation-issue-729) for what that answer is).
  All Products' own **Import products** button keeps issue #875's visibility rules and links
  here with no query parameter, and Admin → Imports' card is a link here too. The breadcrumb reads
  **Products > Import products** (`layout/breadcrumbs/breadcrumb-routes.ts`, parent `PRODUCTS`).

Nothing about the review itself changed with the move: same API calls, same two steps, same
decisions, same applied result.

### The catalogue review screen (issue #739)

`frontend/inventory-app/src/app/components/admin/imports/catalogue-review/CatalogueReviewComponent`
is what **Products → Import products** (`/products/import`) opens, and it is the whole of the
product catalogue import now: there is no direct import behind it any more (decision C2). Issue #888
gave it that page of its own — it was a panel Admin → Imports opened until then (see
[The dedicated Import products page](#the-dedicated-import-products-page-issue-888)). The page
composes it and owns nothing of its workflow, because it is a distinct workflow with its own two-step
state, its own actions and its own loading and error lifecycle — see
[Page composition boundary](#page-composition-boundary-issue-191).

**Two ordered steps, categories first, and the order is a data rule rather than a layout choice.** A
provider product's category is the local category carrying its provider group id, resolved by the
apply against the categories that same apply links or creates. So step one settles the groups —
each unlinked provider group is linked to a local category the operator searches for and names, or
created — and step two shows each product the category it will actually end up in, named as the
provider names it (`categoryAfterImport`), or **none** when its group is linked to no category of
theirs, which is exactly what the apply does with it.

**What the screen states, and what it never offers.**

- Linking a product states that *its name and category will be replaced by the provider's and become
  read-only here*, and linking a category states the same about its name. That is the transition
  `ProviderManagedCatalogueFields` describes, said at the moment the operator chooses it rather than
  discovered afterwards on the edit form.
- **Nothing is negotiated, so the screen offers no field control at all** (issue #792, A2 of #786).
  The price used to be the one choice — keep mine or take the provider's when linking, accept or
  skip when a linked product's provider price had moved — and a product carries no selling price
  any more, so the keep-or-take fieldset, the "Mine … Nayax …" comparison and the applied result's
  accepted/skipped counts are all gone. A stale API response that still proposes a `UnitPrice`
  choice renders nothing and sends nothing: the screen never offers a field it cannot write, and
  the apply would refuse a price decision anyway. See [A product carries no selling
  price](#a-product-carries-no-selling-price-issue-792).
- A **unit/volume** is not offered either, and never was. The provider publishes no unit or volume
  label, so the API proposes none — issue #739's
  out-of-scope note and the owner's decision of 20 October 2026 keep `Product.Unit` locally managed
  until a human decides which Lynx field, if any, means it.
- A provider-owned change on an already-linked row is listed as **applied automatically** with the
  two values, and carries no control at all.
- The link pickers offer only rows **this business maintains itself** (an empty `providerManagedFields`
  on the product or category response): a row already carrying a provider id would be refused by the
  server's own link rule, so offering it would only produce a refusal. Retired products are offered
  and marked, because a deactivated product is still the provider's product and linking it is better
  than creating a duplicate of it.

**Every entry starts on Skip**, and an entry the operator answered nothing about is sent as nothing
at all — a half-decided review must not link the other half by omission. The screen sends decisions
and nothing else: no provider name or group id travels back from the browser, and a link that
names no local row is refused locally with a message rather than sent, because the server refuses the
whole apply over one such decision and would throw away every other answer on the screen. Both calls
are disabled while a support session is active, for the reason every other write on this page is
(issue #661): a session grants `Imports.Run` and the read-only rule refuses the `POST` itself.

### Nayax product catalogue import (issue #300)

**This import no longer exists** (the heading is kept because the sections above and below link to
it). `POST api/imports/products`,
`Inventory.Application.Imports.ImportNayaxProductCatalog`, its `INayaxProductCatalogImportStore`
port, the `EfNayaxProductCatalogImportStore` adapter and `ManualCatalogueImportPolicy` were all
removed by issue #739 (parent #329 decision C2), which replaced them with the catalogue review above
for every business. The section is kept because much of the current design is described against it,
and because what it did is still the right explanation of *why* the review exists:

- It was a one-way write-through sync of the Nayax operator catalogue into the local product and
  category tables: it created a row for every snapshot entry no local row carried the provider id of,
  and overwrote `Name`, `Description`, `UnitPrice` (from the catalogue `ProductDefaultRetailPrice`,
  never the Nayax `ProductCostPrice`) and `CategoryId` on every row that did, plus `UpdatedAt`.
  Stock, costing, supplier and the operator's own local fields were never written. A local product
  Nayax stopped returning was never removed — that drift is reported by the catalogue
  reconciliation below.
- **Two of those four fields are what the review still applies without asking** — the name and the
  category, because the provider owns them (`ProviderManagedCatalogueFields`). The price became a
  per-product decision in issue #738 and then went altogether in issue #792, which deleted the
  product field behind it (see [A product carries no selling
  price](#a-product-carries-no-selling-price-issue-792)); and the **description is no longer taken
  from the provider at all**: it is not one of the fields the review negotiates or applies, so a
  provider description change now leaves the local description alone. That is a deliberate
  consequence of C1/C2 rather than an oversight — the review's contract names exactly the fields it
  writes.
- It had no concurrency token, so two overlapping imports could both decide the same product was new
  and a local edit to a provider-linked row committed between its read and its write was simply
  overwritten. The review's apply is the opposite shape: it re-reads every row it is about to write
  inside its own transaction and decides each link there.
- It refused to run at all for a business holding products with no external id (issue #736), because
  it identified a product only by the provider's id and would have duplicated every manual row. That
  refusal is what the review replaced, and removing both together is what issue #739 is.
- Since issue #735 it set no `Id` at all — the row it created was keyed by the database, with the
